findings.claim: Explicit instruction beats implicit instruction for L2 development, and the advantage has survived two decades of re-analysis.
findings.detail: Norris & Ortega (2000) synthesised 49 studies and found explicit types of instruction outperformed implicit (mean d ≈ 1.13 vs 0.54). Goo, Granena, Yilmaz & Novella (2015) re-ran it on 34 unique samples (11 originals + 23 studies published 1999–2011) and confirmed the direction: explicit g = 1.29, implicit g = 0.77 — note implicit came out substantially higher than in 2000, so the gap narrowed. Li & Sun (2024), 28 reports / 67 samples / N = 3,754, found explicit instruction d = 1.07 within-group and d = 0.81 between-group. Caveat that Norris & Ortega themselves raised and that persists: outcome measures in this literature are heavily biased toward explicit, discrete-point tests, which favours explicit treatments.
findings.implication: Content: every item in the bank ships with a one-line explicit gloss, not just an image-to-hanzi pairing. For 出口 the card carries 'exit — 出 out + 口 mouth/opening', shown at feedback time. Do not build a pure comprehensible-input mode and expect it to compete; make explicit annotation the default and any 'immersion' mode a secondary toggle.

sources.citation: Norris, J. M., & Ortega, L. (2000). Effectiveness of L2 instruction: A research synthesis and quantitative meta-analysis. Language Learning, 50(3), 417–528.

Goo, J., Granena, G., Yilmaz, Y., & Novella, M. (2015). Implicit and explicit instruction in L2 learning: Norris & Ortega (2000) revisited and updated. In P. Rebuschat (Ed.), Implicit and Explicit Learning of Languages (pp. 443–483). John Benjamins.
Li, S., & Sun, H. (2024). Effects of different forms of explicit instruction on L2 development: A meta-analysis. Foreign Language Annals, 57, 229–255.

findings.claim: Corrective feedback produces medium-sized, durable gains; explicit feedback wins on immediate tests, implicit feedback holds up better over time, and prompts (which push the learner to re-produce) beat recasts (which just show the right answer).
findings.detail: Li (2010), meta-analysis of 33 studies, overall d = 0.64, effect maintained and in some analyses growing on delayed posttests; explicit > implicit on immediate and short-delayed posttests, implicit better retained long-term; lab > classroom, shorter treatments > longer, FL context > SL context. Lyster & Saito (2010), 15 classroom studies, significant and durable effects, with prompts producing larger effects than recasts (and recasts larger than explicit correction in their classroom-only set). The prompt/recast asymmetry is the load-bearing bit: feedback that forces a second retrieval attempt outperforms feedback that merely displays the answer.
findings.implication: UX: never end a wrong answer by just showing the right one. On an error, dim the distractors, keep the item on screen, and require one re-tap of the correct hanzi before advancing — a forced second retrieval, not a passive reveal. Budget ~1.5s for this; it is the cheapest effect size in the whole product.

sources.citation: Li, S. (2010). The effectiveness of corrective feedback in SLA: A meta-analysis. Language Learning, 60(2), 309–365.
Lyster, R., & Saito, K. (2010). Oral feedback in classroom SLA: A meta-analysis. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 32(2), 265–302.

findings.claim: On feedback timing, immediate feedback is at least as good as delayed in most L2 comparisons, but the evidence is thinner and more contested than the 'feedback works' finding.
findings.detail: Arroyo & Yilmaz (2018) found the immediate-feedback group outperformed delayed on Spanish gender agreement (45 learners, dyadic Skype text chat, three groups). Li, Zhu & Ellis (2016) is the other anchor study; a registered replication of both (Language Teaching, 2020) was called for precisely because the effect is unstable. A 2023 systematic review of CF timing concluded the optimal-timing question is not settled and that delayed feedback may need to be made more explicit/salient to work at all. Sample sizes here are small (n ≈ 45–90 per study) — this is not meta-analytic ground.
findings.implication: UX: show feedback in the same frame as the answer, within ~300ms of the tap, with no interstitial animation. Do not build an end-of-round 'review your mistakes' screen as the *primary* feedback channel — if you ship one as a secondary recap, make the corrections maximally explicit (correct hanzi enlarged, error struck through), because delayed feedback only works when it is salient.

sources.citation: Arroyo, D. C., & Yilmaz, Y. (2018). An open for replication study: The role of feedback timing in synchronous computer-mediated communication. Language Learning, 68(4).
Optimal timing of treatment for errors in second language learning – A systematic review of corrective feedback timing (2023). PMC9995700.
Nakata, T., & Suzuki, Y. et al. — The timing of corrective feedback in second language learning. Language Teaching (2025, review).

findings.claim: Retrieval practice (testing) beats restudy, and the effect roughly doubles when feedback follows the retrieval attempt.
findings.detail: Rowland (2014), Psychological Bulletin, 159 studies: overall testing effect g ≈ 0.50; recall tests produce larger benefits than recognition tests; feedback is a major moderator — testing with feedback g = 0.73 vs without feedback g = 0.39. Adesope, Trevisan & Sundararajan (2017), Review of Educational Research, 272 independent effect sizes from 118 articles: mean g = 0.51–0.61, with feedback and retrievability the reliable moderators. Notably Adesope found *one* practice test g = 0.70 vs more than one g = 0.51 — i.e. the marginal return on repeated testing within a session is decreasing.
findings.implication: Architecture: the atomic unit of the app is retrieval-attempt → feedback, persisted as an event, never a 'display card' event. Store {item_id, prompt_type, response, correct, latency_ms, timestamp} per attempt — you need the attempt log, not just a mastery score, to run spacing and to A/B anything. UX corollary: prefer more separate short sessions over one long grind (decreasing within-session returns).

sources.citation: Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432–1463.
Adesope, O. O., Trevisan, D. A., & Sundararajan, N. (2017). Rethinking the use of tests: A meta-analysis of practice testing. Review of Educational Research, 87(3), 659–701.

findings.claim: For a reading task, recognition-format retrieval is the correct default; recall formats only pay when you need production (spelling/handwriting), which a reading game never does.
findings.detail: Nakata (2016), 64 English-speaking college students, 60 Swahili–English pairs, computer flashcards, four formats (recognition, recall, hybrid, productive recall): recall formats are more effective than recognition for productive knowledge of orthography; recognition formats are *more desirable* than recall when spelling knowledge is not required — because recognition is far faster per item, so gain-per-minute is higher. Rowland (2014) shows recall > recognition in raw effect size, but that comparison ignores time cost.
findings.implication: UI: the core loop is a 4-alternative recognition tap — one target hanzi/word shown large, four meaning options (or one meaning, four hanzi). Never ask a Dutch/English beginner to write or draw a character. Reserve a 'type the pinyin' recall variant as an optional hard mode only, and only for items already at high recognition mastery.

sources.citation: Nakata, T. (2016). Effects of retrieval formats on second language vocabulary learning. IRAL, 54(3).
Rowland, C. A. (2014). Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432–1463.

findings.claim: Spaced practice beats massed practice for L2 specifically, with a large effect on delayed tests, and longer gaps beat shorter gaps once you measure at a delay.
findings.detail: Kim & Webb (2022), Language Learning 72(1), 269–319: 98 effect sizes from 48 experiments, N = 3,411 L2 learners. Spaced vs massed g = 1.15 on delayed posttests (medium-to-large overall). Shorter spacing was as good as longer spacing on *immediate* posttests but worse on *delayed* posttests — i.e. short gaps buy you session performance and cost you retention, which is exactly the learning-vs-performance dissociation. This is the L2-specific replication of a general-memory finding, so it is not an extrapolation.
findings.implication: Architecture: per-item scheduling state must be durable and offline-first — IndexedDB with {item_id, last_seen_at, next_due_at, successful_retrievals, lapses}, synced opportunistically. A PWA that loses schedule state on cache eviction destroys the single largest effect size available to it. Also: never compute due-ness from session-relative counters; use wall-clock timestamps.

sources.citation: Kim, S. K., & Webb, S. (2022). The effects of spaced practice on second language learning: A meta-analysis. Language Learning, 72(1), 269–319.

findings.claim: The optimal study gap is a function of how far away the test is: roughly 10–20% of the retention interval. This is the single most actionable spacing result and it is almost always ignored by flashcard apps.
findings.detail: Cepeda, Vul, Rohrer, Wixted & Pashler (2008), Psychological Science 19(11), 1095–1102: >1,350 participants, taught facts, reviewed after a gap of up to 3.5 months, final test at delays up to 1 year. At any given test delay, increasing the interstudy gap first raises then gradually lowers final performance — a ridgeline, not a monotone. Optimal gap ≈ 20% of the test delay for delays of a few weeks, falling to ≈ 5–10% at a one-year delay. Backed by Cepeda et al. (2006), a meta-analysis of 254 studies / ~14,000 participants establishing the spacing effect generally.
findings.implication: Architecture + UX: ask the user for a trip date at onboarding and make it the retention interval that drives scheduling. Trip in 28 days → target gaps of ~3–6 days, not the 1-day/3-day/7-day ladder every SRS ships. Trip in 6 months → gaps of ~2–4 weeks. Store `target_retention_date` in the user profile and recompute intervals from it; surface it in the UI as 'tuned for 14 October' so the choice is legible.

sources.citation: Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095–1102.
Cepeda, N. J., et al. (2008). ERIC record ED505660.

findings.claim: Expanding vs uniform spacing: the evidence is genuinely mixed and the difference, where it exists, is small. Do not build product complexity on it.
findings.detail: Kim & Webb (2022), the largest L2 synthesis (48 experiments, N = 3,411), found equal and expanding spacing *statistically equivalent*. Nakata (2015), SSLA 37, 677–711, 128 Japanese college students, 20 English–Japanese pairs, found a 'limited yet statistically significant' advantage for expanding — and explicitly described this as the first L2 study to find expanding superiority, which tells you how weak the prior evidence was. Kang, Lindsey, Mozer & Pashler (2014), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 21, 1544–1550, found equal-interval at least as good as expanding over the long term. In Nakata's own data the *amount* of spacing produced large effects while the *schedule shape* produced a small one.
findings.implication: Architecture: implement a simple, mostly-equal interval ladder derived from the Cepeda 10–20% rule, and spend zero engineering on expanding-vs-equal tuning or on a bespoke SM-2 variant. The ROI is in gap size and in not losing schedule state, not in schedule shape. If you want a knob, make it 'how far away is your trip', not 'expansion factor'.

sources.citation: Kim, S. K., & Webb, S. (2022). Language Learning, 72(1), 269–319.
Nakata, T. (2015). Effects of expanding and equal spacing on second language vocabulary learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 37(4), 677–711.

findings.claim: Interleaving is NOT the right default for vocabulary. The one large meta-analysis finds interleaving helps overall but actively HURTS for word learning — blocking wins for words.
findings.detail: Brunmair & Richter (2019), Psychological Bulletin, 'Similarity matters': 59 studies, 238 effect sizes nested in 158 samples. Overall interleaving effect g = 0.42. But by material: paintings g = 0.67, mathematical tasks g = 0.34, expository texts and tastes non-significant, and **words g = −0.39** — a reliable advantage for *blocked* practice. Their explanation is the similarity moderator: interleaving pays when the learner's job is to discriminate between confusable categories; it costs when the job is to build individual item–meaning associations, where blocking supports elaborative encoding within a theme.
findings.implication: Content: build rounds as semantically blocked scenes — one round is entirely 'subway station signage' (出口 入口 换乘 检票), the next is entirely 'noodle shop menu'. Do not shuffle domains within a round, which is what every generic SRS does. The one legitimate use of interleaving is at the *character* level for visually confusable hanzi (末/未, 日/曰, 千/干, 大/太/犬) — there discrimination is the task, and Brunmair & Richter's similarity account predicts interleaving should help. Tag items with a `confusion_set` field and interleave only within it.

sources.citation: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin, 145(11), 1029–1052.

findings.claim: The generation effect is real and roughly half a standard deviation: producing an answer beats reading it.
findings.detail: Bertsch, Pesta, Wiscott & McDaniel (2007), Memory & Cognition 35(2), 201–210: 445 effect sizes across 86 studies, mean effect ≈ 0.40. Substantial moderator variability across 11 moderators, so the boundary conditions matter — the classic one being that generation benefits require the generated item to be at least partly derivable, and can vanish or reverse when the learner has no basis for generation at all.
findings.implication: UX: the interaction must be commit-then-reveal, never reveal-then-acknowledge. No 'tap to flip the card' — that is reading, not generating. Every card requires a tap on an option before anything is revealed, and there is no skip button on the answer step (a 'don't know' option is fine and is still a commitment).

sources.citation: Bertsch, S., Pesta, B. J., Wiscott, R., & McDaniel, M. A. (2007). The generation effect: A meta-analytic review. Memory & Cognition, 35(2), 201–210.

findings.claim: Guessing before you are taught (pretesting / prequestions) helps — but only for the exact items you guessed at, not for surrounding material.
findings.detail: St. Hilaire, Chan & Ahn (2023), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, preregistered meta-analysis: specific effect (on the pretested material itself) g = 0.54 (k = 97); general effect (on new, non-pretested material in the same lesson) g = 0.04 (k = 91) — essentially zero. Pan & Carpenter (2023), Educational Psychology Review 35:97, review 76 records and conclude prequestioning/pretesting benefits learning *provided there is an opportunity to study the correct answers afterwards*; feedback is the enabling condition, not an optional extra.
findings.implication: UX: a first-exposure item should be presented as a guess-first prompt ('which of these four means "exit"?') with the gloss revealed immediately after, rather than a study-then-test sequence. But the g = 0.04 general effect kills a tempting design: do not assume that pre-quizzing a scene teaches the un-quizzed characters in it. Every character you want learned must itself be an item in the bank with its own retrieval events.

sources.citation: St. Hilaire, K. J., Chan, J. C. K., & Ahn, D. (2023). Guessing as a learning intervention: A meta-analytic review of the prequestion effect. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review.

Pan, S. C., & Carpenter, S. K. (2023). Prequestioning and pretesting effects: A review of empirical research, theoretical perspectives, and implications for educational practice. Educational Psychology Review, 35, 97.

findings.claim: DIRECT ANSWER TO THE WAGER QUESTION, part 1: forcing a metacognitive judgement before answering does NOT reliably improve learning. The best meta-analytic estimate is a small effect that is positive for related material and negative for unrelated material.
findings.detail: This is the closest well-powered analogue to a pre-answer wager — the judgment-of-learning (JOL) reactivity literature. Double, Birney & Walker (2018), Memory 26(6), 741–750: overall g = 0.054, 95% CI [−0.027, 0.135] — not significant; positive only for related word pairs (g = 0.323) and word lists (g = 0.384). Ingendahl, Halamish & Undorf (2025), the much larger successor: 344 effect sizes from 175 independent experiments, N = 15,079 adults. Overall g = 0.22 [0.17, 0.27]; related pairs g = 0.44; **unrelated pairs g = −0.09**, i.e. negative reactivity. A separate line (Journal of Intelligence / Metacognition & Learning, 2023) found essentially no reactivity for general-knowledge facts, the material closest to vocabulary. Mechanism is 'cue strengthening': the judgement makes you notice a relation, which helps only if a relation exists and the final test is sensitive to it.
findings.implication: UX: do not gate every answer behind a confidence wager. A hanzi and its English meaning are an *unrelated* pair in exactly the sense that produced g = −0.09. If you ship the wager, ship it on a subset (see the hypercorrection finding for the subset that is defensible), and instrument it: log `wager_shown: bool` per attempt so you can measure your own delayed-retention delta rather than inheriting a null from the literature.

sources.citation: Double, K. S., Birney, D. P., & Walker, S. A. (2018). A meta-analysis and systematic review of reactivity to judgements of learning. Memory, 26(6), 741–750.
Ingendahl, M., Halamish, V., & Undorf, M. (2025). Do immediate judgments of learning alter memory performance? A meta-analytical review.

findings.claim: DIRECT ANSWER, part 2: confidence-weighted testing / certainty-based marking has essentially no controlled evidence that it improves learning outcomes. It improves measurement reliability and how students feel, and that is it.
findings.detail: Certainty-based marking (Gardner-Medwin, UCL) is 25 years old and its published support is overwhelmingly about *assessment psychometrics* — CBM improves the reliability and validity of exam data in measuring partial knowledge — plus self-report. The one reasonably powered controlled test I could find of CBM as a *learning* intervention: a crossover study in a first-year cell biology course, N = 389 students across two cohorts with different CBM-containing computer-assisted formative assessments. Result: **student examination scores were not affected by CBM**; what changed was course appreciation, and student–instructor interaction duration (median 90s → 110s). 43% of students favoured CBM, 33% saw no merit. Recent enthusiastic CBM papers (e.g. the 2025 physiology AI-assistant implementation) report pre-to-post gains and satisfaction percentages (86.4% 'better recognise knowledge gaps') with no control group — that is not evidence of a learning effect. Note also Double & Birney's finding that JOLs are *less* accurate given prospectively than retrospectively: a pre-answer wager is the worse elicitation point for calibration.
findings.implication: UX: treat the wager as a **scoring and social mechanic**, not a learning mechanic, and say so internally so nobody defends it on pedagogical grounds. In a co-located multiplayer game it earns its place honestly — betting points on your own answer is good table dynamics and creates stakes that a solo SRS cannot. Put it in the multiplayer loop and leave it out of the single-player review loop, where it adds a tap per item and buys nothing measurable.

sources.citation: Schoenmakers, B., & Wens, J. et al. — Certainty-based marking in a formative assessment improves student course appreciation but not summative examination scores. BMC Medical Education (2019), 19:191.
Gardner-Medwin, A. R., & Curtin, N. A. — Certainty-Based Marking (CBM) for reflective learning and proper knowledge assessment.
Certainty-based marking in multiple-choice assessments in physiology (2025). Advances in Physiology Education. (uncontrolled pre/post + satisfaction data)

findings.claim: DIRECT ANSWER, part 3: there IS one real, replicated reason to capture confidence — the hypercorrection effect. Errors made with HIGH confidence are corrected better and more durably than low-confidence errors, given clear feedback.
findings.detail: Butterfield & Metcalfe (2001) and a subsequent line summarised in Metcalfe (2017), Annual Review of Psychology, 'Learning from Errors': high-confidence errors are hypercorrected relative to low-confidence errors following corrective feedback. The mechanism proposed is a metacognitive mismatch that boosts attention to and encoding of the correction — surprise is the active ingredient. Metcalfe & Finn (2011/2012) showed the effect persists at a one-week delay, and that a test after the corrective feedback blocks the return of the high-confidence errors. Important scope limit: this is a claim about *which errors get fixed*, not a claim that eliciting confidence improves learning overall — which is why it coexists with the null JOL-reactivity result above.
findings.implication: UI + architecture: use the wager as a *feedback-routing signal*, not as a learning intervention in itself. If a player wagers high and is wrong, escalate: full-screen correction, the character rendered large with its radical decomposition, a mandatory re-tap, and force a re-test of that item later in the same session (which is what blocks error return). If they wager low and are wrong, a normal inline correction is enough. Store `confidence` on the attempt record and add a `hypercorrection_requeue` flag to the scheduler.

sources.citation: Metcalfe, J. (2017). Learning from errors. Annual Review of Psychology, 68, 465–489.
Metcalfe, J., & Finn, B. (2011). Hypercorrection effect persists over a week, but high-confidence errors return. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 18, 1238–1244.

findings.claim: A word needs roughly 8–10 successful encounters before sizeable gains appear, and more than 10 for full knowledge; but frequency of encounter explains only a moderate share of learning.
findings.detail: Webb (2007), Applied Linguistics 28(1), 46–65: 121 Japanese learners of English, nonsense words substituted into authentic text, 1/3/7/10 encounters, 10 tests across orthography, association, grammatical function, syntax, and meaning-and-form. Gains in at least one knowledge aspect increased at every step up in repetition; ten encounters produced sizeable gains; more than ten needed for full knowledge. Uchihara, Webb & Yanagisawa (2019), Language Learning 69(3), 559–599: meta-analysis of 45 effect sizes from 26 studies, N = 1,918, frequency–learning correlation r = .34 — a medium effect, moderated by learner age, prior vocabulary knowledge, and treatment/method variables. r = .34 means repetition matters and is nowhere near sufficient on its own; quality of the encounter matters as much.
findings.implication: Content: size the item bank against a retrieval budget, not a card count. If the target is 300 characters at ≥10 successful retrievals each, that is ≥3,000 successful retrieval events. At ~4s per recognition trial and ~80% accuracy that is roughly 4 hours of net play — plan content, session length and trip-date scheduling against that number, and refuse feature work that does not increase retrievals-per-minute.

sources.citation: Webb, S. (2007). The effects of repetition on vocabulary knowledge. Applied Linguistics, 28(1), 46–65.
Uchihara, T., Webb, S., & Yanagisawa, A. (2019). The effects of repetition on incidental vocabulary learning: A meta-analysis of correlational studies. Language Learning, 69(3), 559–599.

findings.claim: Deliberate vocabulary study is three to four times more efficient than incidental learning from input. Incidental learning yields under 20% of target words; deliberate activities yield 25–60% at a delay.
findings.detail: Webb, Uchihara & Yanagisawa (2023), Language Teaching: meta-analysis of 24 primary studies, 29 effect sizes, N = 2,771 (1,517 experimental / 1,254 control). Mean proportion of target words learned 9–18% immediate, 6–17% delayed; gains were similar across reading (17%/15%), listening (15%/13%) and reading-while-listening (13%/17%). Webb, Yanagisawa & Uchihara (2020), Modern Language Journal: 100 effect sizes from 22 studies of *intentional* activities — 60.1% (meaning recall) and 58.5% (form recall) on immediate posttests, dropping to 39.4% and 25.1% at delay. Activity-level range 18.4–77.0% immediate, 23.9–73.4% delayed — enormous variation between flashcards, word lists, writing and fill-in-the-blanks, so 'deliberate' is not one thing.
findings.implication: Content: the product should be an explicitly deliberate learning game with contextual scenes as dressing, not an immersion/discovery game. The 25% delayed form-recall figure is also a sober planning number — assume you lose ~half of what the session posttest says you taught, and let the spacing scheduler, not the session summary, define 'learned'.

sources.citation: Webb, S., Uchihara, T., & Yanagisawa, A. (2023). How effective is second language incidental vocabulary learning? A meta-analysis. Language Teaching, 56(2), 161–180.
Webb, S., Yanagisawa, A., & Uchihara, T. (2020). How effective are intentional vocabulary-learning activities? A meta-analysis. The Modern Language Journal, 104(4), 715–738.

findings.claim: Receptive and productive knowledge are distinct constructs with a large asymmetry — recognition scores are systematically higher than recall — so a single mastery number per item is a modelling error.
findings.detail: González-Fernández & Schmitt (2020), Applied Linguistics 41(4), 481–505: eight vocabulary measures administered to English learners, structural equation modelling, showing recognition and recall are different constructs and that word-knowledge components follow a partially ordered acquisition sequence (form-meaning recognition earliest, productive recall latest). Follow-up work (González-Fernández, TESOL Quarterly 2025) further specifies the acquisitional sequence. The practical upshot: a learner at ceiling on hanzi→meaning recognition may be near floor on meaning→hanzi recall.
findings.implication: Architecture: mastery state is a vector per item, not a scalar — at minimum `{recognise_hanzi_to_meaning, recognise_meaning_to_hanzi, recall_pinyin}` each with its own interval and due date. For this product's goal (read a menu, read a sign) only the first two matter; ship them and explicitly do not model production. Getting this wrong means the app declares a character 'learned' on the easy direction and never trains the direction the player actually needs at a ticket machine.

sources.citation: González-Fernández, B., & Schmitt, N. (2020). Word knowledge: Exploring the relationships and order of acquisition of vocabulary knowledge components. Applied Linguistics, 41(4), 481–505.
Schmitt, N. et al. — Conceptualizing L2 vocabulary knowledge. Studies in Second Language Acquisition.

findings.claim: The 95%/98% coverage thresholds are real design constraints, but the underlying relationship is linear, not a cliff — which is better news for a scene-based reading game than the 'threshold' framing suggests.
findings.detail: Hu & Nation (2000) found 98% coverage needed for adequate unassisted comprehension of easy L2 fiction. Laufer & Ravenhorst-Kalovski (2010) proposed two thresholds: 95% coverage (≈4,000–5,000 word families) for 'minimal' comprehension, 98% (≈8,000 families) for 'optimal'. Schmitt, Jiang & Grabe (2011), the key corrective: they found a **relatively linear** relationship between percentage of vocabulary known and degree of comprehension, with **no threshold point where comprehension jumps** — and suggested 98% may be needed only if you want comprehension scores ≥60%. So thresholds are conventions about how much comprehension you demand, not psychological discontinuities.
findings.implication: Content: for a *reading task* — a six-character menu line, a four-character station sign — 95% coverage is meaningless as a per-item statistic; the unit is the scene. Engineer each scene so the player knows every character except at most one, i.e. target 100% minus one unknown per short text, and let the unknown be inferable from context or radical. The linearity result licenses shipping partial-coverage scenes early: partial knowledge yields partial comprehension, which is exactly the real-world win (recognising 出口 on a sign you cannot otherwise read).

Schmitt, N., Jiang, X., & Grabe, W. (2011). The percentage of words known in a text and reading comprehension. The Modern Language Journal, 95(1), 26–43.

findings.claim: Chinese L2 textbooks are a bad content source for real-world reading: a full textbook series reaches only ~81% cumulative coverage of authentic texts, well short of the 95% minimum.
findings.detail: A 2025 study in Language, Culture and Curriculum examined cumulative coverage of Chinese L2 textbook series against authentic real-world texts and found coverage reaching 81% by the final volume — 'a considerable gap from the 95% threshold for acceptable comprehension'. Single study, one textbook corpus, so treat the exact figure as indicative; the direction is consistent with the broader coverage literature.
findings.implication: Content: do not derive the item bank from HSK order or from any textbook syllabus. Build it from a corpus you construct yourself — photograph/scrape real Beijing and Shanghai metro signage, real 小吃 menus, real supermarket label boilerplate (保质期, 生产日期, 净含量, 冷藏), real shopfront category words (药房, 便利店, 面馆). Rank by frequency *within that corpus*, not by HSK level. This is the highest-leverage content decision in the project.

sources.citation: Cumulative coverage of Chinese L2 textbooks: how well do they prepare students for reading real-world texts? Language, Culture and Curriculum, 39(1), 2025.

findings.claim: Chinese character frequency is extremely top-heavy — roughly the top 1,000 characters cover ~90% of running text — so a small, well-chosen character set buys disproportionate real-world reading.
findings.detail: Corpus statistics repeatedly reported: the 1,000 most frequent characters cover ~89–90% of running text (89.25% Hong Kong, 90.26% Mainland, 88.74% Taiwan in one commonly cited comparison); the top ~2,500 reach ~98–99%. I could only reach secondary/aggregator presentations of these corpus counts, not the primary corpus reports, so I am grading this moderate rather than strong. The shape of the distribution (Zipfian, steep) is not in dispute; the exact percentages shift by genre.
findings.implication: Content: set the v1 target at 300–500 characters plus ~200 high-value multi-character words, chosen by frequency *in the signage/menu/label sub-corpus* rather than general text — domain-specific frequency is far steeper still, because a metro sign vocabulary is a few dozen characters. Ship a 'first 100 characters' arc that is explicitly framed as 'you can now read ~40% of what's on the wall'.

sources.citation: Chinese character frequency (corpus coverage statistics, Wikipedia summary of published Mainland/HK/Taiwan corpus counts).
HanziDB — most common Chinese characters ordered by frequency (corpus-derived list).

findings.claim: Radical/orthographic instruction helps L2 Chinese character learning at the beginner level, but the effect is conditional — it fails for semantically opaque characters, and radical *markings* on screen can actively interfere.
findings.detail: Chen & Feng (2020), SAGE Open: radical awareness did not positively affect meaning retention for nontransparent compound characters. A 2022 Frontiers in Psychology study found interference effects of radical markings and stroke-order animations on L2 character learning — i.e. the visual annotation cost attention without paying it back. Against that, work on radical knowledge and character recognition (Journal of Psycholinguistic Research, 2022) supports radical knowledge as a contributor to L2 Chinese reading comprehension, and pedagogical reviews recommend explicit teaching of orthographic regularities including radical position at beginner level. Small samples throughout; no meta-analysis exists. This is the weakest-evidenced area with the strongest folk consensus among Chinese teachers.
findings.implication: UI: do not render radical highlighting by default — the interference finding says a permanently colour-coded character is a cost. Make decomposition a *revealed* layer: on the feedback screen only, and only for characters flagged `semantic_transparency: high` in the item bank (氵 in 河/海/酒 yes; 的/是/了 no). Add that transparency flag to the content schema now, because retrofitting it across 500 characters later is expensive.

sources.citation: Chen, T., & Feng, Y. (2020). Nontransparent compound character learning in L2 Chinese: Does radical awareness always work? SAGE Open.
Interference effects of radical markings and stroke order animations on Chinese character learning among L2 learners (2022). Frontiers in Psychology, 13:783613.
The contribution of radical knowledge and character recognition to L2 Chinese reading comprehension (2022). Journal of Psycholinguistic Research.

findings.claim: Hanzi legibility on small screens is governed by an interaction of size, stroke width and character complexity — and for complex characters stroke WEIGHT matters more than size.
findings.detail: Liu et al. (2016), Human Factors and Ergonomics in Manufacturing & Service Industries: character style and stroke count both significantly affect the legibility threshold; **stroke width is the critical factor for high-complexity characters, while font size is critical for low-complexity characters**; a 12pt size with a 1:10 stroke-width ratio gave best legibility across both complexity levels. Smartphone studies of Traditional Chinese (Applied Ergonomics / Displays, 2017–2019) found Ming (Song) the most legible of Ming/Kai/Li styles, and identified size-and-line-spacing optima (one app study reported 14px with 1.5 line spacing for body text). These are Traditional-character studies mostly, and 'optimal' body-text sizes do not transfer to a game's hero element.
findings.implication: UI: render the target hanzi as a hero element at 96–120px (never below 48px), in a Song/Ming or a Heiti with substantial weight — minimum 500, and set stroke-to-height ratio around 1:10 rather than picking a Light weight for aesthetics. Complex targets (餐, 邊, 藥, 檢) must not be allowed to render thin: gate font-weight on stroke count in the item metadata. Distractor options can be 32–40px. Body/gloss text 16px with 1.5 line-height. Add a `stroke_count` field to every item so the renderer can make this decision.

sources.citation: Liu, N., et al. (2016). Effects of font size, stroke width, and character complexity on the legibility of Chinese characters. Human Factors and Ergonomics in Manufacturing & Service Industries.
Effects of font size and font style of Traditional Chinese characters on readability on smartphones (2018). Displays / International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics.

findings.claim: Dörnyei's L2 Motivational Self System predicts what learners SAY they will do (r = .61) far better than what they actually ACHIEVE (r = .20). Motivational vision features are not a learning lever.
findings.detail: Al-Hoorie (2018), Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching 8(4), 721–754: first meta-analysis of the L2MSS, 32 research reports, 39 unique samples, N = 32,078 learners. Ideal L2 self → subjective intended effort r = .61; ideal L2 self → **objective** achievement measures r = .20. Substantial heterogeneity in most correlations. Al-Hoorie and colleagues have since published a 'validation crisis in the L2MSS tradition' paper in SSLA arguing the instruments themselves are under-validated. r = .20 is ~4% of variance in actual achievement.
findings.implication: UX: an onboarding 'imagine yourself ordering in Chinese' vision exercise will lift self-reported motivation and your survey numbers and will do almost nothing for retention of characters. Spend the onboarding screens on the trip date (which drives the Cepeda scheduler and is causally load-bearing) rather than on identity/vision prompts. If you keep a vision element, keep it to one screen and never let it displace a retrieval opportunity.

sources.citation: Al-Hoorie, A. H. (2018). The L2 motivational self system: A meta-analysis. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 8(4), 721–754.
Al-Hoorie, A. H., et al. The validation crisis in the L2 motivational self system tradition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition.

findings.claim: Foreign language anxiety correlates about r = −0.36 to −0.39 with achievement — one of the largest and most replicated individual-difference effects in SLA. For a co-located multiplayer game this is a direct design risk.
findings.detail: Teimouri, Goetze & Plonsky (2019), SSLA 41(2), 363–387: 97 reports, 105 independent samples, N = 19,933, 23 countries, 216 correlations, mean r = −0.36. Botes, Dewaele & Greiff (2020), Journal for the Psychology of Language Learning: k = 99 effect sizes, N = 14,128, FLCAS vs general academic achievement r = −0.39, with comparable negative correlations for reading, writing, listening and speaking achievement separately. Causality is not established — anxiety and low achievement are mutually reinforcing — but the association is about as solid as SLA correlational findings get, and public performance in front of peers is the canonical FLCA trigger.
findings.implication: UI: in co-located multiplayer, individual wrong answers must not be broadcast by default. Show each player's answer privately on their own device, reveal only the aggregate ('3 of 4 got it') and the correct answer on the shared view, and make per-player error visibility an explicit opt-in. Never show a live per-player accuracy percentage to the table. Scoring can be public; failure should not be.

sources.citation: Teimouri, Y., Goetze, J., & Plonsky, L. (2019). Second language anxiety and achievement: A meta-analysis. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 41(2), 363–387.

Botes, E., Dewaele, J.-M., & Greiff, S. (2020). The Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale and academic achievement: An overview of the prevailing literature and a meta-analysis. Journal for the Psychology of Language Learning, 2, 26–56.

findings.claim: Under self-determination theory, competence is the strongest predictor of self-determined motivation — ahead of autonomy and well ahead of relatedness — and SDT-based interventions reliably raise autonomy and competence need satisfaction.
findings.detail: Wang, Wang et al. (2024), systematic review and meta-analysis of SDT-based interventions in education: 36 intervention studies, N = 11,792; 137 effect sizes from 9,433 participants. Experimental/quasi-experimental: autonomy g = 1.14, competence g = 0.48, intrinsic motivation g = 0.58; pre-post designs: autonomy g = 0.19, competence g = 0.58. Relatedness showed no significant overall effect (g = 0.44, n.s.). A 2025 meta-analysis of need support/thwarting in student populations reports competence as the most positive predictor of self-determined motivation, then autonomy, then relatedness. Note the huge gap between experimental (g = 1.14) and pre-post (g = 0.19) autonomy estimates — design quality is doing a lot of work here.
findings.implication: UX: engineer the difficulty controller to hold accuracy near 80% — high enough for continuous competence signal, low enough to keep retrieval effortful. Concretely: track rolling accuracy over the last 20 attempts and adjust distractor similarity (visually similar hanzi = harder, unrelated = easier) rather than adjusting item difficulty, so the player always faces a real item. Autonomy lever: let players choose the scene domain (menu / metro / supermarket) at the start of each round — a genuine choice that costs nothing.

sources.citation: Wang, J., Wang, Y., et al. (2024). A systematic review and meta-analysis of self-determination-theory-based interventions in the education context. Learning and Instruction.
Need support and need thwarting: A meta-analysis of autonomy, competence, and relatedness supportive and thwarting behaviors in student populations (2025). PMC12276404.

findings.claim: Gamification produces small-to-moderate gains on cognitive learning outcomes (g ≈ 0.49) — but the effect comes from challenge, meaningful goals and narrative, NOT from reward-and-status mechanics.
findings.detail: Sailer & Homner (2020), Educational Psychology Review 32, 77–112 — the best-conducted meta-analysis in this literature: cognitive outcomes g = 0.49, 95% CI [0.30, 0.69], k = 19, N = 1,686; motivational g = 0.36 [0.18, 0.54], k = 16, N = 2,246; behavioural g = 0.25 [0.04, 0.46], k = 9, N = 951. Their moderator finding is the important one: designs built on reward-and-status mechanics alone were far less effective than designs incorporating challenge, meaningful goals and narrative. Note the small k values — 19 studies for the headline cognitive effect.
findings.implication: Content + UX: the game layer should be the *scene fiction* (you are at the ticket machine; the train leaves in 30 seconds; order before the shop closes), not a points economy bolted on top. Build one narrative frame per domain with a concrete goal state ('board the right train'), and let scoring be a byproduct. If forced to choose between building a leaderboard and building three more scene narratives, build the narratives.

sources.citation: Sailer, M., & Homner, L. (2020). The gamification of learning: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 77–112.

findings.claim: Points, streaks and leaderboards have evidence for ENGAGEMENT and behavioural quantity, and essentially no clean evidence for LEARNING or intrinsic motivation. The literature routinely conflates the two and you should not.
findings.detail: Mekler, Brühlmann, Tuch & Opwis (2017), Computers in Human Behavior: points, levels and leaderboards did NOT affect intrinsic motivation and increased only performance *quantity* — more output, not better learning. Hanus & Fox (2015), 16-week longitudinal undergraduate course: leaderboards and badges coincided with *declines* in satisfaction and intrinsic motivation over time. A badges-and-leaderboards meta-analysis (Educational Technology International, 2022, 37 studies) reports SMD = 0.39 on academic performance — positive, but performance measured mostly at course level with heavy confounding. An ETR&D (2023) meta-analysis found gamification enhances intrinsic motivation and perceived autonomy/relatedness but has 'minimal impact on competency'. Duolingo's own streak work is A/B-tested on *retention* metrics (e.g. two streak-freezes → +0.38% daily active learners; a streak-wager test on day-7 retention) — these are engagement outcomes reported in company blog posts, not learning outcomes, and they are not peer-reviewed.
findings.implication: Architecture: instrument learning and engagement as two separate, separately-reported metrics from day one. Learning KPI = accuracy on items at a ≥7-day delay, computed from the attempt log. Engagement KPI = sessions/week, streak length. Ship points and streaks — they are cheap and they plausibly buy sessions, and sessions buy retrievals — but never let a streak-preservation mechanic substitute a trivial task for a due-item review, which is exactly how streaks corrode learning. Rule: a day only counts toward the streak if the player completed their due reviews.

sources.citation: Mekler, E. D., Brühlmann, F., Tuch, A. N., & Opwis, K. (2017). Towards understanding the effects of individual gamification elements on intrinsic motivation and performance. Computers in Human Behavior, 71, 525–534.
Impacts of badges and leaderboards on academic performance: A meta-analysis (2022). Educational Technology International.

Gamification enhances student intrinsic motivation, perceptions of autonomy and relatedness, but minimal impact on competency: a meta-analysis and systematic review (2023). Educational Technology Research and Development.
How streaks keep Duolingo learners committed to their language goals. Duolingo Blog (company A/B results, engagement outcomes only).

findings.claim: The gamification literature has a real publication-bias problem and early effect estimates are inflated; treat any gamification number below g ≈ 0.4 as noise.
findings.detail: Sailer & Homner (2020) explicitly critique the earlier meta-analysis that reported r = .31 [0.11, 0.47] from 14 studies (2013–2015) on two grounds: r cannot correct for small-sample bias and so overestimates, and no publication-bias evaluation was attempted at all. Subsequent meta-analyses have used Hedges' g and run trim-and-fill and fail-safe-N, generally reporting bias as 'unlikely to be an issue' — but fail-safe N is a weak diagnostic and trim-and-fill has low power with the small k values (9–19) typical of this field. Compounding this: novelty effects mean cross-sectional gamification studies over-report what a mechanic does in month six.
findings.implication: Architecture: do not ship gamification mechanics on the strength of the published literature. Build a lightweight client-side experiment framework into the PWA — deterministic bucket assignment from a hashed device id, variant recorded on every attempt event, so any mechanic (wager on/off, leaderboard on/off, streak on/off) can be evaluated against 7-day delayed accuracy in your own population. This is a small amount of work and it is the only way to settle these questions for your product.

sources.citation: Sailer, M., & Homner, L. (2020). Educational Psychology Review, 32, 77–112 (critique of prior meta-analytic practice).

findings.claim: Competition in digital game-based learning has a positive, modest effect (g ≈ 0.39) and it does work for language subjects — so the co-located multiplayer premise is defensible on evidence.
findings.detail: Chen, Chen & Dai (2020), Educational Technology Research and Development: meta-analysis of 25 articles (2008–2019), overall effect size 0.386. Competition in DGBL was effective for maths, science and language, but not for social science; effective for K-12 and college students; effective for puzzle, strategy, role-playing and simulation games but not action games; equally effective for cognitive and non-cognitive outcomes. Barz, Benick, Dörrenbächer-Ulrich & Perels (2024), Review of Educational Research, provides the broader DGBL meta-analysis across cognitive, metacognitive and affective-motivational outcomes. Caveat: none of this is co-located same-room multiplayer specifically, and none of it is L2 reading.
findings.implication: UX: keep the game type in the supported band — turn-based puzzle/quiz with a shared goal, not a reaction-speed action game (the one game type that showed no benefit). Concretely: rounds are simultaneous-answer with a 6–10 second window, not first-to-buzz; a buzzer race converts the task into a speed contest and rewards the fastest reader rather than producing retrieval attempts from everyone. Every player answers every item — that is what preserves retrievals-per-player-per-minute, which is the actual learning currency.

sources.citation: Chen, C.-H., Shih, C.-C., & Law, V. (2020). The effects of competition in digital game-based learning (DGBL): A meta-analysis. Educational Technology Research and Development, 68, 1855–1873.

Barz, N., Benick, M., Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, L., & Perels, F. (2024). The effect of digital game-based learning interventions on cognitive, metacognitive, and affective-motivational learning outcomes in school: A meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research.

findings.claim: 'Desirable difficulties' is a sound framework but a bad slogan: the well-evidenced members are spacing, retrieval practice and generation. Perceptual disfluency — the most UI-tempting member — is a documented failure.
findings.detail: Soderstrom & Bjork (2015), Perspectives on Psychological Science 10(2), 176–199, establish the learning/performance dissociation: conditions that enhance long-term learning often depress performance during training, and vice versa. That framework is solid. But the specific 'make it harder to read' instantiation failed: Taylor, Sanson et al. (2020), Memory 28(7) — four experiments attempting to replicate the Sans Forgetica developers' unpublished findings — found the font was rated harder to read but produced equivalent or *impaired* memory. Wetzler, Pyke & Werner (2021), SAGE Open, replicated the null. The general lesson, which Bjork's own group states: not all difficulties are desirable, and difficulty is a proxy for effortful *retrieval*, not for effortful *perception*.
findings.implication: UI: never degrade hanzi rendering to 'add difficulty' — no low contrast, no thin weights, no obscured strokes, no deliberately hard fonts. Difficulty must come from the retrieval demand (longer gap, more confusable distractors, meaning→hanzi direction) while the pixels stay maximally legible. Concretely: keep hanzi at WCAG AA contrast minimum 4.5:1 against the card, and make distractor visual similarity the difficulty dial.

sources.citation: Soderstrom, N. C., & Bjork, R. A. (2015). Learning versus performance: An integrative review. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 10(2), 176–199.
Taylor, A., Sanson, M., et al. (2020). Disfluent difficulties are not desirable difficulties: The (lack of) effect of Sans Forgetica on memory. Memory, 28(7), 850–857.
Wetzler, E. L., Pyke, A. A., & Werner, A. (2021). Sans Forgetica is not the 'font' of knowledge: Disfluent fonts are not always desirable difficulties. SAGE Open.

findings.claim: Deck/round size has no independent effect on vocabulary learning once spacing is controlled — the apparent benefit of small decks in the folk literature is a spacing confound.
findings.detail: Nakata & Webb (2016), Studies in Second Language Acquisition 38(3), 523–552: earlier block-size studies confounded block size with spacing (small decks necessarily mean shorter gaps between repetitions of the same item). When spacing was manipulated independently, a large block size looked better than a small one only under the confound; with equivalent spacing there was no difference. Part learning produced more correct retrievals *during* learning but not on posttests — a textbook performance-vs-learning dissociation. Whole learning may outperform part learning when spacing between items is longer.
findings.implication: Architecture: do not expose or tune a 'cards per session' parameter, and do not chunk the item bank into small decks on the theory that small is easier. Drive session composition entirely from due-dates plus the semantic-blocking rule from the interleaving finding. This removes a whole class of product decisions that has no evidence behind it.

sources.citation: Nakata, T., & Webb, S. (2016). Does studying vocabulary in smaller sets increase learning? The effects of part and whole learning on second language vocabulary acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 38(3), 523–552.

findings.claim: Vendor efficacy claims for language apps (including Duolingo's) are weak evidence: the reading/listening studies are uncontrolled single-arm designs.
findings.detail: Jiang, Rollinson, Plonsky et al. (2024), CALICO Journal: 245 English learners who completed the A2 'Basic' content of Duolingo courses for Japanese, Spanish or Portuguese speakers, with Duolingo as their only learning tool, scored ACTFL Intermediate High in reading and listening — one sublevel above the expected Intermediate Mid. This is peer-reviewed but single-arm: no control group, self-selected completers, survivorship bias by construction (only people who finished a course are measured). Duolingo's own reports claim parity with four university semesters at roughly half the study time; those are white papers, not controlled trials. The one internal finding worth taking seriously methodologically is that *lessons completed* predicted outcomes better than *time spent* — consistent with retrievals, not minutes, being the currency.
findings.implication: Content: it is defensible to promise a beginner meaningful reading ability in weeks, but set the promise against retrieval counts you control, not against competitor marketing. Ship an honest progress claim tied to measurable coverage — 'you can now read 312 of the 400 most common characters on Chinese signage' — computed from the item bank, rather than a CEFR/HSK level claim you cannot substantiate.

sources.citation: Jiang, X., Rollinson, J., Plonsky, L., et al. (2024). The effectiveness of Duolingo English courses in developing reading and listening proficiency. CALICO Journal, 41(3).
Duolingo Efficacy Studies (company research portal).

findings.claim: Chinese character acuity size rises steadily with stroke count; each extra stroke needs roughly +0.25 arcmin of character size to hold legibility constant.
findings.detail: Zhang, Zhang, Xue, Liu & Yu (2007, IOVS 48:2383-2390) measured acuity for six Chinese character groups spanning 2-4 up to 16-18 strokes plus Sloan letters, in 6 normal-sighted Chinese observers. Acuity size increased steadily with complexity, though more slowly than a pure finest-detail account predicts. Separately, Liu, Yu & Zhang (2016, HFEM 26:381-392, n=36, character search in pseudo-text) found font size and complexity significant but stroke width not; stroke width mattered only for high-complexity characters, font size only for low-complexity ones. Small n in the acuity study; the 0.25 arcmin figure is a single-study slope.
findings.implication: Store strokeCount per character and render size as a function of it: base hanzi size S, then S_effective = S * (1 + 0.012 * max(0, strokes - 8)). Concretely with a 48px base, an 18-stroke character (蔬, 齿, 警) renders at ~54px, a 4-stroke character at 48px. Never let a >12-stroke character render below 32 CSS px anywhere in the UI, including answer chips and score rows.

sources.citation: Zhang J-Y, Zhang T, Xue F, Liu L, Yu C (2007). Legibility Variations of Chinese Characters and Implications for Visual Acuity Measurement in Chinese Reading Population. Investigative Ophthalmology & Visual Science 48(5):2383-2390

Liu N, Yu R, Zhang Y (2016). Effects of Font Size, Stroke Width, and Character Complexity on the Legibility of Chinese Characters. Human Factors and Ergonomics in Manufacturing & Service Industries 26(3):381-392

findings.claim: Chinese readers need substantially larger characters than Latin readers need letters — roughly 1.7-2.0x the ETDRS near-acuity size for traditional characters.
findings.detail: Reported in the traditional-Chinese equivalent-legibility literature: normal-sight readers need a 0.22-0.30 logMAR (1.7-2.0 fold) enlargement over the acuity size measured by an ETDRS near chart to recognise traditional Chinese characters. This is a clinical-optometry finding (small n, Taiwanese sample), abstract-only.
findings.implication: Do not size hanzi with the same scale you size the Dutch/English UI text. Set two independent type scales in CSS custom properties: --latin-base: 16px and --hanzi-base: 32px, with the hanzi prompt at 2-3x the Latin body size. A card showing '出口' with the gloss 'exit' should render 出口 at 48-64px and 'exit' at 16px, not both at 20px.

sources.citation: Equivalent legibility font size for traditional Chinese character compared to early treatment diabetic retinopathy study near visual acuity (2022), PubMed 35399968

findings.claim: Preferred (not minimum) Chinese character size for young adults is ~42 arcmin, and reading at the preferred size rather than the minimum acceptable size lifts proofreading accuracy from 65.4% to 73.3%.
findings.detail: Electronic-paper display study (Ergonomics, 2011) across three age groups: preferred viewing distances 503/455/444 mm and preferred character sizes 42.0/50.0/55.2 arcmin for young/middle-aged/older. Chinese proofreading accuracy was 73.3% at preferred size vs 65.4% at the minimum acceptable size — an ~8 percentage point accuracy cost for sizing at threshold. Earlier CRT work put the all-characters-recognisable threshold at ~20.39 arcmin. Measured smartphone viewing distance is much closer than 500mm: Bababekova & Rosenfield report a mean of 36.2 ± 7.1 cm for text messages, with Lan et al. 33.95 ± 5.9 cm and Boccardo 36.1 ± 7.2 cm converging.
findings.implication: Design for 36 cm viewing distance. 42 arcmin at 360 mm = 4.4 mm ≈ 17 CSS px — that is the *comfort floor for native readers of familiar text*, so treat it as an absolute minimum, not a target. Set the answer-option hanzi at 32 CSS px (~8.5 mm ≈ 81 arcmin) and the prompt hanzi at 48-64 CSS px (~12.7-17 mm ≈ 121-162 arcmin). Never render a hanzi the learner must discriminate below 24 CSS px. Ship a single 'Larger text' toggle that multiplies --hanzi-base by 1.25 rather than a continuous slider.

sources.citation: Electronic paper display preferred viewing distance and character size for different age groups (2011). Ergonomics 54(9)
Bababekova Y, Rosenfield M, et al. Font Size and Viewing Distance of Handheld Smart Phones. Optometry and Vision Science
Hou G, Anicetus U, He J (2022). How to design font size for older adults: A systematic literature review with a mobile device. Frontiers in Psychology 13:931646

findings.claim: Positive polarity (dark text on light background) is measurably more legible than negative polarity, and the advantage grows as character size shrinks — and this holds for Chinese specifically, not just Latin.
findings.detail: Piepenbrock, Mayr & Buchner found a positive-polarity advantage in visual acuity and proofreading for both younger and older adults (2013), with the advantage increasing linearly as character size decreased (2014, Human Factors 56), and smaller pupil size with positive polarity (2014). Mechanism: the bright background contracts the pupil, reducing optical aberration. For Chinese specifically, Dobres, Chahine, Reimer, Gould & Zhao (2016, Displays 41:42-49) found Hei-style type, bold weight, in positive contrast was the most legible combination in a glance-based legibility paradigm; Ming-style MT Sung was the least legible. Two independent literatures converge.
findings.implication: Ship light mode as the default. If you offer dark mode, do not treat it as a free swap: increase --hanzi-base by 15% in dark mode and step the hanzi font-weight from 400 to 500. Use tokens on bare :root for light and redefine only under the dark media query and [data-theme=dark].

Dobres J, Chahine N, Reimer B, Gould D, Zhao N (2016). The effects of Chinese typeface design, stroke weight, and contrast polarity on glance based legibility. Displays 41:42-49

findings.claim: If you do ship dark mode for Chinese text, pure white on pure black is the wrong choice: a dark grey ground with mid-grey text is optimal, and font weight does not matter.
findings.detail: Text Readability of Smartphone in Dark Mode: Effects of Font Type, Font Weight and Color (HCII 2023, Springer LNCS), n=40, Chinese reading-comprehension task, measuring reading time, accuracy and subjective ratings. Font type, background colour and font colour all had significant effects; font weight did not. Optimal combination: Hei font, dark grey background (HSB 0/50/12), light grey text (HSB 0/0/58). Single study, n=40, abstract-only.
findings.implication: Dark-mode tokens: --bg: #1F0F0F-class dark grey (not #000), --fg: #949494-class light grey (not #FFF) — that pairing computes to ~6.1:1 contrast, clearing WCAG AA while avoiding halation on strokes. Set these as :root overrides only; never as the only definition of a colour.

sources.citation: Text Readability of Smartphone in Dark Mode: Effects of Font Type, Font Weight and Color (2023). HCII / Human Aspects of IT for the Aged Population, LNCS

findings.claim: Hei (sans) beats Ming/Song (serif) for on-screen Chinese: faster response times and equal-or-better accuracy, and Ming was the least legible style in a glance paradigm.
findings.detail: Dobres et al. (2016, Displays) rank Hei bold positive-contrast most legible, Ming-style MT Sung least. Smartphone dark-mode work (HCII 2023, n=40) also selected Hei as optimal. Traditional-Chinese smartphone work reports faster response times for Hei than Kai and Ming, with higher accuracy for Hei and Ming than Kai. Countervailing: one traditional-Chinese smartphone study found Ming faster than Hei *only* at 10pt. No study located that tests whether serif/Ming or Kai aids acquisition of character *form* by learners — see gaps.
findings.implication: Use a Hei/gothic face as the single hanzi face: font-family for hanzi = 'Noto Sans SC', 'Source Han Sans SC', 'PingFang SC', 'Microsoft YaHei', sans-serif, with a real fallback stack. Do not ship a Song/Ming or Kai face as body type. If you want a Kai face to show stroke shape, restrict it to a dedicated 'stroke form' detail view at ≥64px, never in the game loop.

sources.citation: Dobres J, Chahine N, Reimer B, Gould D, Zhao N (2016). Displays 41:42-49
Huang S-M (2019). Effects of font size and font style of Traditional Chinese characters on readability on smartphones. International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics
Text Readability of Smartphone in Dark Mode (2023). HCII, LNCS

findings.claim: For simplified Chinese on a phone, 12pt with generous line spacing is the sweet spot; bigger is not monotonically better.
findings.detail: Zhu S, Su X, Dong Y (2021, Interacting with Computers 33(2):177-, n=115, 5.9-inch phone, 3 font sizes x 3 line spacings = 9 conditions): both font size and line spacing significantly affected reading time; only font size affected accuracy; size, spacing and their interaction affected perceived difficulty and visual fatigue. Medium and large font sizes were more comfortable with large line spacing. Independently, Huang (2019) found 10pt gave better reading speed than 14pt on a 5.5-inch phone when viewing distance was free — reading speed does not rise monotonically with size. Liu et al. (2016) found 12pt with a 1:10 stroke-width ratio optimal for legibility at both complexity levels.
findings.implication: For any running-text Chinese block (a menu line, a sign, a sentence item): font-size ~16-17 CSS px equivalent to 12pt at 96dpi, line-height 1.6-1.8 (i.e. the 1.5F-2F range that tested best with medium/large type). Do not exceed ~20px for running text; put the extra size budget into the single isolated target character instead. Cap running-text blocks at 2-3 lines per card.

sources.citation: Zhu S, Su X, Dong Y (2021). Effects of the Font Size and Line Spacing of Simplified Chinese Characters on Smartphone Readability. Interacting with Computers 33(2):177
Huang S-M (2019). International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics
Liu N, Yu R, Zhang Y (2016). HFEM 26(3):381-392

findings.claim: Word-spaced Chinese text helps L2 learners read faster and comprehend better; character-spaced text is worse than word-spaced, and non-word-spaced is the worst of all.
findings.detail: Eye-tracking work with CSL learners (Frontiers in Psychology 2023, 14:783960, building on Bai/Shen/Blythe-style paradigms and the 2012 L2 spaced/unspaced study): word-spaced text produced least disruption; unspaced text produced longer reading times than character-spaced; nonword-spaced produced most disruption. Adding spacing facilitated CSL learners' comprehension, speed and vocabulary learning. Segmenting into *words* beats separating individual characters. Mechanism: spacing makes word boundaries salient, reducing uncertainty about which characters form a word.
findings.implication: Store every reading item pre-segmented into words (an array of word tokens, not a raw string). In the reading UI, render a 0.25em gap between word tokens and zero gap within a word: 火车站 with .w { margin-right: 0.25em }. Add a 'native spacing' toggle that collapses the gap to 0, and switch a learner to native spacing automatically once they clear a level, because real menus and signs have no gaps.

sources.citation: Eye movements of second language learners when reading spaced and unspaced Chinese texts (2023). Frontiers in Psychology 14:783960
Shen D et al. (2012). Eye movements of second language learners when reading spaced and unspaced Chinese text. PubMed 22545927

findings.claim: Visual span for Chinese shrinks as character complexity rises, with an approximately invariant product of ~10 cycles at 1.2 degree character size — complex characters cost you how many you can take in per fixation.
findings.detail: Wang H, He X, Legge GE (2014, Journal of Vision) extended the visual-span trigram method to Chinese; span size in number of characters was smaller for high-complexity than low- or medium-complexity stimuli, and the product of span size and complexity was roughly invariant (~10 cycles at 1.2 deg), suggesting a capacity limit on visual pattern recognition. Aging and Pattern Complexity Effects on the Visual Span (Vision 2019, 3(1):11) replicates the complexity effect across age groups.
findings.implication: Cap the number of hanzi visible in a single reading target at 6-8 characters for low-complexity items and 4-6 for items whose mean stroke count exceeds 12. Compute meanStrokes per item at build time and use it to pick the layout: >12 means one line, larger type, no gloss on the same line.

sources.citation: Wang H, He X, Legge GE (2014). Effect of pattern complexity on the visual span for Chinese and alphabet characters. Journal of Vision
Aging and Pattern Complexity Effects on the Visual Span: Evidence from Chinese Character Recognition (2019). Vision 3(1):11

findings.claim: Simplified characters are visually less complex than traditional but more visually similar to each other — which changes what your distractor set should look like.
findings.detail: Corpus and lexicon-project work (Simplified Chinese Lexicon Project, Behavior Research Methods 2025, 8105 characters + 4864 pseudocharacters) plus perceptual-expertise work (Liu et al. 2016, Cognitive Science) establish that simplified characters need fewer strokes and are visually less complex, but are more visually confusable with one another. Characters with fewer strokes were recognised roughly 100 ms (~9%) faster than high-stroke characters. Complexity did not affect legible contrast threshold except for small (<0.35 deg) characters — i.e. complexity bites hardest exactly at phone sizes.
findings.implication: Ship Simplified only (target is mainland China). Precompute, for every character in the bank, its list of visual neighbours by stroke-edit distance and shared components, and store it as neighbours[]. Draw MC distractors preferentially from that list. Log a per-item p(confusion) from live answer data and keep the top 2 confusable neighbours as the standing distractors.

sources.citation: Simplified Chinese lexicon project: A lexical decision database with 8105 characters and 4864 pseudocharacters (2025). Behavior Research Methods
Liu T et al. (2016). Transfer of Perceptual Expertise: The Case of Simplified and Traditional Chinese Character Recognition. Cognitive Science

findings.claim: Tone-colour coding of Mandarin works, but slightly worse than tone numbers or pitch contours, and adding colour on top of another cue buys nothing.
findings.detail: Godfroid A, Lin C-H, Ryu C (2017). Language Learning 67(4):819-857. n=303 true-novice L2 Mandarin learners (native English speakers), 3-week online training, five conditions: three single-cue (number, pitch contour, colour) and two dual-cue (colour+number, colour+pitch contour). Pretest, immediate posttest, delayed posttest. Multimodal training aided tone perception overall, with a small practical advantage for pitch contours and numbers *over* colour. Dual-cue methods did not beat single-cue. Colour-mediated training gave ~11% item-learning and ~12% system-learning gains. Large, well-powered, randomised, delayed posttest — this is the reference study.
findings.implication: Do not colour-code tones. Where pinyin appears, show the standard diacritic (mā/má/mǎ/mà) and optionally a small pitch-contour glyph; never a colour. If a user asks for tone colours, ship it as an off-by-default accessibility preference, and never combine it with the contour glyph — dual cues add cost with no gain.

sources.citation: Godfroid A, Lin C-H, Ryu C (2017). Hearing and Seeing Tone Through Color: An Efficacy Study of Web-Based, Multimodal Chinese Tone Perception Training. Language Learning 67(4):819-857

findings.claim: Colour-coding visually similar hanzi actively slows learners down — it produces visual overload rather than salience.
findings.detail: Li & Shi et al. (2025). Learning Chinese Characters of Visual Similarity: The Effects of Presentation Style and Color Coding. Languages 10(10):260. n=183 non-tonal native speakers with zero prior hanzi experience. 2x2x2 design: colour coding (with/without) x presentation style (single/paired) x stroke similarity (identical-strokes e.g. 人/入 vs one-extra-stroke e.g. 日/白). Results: (1) characters differing by an added stroke were easier than identical-stroke pairs; (2) simultaneous paired presentation improved discrimination of subtle stroke differences; (3) colour coding *slowed reaction times*, interpreted as visual overload.
findings.implication: Two rules. First: never tint, highlight or outline any part of a hanzi glyph — the target character renders in one flat foreground colour, full stop. Second: when the item is a confusable pair (人/入, 日/白, 未/末, 己/已), present both candidates side by side at equal size in the same row rather than serially — that is what improved discrimination. Tag such items pairType: 'identical-stroke' | 'added-stroke' and schedule identical-stroke pairs later, since they were harder.

sources.citation: Li & Shi et al. (2025). Learning Chinese Characters of Visual Similarity: The Effects of Presentation Style and Color Coding. Languages 10(10):260

findings.claim: Marking radicals inside a character hurts recognition: it increases reaction time and decreases accuracy for L2 learners. Stroke-order animations also decrease accuracy.
findings.detail: Hou F & Jiang X (2022). Interference effects of radical markings and stroke order animations on Chinese character learning among L2 learners. Frontiers in Psychology 13:783613. n=40 L2 learners from alphabetic L1s, split high/low proficiency, four conditions (radical markings x stroke animations). Radical markings increased RT and decreased accuracy on the character-recognition test; stroke-order animations also decreased recognition accuracy. Neither affected character-meaning matching. Authors attribute it to excess visual information raising cognitive load. Single study, n=40, but the direction agrees with the colour-coding finding above.
findings.implication: No radical outlines, no component boxes, no coloured sub-glyph regions, no stroke-order animation anywhere in the answering loop. If the app has a 'how this character is built' explainer, it lives on a separate post-answer screen the user must tap to open, and it shows the components as *separate glyphs beside* the character (木 + 目 → 相), never as an overlay on it.

sources.citation: Hou F, Jiang X (2022). Interference effects of radical markings and stroke order animations on Chinese character learning among L2 learners. Frontiers in Psychology 13:783613

findings.claim: Teaching semantic radicals as explicit content does work and transfers to untaught characters — the payoff is in the item bank, not in the glyph decoration.
findings.detail: Nguyen TP, Zhang J, Li H, Wu X, Cheng Y (2017). Teaching Semantic Radicals Facilitates Inferring New Character Meaning in Sentence Reading for Nonnative Chinese Speakers. Frontiers in Psychology 8:1846. n=54 Vietnamese undergraduates with ~1 year of Chinese, two experimental groups receiving 'old-for-new' semantic-radical teaching plus a control. Sentence-cloze task with four options sharing the same phonetic radical but differing semantic radicals. Pre-to-post gains significant for experimental groups only, and crucially the strategy transferred to semantic radicals that had not been taught. Quasi-experimental, moderate n.
findings.implication: Ship a first-class radical layer in the item bank: ~40-60 high-yield semantic radicals (氵水 water, 木 wood, 口 mouth, 钅金 metal, 艹 grass, 饣食 food, 车 vehicle, 门 gate) as their own item type, introduced before the compound characters that contain them. Item schema needs semanticRadical and phoneticRadical fields per character, and the scheduler must not present a compound before its semantic radical has been seen at least twice. Build cloze items whose distractors share the phonetic radical and differ only in the semantic radical — that is exactly the transfer-tested format.

sources.citation: Nguyen TP, Zhang J, Li H, Wu X, Cheng Y (2017). Frontiers in Psychology 8:1846

findings.claim: Learning with a colour cue and then being tested without it produces the *worst* outcome of all — worse than never having the cue. This is a guidance reversal, not just a smaller benefit.
findings.detail: Skulmowski A (2022). When color coding backfires: A guidance reversal effect when learning with realistic visualizations. Education and Information Technologies 27:3963-. Two experiments, n=125 and n=107. Colour coding helped most when present in both learning and testing materials; learning *with* colour cues and testing *without* them gave the worst retention and transfer scores. Guidance fading (complex model with colour cues, later removed) had no effect. Domain is anatomical visualisation, not Chinese, so this is a transfer-by-analogy argument — but it is the mechanism that matters for a product whose target environment (a real menu, a real subway sign) contains no cues at all.
findings.implication: This is the decisive argument against tone-colour and radical-colour for *this* product. The transfer environment — a Shanghai metro sign — is monochrome black-on-white. Any colour cue present in training and absent in the world is the exact configuration that produced the worst scores. Rule: the character as it appears in the answer options must be pixel-identical in colour and weight to how it would appear on a real sign. Reserve colour strictly for interface chrome (correct/incorrect feedback, player identity, progress), never for linguistic content.

sources.citation: Skulmowski A (2022). When color coding backfires: A guidance reversal effect when learning with realistic visualizations. Education and Information Technologies 27:3963-3985

findings.claim: Across Mayer's own multimedia-learning corpus, the biggest single lever is removing extraneous material (g = 1.00), and signalling/cueing is one of the smallest (g = 0.24).
findings.detail: A Meta-Analysis of Richard Mayer's Multimedia Learning Research (2025, Educational Research Review). 92 articles, 181 studies, 591 effects, 1990-2022. Overall g = 0.37, declining with publication year. Removing seductive detail g = 1.00; modality (no captions vs captions) g = 0.82; personalisation g = 0.70; multimedia g = 0.68; sentence-level coherence g = 0.63; cueing g = 0.24; segmenting g = 0.19; avoiding redundant captions with narration g = 0.14; contiguity g = 0.13; VR immersion g = -0.19. Important caveat the authors state: this meta-analysis is restricted to papers with Mayer as an author, so it is an upper bound on his own principles, not an independent test.
findings.implication: Rank your design budget by these numbers. (1) Coherence first: an answering card contains at most 5 elements — the target hanzi, up to 3 answer options, and a timer/progress affordance. No decorative illustration, no mascot, no confetti during the item, no background pattern. (2) Redundancy: do not simultaneously show hanzi + pinyin + English + play audio. (3) Signalling is cheap but weak — a 2px underline or a subtle weight change is enough; do not spend layout on it. (4) Segmenting is weak — do not over-fragment into 3-item micro-screens on the strength of it.

sources.citation: A meta-analysis of Richard Mayer's multimedia learning research: Searching for boundary conditions of design principles across multiple media types (2025). Educational Research Review
Illinois Experts record for the same meta-analysis

findings.claim: For hanzi + pinyin + English shown together, vertical stacking (pinyin directly above/below its own character) significantly beats a horizontal row — the horizontal layout imposes split attention and hinders character learning for beginners.
findings.detail: Lee CH & Kalyuga S (2011). Effectiveness of Different Pinyin Presentation Formats in Learning Chinese Characters: A Cognitive Load Perspective. Language Learning 61(4):1099-1118. Experiment comparing vertical vs horizontal layouts of character / pinyin / English translation. Significant advantage for the vertical format, attributed to eliminating split attention by placing each pinyin segment exactly under its matching character. The commonly used horizontal format was concluded to impose high cognitive load and hinder character learning at beginner level. Related: Wang & Kalyuga (2010, Computers in Human Behavior) found an expertise reversal — *partial* on-screen pinyin beat both full pinyin and no pinyin for more experienced learners.
findings.implication: When pinyin is shown at all, use HTML ruby: <ruby>火<rt>huǒ</rt></ruby><ruby>车<rt>chē</rt></ruby> — per-character, vertically aligned, ruby text at 0.45em of the hanzi size. Never a separate pinyin line under the whole phrase. And gate it: full ruby for a learner's first 3 exposures to an item, then *partial* ruby (only the characters that item's error history flags as weak), then none. Store exposureCount and perCharacterErrorRate to drive this.
