findings.claim: Playing audio while showing the written form is worth more for Chinese than for European L2s, precisely because the orthographic distance from English/Dutch is so large.
findings.detail: Koh (2024). Deconstructing the benefits of reading-while-listening on L2 reading comprehension: The influence of cross-orthographic distance. Foreign Language Annals. L1 Korean intermediate undergraduates learning Chinese (non-alphabetic), English (alphabetic deep) and Spanish (alphabetic shallow), reading vs reading-while-listening authentic texts, untimed written MC comprehension. Learners of the *most* orthographically distant L2 (Chinese) benefitted most from RWL. Mechanism: the spoken form supports establishing a stable phonology-orthography link. Broader RWL literature is mixed (Hui 2024/2026 in MLJ and Language Learning), so grade moderate not strong.
findings.implication: Autoplay the audio for the correct answer at reveal, every time, with the hanzi still on screen — this is a post-answer feedback event, not a simultaneous presentation during the item (which would trip redundancy). Ship audio as pre-cached per-item files in the PWA's Cache Storage so it works offline in a Beijing basement restaurant; budget ~15-25 KB per item at 48 kbps mono Opus.

sources.citation: Koh (2024). Foreign Language Annals
Hui B (2026). Listening, Reading, or Both? Rethinking the Comprehension Benefits of Reading-While-Listening. Language Learning

findings.claim: Multiple choice is not a weak substitute for recall in this product — meta-analytically it produced a *larger* testing effect than short answer (g = 0.70 vs 0.48), and matching practice format to the target format adds more (g = 0.63 vs 0.53).
findings.detail: Adesope OO, Trevisan DA, Sundararajan N (2017). Rethinking the Use of Tests: A Meta-Analysis of Practice Testing. Review of Educational Research 87(3). Overall retrieval-practice effect g = 0.61. Multiple-choice practice g = 0.70; short-answer practice g = 0.48. Testing effects larger when practice and final test formats were identical (g = 0.63) than when they mismatched (g = 0.53). This overturns the theoretical prediction that recall must beat recognition. Directly relevant because the product's real-world target task — 'is that shopfront 药店 or 酒店?' — *is* a recognition task.
findings.implication: Keep MC as the core loop; you do not need to bolt on typing or handwriting to be pedagogically respectable. And make the practice format mirror the criterion task: the stem should be the hanzi as it appears in the world and the options should be meanings/functions in Dutch or English ('pharmacy' / 'hotel' / 'bank'), not the reverse. Reverse-direction items (English stem, hanzi options) train production, which is not the stated goal — cap them at ~20% of the bank.

sources.citation: Adesope OO, Trevisan DA, Sundararajan N (2017). Rethinking the Use of Tests: A Meta-Analysis of Practice Testing. Review of Educational Research 87(3):659-701

findings.claim: The negative suggestion effect is real but small and quantified: exposure to MC lures raised the rate of producing those specific wrong answers a week later from 5% to 12%.
findings.detail: Roediger HL III & Marsh EJ (2005). The Positive and Negative Consequences of Multiple-Choice Testing. JEP:LMC 31(5):1155-1159. Participants studied prose passages, took MC tests with 2-6 alternatives, returned one week later for open-ended short answer with explicit instructions not to guess. Net positive testing effect on correct retention. Negative effect: MC lures were produced on 5% of questions when not previously tested, rising to 12% after testing. Increasing the number of alternatives decreased MC accuracy. Replicated in Marsh, Roediger, Bjork & Bjork (2007, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review) and in Butler & Roediger (2010, Memory & Cognition) showing both effects persist after 1 week.
findings.implication: Budget for it rather than fear it: the net effect of MC is positive, and 7 percentage points of lure intrusion is the price. Mitigate structurally — (a) never reuse a wrong option as a *correct* answer for a different item in the same session; (b) after a wrong answer, immediately re-present the same item with the chosen lure removed, so the last thing the player sees is the correct pairing; (c) log every chosen-lure event as {itemId, lureId, timestamp} and force a corrective re-test of that item within 24 hours.

sources.citation: Roediger HL III, Marsh EJ (2005). The Positive and Negative Consequences of Multiple-Choice Testing. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 31(5)
Marsh EJ, Roediger HL, Bjork RA, Bjork EL (2007). The memorial consequences of multiple-choice testing. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review

findings.claim: Feedback is the fix for distractor reinforcement: both immediate and delayed feedback raise correct responses and cut lure intrusions, and they are equally effective at cutting intrusions.
findings.detail: Butler AC & Roediger HL III (2008). Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing. Memory & Cognition 36(3):604-616. Subjects studied passages then took an MC test with immediate feedback, delayed feedback, or no feedback, followed by a delayed cued-recall test. Both feedback conditions increased correct responses and reduced lure intrusions relative to no feedback, and the two timings were equally effective at reducing intrusions.
findings.implication: Feedback is mandatory on every item, and the timing is yours to choose — which is a gift for a co-located multiplayer format. Two valid designs: reveal per item (immediate), or hold reveals to the end of a 5-item round (delayed) so opponents cannot read your answer off your face. Pick end-of-round batch reveal for the multiplayer mode and immediate reveal for single-player. Feedback must show the correct hanzi + its meaning + play audio; simply showing a red X is not the manipulation that was tested.

sources.citation: Butler AC, Roediger HL III (2008). Memory & Cognition 36(3):604-616

findings.claim: Three options are optimal for multiple-choice items — you get more items per unit of time with no loss of psychometric quality.
findings.detail: Rodriguez MC (2005). Three Options Are Optimal for Multiple-Choice Items: A Meta-Analysis of 80 Years of Research. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice 24(2):3-13. Random-effects meta-analysis. More 3-option items can be administered per unit of testing time while improving content coverage, without detriment to score quality. Important qualifier the paper states: reducing options while holding item count constant *does* reduce difficulty, discrimination and reliability — unless the removed options were the ineffective ones. Random removal is harmful.
findings.implication: Use exactly 3 options per item, and spend the saved screen space and time on more items per round. On a 390px-wide phone this also lets each option be a full-width row ≥56px tall (see touch targets) inside the thumb zone. Critically: the third option must be a *real* competitor drawn from the visual-neighbour or semantic-field list, never filler — Rodriguez's result only holds when the retained options are the effective ones.

sources.citation: Rodriguez MC (2005). Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice 24(2):3-13

findings.claim: Distractors that are orthographically or semantically close to the key raise both item difficulty and item discrimination; distractors generated from real learner errors are measurably more competitive than hand-written ones.
findings.detail: Ludewig U, Schwerter J, McElvany N (2023). The Features of Plausible but Incorrect Options: Distractor Plausibility in Synonym-Based Vocabulary Tests. Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment 41(7):711-731 — options with distracting features (semantic relatedness, orthographic similarity) increased item difficulty and discrimination; distractors less synonymous than the key decreased discrimination. Generating Competitive Distractors from Student Error Data (ACM Learning @ Scale 2025) — a scalable data-driven method generating orthographically related distractors from common incorrect responses in open-answer retrieval practice, aligned with learners' shared misconceptions. Also Generating Plausible Distractors via Student Choice Prediction (arXiv 2501.13125).
findings.implication: Distractor generation policy, in priority order: (1) a visual neighbour of the target character sharing ≥1 component (药店 vs 酒店, 大 vs 太 vs 犬); (2) a same-semantic-field item the learner would plausibly meet in the same physical place (on a menu: 牛肉/羊肉/猪肉); (3) a homophone or near-homophone. Never a random unrelated character. Then close the loop: after ~500 responses per item, replace the least-chosen distractor with the most-frequent wrong open-answer if you ever collect one, or with the most-confused neighbour from live logs.

findings.claim: 9.2 mm is the empirically established minimum comfortable touch target for one-handed thumb use on a phone; error rate stops improving above 9.6 mm for discrete taps. For use while walking, you need 14 mm.
findings.detail: Parhi P, Karlson AK, Bederson BB (2006). Target Size Study for One-Handed Thumb Use on Small Touchscreen Devices. MobileHCI '06. n=20 right-handed participants, 5 target sizes (3.8, 5.8, 7.7, 9.6, 11.5 mm) x 9 screen locations x 5 repetitions, one-handed. Full text read. Result: speed improved as targets grew, but there were NO significant error-rate differences between sizes ≥9.6 mm (discrete) and ≥7.7 mm (serial); recommendation 9.2 mm discrete, 9.6 mm serial. Independently, Conradi J et al. (2015, Procedia Manufacturing / AHFE) tested 5, 8, 11 and 14 mm squares standing vs walking: 8 mm is usable standing but still error-prone; only 14 mm gave low error rates both walking and standing. Note the '44px folklore' has no comparable published experiment behind it — Parhi does.
findings.implication: Minimum interactive height 48 CSS px (~12.7 mm) — above Parhi's 9.2 mm floor with margin. For the answer-option rows, which are the only thing that matters, use 56 CSS px height, full content width, 8px gap. For any mode intended for use on the move (a 'read the subway sign' street mode), raise every target to 56 CSS px minimum height *and* 56 px minimum width, hitting Conradi's 14 mm. Do not put destructive controls (skip, quit, end game) within 24 px of an answer option.

sources.citation: Parhi P, Karlson AK, Bederson BB (2006). Target Size Study for One-Handed Thumb Use on Small Touchscreen Devices. Proc. MobileHCI '06

findings.claim: The thumb's reachable area on a phone is a predictable quadratic function of surface size, hand size and index-finger position on the back — it is not a fixed 'thumb zone' graphic.
findings.detail: Bergstrom-Lehtovirta J & Oulasvirta A (2014). Modeling the functional area of the thumb on mobile touchscreen surfaces. CHI '14. Predictive model derived from gripping-hand kinematics; thumb maximum range described by quadratic curves fitted to each thumb trajectory; high model fit across 20 participants. Later work (Grip-Reach-Touch-Repeat, CHI 2024) refines it for arbitrary form factors. n=20, model-fitting rather than an outcome experiment.
findings.implication: Put the three answer options in the bottom 45% of the viewport, stacked, full-width, and put nothing the player must hit during timed play in the top 25% or in the top corners. Anchor the option stack to the bottom with `position: sticky; bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` so it stays reachable on a 6.7-inch device. The hanzi prompt goes above the options in the upper-middle third — it is looked at, not tapped, so reach does not constrain it.

findings.claim: Time pressure costs accuracy (d ≈ 0.35) over and above simply making people faster, and it hits difficult items and high-ability participants hardest.
findings.detail: Review and experiment with Raven's Matrices (Journal of Intelligence 2023, 11(6):120): time pressure produced a substantial decrease in accuracy (d = 0.35) even when controlling for response time at item level, indicating degraded processing not just speeding. Even mild time pressure induced speeding throughout the task, with participants speeding more than required. Time pressure disproportionately shortened RTs for difficult items and for participants with high ability, working memory capacity or need for cognition. Separately, in Kahoot research, time-based scoring offered no advantage over accuracy-based metrics in predicting learning outcomes, and speed scoring is reported to reduce reflection and encourage guessing. Visual timers reduced *anticipatory* anxiety without changing performance in an elementary maths assessment.
findings.implication: Do not award points for speed. Score correctness only, and break ties on total time across the round rather than per item. Give a generous per-item deadline — 10 s for a 1-2 character recognition item, 15 s for a 4+ character phrase — long enough that it almost never binds for a prepared player, and show it as a depleting bar (visual timer, anxiety-reducing) rather than counting digits. On timeout, score as incorrect but still run the full feedback reveal.

sources.citation: Should Intelligence Tests Be Speeded or Unspeeded? A Brief Review of the Effects of Time Pressure on Response Processes and an Experimental Study with Raven's Matrices (2023). Journal of Intelligence 11(6):120

findings.claim: Being watched impairs accuracy on complex tasks and speeds simple ones — and in games specifically, *supportive* spectators hurt performance more than critical ones.
findings.detail: Bond CF & Titus LJ (1983). Social facilitation: a meta-analysis of 241 studies. Psychological Bulletin — 241 studies, ~24,000 participants: presence of others increases speed on simple tasks and decreases speed on complex tasks; impairs complex-task accuracy and slightly facilitates simple-task accuracy. Effects are small: 0.3%-3% of variance, with >40% of results on some measures opposing the mean. The trigger is the ability to *monitor* performance, not mere presence. In a game context, Killing with Kindness (Proc. ACM HCI / CSCW 2025), mixed-methods lab experiment n=85 in a competitive racing game, found counter-intuitively that supportive spectatorship was MORE detrimental to performance than critical spectatorship, attributed to expectation threat, nervous activation and presentational concerns.
findings.implication: Design the co-located round so opponents cannot monitor the answering keystroke. Concrete: (a) options are revealed and answered on the answering player's own device with no mirrored public state until lock-in; (b) the shared/spectator view shows only 'Player 2 is answering' and a progress bar, never the live selection; (c) no 'X got it right in 2.1s' banner mid-round. Also: because the effect is *smallest* on simple tasks, put the easiest items (2-stroke, high-frequency: 出, 入, 男, 女) in the first round when observation salience is highest, and the hard multi-character items in later rounds when players have habituated.

findings.claim: Co-located mobile games get their social value from shared physical space plus per-device private information; shared-device 'pass the phone' formats physically draw players closer and keep everyone engaged, but the CHI evidence here is qualitative, not effect-sized.
findings.detail: Design-research literature: co-located multiplayer games are characterised by shared physical spaces promoting physical awareness plus individual devices supporting both public and private information; mobility affords asymmetric design with information and interaction (Designing for Social Play in Co-located Mobile Games). Emmerich & Masuch (CHI PLAY 2017), The Impact of Game Patterns on Player Experience and Social Interaction in Co-Located Multiplayer Games, examines competition vs collaboration patterns. Kappen et al. (CHI PLAY '14) on co-located audiences and social player experience. Studies of shared-phone games report participants physically moving closer and coordinating to pass the device. All qualitative/small-n; no controlled learning-outcome study located.
findings.implication: Support two co-located topologies from the same codebase: (a) one-device pass-and-play, where the phone is handed round and each turn opens with a 'Hand to <name> — tap when ready' interstitial that hides the item until tapped; (b) multi-device over local peer connection with a shared scoreboard. Architecturally that means the game state machine must be transport-agnostic: a pure reducer over {playerId, itemId, choice, elapsedMs} events, with the transport (same-device turn handoff, BroadcastChannel, WebRTC datachannel) swapped underneath. Do not build the rules into the networking layer.

findings.claim: Gamification's effect on cognitive learning outcomes is real but small-to-medium (g = 0.49), and the elements that moderate behavioural outcomes are game fiction and competition combined with collaboration — not points and leaderboards.
findings.detail: Sailer M & Homner L (2020). The Gamification of Learning: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review 32:77-112. Random-effects: cognitive g = 0.49 [0.30, 0.69], k=19, N=1686; motivational g = 0.36 [0.18, 0.54], k=16, N=2246; behavioural g = 0.25 [0.04, 0.46], k=9, N=951. The cognitive effect was stable in a high-methodological-rigour subsplit; motivational and behavioural effects were not. Significant moderators of behavioural outcomes: inclusion of game fiction, and combining competition with collaboration. Counterweight: Almeida et al. (2023, Information and Software Technology / arXiv 2305.08346) systematic mapping found badges, leaderboards, competitions and points are the elements most often reported as causing negative effects, with lower-performing learners specifically demotivated by leaderboards.
findings.implication: Invest in fiction and in competition-plus-collaboration, not in a points economy. Concretely: frame each round as a place ('the noodle shop', 'Line 2 to the airport', 'the supermarket aisle') with the real item set for that place, and add a co-op mode where the table plays *against the menu* rather than each other. Ship no global leaderboard. Ship a per-session result screen only, and rank by 'characters you can now read' rather than by points, so the bottom player still sees a positive number.

sources.citation: Sailer M, Homner L (2020). The Gamification of Learning: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review 32:77-112
Almeida C, Kalinowski M, Uchôa A, Feijó B (2023). Negative effects of gamification in education software: Systematic mapping and practitioner perceptions. Information and Software Technology

findings.claim: Push reminders reliably raise studying on the days they fire, but a controlled comparison found no net increase in study frequency versus a never-reminded control — they appear to substitute for, not add to, self-initiated study.
findings.detail: Nobbe L, Breitwieser J, Biedermann D, Brod G (2024). Smartphone-based study reminders can be a double-edged sword. npj Science of Learning. n=85 students aged 10-12, 36-day intervention with a vocabulary-learning app, reminders scheduled on 16 days, combining between- and within-person experimental manipulation with app logfile data. Students were more likely to study on reminder days than non-reminder days, but relative to a never-reminded control group the within-person effect was not a net increase — implying reminders may reduce motivation to study independently on other days. Converging: a MALL RCT (n=150, 9 weeks) found the push-notification group hit 82% daily adherence vs 67% self-scheduled and 49% control, but showed a sharp consistency collapse once reminders ceased, indicating extrinsic dependency. Sample is children in the npj study; generalisation to adult Dutch/English learners is an inference.
findings.implication: Cap notifications at one per day maximum, and make it a *self-scheduled* one the user picks during onboarding ('when do you want your daily 5 minutes?') rather than an algorithmically timed one. Build an explicit wean: after 21 consecutive days of on-time self-initiated opens, the app offers to turn reminders off and says why. Never send a second 'you're about to lose your streak' notification the same day — that is the dependency-building pattern. Track selfInitiatedOpens vs notificationOpens separately so you can see substitution happening.

findings.claim: Spacing beats massing for L2 learning with g = 0.40 on delayed tests, and longer inter-session gaps beat shorter ones specifically on delayed tests; expanding and equal schedules are statistically equivalent.
findings.detail: Kim SK & Webb S (2022). The Effects of Spaced Practice on Second Language Learning: A Meta-Analysis. Language Learning 72(1):269-319. 98 effect sizes from 48 experiments, N=3,411. Medium-to-large effect of spacing on L2 learning overall; short spacing was as effective as long spacing on immediate posttests but LESS effective on delayed posttests; the short-vs-long comparison gave g = 0.40 on delayed posttests (delayed = ≥1 day). Equal and expanding spacing were statistically equivalent. Moderators: learning target, number of sessions, practice type, activity type, feedback timing, retention interval. Broader distributed-practice base: Cepeda et al. 2006 (317 experiments, 184 articles) and a 2025 classroom meta-analysis (22 studies, >3,000 participants, d = 0.54).
findings.implication: Two direct consequences. (1) Since expanding ≈ equal, do not build a complicated FSRS-style expanding scheduler for v1 — a fixed-ladder schedule (1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 21 days, 60 days) is defensible and vastly simpler; store nextDueAt and intervalIndex per item. (2) Bias toward LONGER gaps than feel comfortable, because short gaps only match long gaps on immediate tests. Never show the same character twice within one session unless it was answered wrong; enforce a minimum 24-hour gap between correct repetitions of an item.

sources.citation: Kim SK, Webb S (2022). The Effects of Spaced Practice on Second Language Learning: A Meta-Analysis. Language Learning 72(1):269-319

findings.claim: Microlearning sessions under ~10 minutes produce meaningful L2 gains, but the meta-analytic estimate is unstable (SMD = 1.43 with I² = 66% from only 10 studies) and should not be trusted as a number.
findings.detail: Prasittichok et al. (2024). The Effects of Microlearning on EFL Students' English Speaking: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research. 10 peer-reviewed studies, 743 EFL participants, SMD = 1.43, p < .05, I² = 66% (moderate-to-high heterogeneity). An SMD of 1.43 from k=10 in an area with obvious publication-bias pressure is not credible at face value; the direction is supportable, the magnitude is not. Outcome is speaking, not reading. Duolingo's own efficacy study gives a more usable anchor: Jiang X, Rollinson J, Plonsky L, Gustafson E, Pajak B (2021, Foreign Language Annals), n=225 adult US learners using Duolingo as their only tool, median 112 hours (mean 141) of study to reach ACTFL Intermediate Low reading / Novice High listening, comparable to end-of-fourth-semester university students.
findings.implication: Design the default round to be completable in 3-5 minutes (roughly 12-20 three-option items at 10-15 s each) and make that the unit that gets scheduled, saved and resumed. Do not promise learning outcomes proportional to microlearning meta-analytic effect sizes. Do use the Duolingo anchor for honest goal-setting copy and for capacity planning: an item bank and schedule that assumes ~100-140 hours to functional reading, i.e. ~20 minutes/day for a year, or a much smaller targeted bank (300-600 characters covering menus, transit, signage, labels) for a 20-30 hour 'survive a trip' goal.

findings.claim: Task resumption after an interruption costs time that grows with interruption duration and demand — the cost is a decay-plus-interference effect on the suspended goal, and it is mitigated by cues that reinstate the goal.
findings.detail: Altmann EM & Trafton JG (2002) memory-for-goals model; Monk CA, Trafton JG, Boehm-Davis DA (2008), The Effect of Interruption Duration and Demand on Resuming Suspended Goals, JEP: Applied — three experiments with an interleaved-tasks paradigm showed longer and more demanding interruptions produce longer resumption lags; the resumption-time profile up to 1 min supports decay, and the duration x demand interaction supports goal rehearsal mitigating decay. Altmann & Trafton (CogSci 2004) on resumption lag and the role of cues. Individual differences: working-memory capacity strongly negatively predicts resumption lag and moderates the duration effect (JEP:LMC 2016).
findings.implication: A phone learning app is interrupted constantly. Persist the full item state (itemId, options in their shown order, elapsedMs, selection-in-progress) to IndexedDB on every visibilitychange and on every option focus, not just at item boundaries. On resume, do NOT drop the player straight back into a running timer — show a 2-second reinstatement card that redisplays the target hanzi and the round context ('Round 2, the noodle shop, 7 of 12'), then restart the item's timer from full. That card is the goal-reinstating cue the literature says reduces the lag.

findings.claim: One-item-per-screen (paging) costs completion time relative to scrolling but does not cost completion rate — so the coherence benefit is bought with time, not with drop-off.
findings.detail: Mavletova A & Couper MP (2014). Mobile Web Survey Design: Scrolling versus Paging, SMS versus E-mail Invitations. Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology 2(4):498-. Scrolling produced significantly faster completion times, non-significantly lower breakoff, fewer technical problems and higher subjective ratings; respondents were equally likely to complete under either design, and the number of skipped questions was similar. This is survey research, not learning research — the transfer is an argument, not a finding. It is paired here with the coherence/seductive-detail results (g = 0.63 and g = 1.00) which favour a minimal single-focus screen.
findings.implication: Use one item per screen — the coherence evidence is much stronger than the paging time cost, and in a timed game the per-item time is set by the deadline anyway. But budget for the cost: expect ~10-20% more wall-clock time per item than a scrolling list would take, and design the round length around that (12 items, not 20, for a 5-minute round). Do not show the next item's hanzi in a peek/preview — that reintroduces exactly the extraneous material coherence tells you to remove.

findings.claim: Glosses help L2 reading, with the largest benefit for beginners, and multimodal (text + image) glosses beat text-only.
findings.detail: Abraham LB (2008). Computer-mediated glosses in second language reading comprehension and vocabulary learning: A meta-analysis. Computer Assisted Language Learning 21(3) — 11 studies, medium effect on reading comprehension, large effect on incidental vocabulary. Yun J (2011) — 10 studies, g = 0.46 for digital reading with lexical glosses on L2 vocabulary. Multimedia glosses and second language vocabulary learning: A second-round meta-analysis (2024, System) — multiple-mode (text+visual) glossing has a large positive effect vs text-only. Reported moderation by proficiency: large effect for beginners, medium for advanced, small/inconsistent for intermediate. These meta-analyses are small-k and the proficiency moderation is not robustly established.
findings.implication: On the post-answer reveal card, pair the hanzi with a small photograph or line icon of the referent, not just the Dutch/English word — that is the text+visual gloss configuration that outperformed text-only. Budget one ~120x120px WebP per concrete noun item (a bowl of noodles for 面, a subway car for 地铁), inlined or cached. Skip images for abstract/functional items (出口, 禁止) where a photo would be a seductive detail rather than a gloss.

findings.claim: The large majority of Chinese characters are semantic-phonetic compounds (xíngshēngzì), so component structure — not whole-character shape — is the dominant statistical regularity in the script.
findings.detail: Corpus counts converge on ~80-85%. Shu et al. (2003), analysing the characters in Beijing primary textbooks, report ~80% phonetic-semantic compounds and only ~8% pictographs; other corpus analyses cited in the recognition literature give 84%. Estimates vary with the character set sampled (textbook set vs. full standard list) but never fall below ~72%. NOTE: read from abstracts/secondary summaries only; the exact denominators differ between sources.
findings.implication: The item bank must store every character as a decomposition (component list + structure type), not as a bitmap or a single glyph string. Ship a component table of ~200 semantic radicals + ~300 high-yield phonetics as first-class learnable objects, and let the game generate 'which component is shared?' rounds. Do NOT build a pictograph-story pipeline as the primary path — it covers under 10% of the script.

findings.claim: The phonetic component is an unreliable pronunciation cue: only roughly a quarter to a third of compounds are fully regular once tone is counted, and about half are at best segmentally identical.
findings.detail: Reported corpus figures, all from secondary/abstract sources: phonetics give a valid cue in at most ~50% of semantic-phonetic characters; ~26% cueing validity for phonetic radicals; 'less than 20% when tone information is considered'; ~38% of characters have a phonetic radical that indicates pronunciation; average cueing validity of both radical types ~30-40%. Regular + semi-regular (shared onset or rime) together ≈ half of phonetic compounds. The spread (20%-50%) is real and reflects different databases, different treatment of tone, and different definitions of 'regular'. I could not open the primary databases (Hsiao & Shillcock 2006; Zhou 1978) to pin one number.
findings.implication: Never present the phonetic component as a pronunciation rule. Model it as a probabilistic hint with a stored per-character reliability field (regular / segmental-only / irregular) and surface it only as a *narrowing* aid: 'this one probably sounds like the 青 family — check the tone'. Budget for ~1 in 3 phonetic hints being wrong and design the feedback copy so a wrong hint is not experienced as the app lying.

sources.citation: Hsiao, J. H., & Shillcock, R. (2006). Analysis of a Chinese phonetic compound database. Journal of Psycholinguistic Research, 35, 405-426
Williams, C., & Bever, T. (2010). Chinese character decoding: a semantic bias? Reading and Writing

findings.claim: Compound characters are overwhelmingly left-right structured, and within those, the semantic component is on the left about nine times out of ten.
findings.detail: Hsiao & Shillcock (2006): ~72% of phonograms are left-right structured; of left-right phonetic compounds, ~90% are semantic-left/phonetic-right (SP) versus ~10% PS. Their analysis covered the 3,027 most common left-right compounds. Read from abstract/secondary summary only.
findings.implication: A single reusable card layout handles ~72% of the bank: a two-box split with the left box tinted as 'meaning slot' and the right as 'sound slot'. Store a structure enum (left-right, top-bottom, enclosure, single) per character and drive the decomposition animation off it. Teach 'left side = what it is about' as an explicit, early rule — it is right ~90% of the time within left-right characters.

findings.claim: Orthographic awareness correlates with L2 Chinese word reading at about the same strength as phonological and morphological awareness — all moderate, none dominant.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of CSL/CFL learners: 42 effect sizes, N = 1,103. Phonological awareness r = 0.41, orthographic awareness r = 0.38, morphological awareness r = 0.36, RAN r = -0.32. This is correlational, so it establishes that component knowledge matters, not that teaching it causes gains. Author list not verified (Frontiers and PMC both blocked).
findings.implication: Do not build the whole game on radicals alone. The item bank needs three parallel retrieval routes per character — form (which glyph), sound (which pinyin+tone), meaning (which gloss) — and the session scheduler should rotate across all three rather than drilling form only. Store per-route mastery, not one scalar 'known' flag.

findings.claim: Explicit radical/orthographic instruction produces measurable gains — but adding radical highlighting and stroke animation *to a recognition task* actively hurts recognition.
findings.detail: FOR: Chen, Hsu, Chang, Lin, Chang & Sung (2013, Language Learning & Technology) ran a nonequivalent pretest-posttest quasi-experiment, N=129 (69 experimental / 60 comparison), 3 weeks, ≥7 phonetic/semantic radicals + derivatives per week; the experimental group beat the comparison group on phonetic-radical awareness, semantic-radical awareness, and orthographic knowledge. AGAINST: Hou & Jiang (2022, Frontiers in Psychology), N=40 alphabetic-L1 learners, 2x2 within design (radical colour markings x stroke-order animation): radical markings *increased* RT and *decreased* accuracy on character recognition; stroke animations also decreased recognition accuracy; neither affected character-meaning matching. Interpretation: teaching the component system as content works; decorating the character with component cues at recognition time adds extraneous load. Both read from abstracts only; Hou & Jiang is small (n=40) and quasi-experimental designs cannot rule out selection.
findings.implication: Split the two. Have a dedicated 'component lesson' mode where radicals are taught explicitly with colour and animation, and a 'read it' game mode where characters are rendered plain, single-colour, no highlighting, no stroke animation. Never colour-code radicals inside a timed recognition round.

sources.citation: Chen, H.-C., Hsu, C.-C., Chang, L.-Y., Lin, Y.-C., Chang, K.-E., & Sung, Y.-T. (2013). Using a radical-derived character e-learning platform to increase learner knowledge of Chinese characters. Language Learning & Technology, 17(1)
Hou, F., & Jiang, X. (2022). Interference effects of radical markings and stroke order animations on Chinese character learning among L2 learners. Frontiers in Psychology, 13:783613

findings.claim: Colour coding and extra visual salience on characters slow learners down; paired presentation of confusable characters helps.
findings.detail: Li, Shi & Wang (2025, Languages), N=183 non-tonal-L1 absolute beginners, 2x2x2 (colour coding x single/paired presentation x identical/different strokes): characters differing by an added stroke (日/白) were easier than identical-stroke pairs (人/入); simultaneous paired presentation improved discrimination of subtle stroke differences; colour coding slowed reaction times, interpreted as visual overload. Converges with Hou & Jiang (2022). Abstract-only.
findings.implication: Present confusable characters as a side-by-side pair when introducing them (人/入, 日/白, 千/干, 未/末), not one at a time. Keep hanzi rendered in a single ink colour on a plain ground; reserve colour for scoring/turn state, not for glyph parts. Precompute a visual-confusability neighbour list per character and use it to pick distractors.

sources.citation: Li, J., Shi, M., & Wang, X. (2025). Learning Chinese Characters of Visual Similarity: The Effects of Presentation Style and Color Coding. Languages, 10(10):260

Chang, L.-Y., Tang, Y.-Y., Lee, C.-Y., & Chen, H.-C. (2022). The Effect of Visual Mnemonics and the Presentation of Character Pairs on Learning Visually Similar Characters for CSL Learners. Frontiers in Psychology, 13:783898

findings.claim: Visual similarity, not phonology, drives most character errors — around three quarters of miswritten characters are attributable to it, and stroke-level omission/addition dominates.
findings.detail: Reported figures from the CSL error-analysis literature: visual similarity accounted for 75% of errors in a set of 4,100 incorrectly written characters (computational-linguistics study); in 4,305 written responses from 144 CSL learners, stroke-level errors accounted for the most variance in accuracy, with over 50% of stroke errors being omissions and additions. Figures taken from secondary summaries; primary sources not opened.
findings.implication: Distractor generation must be visual-first. For each target, generate the 3 distractors from a stored orthographic-neighbour list (edit distance over component/stroke graph), not from same-pinyin or same-meaning sets. A distractor set of semantically related but visually distinct characters will make the game feel easy and teach nothing.

sources.citation: Chang, L.-Y., Tang, Y.-Y., Lee, C.-Y., & Chen, H.-C. (2022). The Effect of Visual Mnemonics and the Presentation of Character Pairs on Learning Visually Similar Characters for CSL Learners. Frontiers in Psychology, 13:783898

findings.claim: Character frequency is brutally skewed: ~2,500 characters cover ~98% of running text and 3,500 cover ~99.5%.
findings.detail: The Chinese state validation of the 现代汉语常用字表 (1988) reports 2,500 常用字 = 97.97% coverage, the additional 1,000 次常用字 = 1.51%, total 3,500 = 99.48%. Independent corpus summaries give top ~100 ≈ 42%, top ~1,000 ≈ 90%, top ~2,500 ≈ 98-99%. Jun Da's Modern Chinese Character Frequency List (built from ~110MB of online text, ~9,933 characters ranked) is the standard machine-readable source; SUBTLEX-CH gives a subtitle-based alternative and BCC a 15-billion-character one. I could not fetch Jun Da's cumulative table directly (host blocked), so the intermediate ranks are from secondary summaries.
findings.implication: For a travel-reading product the curve says the whole product lives in the first ~600-1,000 characters. Ship the bank in strict frequency bands of 50, with band 1-12 (600 chars) as the core game and everything beyond band 20 (1,000) as optional. Show the player a coverage meter driven by real corpus cumulative-frequency values stored per character, not a raw 'characters learned' count — 'you can now read 78% of the characters on an average sign' is the motivating number.

sources.citation: 国家语言文字工作委员会 / 国家教育委员会 (1988). 现代汉语常用字表 (Modern Chinese Common Character List), 2,500 + 1,000 characters, with reported coverage 97.97% / 99.48%
Da, J. Modern Chinese Character Frequency List (汉字单字频率列表), Chinese Text Computing, Middle Tennessee State University

findings.claim: The official mainland character inventories give ready-made, defensible cut points: 8,105 total (3,500 / 3,000 / 1,605 tiers) in the 2013 General Standard table, and 3,000 characters across HSK 3.0's nine bands.
findings.detail: 通用规范汉字表 (Table of General Standard Chinese Characters), promulgated by the Ministry of Education and State Language Commission, 5 June 2013: 8,105 characters in three tiers of 3,500 / 3,000 / 1,605. HSK 3.0 (汉语水平等级标准, effective 1 July 2021): 3 levels / 9 bands, 3,000 characters and 11,092 words in total, with roughly 300 new characters per band. The per-band breakdown came from secondary sources (Skritter, ChineseFor.Us, HanziExpress) and should be checked against the official standard before shipping it as a label.
findings.implication: Tag every item with (a) Tier 1/2/3 of the 2013 standard and (b) HSK 3.0 band. Tier 1 is the outer boundary of what the product should ever contain. Use HSK band only as a secondary display label — do not let it drive ordering, because HSK band order is not frequency order and a travel-reading player needs 出口 and 元 before HSK's sequencing would give them.

sources.citation: 中华人民共和国教育部 / 国家语言文字工作委员会 (2013). 通用规范汉字表 (8,105 characters; tiers of 3,500 / 3,000 / 1,605)

findings.claim: Subtitle-based frequency (SUBTLEX-CH) predicts Chinese lexical processing better than written-text frequency.
findings.detail: Cai & Brysbaert (2010, PLoS ONE 5(6):e10729): corpus of film/TV subtitles, 46.8 million characters / 33.5 million words. The subtitle-derived word and character frequencies explained significantly more variance in Chinese word naming and lexical decision than measures based on written texts. It also added contextual diversity measures. Abstract-only.
findings.implication: Rank items by a blend, not one list: SUBTLEX-CH contextual diversity for anything the player will hear or say, and a written/web corpus (Jun Da, or BCC's 15-billion-character set) for signage and label reading. Store both frequency values per character so the ordering weight can be tuned later without re-authoring content.

sources.citation: Cai, Q., & Brysbaert, M. (2010). SUBTLEX-CH: Chinese word and character frequencies based on film subtitles. PLoS ONE, 5(6):e10729
Xun, E., Rao, G., Xiao, X., & Zang, J. (2016). The construction of the BCC corpus in the age of big data. Corpus Linguistics, 3(1), 93-109 (15 billion characters)

findings.claim: Character coverage is not comprehension coverage: the reading threshold literature puts adequate comprehension at 95-98% of *word* tokens known, and L2 Chinese textbooks fall far short.
findings.detail: Hu & Nation's 98% (good comprehension) / 95% (minimally acceptable) thresholds are the reference points and have been directly replicated (Kremmel et al., 2023, Language Learning). Shen et al. (2025, Language, Culture and Curriculum 39(1)) measured cumulative *word-token* coverage of a full CSL textbook series against a balanced corpus: 81% by the final volume, well short of 95%. Note there is no established character-level threshold for L2 Chinese — the thresholds are word-based, and one Chinese-EFL study testing seven coverage levels (90-100%) found no clean threshold at all. Abstract-only throughout.
findings.implication: Do not promise comprehension. Frame the product's win condition as *targeted item recognition* — 'you can find the exit, read this menu line, spot 女 on a toilet door' — and build the scoring around identifying known items inside authentic photographed text where most of the text is unknown. A 'read this whole sentence' mode at beginner level will produce failure, because 600 characters ≈ well under 95% word coverage of any real sign.

sources.citation: Shen, M. et al. (2025). Cumulative coverage of Chinese L2 textbooks: how well do they prepare students for reading real-world texts? Language, Culture and Curriculum, 39(1)
Kremmel, B. et al. (2023). Unknown Vocabulary Density and Reading Comprehension: Replicating Hu and Nation (2000). Language Learning

findings.claim: Chinese has no word spaces, and word segmentation is a genuine, measurable L2 bottleneck — L2 readers fall back to character-by-character reading.
findings.detail: Eye-tracking studies of L2 Chinese readers converge: L2 readers read more slowly than L1 readers and adopt a cautious character-by-character strategy; word-spaced text produces the least disruption, unspaced text more, character-spaced text more still, and *nonword*-spaced text the most disruption — i.e. the benefit is genuinely from correct word boundaries, not from white space per se. A 2025 eye-tracking study found colour cues can also guide segmentation. Multiple independent labs (Frontiers in Psychology 2023, 14:783960; Bilingualism: Language and Cognition; Behavioral Sciences 2025), abstract-only.
findings.implication: Add a segmentation aid as a first-class, toggleable rendering mode: alternating subtle background tints per word (not spaces, which change layout, and not per-character colour). Store every text item pre-segmented into words at authoring time — segmentation must be a stored field, not computed on device. Ship a 'boundary' game mode: show an unspaced string and have players tap where words split; wrong boundaries are the actual failure mode worth training.

sources.citation: Eye movements of second language learners when reading spaced and unspaced Chinese texts (2023). Frontiers in Psychology, 14:783960
Unpacking word segmentation processes by L2 Chinese readers: Evidence from eye movements. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition
The Impact of Color Cues on Word Segmentation by L2 Chinese Readers: Evidence from Eye Movements (2025). Behavioral Sciences, 15(7):904

findings.claim: Knowing the characters does not give you the word: multi-character word meaning depends on semantic transparency and morphological awareness, which are separate, trainable competencies.
findings.detail: L2 Chinese lexical-inference studies (Reading and Writing 2019/2020; Frontiers in Psychology 2022) find that success at inferring a compound's meaning from its characters depends on an interaction between learner linguistic knowledge and the word's semantic transparency, and that morphological awareness contributes over and above character knowledge. Heritage learners benefit more from morphological awareness because oral vocabulary seeds morpheme recognition. Abstract-only; these are correlational/path-analytic, not interventions.
findings.implication: Ship words, not just characters, as the primary item type, and tag each multi-character word with a transparency rating (transparent 电脑, semi 出口, opaque 东西). Sequence transparent compounds early — they double as free component practice — and teach opaque high-frequency travel words (东西, 小心, 洗手间) as unanalysed wholes with no component story attached.

sources.citation: Word-meaning inference in L2 Chinese: an interactive effect of learners' linguistic knowledge and words' semantic transparency. Reading and Writing
Word Knowledge in L2 Chinese Lexical Inference: A Moderated Path Analysis of Language Proficiency Level and Heritage Status (2022). Frontiers in Psychology, 13:869368

findings.claim: HANDWRITING, SIDE A: hand-copying characters improves orthographic (form) and meaning knowledge relative to pinyin typing, which instead strengthens phonology.
findings.detail: Guan, Liu, Chan, Ye & Perfetti (2011, Journal of Educational Psychology 103(3), 509-522): N=48 adult learners at Pittsburgh, five consecutive days, character-writing-to-read vs. alphabet-typing-to-read. Handwriting group better on form recognition and character-meaning; pinyin-typing group better on character-phonology. Xu, Chang, Zhang & Perfetti (2013, Foreign Language Annals) replicated the writing advantage for form recognition and character-meaning links, with animation also helping form recognition. Chai & Ma (2022, Frontiers in Psychology 12:779190) found, in HSK data from 74,362 CSL learners across 67 L1s, a significant effect of Chinese character writing proficiency on reading proficiency, with a language-distance interaction — but this is correlational and heavily confounded with total study effort. All abstract-only.
findings.implication: Offer a finger-tracing mode as an *optional* deep-dive on a small set (the ~50 highest-value characters and the ~30 most-used semantic radicals), not as a gate on progression. Architecturally this means the stroke-path data (SVG medians) only needs to ship for a few hundred characters, not the whole bank — a large asset saving for a PWA.

sources.citation: Guan, C. Q., Liu, Y., Chan, D. H. L., Ye, F., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Writing strengthens orthography and alphabetic-coding strengthens phonology in learning to read Chinese. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 509-522
Xu, Y., Chang, L.-Y., Zhang, J., & Perfetti, C. A. (2013). Reading, Writing, and Animation in Character Learning in Chinese as a Foreign Language. Foreign Language Annals

Chai, X., & Ma, M. (2022). Exploring Relationships Between L2 Chinese Character Writing and Reading Acquisition From Embodied Cognitive Perspectives: Evidence From HSK Big Data. Frontiers in Psychology, 12:779190 (N = 74,362)

findings.claim: HANDWRITING, SIDE B: under equal total practice time, handwriting practice makes recognition *worse*, because the time comes out of recognition practice.
findings.detail: Lu, Ostrow & Heffernan (2019, AERA Open 5(4)) — a registered-report replication of their own pilot, run inside the ASSISTments platform, manipulating handwriting vs. no-handwriting practice with posttests immediate / 1-day / 1-week. Learners who spent 30% of practice time on hand-copying scored significantly *lower* on online word-recognition posttests at all three time points, and the on-paper posttests showed no compensating gain for the copying group. The authors note instructors report devoting at least a third of course time to handwriting. Abstract-only; I could not read the exact n or effect sizes.
findings.implication: This is the decisive finding for a travel-reading product: handwriting must never be on the critical path. Make the default loop 100% recognition (see glyph → choose meaning/sound → confirm), and if tracing ships, it must be additive time, explicitly framed as 'extra', never substituted for recognition reps. Do not make stroke-order accuracy a scoring dimension.

sources.citation: Lu, X., Ostrow, K. S., & Heffernan, N. T. (2019). Save Your Strokes: Chinese Handwriting Practice Makes for Ineffective Use of Instructional Time in Second Language Classrooms. AERA Open, 5(4)
Lu, X., Ostrow, K. S., & Heffernan, N. T. (2020). Reflections on the Registered Report Process for 'Save Your Strokes'

findings.claim: The handwriting disagreement is real and is best read as a process-vs-opportunity-cost conflict, not as one side being wrong.
findings.detail: The two literatures are not testing the same question. Guan et al. (2011) and Xu et al. (2013) hold *exposure to the character* roughly constant and vary the encoding process, finding writing improves form memory. Lu et al. (2019) hold *total instructional time* constant and vary the activity, finding writing loses to more recognition practice. Chai & Ma (2022) is observational at huge n and cannot separate writing skill from overall investment. A synthetic review of typing vs. handwriting in Chinese learning (International Journal of Educational Research, 2021) exists but I could not read it. No registered replication reconciles the two designs. All abstract-only.
findings.implication: Instrument for it rather than betting on it. Ship tracing as an A/B-able module behind a flag, log per-character (mode, seconds spent, subsequent recognition accuracy at 1 day / 7 days), and let your own telemetry settle it for your population. That requires storing per-attempt event records with a mode field from day one — retrofitting this later is expensive.

sources.citation: Comparison studies of typing and handwriting in Chinese language learning: A synthetic review (2021). International Journal of Educational Research
Lu, X., Ostrow, K. S., & Heffernan, N. T. (2019). AERA Open, 5(4)

findings.claim: Character amnesia is real and measurable in native writers, and it is a production deficit, not a recognition deficit.
findings.detail: A mega-study analysis (Journal of Neurolinguistics, 2021) reports character amnesia occurring for about 42% of characters and about 6% of the time in university students, with the strongest predictors being character frequency, familiarity of the containing word, and age of acquisition, plus stroke count, orthographic regularity and imageability. A 30-item standardised test has since been constructed (Reading and Writing, 2023). Sociolinguistic work finds IME preference among the strongest predictors. A dissenting paper ('Reassessing the Evidence of Chinese Character Amnesia', 2018) argues media surveys overstate the effect. All abstract-only.
findings.implication: Two consequences. (1) It confirms recognition and production dissociate, which licenses a recognition-only product without apology — put that in the onboarding copy. (2) If any writing feature ships, score it on *recognisability of the result*, not stroke fidelity, since even natives fail production while retaining recognition.

sources.citation: Character amnesia in Chinese handwriting: a mega-study analysis (2021). Journal of Neurolinguistics
Constructing a 30-item test for character amnesia in Chinese (2023). Reading and Writing

findings.claim: There is no good evidence that early pinyin harms character acquisition; the 'pinyin crutch' claim is folklore. What *is* supported is that pinyin's on-screen placement matters a lot.
findings.detail: Curriculum-level comparisons are weak and mixed: a four-arm study of ~98 learners aged 14-16 (rote memorisation vs. delayed character introduction vs. character colour-coding vs. control) found rote memorisation best for short-term character memorising; other work splitting delayed-character-introduction into LS-RW vs. LSR-W found the LSR-W variant (delay writing only, not reading) more effective. Practitioner sources assert pinyin slows reading and creates dependence, but the empirical claim I could locate on the other side is that pinyin ability and pinyin study time were not correlated with character recognition in beginners aged 12-14. Meanwhile at least one study finds highly experienced learners activate character orthography when reading pinyin (Bilingualism: Language and Cognition), which argues against pinyin being a competing representation. No adequately powered RCT of pinyin-first vs. character-first exists that I could find. Abstract-only.
findings.implication: Don't withhold pinyin on ideological grounds, but make it *revealable rather than ambient*: character shown alone by default, pinyin behind a tap or auto-revealed only after a response. This satisfies both camps and is cheap. Log reveal-rate per player as a difficulty signal.

sources.citation: Which is more effective in introducing Chinese characters? An investigative study of four methods used to teach CFL beginners (authors not verified)

findings.claim: Pinyin layout is a split-attention problem with a measured answer: put pinyin adjacent to (directly under) each character, and show the character before the prompts.
findings.detail: Lee & Kalyuga (2011, Language Learning 61(4), 1099-1118): vertical format (pinyin directly under each character) significantly beat the conventional horizontal format (pinyin after the string), attributed to eliminating split attention; the horizontal layout imposes high extraneous cognitive load at beginner level. A later SSLA study (2023, N=69 English natives, 30 Chinese words) compared horizontal / vertical / adjacent and found the adjacent format produced the highest gain scores — and was the *least preferred* format, with preference ratings unrelated to gains. Chung (2007, Educational Psychology 27(1), 1-20) found acquisition faster when the character was presented *before* rather than after the pinyin/English prompts, and that colour-coded prompts improved learning and two-week retention. All abstract-only.
findings.implication: Concrete card spec: hanzi first, alone, for a beat; pinyin rendered directly beneath each individual character (per-character alignment, not one pinyin string under the whole word); English/Dutch gloss adjacent, not on a separate line far below. Colour-code the *gloss text*, not the glyph. And ignore player preference surveys about layout — the evidence says preference does not track learning.

findings.claim: T2/T3 is the hardest Mandarin tone contrast for non-tonal-L1 adults, including Dutch speakers specifically, and the cue they fail to use is the timing of the F0 turning point.
findings.detail: T2 and T3 start at similar F0 height; the discriminating cue for natives is the location of the turning point — near onset for T2, around the middle for T3 — plus the depth of the dip. L2 listeners instead lean on duration, an unreliable cue. Zou, Caspers & Chen (2022, Frontiers in Psychology 13:891756) tested beginning and advanced *Dutch* learners with a sub-lexical sequence-recall task and an auditory lexical-decision task: T2-T3 was the most error-prone contrast for both groups; advanced learners improved on it sub-lexically but *not* in lexical decision; advanced learners showed strongest sensitivity to T1 and weakest to T4. A 2026 Speech Prosody paper revisits the confusion. Multiple labs, abstract-only.
findings.implication: If tone appears in the game at all, treat T2-vs-T3 as its own dedicated minimal-pair mode and stop treating the four tones as symmetric. Do not visualise tones as four equal icons — draw T2 and T3 as contours with the turning point marked, since that is the cue learners are missing. Tag every audio item with its tone pair so the scheduler can over-sample T2/T3 confusions by roughly 3x relative to their base rate.

sources.citation: Zou, T., Caspers, J., & Chen, Y. (2022). Perception of Different Tone Contrasts at Sub-Lexical and Lexical Levels by Dutch Learners of Mandarin Chinese. Frontiers in Psychology, 13:891756

Jongman, A. et al. Perception and Production of Mandarin Chinese Tones (book chapter)

findings.claim: High-variability phonetic training works, with meta-analytic effect sizes around g = 0.67-0.92 for perception — one of the strongest evidence bases in applied L2 research.
findings.detail: Uchihara, Karas & Thomson (2025, Studies in Second Language Acquisition): meta-analysis of 79 studies; g = 0.92 for pretest-posttest (k = 96) and g = 0.67 for treatment-vs-control (k = 32); moderators include length of L2 learning, response labels, training and testing task type, total training time, target phones, and number of talkers. Mahdi & Mohsen (2024, Language Teaching Research Quarterly 40, 29-45): 18 studies, 22 effect sizes, overall g = 0.77 on pronunciation, with a *large* effect specifically for lexical tones; five-to-eight talkers gave g = 0.77 versus g = 0.55 for two-to-four talkers. Abstract-only, but two independent meta-analyses agree.
findings.implication: If the app ships audio, ship at least 5 distinct speakers per audio item, not one studio voice. That is a storage decision: ~5x audio assets, so use short single-word/short-phrase clips, Opus-encoded, cached in the PWA's Cache Storage with per-item eviction. Randomise speaker per presentation and never let a player hear the same clip twice in a session.

sources.citation: Uchihara, T., Karas, M., & Thomson, R. I. (2025). High variability phonetic training (HVPT): A meta-analysis of L2 perceptual training studies. Studies in Second Language Acquisition
Mahdi, H. S., & Mohsen, M. A. (2024). Enhancing Pronunciation Learning through High Variability Phonetic Training: A Meta-analysis. Language Teaching Research Quarterly, 40, 29-45

findings.claim: The canonical Mandarin tone HVPT protocol is short and specific: ~8 sessions over 2 weeks with trial-by-trial feedback yields ~21% perception gain that generalises to new talkers and survives 6 months.
findings.detail: Wang, Spence, Jongman & Sereno (1999, JASA 106(6):3649): 8 American learners of Mandarin, 8 training sessions over 2 weeks, natural words from multiple native talkers, identification with feedback. Identification improved 21%; gains generalised to new stimuli and new talkers (18% on novel stimuli) and were retained at 6-month follow-up. n = 8 is small, but the protocol has been reproduced across dozens of HVPT studies (see the 79-study meta-analysis above), which is what earns the 'strong' grade — not this study alone. Abstract-only.
findings.implication: Design the tone module as a bounded 8-session course of ~20-30 minutes, not an infinite daily drip: that is the dose with evidence behind it. Trial-by-trial immediate feedback is mandatory (correct/incorrect plus replay of the target), which means the answer key and audio must be local — the module has to work fully offline in the PWA, since a co-located game in a Chinese restaurant may have no usable network.

sources.citation: Wang, Y., Spence, M. M., Jongman, A., & Sereno, J. A. (1999). Training American listeners to perceive Mandarin tones. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 106(6), 3649-3658

findings.claim: Perceptual training transfers to production, but at roughly half the effect size — you get production gains for free, not equally.
findings.detail: Wang, Jongman & Sereno (2003, JASA 113(2), 1033-1043) recorded trainees producing Mandarin words before and after perceptual training and had native listeners judge them; production accuracy increased significantly. Sakai & Moorman (2018, Applied Psycholinguistics — venue inferred from secondary sources) meta-analysed 25 years / 18 perceptual-training studies (k = 24): perception d = 0.92, production d = 0.54; effects larger for obstruents than vowels or sonorants. A separate meta-analysis specifically on the HVPT perception-production connection (Applied Psycholinguistics, 2024) reports that talker count from 3 to 30 did not significantly predict production transfer, with 3 talkers apparently sufficient for significant production gains. Abstract-only.
findings.implication: Do not build speech recognition / pronunciation scoring for v1. Perception training buys most of the production benefit at a fraction of the engineering cost, and on-device Mandarin tone ASR is unreliable. Spend the budget on multi-talker audio and feedback latency instead.

sources.citation: Wang, Y., Jongman, A., & Sereno, J. A. (2003). Acoustic and perceptual evaluation of Mandarin tone productions before and after perceptual training. JASA, 113(2), 1033-1043

Sakai, M., & Moorman, C. (2018). Can perception training improve the production of second language phonemes? A meta-analytic review of 25 years of perception training research. Applied Psycholinguistics (venue not verified)
Does perceptual high variability phonetic training improve L2 speech production? A meta-analysis of perception-production connection (2024). Applied Psycholinguistics

findings.claim: Drilling tones on isolated syllables transfers poorly: learners who identify isolated tones near-perfectly can perform *below chance* on the same syllables inside disyllabic words.
findings.detail: Around 70% of Mandarin words are disyllabic. Studies of advanced L2 learners report that despite strong isolated-tone identification, most learners performed below chance at rejecting tonal nonword competitors of real disyllabic Mandarin words — i.e. tone is not being encoded in the lexical representation even when it is perceptible. Related work finds advanced learners show persistent deficits for lexical tone in picture-to-word matching, and that advanced Dutch learners reached near-native sandhi discrimination on simple tasks but degraded on complex ones. On sandhi itself: T3 sandhi is highly productive and L2 learners apply it above 77% even on pseudowords, and the phonetically motivated half-third sandhi is acquired more easily than full T3 sandhi. Abstract-only; different labs, different tasks, so the effect is directionally solid but the magnitude is not.
findings.implication: Make the disyllabic word, not the syllable, the atomic tone item. Every tone item in the bank is a real two-syllable word with its citation tone pair AND its surface (post-sandhi) tone pair stored as separate fields, because 你好 is stored T3+T3 and heard T2+T3. A tone game that drills mā/má/mǎ/mà will produce players who fail on 老板 and 好吃.

sources.citation: Advanced second language learners' perception of lexical tone contrasts. Studies in Second Language Acquisition
Advanced Second Language Learners of Mandarin Show Persistent Deficits for Lexical Tone Encoding in Picture-to-Word Form Matching (2021). Frontiers in Communication, 6:689423
Mechanisms of tone sandhi rule application by tonal and non-tonal non-native speakers. Speech Communication

findings.claim: Experimenter-supplied imagery mnemonics beat rote on immediate tests but produce MORE forgetting than rote at delay — the classic finding is the opposite of the marketing claim.
findings.detail: Wang & Thomas (1992, Language Learning 42(3)): two 2x2 studies (mnemonic vs. rote x immediate vs. delayed) on English translations of Chinese characters. Study 1 equated exposure time, tested at immediate and 2 days; Study 2 gave the rote group extra time to equate immediate performance and extended the delay to 1 week. In neither study did imagery mnemonics show any advantage beyond the immediate test, and greater forgetting was observed under mnemonic learning. The authors attribute this to experimenter-imposed vs. subject-generated encoding — which matters, because it predicts *learner-generated* mnemonics may behave differently. A 2023 mixed-method study reports gains from visual mnemonics, but it is not a controlled delayed-retention comparison. Abstract-only.
findings.implication: Do not ship a fixed mnemonic story per character as the core mechanic. If mnemonics appear, make them player-generated and shareable between co-located players (a 'pitch your story, table votes' round) — that keeps the generation effect and turns a weakness into a multiplayer feature. Store user-authored mnemonics locally per player; never treat a shipped story as the canonical meaning.

sources.citation: Wang, A. Y., & Thomas, M. H. (1992). The Effect of Imagery-Based Mnemonics on the Long-Term Retention of Chinese Characters. Language Learning, 42(3)
Applying Visual Mnemonics Enhances Chinese Characters Learning for Chinese as Second Language Learners: A Mixed-Method Study (2023). ICDTE '23, ACM

findings.claim: The keyword method has genuine meta-analytic support for foreign-vocabulary recall, but almost all of it is against rote-repetition controls, and none of it is about Chinese characters.
findings.detail: Pressley, Levin & Delaney (1982, Review of Educational Research 52(1), 61-91) is the foundational review and reports the keyword mnemonic superior to rote repetition for foreign vocabulary. Subsequent commentary notes the comparison is almost always against rote repetition rather than against other elaborative strategies, which inflates the apparent advantage. Critically, the keyword method links an L2 *sound* to an L1 word — it addresses pinyin-to-meaning, not glyph-to-meaning, so it does not transfer to character recognition. Abstract-only.
findings.implication: Use keyword mnemonics only in the audio/pinyin track (e.g. linking chū in 出口 to an English keyword), and keep them out of the visual character track where the Wang & Thomas result applies. Two different mnemonic affordances, two different item types in the schema.

sources.citation: Pressley, M., Levin, J. R., & Delaney, H. D. (1982). The Mnemonic Keyword Method. Review of Educational Research, 52(1), 61-91

findings.claim: Heisig-style and Mandarin Blueprint-style character systems have no controlled efficacy evidence for Chinese; Chineasy additionally rests on etymology that specialists say is false and covers a fraction of the script.
findings.detail: I could find no peer-reviewed trial of Remembering the Simplified Hanzi, Remembering the Traditional Hanzi, or Mandarin Blueprint. All located evaluations are practitioner reviews and blog posts; even sympathetic sources note SLA has largely neglected logographic method research. For Chineasy specifically, the criticism is documented but is expert commentary rather than a controlled study: Victor Mair's Language Log critique quotes a US university Chinese program director saying 'what she is teaching is not reading… at best it will enable one to recognize a few Chinese pictographic characters in isolation', and notes the subtitle is misleading. The structural objection is decisive and quantitative: pictographs are ~8-10% of characters (Shu et al. 2003), so a pictograph-based system cannot scale past a few hundred items. Common Heisig criticisms (no pronunciation taught, writing-focused, questionable keyword choices, ordering) are practitioner consensus, not measured.
findings.implication: Do not license, imitate, or cite these systems as validated. Where the product needs decomposition stories, generate them from *actual* component semantics (semantic radical + phonetic series) with a per-story provenance flag ('etymological' vs 'memory aid only'), and label memory aids as such in the UI. This is also a legal/brand safety point: repeating Chineasy-style false etymologies is a known reputational liability among Chinese-teaching professionals.

sources.citation: Mair, V. (2014). Chineasy? Not. Language Log, University of Pennsylvania

Zhang, S. (2024). Effective character teaching methods for L1 English Chinese-as-a-foreign-language learners: A review of empirical research. Chinese as a Second Language (systematic review of 22 articles, 39 methods; no Heisig/Chineasy trials among them)

findings.claim: Character legibility on screen depends on size interacting with stroke complexity: each extra stroke costs roughly 0.25 arcmin of required character size.
findings.detail: Liu & Yu (2016, Human Factors and Ergonomics in Manufacturing & Service Industries): font size and character complexity had significant effects on legibility; stroke width was not significant overall but became critical for high-complexity characters, while font size was the critical factor for low-complexity characters; best combination reported as 12pt with a 1:10 stroke-width ratio. Earlier legibility-threshold work reports that each additional stroke must be compensated by roughly 0.25 min of arc of character size, with complexity bands of 2-9, 10-17, and 18-25 strokes. VR work on older adults reports minimum recognisable sizes roughly double those for young adults. These are lab ergonomics studies on specific displays; the arcmin rule generalises better than the point sizes. Abstract-only.
findings.implication: Set hanzi size from stroke count, not one global value. On a phone at ~35cm viewing distance, floor the simple characters (2-9 strokes) at ~48px and scale complex ones (18+ strokes) to ~64-72px; expose it as `font-size: clamp(48px, calc(44px + strokes * 1.1px), 80px)` driven by a stored stroke-count field. Use a high-contrast, generous-stroke face (Noto Sans SC Medium or heavier — never Light) and never render game-critical hanzi below 48px. Store stroke count per character: it is needed for typography, for difficulty estimation, and (per the character-amnesia predictors) for scheduling.

sources.citation: Liu, N., & Yu, R. (2016). Effects of Font Size, Stroke Width, and Character Complexity on the Legibility of Chinese Characters. Human Factors and Ergonomics in Manufacturing & Service Industries
The legibility threshold of Chinese characters in three type styles. International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics

findings.claim: For mainland travel the answer is unambiguously simplified — it is the legally mandated script for public and official use — and the transfer asymmetry favours learning simplified anyway.
findings.detail: The Law of the PRC on the Standard Spoken and Written Chinese Language (adopted 31 Oct 2000, in force 1 Jan 2001) makes Putonghua and standardised (simplified) characters the official spoken and written language for state organs and public use; the 2013 通用规范汉字表 is the operative character inventory. On transfer: Liu et al. (2016, Cognitive Science) found simplified-Chinese readers transferred their analytic processing to traditional characters, whereas traditional readers processed simplified characters more holistically — an asymmetry the authors attribute to the greater variance in simplified character forms. A 2025 study of Hong Kong students converting between scripts found systematic component-level errors going simplified→traditional and stroke-level errors going traditional→simplified. Abstract-only; the transfer studies are on native readers, not L2 adults, so the generalisation to a Dutch/English beginner is an inference.
findings.implication: Ship simplified only, and say so in onboarding. Do not build a script toggle for v1 — it doubles the glyph, decomposition, and confusability data with no benefit to the stated goal. Do store the traditional variant as a nullable field per character so a later Taiwan/HK mode is a data change, not a schema migration. One exception worth authoring: a handful of traditional forms genuinely appear on mainland shopfronts and restaurant signage (餐廳, 麵), so add a short 'signboard variants' module rather than a full script mode.

sources.citation: Law of the People's Republic of China on the Standard Spoken and Written Chinese Language (2000/2001). Ministry of Education of the PRC
Liu, T., Chuk, T., Yeh, S.-L., & Hsiao, J. H. (2016). Transfer of Perceptual Expertise: The Case of Simplified and Traditional Chinese Character Recognition. Cognitive Science

findings.claim: L1-writing-system background changes which radical information L2 learners actually use, and Dutch/English learners sit in the weakest group.
findings.detail: Yu & Chan (2026, International Journal of Bilingualism) compared alphabetic-L1, Japanese-L1 and Korean-L1 learners on perception of and reliance on orthographic, phonological and semantic information carried by radicals, finding L1 writing system and Chinese proficiency both shape radical use. The meta-analysis of reading-related skills also notes that for Sinographosphere learners the phonological aspect is comparatively more critical. Single recent study, abstract-only, and I could not read the direction or size of the alphabetic-L1 effect — hence 'weak'.
findings.implication: Assume zero prior orthographic scaffolding for this audience and teach the component system explicitly rather than expecting it to be induced from exposure. Practically: a mandatory ~30-radical onboarding module (口 木 氵 女 人 心 门 车 食 etc.) before the frequency-ordered character bank unlocks, because a Dutch or English speaker has no Japanese kanji knowledge to fall back on.

sources.citation: Yu, M., & Chan, Y. H. C. (2026). Radical perception and reliance in Chinese character recognition by L2 Chinese learners: A comparison of alphabetic, Japanese, and Korean learners. International Journal of Bilingualism
