findings.claim: Mandarin is FSI Category IV ('super-hard'): 88 weeks / ~2,200 class hours to ILR Speaking-3 / Reading-3, more than double Category III. The jump from III to IV is the single largest step in the framework.
findings.detail: FSI groups languages I–IV; Cat I (Dutch, Afrikaans, Danish, Spanish…) ≈ 24–30 weeks / 600–750 hours; Cat III ≈ 44 weeks / 1,100 hours; Cat IV (Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic) = 88 weeks / 2,200 hours, split across US and in-country study. Target is ILR 3/3 (professional working proficiency, roughly upper-B2/low-C1), not colloquial 'fluency'. Note: these are institutional course-length policies for selected, aptitude-screened full-time adult diplomats, not published research data with variance figures. Dutch itself is Category I for English speakers — the FSI scale says nothing about the Dutch→Mandarin direction, and no European agency publishes an equivalent hour table.

sources.citation: US Department of State, Foreign Service Institute, School of Language Studies — Foreign Language Training (official language category/duration table)
13 FAH-1 H-220, Foreign Affairs Handbook — language designations and training

findings.implication: Do not scope the product as 'learn Mandarin'. 2,200 hours is unreachable for the target user, so ship a deliberately narrow reading-recognition goal: a ~600–900 character / ~1,200 item bank covering menu, transit, retail-label and shopfront Chinese only. Set the in-app goal metric to 'signs you can read', never a CEFR/HSK level.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: DLI runs Category IV Chinese at 64 weeks full-time with a minimum aptitude screen (DLAB ≥ 111) and still sees 5–40% attrition and roughly 64% DLPT success once attrition and retests are counted.
findings.detail: US Army Research Institute / DLI student-achievement analyses. Higher DLAB correlates with lower attrition. This is the best available quantification of dropout under near-ideal conditions (paid, full-time, screened, taught by native instructors).

sources.citation: Student Achievement Indicators at the Defense Language Institute Foreign Language Center (US Army Research Institute technical report, AD1150437)
Defense Language Institute — course categories and durations (overview)

findings.implication: Architect for churn as the primary failure mode, not for depth. Persist every player's state server-side (or in IndexedDB with an export/restore path) so a 3-week gap does not reset progress, and make the first re-entry after a lapse a 60-second 'what you still know' review built from their own scheduler state rather than a fresh lesson.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Chinese character frequency is close to Zipfian: the top 100 characters cover ~42% of running text, top 500 ~75%, top 1,000 ~89–90%, and 3,000 ~99%. Coverage climbs steeply then flattens hard.
findings.detail: Consistent across mainland, Taiwan and Hong Kong corpora. The corollary is that the marginal value of character 1,001 is roughly two orders of magnitude below character 10. Crucially, this is *running-text* frequency; menu, signage and label Chinese has a materially different distribution (出口, 推, 拉, 收银, 麻辣, 禁止, 优惠 are far more frequent in the domain than in a general corpus).

sources.citation: Chinese character frequency — corpus coverage statistics (secondary compilation of Jun Da / Academia Sinica frequency corpora)
Wenlin Institute Guide — Frequency Statistics
HanziCraft — Most Common Chinese Characters: Frequency List

findings.implication: Order the item bank by *domain* frequency, not general frequency, and compute it yourself: scrape/compile a corpus of real menus, station signage, product labels and shopfronts, then rank. Ship the first 100 domain characters as tier 1 (target: player reads ~40% of a real menu after tier 1). Store two frequency fields per character — general rank and domain rank — and drive unlocking from the domain rank.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Mandarin offers no cognates to Dutch or English, removing a facilitation effect that is robust and large in the learning literature: cognates are learned significantly faster than non-cognates in both recognition and production, including when the orthography is logographic.
findings.detail: Cognate facilitation is one of the most replicated effects in bilingual lexical processing; it survives into learning (not just processing) and into trilingual settings, and it also transfers to grammar — cognate-vocabulary learners applied L2 grammatical rules better than non-cognate learners (Sanahuja & Erdocia, Language Teaching Research 2024). For Mandarin every item is therefore a pure arbitrary paired associate — form, sound and meaning all novel — which is the most expensive kind of vocabulary item to acquire.

sources.citation: Sanahuja, N. & Erdocia, K. (2024). The impact of cognate vocabulary on explicit L2 rule learning. Language Teaching Research.
Bosma, E. et al. / Frontiers in Psychology (2022). How does bilingual experience influence novel word learning? Evidence from comparing L1-L3 and L2-L3 cognate status.
Chen et al. (2025). The Cognate Facilitation Effect of L2–L3 Cognates in Chinese–English–Spanish Trilinguals. International Journal of Applied Linguistics.

findings.implication: Budget far more exposures per item than a European-language app would: plan ~8–12 successful retrievals to durable recognition, not 3–4, and size the item bank down accordingly (900 characters × 10 retrievals is already ~9,000 events). Compensate for the missing form-similarity hook by making the *visual* hook do the work — every item card carries a photograph of the real-world referent in situ (a photo of the actual 出口 sign, the actual bowl of 牛肉面), not a clip-art icon.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: The Tone 2 / Tone 3 confusion is the dominant tone error for non-tonal-L1 learners and it is acoustically driven, not L1-driven — English, Dutch and even Cantonese L1 learners all show it.
findings.detail: T2 (rising) and low-onset T3 share a low F0 turning point and a rising tail; learners weight the low-pitch cue over the concave contour, so a low flat token is read as T3 regardless of contour. Hao (2012, Journal of Phonetics) found mutual T2/T3 confusion as the most common error for English learners in both syllable positions of disyllables, and found it in Cantonese learners too. Experimentally expanding F0 range reduces the T2-as-T3 error only slightly (0.30 → 0.27 proportion incorrect), which is evidence the confusion is categorical rather than merely audibility-limited.

sources.citation: Hao, Y.-C. (2012). Second language acquisition of Mandarin Chinese tones by tonal and non-tonal language speakers. Journal of Phonetics, 40(2).
Enhancing lexical tone learning for second language speakers: effects of acoustic properties in Mandarin tone perception (2024). PMC11371754.
A Cross-Language Study of Tonal Variants in Mandarin in Different Attentional Conditions (2025). PMC11939136.

findings.implication: In a reading game, never let a T2/T3 discrimination gate progress. Concretely: when generating multiple-choice pinyin distractors, exclude the T2↔T3 swap from the distractor pool for the first 200 items, and if tone is scored at all, score T2 and T3 as a single merged category until a player has cleared a dedicated, opt-in T2/T3 contrast drill.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Dutch L1 beginners process segmental and tonal information *separately* — like Dutch listeners with no Mandarin at all — and only integrate them at advanced level. T2/T3 is their worst contrast in both a sub-lexical recall task and a lexical decision task.
findings.detail: Zou, Caspers & Chen (Frontiers in Psychology 2022; and Zou's 2017 Leiden LOT dissertation, supervised by Van Heuven) tested beginning and advanced Dutch learners with a sequence-recall task and an auditory lexical decision task. Advanced learners improved on T2/T3 in the sub-lexical task but *not* in the lexical decision task — using tone in on-line word recognition is harder than using it in a memory task. Advanced learners showed strongest sensitivity to T1 and weakest to T4. The authors attribute part of the difficulty to interference from the tonal contrasts of Dutch *intonation*. This is the only body of work I found that studies Dutch L1 Mandarin learners directly.

sources.citation: Zou, T., Caspers, J. & Chen, Y. (2022). Perception of Different Tone Contrasts at Sub-Lexical and Lexical Levels by Dutch Learners of Mandarin Chinese. Frontiers in Psychology. PMC9207513.
Zou, T. (2017). Production and perception of tones by Dutch learners of Mandarin. PhD dissertation, Leiden University / LOT 472.
Zou, T. et al. The developmental trajectories of attention distribution and segment-tone integration in Dutch learners of Mandarin tones. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition.

findings.implication: Split the audio channel from the tone channel in the data model and in the UI. An item's pronunciation should be storable and testable as (segments) and (tone) as two independently-scheduled attributes, so a Dutch beginner can be credited for knowing 'chu-kou' while still failing the tone. On the card, render the tone as a separate coloured diacritic badge next to the syllable rather than only as a mark over the vowel, so the two channels are visually separable too.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: High-variability phonetic training works, with a large effect on tone specifically, and identification training beats discrimination training by a wide margin.
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of L2 perceptual training: g = 0.92 pretest–posttest (k = 96) and g = 0.67 treatment–control (k = 32). By target phone, tone g ≈ 1.00 (comparable to vowels, above obstruents at 0.69). By task, identification training g = 0.95 vs discrimination training g = 0.57; identification *testing* g = 1.08 vs discrimination testing g = 0.77. A separate meta-analysis puts overall HVPT effect on pronunciation at g = 0.77 with the largest gains for consonants and tones and for more advanced learners.

sources.citation: Zhang, X., Cheng, B., Qin, D. & Zhang, Y. High variability phonetic training (HVPT): A meta-analysis of L2 perceptual training studies. Studies in Second Language Acquisition.
Enhancing Pronunciation Learning through High Variability Phonetic Training (meta-analysis). ERIC EJ1425175.
Does perceptual HVPT improve L2 speech production? A meta-analysis of the perception–production connection. Applied Psycholinguistics.

findings.implication: Wherever the game plays audio, make the task 'which of these four is it?' (identification), never 'same or different?' (discrimination) — the meta-analysis puts a ~0.4 g gap between them. And ship at least 4–6 distinct recorded voices per item (male/female, different regional accents), rotating talker per presentation. Architecturally that means the audio asset table is keyed (item_id, talker_id) and the client must pre-cache several talkers per item for offline play.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: The 'musicians learn tone better' claim is contested. The original finding is real but correlational, and the current review position is that replications frequently fail and that musical *aptitude*, not training, carries the association.
findings.detail: Wong & Perrachione (2007, Applied Psycholinguistics) trained native English speakers on 18 pseudo-words (6 pseudosyllables × 3 pitch patterns) and found learning success predicted by pre-training non-lexical pitch-pattern identification and by prior musical experience; Wong et al. (2007, Nature Neuroscience) added brainstem-encoding evidence. Against this: Schellenberg & Lima (2024, Annual Review of Psychology) conclude that replication attempts frequently fail (citing Boebinger et al. 2015; Schellenberg et al. 2023; Whiteford et al. 2025), that experimental and longitudinal studies report small/mixed effects, and that music-training associations disappear when music aptitude is held constant — i.e. selection, not transfer.

sources.citation: Wong, P. C. M. & Perrachione, T. K. (2007). Learning pitch patterns in lexical identification by native English-speaking adults. Applied Psycholinguistics, 28(4).
Perrachione, T. K. et al. Individual variability in cue-weighting and lexical tone learning. PMC2921440.
Schellenberg, E. G. & Lima, C. F. (2024). Music Training and Nonmusical Abilities. Annual Review of Psychology.
Revisiting the association between musical expertise and second-language proficiency (2026). Royal Society Open Science.

findings.implication: Do not ask 'do you play an instrument?' in onboarding and do not branch content on it — the evidence does not support it and it wastes an onboarding slot. If you want an adaptive signal, use the thing that actually predicted learning: a 60-second, 12-trial pre-test of *pitch-contour identification on non-speech tones*. Store the score as a single float and use it only to set the initial tone-drill difficulty, not to gate content.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: The three-way sibilant contrast (retroflex zh/ch/sh vs alveolo-palatal j/q/x vs alveolar z/c/s) is genuinely hard for English speakers, with accuracy floors near 30%, and perception and production are largely decoupled.
findings.detail: 25 native English CFL learners read the eight consonants j /tɕ/, q /tɕʰ/, x /ɕ/, zh /tʂ/, ch /tʂʰ/, sh /ʂ/, z /ts/, c /tsʰ/ in sentences and did a forced-choice identification task. Perception accuracy ranged 29–80%, production 25–88%. Only 2 of 8 sounds showed a moderate perception–production correlation. The structural cause: English has one postalveolar series (/ʃ tʃ dʒ/) sitting acoustically *between* Mandarin's retroflex and alveolo-palatal series, so both Mandarin categories assimilate to a single English category.

sources.citation: The Acquisition of Mandarin Consonants by English Learners: The Relationship between Perception and Production. Languages, 5(2), 20 (2020). n=25.
How to Teach Mandarin Alveolo-palatal [ɕ]: Pedagogical Suggestions Based on Articulatory Comparisons of Mandarin [ɕ] and English [ʃ].

findings.implication: Build an explicit three-column contrast set into the item bank — every syllable tagged sibilant_series ∈ {retroflex, alveolopalatal, alveolar, none} — and generate identification drills that force a 3-way choice (shī / xī / sī) rather than a 2-way one. Do not include sibilant-series errors in the main progress score; surface them in a separate 'sounds' meter, because a 30% floor inside the main score will read as failure and drive churn.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Pinyin's orthography actively misleads alphabetic-L1 learners about syllable structure: where pinyin elides the main vowel (iu, ui, un), English beginners literally count one fewer vowel than in the spelled-out equivalent.
findings.detail: Bassetti (2007) showed English beginner learners counted fewer vowels in syllables whose pinyin spelling omits the main vowel (e.g. dui, written for [twei]) than in syllables where it is written (wei). This is orthographic interference on phonological representation, not just a spelling nuisance. Related work on pinyin vs zhuyin found the predicted grapheme-to-phoneme interference effects were *not* always borne out, and that most mispronunciations traced to intrinsic English phonology rather than to pinyin per se — so the general 'pinyin causes English-like pronunciation' claim is weaker than the specific elided-vowel claim.

sources.citation: Bassetti, B. (2007). Effects of hanyu pinyin on pronunciation in learners of Chinese as a Foreign Language. Birkbeck ePrints.
The Influence of the Pinyin and Zhuyin Writing Systems on the Acquisition of Mandarin Word Forms by Native English Speakers. Frontiers in Psychology 7:785 (2016).
Bassetti, B. & Atkinson, N. The influence of orthography in second language phonological acquisition. Language Teaching (Cambridge).

findings.implication: Add a per-syllable boolean `elided_vowel` to the pinyin data (true for -iu, -ui, -un, -ün rimes) and, on those cards only, render the expanded form as small grey text under the standard pinyin — `duì  ⟨du-ei⟩`. Do this for roughly the ~40 affected rime/syllable combinations, not globally, so the extra ink is paid only where it buys something.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Two independent meta-analyses agree: glossing beats no glossing, and L1 glosses beat L2 glosses — with the L1 advantage largest for exactly the population this product serves (beginners) and on immediate recall.
findings.detail: Kim, H. S., Lee, J. H. & Lee, H. (2024, Language Teaching Research): 78 effect sizes, 26 studies, 30 independent samples, N = 2,189; L1 glossing > L2 glossing, Hedges' g = 0.33, p < .001; advantage particularly clear for beginners vs intermediate-plus, and supported by immediate vocabulary posttests more than delayed posttests or reading comprehension. Yanagisawa, Webb & Uchihara (SSLA): 359 effect sizes, 42 studies, N = 3,802; glossed reading > unglossed; L1 glosses > L2 glosses; **multiple-choice glosses were the most effective gloss type, in-text glosses and glossaries the least**. A more recent single study (Chen, 2025, TESOL Quarterly) reports both gloss languages at medium effect and argues the choice can follow learner preference — a real dissent, but one study against two meta-analyses.

sources.citation: Kim, H. S., Lee, J. H. & Lee, H. (2024). The relative effects of L1 and L2 glosses on L2 learning: A meta-analysis. Language Teaching Research.
Yanagisawa, A., Webb, S. & Uchihara, T. How do different forms of glossing contribute to L2 vocabulary learning from reading? Studies in Second Language Acquisition.
Chen, X. (2025). The Effects of Gloss Language on L2 Vocabulary Learning from Reading. TESOL Quarterly.

findings.implication: Two decisions fall straight out. (1) Gloss language: default to the user's L1 (Dutch for nl locale, English for en) — not a shared English gloss for everyone. (2) Gloss *format*: the reveal should be a 4-option forced choice on meaning, not a passive tooltip — 'multiple-choice gloss' is the meta-analytically best type and 'in-text gloss / glossary' the worst, which is precisely the difference between a game mechanic and a dictionary popup. Kill any always-visible translation under the hanzi.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Picture/multimedia glosses add on top of text glosses; for a concrete-noun, real-world-referent domain this is the highest-leverage gloss decision, above the L1-vs-L2 question.
findings.detail: Multiple meta-analyses of multimedia glossing (text+picture vs text-only) find an advantage for combined glosses on L2 vocabulary acquisition. For a menu/signage/label item bank, nearly every target is a concrete, photographable referent, which is the condition where dual coding is strongest and where the L1-vs-L2 translation problem partly dissolves (a photo of a bowl of 牛肉面 needs no language).

sources.citation: Multimedia glosses and second language vocabulary learning: A second-round meta-analysis (2024). System.
Efficacy of Multimodal Glossing on L2 Vocabulary Learning: A Meta-Analysis.
Ramezanali, N., Uchihara, T. & Faez, F. Efficacy of multimodal glossing on L2 vocabulary learning (TESOL Quarterly line of work).

findings.implication: Make the photograph mandatory in the item schema (`image_url` non-null) and treat text-only items as incomplete content. Budget the photo pipeline early: ~900 in-situ photos of real Chinese menus, signs, labels and shopfronts. On the card, photo above, hanzi below, gloss text last — and for a PWA, ship them as WebP/AVIF at two resolutions with a service-worker cache, because offline play in China is a core use case.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: For a Dutch adult fluent in English, the evidence does NOT support switching to English glosses — but the evidence base for the specific L1-vs-L2-mediation question in L3 learning is thin and the one directly relevant study is mixed.
findings.detail: There is no study of Dutch–English bilinguals learning Mandarin. The nearest evidence: a Polish-L1 / English-L2 / Italian-L3 study found the instrument version with *keywords in L2-English and instructions in L1-Polish* was most effective at eliciting L3 vocabulary — but this is a measurement instrument, not learning, and Italian shares cognates with English while Mandarin shares none. Theory splits: the L2 Status Factor (Bardel & Falk) predicts English would be the privileged transfer source because of shared late-learned/metalinguistic status; the Typological Primacy Model (Rothman) predicts transfer follows (psycho)typological proximity — and Mandarin is typologically remote from both Dutch and English, so TPM predicts *no* strong anchor from either, which drains the L3 argument for English. Meanwhile the glossing meta-analyses point the other way (L1 > L2, strongest for beginners).

sources.citation: Adapting the Vocabulary Knowledge Scale to measure L3 lexical knowledge (2025). International Journal of Bilingual Education and Bilingualism.
Rothman, J. (2011). L3 syntactic transfer selectivity and typological determinacy: The Typological Primacy Model. Second Language Research.
Rothman, J. Linguistic and cognitive motivations for the Typological Primacy Model (TPM) of L3 transfer. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition.
Third language acquisition: L2 status factor vs TPM (review). Arizona Working Papers in SLAT 25 (2018).

findings.implication: RECOMMENDATION — ship Dutch as the default gloss for nl-locale users, English for everyone else, with a per-user override in settings; do NOT ship English-only to Dutch users, and do NOT ship an always-on bilingual Dutch+English gloss (no meta-analytic support, and it adds extraneous load to a small phone card). Make English a tap-to-reveal *second* line on the answer side only. Architecturally: `gloss: {nl, en}` on every item from day one (retrofitting a second gloss language into a live item bank is the expensive version of this decision), one language rendered, the other behind a tap. Instrument it — log gloss language and retention so you can settle this empirically with your own data, since the literature cannot settle it for this exact triad.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Colour-coding radicals inside characters and playing stroke-order animations actively HURT L2 character recognition — slower reaction times and lower accuracy.
findings.detail: Hou & Jiang (2022, Frontiers in Psychology): presenting radical markings (radicals highlighted in different colours) increased participants' reaction times and decreased accuracy in character recognition tests; presenting stroke-order animations also decreased recognition accuracy. This is a direct negative result against two of the most common design choices in character-learning apps. Related nuance: radical awareness helps *transparent* compound characters but not semi-opaque or opaque ones, which are better memorised as whole units (Chen & Feng, 2020, SAGE Open).

sources.citation: Hou, F. & Jiang, X. (2022). Interference effects of radical markings and stroke order animations on Chinese character learning among L2 learners. Frontiers in Psychology, 13:783613.
Chen, T. & Feng, Y. (2020). Nontransparent Compound Character Learning in L2 Chinese: Does Radical Awareness Always Work? SAGE Open.

findings.implication: Render the hanzi as a single solid-colour glyph on every recognition item — no per-radical colouring, no animated stroke order on the recognition card. If radical information is shown at all, put it *outside* the glyph as a separate small annotation chip ('氵 water') on the answer/review side, and only for characters tagged `semantic_transparency = transparent`. This means the item schema needs a transparency flag per character, hand-graded or taken from an existing transparency norm.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Teaching semantic radicals does pay off in one specific way: learners transfer the strategy to infer meanings of *untaught* characters in sentence reading.
findings.detail: Frontiers in Psychology (2017): after a three-week course covering Chinese orthographic knowledge and ≥7 phonetic/semantic radicals per week with their derivative characters, the experimental group outperformed controls on phonetic-radical awareness, semantic-radical awareness and orthographic knowledge tests, and successfully inferred meanings of unfamiliar characters containing *untaught* semantic radicals. Beginners also benefit from radical-based *grouping* of items over distributed presentation.

sources.citation: Teaching Semantic Radicals Facilitates Inferring New Character Meaning in Sentence Reading for Nonnative Chinese Speakers. Frontiers in Psychology 8:1846 (2017). PMC5660119.
Radical Awareness Among L2 Chinese Learners. Chinese as a Second Language Learning & Teaching 2(1) (2022).

findings.implication: Add a distinct 'radical' round to the game — not radical colouring on recognition cards (see previous finding), but a separate mode that groups items by shared semantic radical. Prioritise the ~15 radicals that carry the domain: 饣/食 (food), 月 (meat), 鱼, 肉, 辶 (movement/transit), 门 (door), 车 (vehicle), 钅(metal), 氵(liquid), 酉 (alcohol/fermented), 米 (grain), 艹 (plant), 女/男, 口, 页. Batch new items into radical-based sets of 6–8 for beginners rather than interleaving them across radicals.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Alphabetic-L1 beginners do not develop sublexical orthography-to-phonology mapping in Chinese; the phonetic component is not usable as a pronunciation cue until advanced proficiency.
findings.detail: ERP evidence (Cognitive, Affective & Behavioral Neuroscience 2015) that while skilled native Chinese readers access sublexical phonological units when recognising phonograms, sublexical orthography-to-phonology mapping is *not* found among beginning L2 Chinese learners with alphabetic L1s. Separately, only advanced L2 learners show the left-lateralised N170 visual specialisation characteristic of native readers.

sources.citation: Electrophysiological evidence of sublexical phonological access in character processing by L2 Chinese learners of L1 alphabetic scripts. Cognitive, Affective, & Behavioral Neuroscience (2015).
The left-lateralized N170 for visual specialization in advanced L2 Chinese learners. PMC11390388.
Neural tuning for Chinese characters in adult Chinese L2 learners: an ERP study. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition.

findings.implication: Never teach or test 'guess the pronunciation from the phonetic component' for beginners, and do not let the scheduler assume that learning 青 qīng transfers to 清/请/情. Model pronunciation as an independent learnable attribute per character with its own scheduling state — three fields (form→meaning, form→sound, sound→form) with separate intervals — rather than one merged 'known' bit.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Spaced practice reliably beats massed practice for L2 vocabulary and grammar.
findings.detail: Kim & Webb (2022) meta-analysis: 48 experiments, 3,411 L2 learners; spaced practice significantly outperformed massed practice across vocabulary and grammar outcomes. Retrieval practice (the testing effect) is separately well established for long-term retention, including for L3 vocabulary.

sources.citation: Kim, S. K. & Webb, S. (2022). The Effects of Spaced Practice on Second Language Learning: A Meta-Analysis. Language Learning.
The influence of the spacing effect on L2 vocabulary learning. System (2023).
The Benefits of Covert Retrieval Practice on Short- and Long-Term L3 Vocabulary Retention. Behavioral Sciences 16(7):1124.

findings.implication: The scheduler is a first-class architectural component, not a feature: per-player, per-item, per-attribute state (last_seen, interval, ease, lapses) persisted locally in IndexedDB and synced. Critically for a *co-located multiplayer* game — every card a player answers in a shared session must write back to that player's individual schedule, so the multiplayer round is a delivery mechanism for spaced retrieval rather than a separate, unscored mode. Design the sync as last-write-wins per (player_id, item_id, attribute) so offline sessions on four phones in a Beijing restaurant merge cleanly.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Game-based and mobile-app language learning shows large effects, but almost entirely on vocabulary and pronunciation — not on grammar, reading comprehension, or writing — and the large effects require sustained treatment (10+ weeks).
findings.detail: Meta-analysis of mobile games for language learning: 38 (quasi-)experimental studies, 4,102 participants, overall g = 0.962 [0.688–1.235]; vocabulary g = 1.251 (k = 16); ~83% of game-using learners outperformed non-users. A mobile-app vocabulary meta-analysis found g = 1.28 when restricted to treatments of ≥10 weeks. Moderator analyses confirm significant positive effects on vocabulary and pronunciation but 'less clear' effects on speaking, reading, writing, grammar and literacy, and mostly for English as the target language.

sources.citation: Do mobile games improve language learning? A meta-analysis (2025). Computer Assisted Language Learning.
A meta-analysis on mobile-assisted vocabulary learning: Do mobile applications help? ReCALL.
Digital game-based second-language vocabulary learning and conditions of research designs: A meta-analysis. Computers & Education.

findings.implication: Keep the core loop lexical — character/word recognition — and resist adding grammar levels; that is the outcome where games measurably win. Design the progression for a 10–12 week arc (the duration at which effects reach g ≈ 1.28): a visible 'trip countdown' schedule of ~70 daily sessions of 5–8 minutes, not an endless level ladder. Note the caveat honestly: nearly all of this evidence is for English as the target language, so treat the effect size as an upper bound for Mandarin.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Font size and character complexity both significantly affect Chinese legibility, and stroke *width* becomes the critical variable for complex characters — each extra stroke needs roughly 0.25 arcmin more character size to hold legibility constant.
findings.detail: Liu et al. (2016, Human Factors and Ergonomics in Manufacturing): font size and complexity both significant; stroke width not significant overall, but critical for high-complexity characters, while size is the critical factor for low-complexity ones; best combination tested was 12 pt with a 1:10 stroke-width ratio. A separate regression gives the ~0.25 arcmin-per-stroke compensation rule. Smartphone-specific studies confirm size and line spacing effects on readability.

sources.citation: Liu, N. et al. (2016). Effects of Font Size, Stroke Width, and Character Complexity on the Legibility of Chinese Characters. Human Factors and Ergonomics in Manufacturing & Service Industries.
Effects of the Font Size and Line Spacing of Simplified Chinese Characters on Smartphone Readability.
Effects of font size, display resolution and task type on reading Chinese fonts from mobile devices. Displays (2008).

findings.implication: Concrete type spec: hanzi on the primary recognition card at 96 px minimum (a single character is the hero element — it is a picture, not text); hanzi in multi-character reading strings at 40 px minimum, scaling to 48 px for any string containing a character of >15 strokes (store `stroke_count` per character and drive the size class from it). Use a Regular or Medium weight CJK face (Noto Sans SC 400/500) and never Light/Thin — stroke width is the binding constraint on complex glyphs. Latin gloss text sits at 15–16 px; do not set hanzi at body-text size.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Inserting inter-word spaces into Chinese text speeds word reading for elementary-proficiency L2 learners, even though authentic Chinese is unspaced.
findings.detail: Eye-tracking study of L2 Chinese learners' processing unit: participants read target words faster in the spaced condition than the unspaced condition. Single study; the tension is that all real-world signage and menus are unspaced, so spacing is a scaffold that must be removed.

sources.citation: Yao, P. et al. (2025). Explore the processing unit of L2 Chinese learners in online reading (eye-tracking).

findings.implication: Ship word-segmentation metadata in the item bank (each reading string stored as an array of word tokens, not a raw string) and render a 0.2–0.25 em gap between words in beginner mode, collapsing to zero as the player levels up on that item. Make the final review of every item unspaced, since the transfer target is an unspaced sign. This is a schema decision that must be made before content authoring starts.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: L2 learners of Chinese over-rely on the general classifier 个 ge and are near-native on high-frequency classifiers but error-prone on low-frequency ones; the bottleneck is lexical knowledge, not the syntactic category.
findings.detail: Study with 34 English-speaking learners and 33 native Chinese speakers using elicited production, self-paced reading, lexical decision and a classifier knowledge test: learners over-produced 个 and under-used specific classifiers; they were insensitive to classifier *omission* online but sensitive to classifiers semantically inconsistent with the noun. L2 adults overgeneralise 个 much as L1 children do. Error rates were comparably low for both L1 groups on high-frequency classifiers and significantly higher on low-frequency ones. Conclusion: establishing the functional category is attainable; the real constraint is lexical.

sources.citation: The L2 acquisition of Chinese classifiers: Comprehension and production (PhD dissertation, Michigan State University).
Chinese Classifier Acquisition (University of Montana thesis).
A Review on the Acquisition of Chinese Classifiers by CSL Learners (2025).

findings.implication: Do not teach the classifier system. Ship exactly the classifiers a menu/shop reader must recognise as frozen chunks inside larger strings — 个, 份, 碗, 杯, 瓶, 张, 位, 条 — and always as part of a whole item (一碗牛肉面, 两瓶啤酒), never as a standalone grammar drill. Tag them `chunk_only = true` in the bank so the generator never isolates them as a target.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Aspect markers 了/过/着 map onto no Germanic category: Chinese has rich aspect and no morphological tense, English/Dutch the reverse. Acquisition order is 了 and 过 before 着, and the tense→aspect remapping is a persistent, long-term difficulty.
findings.detail: Feature Reassembly Hypothesis studies of 了 and 过 by English-speaking learners (Guo, Linguistic Approaches to Bilingualism 2025) frame this as a complex L1-tense to L2-aspect mapping that produces persistent errors. Instructional comparison (Researching and Teaching CFL): a communicative approach beat grammar-translation for use in context, but the gains did not last without further treatment. Note there is also documented *positive* transfer for sentence-final 了 from English 'already'.

sources.citation: Guo (2025). Disentangling aspect and tense in L2 acquisition: A feature reassembly approach to perfective markers le and guo in L2 Chinese grammars. Linguistic Approaches to Bilingualism.
Investigating the teaching of Chinese aspect markers zai, zhe, le and guo. Researching and Teaching Chinese as a Foreign Language.
Positive cross-linguistic influence in the representation and processing of sentence-final particle le by L2 and heritage learners of Chinese. Frontiers in Psychology 14:1145493 (2023).

findings.implication: Exclude 着 from the item bank entirely at launch. Treat 了 and 过 purely as visual tokens the player must recognise inside signage strings (卖完了, 到了) with a gloss like 'marks: done / changed state' — never as a grammar exercise and never with an English tense equivalent, since the tense mapping is the source of the persistent error.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: English-speaking learners systematically transfer subject-prominence onto topic-prominent Chinese until fairly high proficiency; topic chains and zero anaphora are the structures they misparse.
findings.detail: Jin (1994, Language Learning, ERIC EJ483574) is the reference study: native English speakers learning Chinese showed systematic transfer of English subject-prominence features before reaching the topic concept. Later work confirms topic chain plus zero anaphora as the core topic-prominent discourse structure and shows form-focused instruction can raise L2 Chinese topic-chain use. Dutch adds a further wrinkle: Dutch is verb-second in main clauses and verb-final in subordinate clauses, so English SVO is actually the closer word-order analogy to Mandarin for a Dutch learner — a typological argument, not an empirically tested one.

sources.citation: Jin, H. G. (1994). Topic-Prominence and Subject-Prominence in L2 Acquisition: Evidence of English-to-Chinese Typological Transfer. Language Learning. ERIC EJ483574.
Enhancing Syntactic Complexity in L2 Chinese Writing: Effects of Form-Focused Instruction on the Chinese Topic Chain. PMC9037319.
Topic prominence in L2 acquisition: Evidence of Chinese-to-English typological transfer. Journal of Second Language Studies.

findings.implication: Cap reading items at 4 characters for the first tier and 8 for the second, and hard-exclude any string with a dropped subject or a topic-comment fronting from tiers 1–2 — learners will silently misparse them and score them as 'known'. This is content-authoring guidance worth encoding as a lint rule over the item bank (reject items whose segmentation lacks an overt subject when a verb is present).
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Directional complements (进/出/上/下/回/过 + 来/去) are a documented major difficulty for English L1 learners because English encodes path with satellites only, while Chinese directional morphemes double as independent verbs.
findings.detail: Wu, S.-L. (2011, Language Learning), 'Learning to Express Motion Events in an L2: The Case of Chinese Directional Complements': difficulty traced to the syntactic complexity of DC patterns, Chinese serial-verb typology, and the dual verb/satellite function. Resultative verb complements show a parallel markedness-graded difficulty (more arguments = harder), with success rates as high as 94.1% on the least marked types.

sources.citation: Wu, S.-L. (2011). Learning to Express Motion Events in an L2: The Case of Chinese Directional Complements. Language Learning, 61(2).
Acquisition of the Chinese resultative verb complements by L2 learners (Penn State dissertation).
A Study of the Acquisition of Chinese Resultative Verb Complements and Corresponding Teaching Strategies.

findings.implication: Good news for this product: the signage domain is saturated with exactly these morphemes (入口, 出口, 上车, 下车, 进站, 出站, 过街, 回收) and they are all *fixed lexical signs*. Ship them as whole two-character units with photographs, tagged `atomic = true`, and never decompose them into a complement analysis. Add a tier-1 'directions and doors' set of ~20 such signs — highest real-world payoff per item in the bank.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: In the Netherlands, Chinese has been a VWO exam subject since 2015–16, examined only as a schoolexamen (no centraal examen), with PTA tests structurally based on HSK, and requiring active mastery of 400 characters.
findings.detail: SLO (Stichting Leerplanontwikkeling) publishes the curriculum proposal 'Chinees op school' and the handreiking schoolexamen Chinees havo/vwo. Chinese Language and Culture holds the same curricular position and study load as other modern foreign languages other than English. The exam candidate must actively master 400 characters (read and write). I could not read the SLO documents directly (egress-blocked), so the per-skill CEFR level claims in the exam programme remain unverified.

sources.citation: SLO — Chinees vwo (curriculum and exam programme portal).
SLO — Chinees op school: voorstel voor een leerplan Chinees.
SLO — Handreiking schoolexamen Chinees havo/vwo, algemene informatie.

findings.implication: There is a ready-made, officially-defined 400-character tier for the Dutch market. Ship a 'VWO Chinees' mode: tag every item with `vwo_400 = true/false` and `hsk3_band`, and offer Dutch secondary students a filtered deck. This is a distribution wedge (Dutch schools with a Chinees programme are a small, enumerable list) and it costs only two boolean/enum columns in the item schema.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: HSK 3.0 (the International Chinese Language Education Chinese Proficiency Grading Standards) restructured Chinese proficiency into 9 levels in 3 bands, topping out at 11,092 words and 3,000 characters, with revised standards published Nov 2025 and full implementation July 2026.
findings.detail: Released by Hanban/CLEC in 2021, implemented from 2022; 5,207 words changed level in the 2026 update. Official framing maps the three bands (1–3 foundational, 4–6 developmental, 7–9 proficiency) onto CEFR A/B/C. No official study-hour table is published for HSK 3.0 — the widely-cited hour figures (80–150 h for HSK 1, 500–1,000 h for HSK 4) are unsourced planning estimates and should be treated as folklore.

sources.citation: HSK 3.0 / Chinese Proficiency Grading Standards for International Chinese Language Education — overview.
What Is HSK 3.0? 9 Levels and Current Exam Status (2026 update, incl. 5,207 word level changes).
HSK to CEFR conversion charts (2026).

findings.implication: Tag items with HSK 3.0 band for credibility and filtering, but do NOT order the curriculum by it — HSK wordlists are oriented to spoken/general proficiency and will not surface 出口, 推, 拉, 收银台, 禁止吸烟, 微信支付 or 麻辣 at the right time. The ordering key must be your own domain-frequency rank; HSK is a secondary tag. Also: the July 2026 full implementation means any HSK tags you ship now need a versioned field (`hsk_version`, `hsk_band`) so the 5,207 reclassified words can be migrated without re-authoring.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: Handwriting practice measurably improves L2 character recognition and orthographic knowledge — but the effect requires a large volume of practice, and pinyin typing does not produce the same sensorimotor activation.
findings.detail: Writing practice improved accuracy on writing and meaning assignments vs no writing practice; drawing facilitated visual word recognition relative to viewing; handwriting produced stronger bilateral superior parietal and right postcentral activation than pinyin typing, and for hand-learned characters, left sensorimotor activation correlated with lexical processing accuracy. The explicit caveat in this literature is that L2 learners need a large amount of writing practice for the effect to appear.

sources.citation: Effect of stroke-order learning and handwriting exercises on recognizing and writing Chinese characters by CFL learners. Computers in Human Behavior.
Neural Correlates of Handwriting Effects in L2 Learners. PMC9330472.
Activation of writing-specific brain regions when reading Chinese as a second language: effects of training modality and transfer to novel characters. Neuropsychologia.
Comparison studies of typing and handwriting in Chinese language learning: A synthetic review. Learning and Instruction.

findings.implication: Do not put handwriting on the critical path of a phone reading game — the effect needs volume you cannot extract from a 6-minute session, and a finger-trace requirement will kill the multiplayer loop. Instead offer a single optional finger-trace on *first encounter only*, for the ~150 highest-domain-frequency characters, as a 3-second 'stamp it in' gesture with no scoring and no retry. Store `traced_at` per character so it never repeats.
findings._topic: Mandarin acquisition by Dutch and English L1 speakers — difficulty, phonology, grammar transfer, gloss language, and the Dutch teaching context; implications for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin *reading* game

findings.claim: On the largest independent spaced-repetition benchmark, FSRS's advantage over trivial baselines is small, and a zero-parameter moving average beats every FSRS version on calibration.
findings.detail: Open Spaced Repetition SRS Benchmark, read in full this session. Dataset: 9,999 Anki collections, 349,923,850 reviews used for evaluation (from ~727M raw), sklearn TimeSeriesSplit so older reviews train and newer reviews test. Log Loss (lower better), 99% CIs, excluding same-day reviews: RWKV-P 0.2773±0.0036; LSTM 0.3332±0.0041; GRU 0.3333±0.0041; MOVING-AVG (0 parameters) 0.3369±0.0042; Logistic Regression (34 hand-built features) 0.3393±0.0042; FSRS-7 recency 0.3414±0.0043; FSRS-7 (35 params) 0.3437±0.0043; FSRS-6 (21 params) 0.3460±0.0042; FSRS-5 0.3560±0.0045; FSRS-4.5 0.3624±0.0046; FSRS-7 with DEFAULT parameters (no per-user optimisation) 0.3629±0.0044; AVG (constant = user's mean retention) 0.3945±0.0051. AUC: FSRS-7 0.7069±0.0023, Logistic Regression 0.7108±0.0023, MOVING-AVG 0.7001±0.0026, AVG 0.4997. So: (a) a 0-parameter moving average outperforms the flagship 35-parameter FSRS-7 on log loss; (b) the entire gain from per-user optimisation of FSRS-7 is 0.3629→0.3437 = 0.019 log loss. Caveats the benchmark does not state but that matter: all data was generated under Anki's own SM-2-derived scheduling (selection bias — intervals are not randomised), and the metric is recall prediction, not learning outcome. SM-2 itself is no longer a row in the current benchmark table.

findings.implication: Do not build, tune or research a scheduler. Install `ts-fsrs` (FSRS-6, pure TypeScript, runs client-side) with the 21 shipped default parameters and never write a per-user optimiser: the whole prize is 0.019 log loss, which is invisible in a party game of ~30 rounds. Spend the saved engineering on item-bank quality and on the group-selection layer, which has no off-the-shelf answer. Budget: scheduler = one npm dependency and ~40 lines of glue.

findings.claim: Half-Life Regression — Duolingo's published, widely-cited scheduling model — is one of the worst performers on independent data, worse than predicting the user's constant average retention.
findings.detail: Same SRS Benchmark, read in full. HLR: Log Loss 0.4694±0.0073, RMSE(bins) 0.1275±0.0019, AUC 0.6369±0.0026. HLR-short: 0.4929±0.0078 / 0.1397 / 0.6115. Compare AVG (a constant equal to the user's overall retention, 0 parameters): 0.3945±0.0051. HLR is therefore worse-calibrated than a constant. Ebisu v2 (Bayesian) is worse still at 0.4989±0.0078. Note HLR retains some discrimination (AUC 0.637 > 0.500) — it ranks items better than chance but its absolute probabilities are badly wrong, which is exactly what matters if you use predicted recall to select items.

findings.implication: Do not implement half-life regression, despite its convenient closed form p = 2^(-t/h) and its fame in the language-learning literature. If you want a tiny closed-form model for the group-selection scoring function, use FSRS-6's retrievability instead: R(t,S) = (1 + FACTOR·t/S)^(−DECAY) with FSRS-6 default decay 0.1542 — same computational cost, far better calibrated, and it comes with the library you are already installing.

findings.claim: The famous "+12% Duolingo engagement" from Settles & Meeder 2016 is NOT the result of HLR beating Leitner. HLR versus Leitner produced no significant engagement gain and a significant 7.3% DROP in practice sessions.
findings.detail: Read from the paper PDF (full text extracted this session). Table 4, "Change (%) in daily student retention for controlled user experiments", * = p<0.001. Experiment I — HLR (treatment) vs Leitner (control), 6 weeks, "just under 1 million students", randomised: Any activity +0.3 (n.s.), New lesson +0.3 (n.s.), Practice −7.3*. The only statistically significant effect of replacing Leitner with HLR was a 7.3% decrease in practice-session retention. Experiment II — HLR-lex (treatment; HLR with the lexeme-tag features REMOVED) vs HLR (control), 2 weeks, 3.3 million students: Any +12.0*, New lesson +1.7*, Practice +9.5*. The abstract's headline "+12% daily student engagement" is Experiment II — i.e. the gain came from making the model SIMPLER, not from spaced repetition modelling beating the Leitner box system. Also note: the outcome measured throughout is *daily retention* (did the user come back the next day), never vocabulary gain. No learning outcome was measured in either experiment.

sources.citation: Settles, B. & Meeder, B. (2016). A Trainable Spaced Repetition Model for Language Learning. Proc. ACL 2016, pp. 1848–1858. §4.3, §4.4, Table 4. n≈1M and n=3.3M randomised users.
ACL Anthology record P16-1174

findings.implication: Never justify a design decision — internally or in the app's copy — on the grounds that a smarter scheduler drives engagement or learning; the single largest industry experiment on exactly this question found the opposite. Correspondingly, do not instrument the PWA to optimise next-day return. Instrument it to measure reading gain (see the yes/no test finding) and treat session-return as a guardrail metric only. Concretely: two analytics events matter — `session_completed` and `checkin_test_score`; everything else is diagnostic.

findings.claim: No published spaced-repetition model discriminates item-level recall much above chance in a real language-learning product — and in Duolingo's own evaluation the crude Leitner box system had the highest AUC of all models tested.
findings.detail: Settles & Meeder 2016 Table 2, read from the PDF. Evaluation on two weeks of Duolingo logs, 12.9 million student-word lesson and practice traces. MAE↓ / AUC↑ / Spearman correlation with half-life↑: HLR 0.128 / 0.538 / 0.201; HLR-lex 0.128 / 0.537 / 0.160; HLR−h 0.350 / 0.528 / −0.143; Leitner 0.235 / 0.542 / −0.098; Pimsleur 0.445 / 0.510 / −0.132; Logistic Regression 0.211 / 0.513 / n/a; constant p̄=0.859 baseline 0.175 / n/a / n/a. HLR's celebrated "45%+ error reduction" is MAE only (0.235→0.128 vs Leitner). On AUC — the ability to tell a recalled item from a forgotten one — Leitner (0.542) is nominally the best model in the table and HLR (0.538) is second; every model is within 0.04 of chance. The independent Anki benchmark reaches AUC ~0.71 (FSRS) to 0.83 (RWKV-P) on flashcard data, so this is partly a property of Duolingo's noisy in-lesson exposure data rather than of memory modelling in general — but the language-learning-in-the-wild number is the relevant one for this product.

sources.citation: Settles, B. & Meeder, B. (2016). ACL 2016, Table 2 and §4.1. 12.9M traces, two weeks of production logs, significance at p<0.001.
Open Spaced Repetition, SRS Benchmark AUC column (FSRS-7 0.7069±0.0023; RWKV-P 0.8329±0.0017), 9,999 collections

findings.implication: Never show the player a numeric strength/mastery percentage for an item — the model cannot support that precision and a wrong number is a trust-destroying, visible lie (Duolingo's users complained about exactly this; see the overfitting finding). Show at most three coarse states per item, distinguished by colour and shape, not by a bar: NEW (outline chip), LEARNING (half-filled chip), SOLID (filled chip). Aggregate progress is shown at the deck/domain level only ("metro signs: 62 of 180 solid"), where averaging over ~100 items makes the estimate defensible.

findings.claim: Rich per-item difficulty features overfit, produce user-visible unfairness, and break cold start — and the documented industrial fix was to delete them.
findings.detail: Settles & Meeder 2016 §4.4, read from the PDF. After HLR was deployed to all Duolingo students, "active students pointed out that particular words or skills would decay rapidly, regardless of how often they practiced. Upon closer investigation, these complaints could be traced to lexeme tag features with highly negative weights in the HLR model... This implied that some feature-based overfitting had occurred, despite the L2 regularization term in the training procedure." Simultaneously, Duolingo was launching new language courses for which "no training data yet existed to fit lexeme tag feature weights" — the cold-start problem. Their fix: HLR-lex, which uses interaction-count features only (no linguistic features). Result was Experiment II above: all three retention metrics significantly higher, and the previously complaining users "were also positive about the change". The two top HLR variants were "virtually tied" on offline predictive metrics — i.e. offline metrics gave no signal that the feature-rich model was harmful.

sources.citation: Settles, B. & Meeder, B. (2016). ACL 2016, §4.4. Single company, n=3.3M randomised users; findings are an industrial post-mortem, not a controlled test of the overfitting mechanism.

findings.implication: For cold-starting a new hanzi/word item's difficulty, use item features only as a heavily shrunken prior, and clamp it. Concretely: predicted_initial_difficulty = global_mean + 0.3 × (feature_model_prediction − global_mean), where the feature model uses only stroke count, character count, character-frequency band and whether all component characters are already introduced; then hard-clamp the resulting initial interval to [0.5×, 1.5×] the global new-item interval, and let observed responses fully override the prior after 5 responses on that item (empirical-Bayes shrinkage weight n/(n+5)). Store `prior_difficulty` and `observed_difficulty` as separate columns so you can turn the prior off in one line if the same failure appears.

findings.claim: Deep knowledge tracing does not reliably beat logistic regression over hand-built count features; across eight standard datasets the two split the wins evenly and the gaps are 0.01–0.06 AUC.
findings.detail: Results table read in full from the authors' own repository for Gervet, Koedinger, Schneider & Mitchell, "When is Deep Learning the Best Approach to Knowledge Tracing?" (JEDM 2020). AUC, Best-LR (logistic regression on item + skill + counts + time-window features) vs DKT vs SAKT across assistments09 (3,241 users / 278,868 interactions), assistments12 (29,018 / 2.71M), assistments15 (14,567 / 658,887), assistments17 (1,708 / 942,814), bridge_algebra06 (1,146 / 1.82M), algebra05 (574 / 607,025), spanish (182 / 578,726), statics (282 / 189,297). Best-LR wins or ties: assist09 0.77 vs DKT 0.75; bridge06 0.80 vs 0.79; algebra05 0.83 vs 0.82 (tie with DAS3H); spanish 0.86 vs 0.83. DKT wins: assist12 0.77 vs 0.75; assist15 0.73 vs 0.70; assist17 0.77 vs 0.71; statics 0.83 vs 0.82. Classic IRT-only is clearly worse everywhere (0.64–0.79); PFA is erratic (0.62 on assist17, 0.85 on spanish). Note the datasets where DKT wins are the large, long-sequence ones (assist12: 2.7M interactions; assist17: median sequence length 441) — this product will never have sequences of that length. Corroborating direction, though I could not read them this session: Khajah/Lindsey/Mozer (EDM 2016) and Xiong et al. (EDM 2016) are the well-known replications reporting that DKT's reported advantage shrinks or vanishes under correct evaluation, and pyKT (NeurIPS D&B 2022) rebuilt the DLKT evaluation protocol after finding methodological problems in prior comparisons.

findings.implication: The learner model is a logistic regression, computed in the browser, over six integers per (player, item-skill): total attempts, total correct, attempts on this character/word, correct on this character/word, days since last attempt (log1p), and item difficulty. That is ~24 bytes per player-item, trains with SGD in milliseconds on a phone, and needs no server, no model file and no ML dependency. Explicitly do not ship an RNN/transformer knowledge tracer: the datasets where deep models win have median sequence lengths in the hundreds, and a party game produces ~30 responses per player per evening.

findings.claim: HSK 3.0 (2021) exact counts, verified against the official list: 11,092 words and 3,000 characters over 9 levels, with levels of very unequal size — and it formally separates reading recognition from handwriting.
findings.detail: Counted directly from the OCR of the official Ministry of Education standard 《国际中文教育中文水平等级标准》 (GF0025-2021). Words per level: L1 500, L2 772, L3 973, L4 1000, L5 1071, L6 1140, L7–9 (a single combined band) 5636. Cumulative: L1 500, L1-2 1272, L1-3 2245, L1-4 3245, L1-5 4316, L1-6 5456, all 11,092. Characters: exactly 300 at each of L1–L6, plus 1200 for the combined L7–9 band = 3,000 total. Separately and importantly, the standard publishes three *handwriting* character lists — 初等 300, 中等 400, 高等 500 (1,200 total) — which are a strict subset of the reading requirement. So HSK 3.0 itself asserts that a learner at every level is expected to read four to six times more characters than they can write. Caveat: source is a community OCR of the official PDF, marked "OCR'ed but not extensively proofread"; the totals (11,092 words / 3,000 characters) match the officially announced figures, which is a good consistency check, but individual entries may contain OCR errors.

sources.citation: Ministry of Education of the PRC / Chinese Proficiency Grading Standards for International Chinese Language Education (GF0025-2021), word and character lists; counted from the Pleco OCR extraction (elkmovie/hsk30), 11,092 word entries and 4,200 character entries parsed 2026-08-22.

findings.implication: Two content decisions follow. (1) A reading-only product is not a shortcut around HSK — it is aligned with the official standard, which itself demands 3,000 read characters against only 1,200 written ones. Say so in the onboarding copy; it removes the "but shouldn't I learn to write?" objection in one sentence. (2) Levels are not equal-sized (L1→L2 is +54% words, L6→L7-9 is +394%), so never render HSK progress as equal-width segments in a progress bar — use area-proportional segments or drop the HSK framing from the progress UI entirely.

findings.claim: Character coverage of the HSK 3.0 word list is steeply non-linear: the first 300 characters unlock 97% of HSK-1 words but only 13% of the whole list; 900 characters cross the 50% line.
findings.detail: Computed this session over the official HSK 3.0 lists. A word counts as "fully decodable" when every one of its characters is in the cumulative character set. Cumulative characters → fully-decodable words out of 11,092: 300 chars → 1,415 (12.8%); 600 → 3,544 (32.0%); 900 → 5,787 (52.2%); 1,200 → 7,318 (66.0%); 1,500 → 8,346 (75.2%); 1,800 → 9,367 (84.4%); 3,000 → 11,092 (100%). Within level 1, the 300 L1 characters fully cover 487 of the 500 L1 words (97.4%). Separately, 330 characters account for 50% of all hanzi token occurrences inside the wordlist, and 996 characters account for 80%. Caveat: this is type coverage within a curated pedagogical wordlist, not token coverage of running text; corpus-based running-text coverage figures are a different (and generally more favourable) statistic that I could not verify this session.

sources.citation: Computed 2026-08-22 over the GF0025-2021 word list (11,092 entries) and character list (3,000 reading characters), parsed from the Pleco OCR extraction.

findings.implication: Make the item bank character-first with an explicit dependency graph, not word-first. Every word item stores `component_char_ids[]`, and a word item is ineligible for selection until all its component characters have been introduced. This is a hard constraint in the selection query, not a soft preference. It also gives you the single most motivating progress display available: "you know 312 characters → 1,502 words are now readable", a number that jumps by tens of words each time one character lands, which is far more rewarding than a per-item percentage.

findings.claim: HSK level ordering is close to useless as the content spine for a survival-reading product: of a 125-item menu/metro/supermarket/shopfront set, only 16% appear in HSK 1–2 and 40% are absent from the entire 11,092-word HSK 3.0 list.
findings.detail: Audit computed this session. A 125-item hand-built survival set was matched against the official HSK 3.0 word list. Menu (n=40): 18% in HSK 1-2, 22% in HSK 1-3, 40% absent from HSK 3.0 entirely (面条 炒饭 牛肉 猪肉 羊肉 鸡肉 红烧 凉拌 结账 服务员 …). Metro (n=29): 17% in HSK 1-2, 24% in HSK 1-3, 45% absent (换乘 末班车 刷卡 充值 单程票 闸机 开往 下一站 终点站 请勿 扶梯 …). Supermarket labels (n=30): 0% in HSK 1-2, 3% in HSK 1-3, 50% absent (生产日期 净含量 配料 原产地 冷藏 收银台 无糖 低脂 脱脂 全脂 …). Shopfronts (n=26): 31% in HSK 1-2, 38% in HSK 1-3, 23% absent. The picture inverts at the character level: across all 125 items there are 202 distinct characters, of which only 1 (荤) falls outside the HSK 3,000 at all; 26% fall outside the HSK 1-3 900-character set and 42% outside the HSK 1-2 600-character set. Honest limitation: the survival set is my own construction, not a corpus sample, so the exact percentages are illustrative; the direction and the character-level result (99.5% inside HSK 3000, 74% inside HSK 1-3) are robust to reasonable changes in the item list.

sources.citation: Audit computed 2026-08-22: 125 hand-constructed survival items across four signage domains matched against the GF0025-2021 word and character lists.

findings.implication: Do not order the item bank by HSK level, and do not promise "HSK 1 lets you read a menu" — it demonstrably does not. Build the bank from a signage/menu/label corpus (photograph 200 real menus, metro signs and product labels; extract and frequency-rank), order by real-world frequency within domain, and carry HSK level only as a metadata annotation used for difficulty priors and for players who also want an HSK narrative. Ship four domain decks — MENU, METRO, SHOP LABEL, SHOPFRONT — and let players pick the trip they are taking. Use the 900-character HSK 1-3 set as the character spine (it covers 74% of survival characters) and add the ~53 out-of-band survival characters (乘 促 储 冻 刷 勿 厅 厢 售 巾 扶 招 料 炒 烧 禁 素 腐 荐 藏 袋 询 账 质 购 辣 递 酸 铺 销 闸 馒 鲜 …) as a fifth, explicitly named "street characters" deck.

findings.claim: FSRS's own headline efficiency claim — "20–30% fewer reviews than SM-2 for the same retention" — is explicitly stated by the project to be simulation-based, and the project has published no A/B test or user study.
findings.detail: Read this session from the FSRS project's own wiki (page last updated 2026-02-12): FSRS users need "20–30% fewer reviews than with SM-2 algorithm to achieve the same retention level", with the project's own note that this "figure is based on simulation results". Corroborating: I enumerated all repositories in the open-spaced-repetition GitHub organisation (~28 repos: implementations in TS/Rust/Python/Go/Swift/Ruby/Dart/PHP/R, srs-benchmark, srs-simulator, fsrs-optimizer, Anki add-ons) and there is no A/B test, user study, or learning-outcome experiment repository. The benchmark measures recall *prediction* accuracy only. There is peer-reviewed work behind the underlying memory model — Ye, Su & Cao's SSP-MMC (KDD 2022, over 220 million MaiMemo memory-behaviour logs) and its TKDE 2023 successor — but I could not retrieve either full text this session (dl.acm.org, ieeexplore.ieee.org and maimemo.com are all egress-blocked), so I cannot confirm what outcome measures those papers used.

findings.implication: Never put a numeric efficiency claim ("learn 30% faster", "half the reviews") anywhere in the product, the store listing or the onboarding. There is no experimental evidence behind the industry's most-cited such number. If you want a defensible on-screen claim, make it about the item bank instead — "every word in this deck was photographed off a real Beijing menu" — which is true and verifiable.

findings.claim: FSRS-6 is a 21-parameter closed-form model with a per-item state of two floats, and both scheduler and optimiser have production-grade browser implementations — so the whole adaptive layer can run offline in a PWA with no backend.
findings.detail: Read from source this session. Forgetting curve: R(t,S) = (1 + FACTOR · t/S)^DECAY, defined so that R = 0.9 when t = S; FSRS-4.5 used DECAY = −0.5, FACTOR = 19/81; FSRS-6 makes decay a fitted parameter with default 0.1542. Inverse for scheduling: I(r,S) = (S/FACTOR)·(r^(1/DECAY) − 1), so I = S when r = 0.9. Per-item memory state is exactly (stability: f32, difficulty: f32); FSRS-6 has 21 default parameters shipped as a constant vector "fitting the average person's learning habits" (fsrs-rs `DEFAULT_PARAMETERS`, values 0.212, 1.2931, 2.3065, 8.2956, 6.4133, 0.8334, 3.0194, 0.001, 1.8722, 0.1666, 0.796, 1.4835, 0.0614, 0.2629, 1.6483, 0.6014, 1.8729, 0.5425, 0.0912, 0.0658, 0.1542). Default desired retention is 0.9 throughout the reference implementations; the project states 0.70–0.97 is the reasonable range. Implementations: `ts-fsrs` (npm, pure TypeScript, FSRS-6, requires Node ≥20 to build), `@open-spaced-repetition/binding` (WASI/WASM optimiser), and `fsrs-browser` (browser-based FSRS with optimizer and scheduler).

findings.implication: Per-(player, item) scheduling state is 16 bytes: stability f32, difficulty f32, last_review int64-as-f64. A full bank of 3,000 characters + 3,000 words × 8 local players is 48,000 rows ≈ 800 KB in IndexedDB — trivially within a PWA budget and fully offline. Compute R(t,S) inline at selection time from the stored state rather than persisting a due-date, so a device that has been asleep for three weeks needs no catch-up job on wake. Ship the 21 default parameters as a frozen constant; wire the WASM optimiser behind a dev flag only.

findings.claim: There is a de-facto standard review-log schema for spaced repetition, and adopting it now costs nothing while keeping every future analysis option open.
findings.detail: Read in full from the FSRS Optimizer specification, which is explicitly intended as "a standardized, universal optimizer to various FSRS implementations" and "a ubiquitous standard for spaced repetition review logs". Required: card_id (int or string), review_time (timestamp in MILLISECONDS, UTC), review_rating (int, {1 Again, 2 Hard, 3 Good, 4 Easy}). Optional but recommended: review_state (int, {0 New, 1 Learning, 2 Review, 3 Relearning}), review_duration (int, milliseconds — "measures the cost of the review"). Per-user extras: timezone (IANA string) and day_start (hour 0–23, "used to separate reviews that are divided by sleep into different days").

sources.citation: Open Spaced Repetition, FSRS Optimizer review_logs schema specification (read in full 2026-08-22)

findings.implication: Store exactly this schema from day one, plus three product-specific columns this game needs: `player_id`, `mode` (solo | group), and `role` (answered | observed | co_committed). `review_duration` in particular must be captured now — it is free to record, it is what any future optimiser needs to weigh cost, and in a party game it is also your only signal for "was this player actually looking at the screen". Use `day_start` = 4 (04:00 local) so a late-night session counts as one day, not two.
