findings.claim: I could not establish that a literature on co-located, simultaneous, multi-learner spaced-repetition item selection exists — and I could not run the searches needed to establish that it does not.
findings.detail: HONEST STATEMENT OF METHOD LIMITS. This session's web-search budget was exhausted before I began (200/200 calls used), and the egress proxy blocks arxiv.org, aclanthology.org, api.semanticscholar.org, osf.io, openreview.net, dl.acm.org, ieeexplore.ieee.org, nature.com, pnas.org, files.eric.ed.gov, educationaldatamining.org, ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, doi.org and every publisher host I probed; only github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com were reachable. So I ran no database searches for "group spaced repetition", "collaborative spaced repetition", "group-adaptive sequencing" or "multi-learner item selection". From prior knowledge I am not aware of a substantive literature on simultaneous multi-learner item selection; the nearest adjacent bodies of work are group knowledge tracing / group-level student modelling, group formation in CSCL, and reciprocal peer tutoring — none of which solve "one item, N learners, one screen, right now". That is a plausible but UNVERIFIED gap claim and must be checked before it is relied on. The design consequence below is derived from first principles plus the transferable evidence above, not from a located source.
findings.implication: Treat the group-selection layer as the one genuinely novel component of the system and budget accordingly — it is the part with no library, no benchmark and no paper to copy. Architecturally, keep per-player scheduling state strictly per-player (never a shared group state), and make the group layer a pure, stateless selection function: `pickItem(candidates, players[]) -> item`, taking each player's R for each candidate and returning one item. Because it is pure and stateless you can swap the objective, log the counterfactual (what each alternative objective would have chosen), and A/B it later without touching storage. Do NOT collapse players into a single averaged learner — that discards the information the selection function exists to use.
findings._topic: Scheduling, adaptivity and measurement for a co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA — spaced repetition algorithms, knowledge tracing, group-adaptive sequencing, vocabulary-gain measurement, cold start and adaptive-system failure modes

findings.claim: Buzzer-race scoring destroys the measurement the scheduler depends on; simultaneous hidden commit followed by reveal restores it and collapses most of the per-learner/shared-item tension.
findings.detail: Reasoned from the evidence above, not from a located study on group play. The mechanism: FSRS-style state updates require a *retrieval attempt outcome* per learner per item. In a first-to-buzz format, one player answers and N−1 players produce no observable outcome — their exposure is a study event, not a retrieval, and the literature the schedulers are fitted on contains no such event type, so any grade you invent for them is fabricated data being fed back into the model. Duolingo's own failure mode (the overfitting finding above) shows how quickly bad per-item signal becomes user-visible unfairness. If instead every player commits an answer privately within the same time window and all answers reveal together, every round yields a genuine, independent retrieval outcome for every player — the shared-item constraint stops being a measurement problem and becomes purely a difficulty-targeting problem, which is solvable separately (see the response-format finding). Boundary condition: this only works if commit is genuinely blind — visible partial input, or a visible "3 of 4 have answered" counter that names people, reintroduces copying.

sources.citation: Derived from the requirement structure of FSRS/HLR review logs (review_rating per card per review) — Open Spaced Repetition FSRS Optimizer schema

findings.implication: Core interaction loop: item appears → all players get a fixed commit window (start at 7 s for recognition items; the window is the same for everyone) → each player taps their answer on their own phone with no visual feedback to others beyond an anonymous filled-dot count → window closes or all committed → simultaneous reveal with per-player correctness. Never award points for speed-to-buzz. If you want a speed dimension, award it *within* the commit window as a tiebreaker on an already-correct answer, so the incentive is to be right, not to be fast and wrong. Log one review row per player per round, always — `role: co_committed`, never a fabricated grade for a non-responder.
findings._topic: Scheduling, adaptivity and measurement for a co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA — spaced repetition algorithms, knowledge tracing, group-adaptive sequencing, vocabulary-gain measurement, cold start and adaptive-system failure modes

findings.claim: With one shared item and mixed-ability players, the defensible way to restore per-learner difficulty is to vary the response format per player, not the item.
findings.detail: Reasoned from first principles given the group-SRS gap, and constrained by the retrieval-practice requirement that the task be effortful but succeed. The shared item is what makes co-located play work (shared attention, shared reaction, one thing to point at). The per-learner variable that can differ without breaking that is the *response affordance*: the same 出口 on the shared display can be a 2-alternative forced choice for a beginner, a 4-alternative choice for an intermediate, and free pinyin/meaning entry for the strongest player. Difficulty is then targeted per player against their own R for that item, while the stimulus, the timing and the social moment stay shared. This also gives a clean, monotone difficulty ladder for the success-rate controller (next finding) that does not require re-selecting the item mid-round. Caveat: the three formats are not psychometrically equivalent — a 2AFC correct is much weaker evidence of knowledge than a free-recall correct — so the grade fed to the scheduler must be discounted by format.
findings.implication: Ship three response formats per item, generated from the same item record: TIER-1 two large tappable options; TIER-2 four options; TIER-3 free entry (pinyin, or Dutch/English meaning). Each player's tier is chosen independently at round start from their own predicted R. Map format to FSRS grade with an explicit discount: free-recall correct → Good/Easy (3/4); 4-choice correct → Good (3); 2-choice correct → Hard (2), because a 50% guess rate means a single correct is weak evidence; any incorrect → Again (1). Store `format_tier` on every review row so the discount can be re-derived later. UI consequence: the shared display shows only the hanzi stimulus; all options live on the individual phones, which is also what lets the tiers differ invisibly.
findings._topic: Scheduling, adaptivity and measurement for a co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA — spaced repetition algorithms, knowledge tracing, group-adaptive sequencing, vocabulary-gain measurement, cold start and adaptive-system failure modes

findings.claim: A defensible group item-selection objective is to minimise squared deviation from a target retrievability across players, with an explicit fairness rotation — not to maximise mean expected gain.
findings.detail: Reasoned from first principles. Maximising the group mean systematically starves the extremes: in a mixed group, the mean-optimal item is one the strongest player finds trivial and the weakest cannot attempt. Two components are needed. (1) Difficulty targeting: score each candidate item i by U(i) = −Σ_p w_p·(R_p(i) − r*)², where R_p(i) is player p's FSRS retrievability and r* is the target (see the 85% finding). Squared deviation, not mean, is what penalises serving one player badly. (2) Fairness rotation: give each player a weight w_p that increases the longer it has been since an item was selected primarily for them — e.g. w_p = 1 + 0.5·(rounds_since_p_was_pivot), reset when p is the argmin contributor. Without (2), the player whose due-queue happens to overlap the group's gets all the practice. Constraint layer on top: an item is only a candidate if all its component characters have been introduced for every player (the dependency-graph finding), and never re-show an item within the same session for scoring purposes (the massed-practice failure mode).
findings.implication: Implement `pickItem` as: filter candidates by the character-dependency constraint and the no-repeat-this-session constraint → score by U(i) = −Σ_p w_p·(R_p(i) − 0.85)² → take a softmax sample over the top 8 rather than the argmax, so the same evening never produces the same sequence twice. Persist per-player `rounds_since_pivot` and the chosen item's per-player R vector on the review rows, so the selection can be evaluated retrospectively. Cost: 6,000 candidates × 8 players × one pow() = ~50k float ops per round, i.e. under 2 ms on a phone — no need for indexing tricks or a server.
findings._topic: Scheduling, adaptivity and measurement for a co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA — spaced repetition algorithms, knowledge tracing, group-adaptive sequencing, vocabulary-gain measurement, cold start and adaptive-system failure modes

findings.claim: The "85% rule" is a real result for a specific class of tasks, but it is a result about training error in continuously-tunable perceptual/classification learning, not about retention targets in discrete-item memory — and conflating the two is a design error.
findings.detail: Wilson, Shenhav, Straccia & Cohen (2019), "The Eighty Five Percent Rule for optimal learning", Nature Communications 10:4646, derives an optimal training error rate of ≈15.87% (accuracy ≈84.13%, i.e. the normal-distribution point at one standard deviation) for a family of gradient-descent-trained binary classifiers on two-alternative perceptual discrimination where task difficulty is a continuous, freely-tunable parameter. IMPORTANT: I could NOT retrieve this paper this session (nature.com and doi.org are egress-blocked); I did verify that the authors' figure-replication repository exists and is described as "Code to replicate the figures from 'The Eighty Five Percent Rule for Optimal Learning'" (MATLAB, created 2019). Treat the 15.87% figure as cited-from-record and verify before quoting. The boundary conditions matter more than the number: the derivation assumes a learner doing gradient descent on a decision boundary with continuously variable stimulus difficulty. Vocabulary recognition is discrete-item retrieval from declarative memory, where the governing quantity in the deployed systems is *desired retention*, an economic trade-off (review cost vs forgetting cost) rather than a learning-rate optimum. FSRS's own analysis frames it exactly that way — minimise workload/knowledge, i.e. "minutes of studying divided by" the sum of recall probabilities — solved numerically with Brent's method per user, with 0.70–0.97 stated as the reasonable range and 0.9 the default everywhere in the reference implementations. So there are two different targets and they should not be set from the same number.

sources.citation: Wilson, R. C., Shenhav, A., Straccia, M. & Cohen, J. D. (2019). The Eighty Five Percent Rule for optimal learning. Nature Communications 10, 4646. NOT RETRIEVED THIS SESSION (nature.com egress-blocked) — cited from record; the 15.87% optimal error rate should be re-verified against the paper.
Authors' figure-replication code repository (existence and description verified 2026-08-22)

Open Spaced Repetition, "The Optimal Retention" wiki — objective is min(workload/knowledge), knowledge = Σ R_i, solved with Brent's method; 70–97% stated as the reasonable desired-retention range (read in full 2026-08-22)

findings.implication: Use two separate knobs and never let one drive the other. (1) FSRS desired retention stays at its default 0.90 — it governs when an item comes back across days. (2) Session accuracy is targeted at ~85% and is controlled by response format, which is the continuously-tunable difficulty parameter the 85% derivation actually assumes. Concrete controller, per player, evaluated each round: rolling accuracy over that player's last 10 committed answers; if <0.75 drop one format tier (4-choice → 2-choice) and inject one already-solid item; if >0.92 raise one tier (2-choice → 4-choice → free entry). Clamp at one tier change per three rounds so the difficulty does not oscillate visibly.
findings._topic: Scheduling, adaptivity and measurement for a co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA — spaced repetition algorithms, knowledge tracing, group-adaptive sequencing, vocabulary-gain measurement, cold start and adaptive-system failure modes

findings.claim: Elo-style rating is the right cold-start mechanism for item difficulty in this product, because it converges in tens of responses where IRT calibration needs hundreds — but I could not verify the published deployment descriptions this session.
findings.detail: NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION — every host carrying these papers was egress-blocked. From record: Pelánek's group deployed Elo-based item/learner rating in production adaptive-learning systems (slepemapy.cz geography practice, later the Umíme/ProblemSolving.cz family), reporting that Elo item-difficulty estimates converge quickly and correlate strongly with IRT-derived difficulties while being computable online with O(1) work per response. The key published refinement is an uncertainty-decaying update constant, K(n) = a/(1 + b·n), so early responses move an estimate a lot and later ones barely at all — functionally a cheap Glicko. The relevant references are Papoušek, Pelánek & Stanislav (EDM 2014, "Adaptive Practice of Facts in Domains with Varied Prior Knowledge") and Pelánek (2016, Computers & Education, "Applications of the Elo rating system in adaptive educational systems"). Sample sizes and exact convergence figures must be re-checked. The contrast with IRT is the load-bearing part and is standard psychometrics: 2PL item calibration wants on the order of several hundred responses per item for stable discrimination estimates, Rasch/1PL rather fewer — either way far more than a party game will generate per item in its first months.

sources.citation: Pelánek, R. (2016). Applications of the Elo rating system in adaptive educational systems. Computers & Education 98, 169–179. NOT RETRIEVED — publisher and DOI hosts egress-blocked.
Papoušek, J., Pelánek, R. & Stanislav, V. (2014). Adaptive Practice of Facts in Domains with Varied Prior Knowledge. EDM 2014. NOT RETRIEVED — educationaldatamining.org and fi.muni.cz egress-blocked.

findings.implication: Store two scalars per item (difficulty θ_i, response count n_i) and two per player (ability θ_p, count n_p), 16 bytes each. Update both after every committed answer with K = 0.4/(1 + 0.05·n), which gives a large early move that has decayed to ~0.13 by the 40th response. Use θ_i as the shrunken prior for FSRS initial difficulty (see the overfitting finding) and as the *only* difficulty signal for an item with fewer than 5 responses. Practical consequence: a brand-new item photographed off a menu becomes usably calibrated after roughly 30 responses — one evening with six players seeing it five times — so you can add content continuously without a pretesting pipeline.
findings._topic: Scheduling, adaptivity and measurement for a co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA — spaced repetition algorithms, knowledge tracing, group-adaptive sequencing, vocabulary-gain measurement, cold start and adaptive-system failure modes

findings.claim: A yes/no vocabulary test with pseudoword false-alarm correction is the cheapest valid measure of reading-vocabulary gain and is the right instrument for this product — with the caveat that Chinese requires pseudo-WORDS built from real characters, not pseudo-characters.
findings.detail: NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION — Language Testing, ERIC and all publisher hosts were egress-blocked. From record: the yes/no (checklist) vocabulary format asks "do you know this word?" over a list seeded with non-existent items; the non-words measure overclaiming and the score is corrected accordingly (hits minus false alarms, or the Isec / Δm corrections). Foundational and validation references: Meara & Buxton (1987, Language Testing 4(2)) introducing the format with imaginary words; Mochida & Harrington (2006, Language Testing 23(1)) validating yes/no scores against the Vocabulary Levels Test; Pellicer-Sánchez & Schmitt (2012, Language Testing 29(4)) on scoring-formula behaviour. Sample sizes and the relative merits of the correction formulas must be re-checked before any of this is quoted. The Chinese-specific adaptation is a genuine design constraint: a pseudo-character (an invented glyph) is trivially rejectable and would collapse the false-alarm rate to zero, destroying the correction. The valid analogue is a pseudo-word — a string of two real, well-formed characters that is not a word (the standard stimulus type in Chinese lexical-decision work). Related instruments I could not verify: Nation & Beglar's Vocabulary Size Test (2007) and its Chinese analogues, which are longer, norm-referenced, and much less suited to a 90-second in-app check-in.

sources.citation: Meara, P. & Buxton, B. (1987). An alternative to multiple choice vocabulary tests. Language Testing 4(2), 142–154. NOT RETRIEVED — egress-blocked.
Mochida, A. & Harrington, M. (2006). The Yes/No test as a measure of receptive vocabulary knowledge. Language Testing 23(1), 73–98. NOT RETRIEVED — egress-blocked.
Pellicer-Sánchez, A. & Schmitt, N. (2012). Scoring Yes–No vocabulary tests: Reaction time vs. nonword approaches. Language Testing 29(4), 489–509. NOT RETRIEVED — egress-blocked.

findings.implication: Ship a 60-item check-in: 40 real items sampled proportionally across the player's covered frequency bands + 20 pseudowords, each pseudoword built by pairing two real characters the player has already met into a non-word (e.g. 票冷). Present one item per screen, two buttons (读得懂 / 读不懂), no time pressure, ~90 seconds total. Score as corrected hit rate = hits/40 − false_alarms/20, floored at 0. Run it at first launch, then every 10 completed sessions, then on demand. Store `checkin_id, timestamp, hits, false_alarms, corrected_score, band_breakdown` — that is the product's only real learning-outcome metric and it costs one screen and no backend. Do NOT use pseudo-characters; they are rejected on sight and make the correction term zero.
findings._topic: Scheduling, adaptivity and measurement for a co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA — spaced repetition algorithms, knowledge tracing, group-adaptive sequencing, vocabulary-gain measurement, cold start and adaptive-system failure modes

findings.claim: HSK level-to-CEFR alignment is contested and should not appear in the product; report progress against the official HSK word/character lists instead, which you can compute exactly.
findings.detail: NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION — I could not retrieve the critical literature (all journal and repository hosts egress-blocked) and I could not search. From record, the contested points are: HSK 2.0's official CEFR mapping (HSK 6 ≈ C2) was widely criticised as inflated relative to the vocabulary and character load actually required, with HSK 6's ~5,000 words being far below the lexical demands of C2 in European-language frameworks; HSK 3.0 (GF0025-2021) restructured to nine levels across three bands and expanded the vocabulary requirement substantially, which is generally read as an implicit acknowledgement of the earlier gap. What I CAN state with certainty from the official lists I parsed is the objective side of the argument: HSK 3.0 requires 11,092 words and 3,000 reading characters in total, versus HSK 2.0's roughly 5,000 words at level 6 — i.e. the top-end requirement roughly doubled between the two standards, which is itself evidence that the earlier level claims were not stable. The specific published criticisms and any CEFR-alignment studies must be located and read before any of this is asserted in writing.

sources.citation: Chinese Proficiency Grading Standards for International Chinese Language Education (GF0025-2021) — official word and character lists, counted directly this session: 11,092 words, 3,000 reading characters, nine levels in three bands.
Ministry of Education of the PRC announcement of GF0025-2021. NOT RETRIEVED — moe.gov.cn egress-blocked.

findings.implication: Put no CEFR letter anywhere in the UI and make no equivalence claim between an HSK level and a real-world ability. Express progress in two ways only, both of which you can compute and defend: (1) counts against the official lists — "312 / 900 HSK 1-3 characters solid"; (2) domain coverage against your own photographed corpus — "you can read 62% of the words on an average Beijing metro sign". The second is the one to make the hero number, because it is the promise the product actually makes and it is measured on the actual target material.
findings._topic: Scheduling, adaptivity and measurement for a co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA — spaced repetition algorithms, knowledge tracing, group-adaptive sequencing, vocabulary-gain measurement, cold start and adaptive-system failure modes

findings.claim: The documented failure modes of adaptive selection are massed-practice inflation, the all-hard death spiral, and sustained-failure demotivation; the mitigations are cheap, hard constraints rather than tuning.
findings.detail: Partly evidenced, partly reasoned. Directly evidenced from this session: the Duolingo post-mortem (Settles & Meeder §4.4) is a documented instance of an adaptive system driving a subset of items to punishingly short intervals, producing user complaints that specific words "would decay rapidly, regardless of how often they practiced" — an all-hard spiral confined to a feature-defined slice of the item bank, invisible in offline metrics because the two model variants were "virtually tied". Also evidenced: FSRS's own retention analysis frames scheduling as minimising workload/knowledge, which makes explicit that pushing retention up drives review volume up superlinearly — the mechanism behind session bloat. Reasoned (NOT located in the literature this session): massed-practice inflation, where re-showing an item within a session produces an easy correct that the scheduler reads as evidence of durable learning; and the demotivation path from sustained failure, which is a well-established motivational finding I could not verify a source for here. Note the massed-practice point interacts with the group format: in a party game the same item may recur naturally within an evening, so this is not a hypothetical.

sources.citation: Settles, B. & Meeder, B. (2016). ACL 2016, §4.4 — documented production failure: over-short intervals on a feature-defined item slice, user complaints, offline metrics blind to it.
Open Spaced Repetition, "The Optimal Retention" wiki — workload/knowledge objective, showing the superlinear review-volume cost of raising retention.

findings.implication: Four hard constraints in the selection function, none of them tunable by the difficulty controller. (1) No item is scored twice in one session — if it must recur, log it with `role: exposure` and do not update stability. (2) An item may not advance out of LEARNING on the strength of same-session corrects; require one correct in a later session. (3) Cap consecutive incorrect answers for any player at 2 — on the third, force-inject an item where that player's R > 0.95, regardless of what the group objective wants. (4) Cap any item's per-player minimum interval at 1 day, so no word can ever be scheduled into the punishing sub-daily loop Duolingo's users hit. Add one monitoring query you actually look at: the per-item distribution of mean interval, so a slice of the bank collapsing to the floor is visible before players complain.
findings._topic: Scheduling, adaptivity and measurement for a co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA — spaced repetition algorithms, knowledge tracing, group-adaptive sequencing, vocabulary-gain measurement, cold start and adaptive-system failure modes

findings.claim: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing and Performance Factors Analysis remain the correct reference baselines, and mature open implementations exist — but BKT's binary-mastery framing is a poor fit for a forgetting-dominated reading task.
findings.detail: Partly verified. Verified this session from the pyBKT repository: BKT and its standard variants (individual student priors/learn-rate/guess/slip; per-item guess and slip; per-item or per-resource learn rate) have a maintained Python implementation, documented in Badrinath, Wang & Pardos (EDM 2021, pp. 468–474) and Bulut et al. (2023, Psych 5(3), 770–786), with the variant lineage traced to Pardos & Heffernan (UMAP 2010), KT-IDEM (UMAP 2011), Pardos et al. (EDM 2013) and Xu, Johnson & Pardos (ICML ML4Ed 2015). Not verified this session: the original BKT formulation (Corbett & Anderson 1995) and PFA (Pavlik, Cen & Koedinger, AIED 2009) — both egress-blocked. The structural objection is model-theoretic and does not need a citation: BKT's latent state is a binary "mastered / not mastered" with a monotone learn transition and NO forget transition in its standard form. For a Dutch or English speaker learning hanzi recognition, forgetting is the dominant dynamic — which is precisely why the spaced-repetition family (FSRS, HLR, DASH) models a continuous, decaying retrievability instead. PFA, being a logistic model over prior successes and failures, is closer to the Best-LR baseline that performed well in Gervet et al., but its per-dataset variance there was large (AUC 0.62 to 0.85).

sources.citation: pyBKT repository and its variant/citation list, read in full 2026-08-22: Badrinath, A., Wang, F. & Pardos, Z. A. (2021), pyBKT: An Accessible Python Library of Bayesian Knowledge Tracing Models, EDM 2021, 468–474; Bulut, O. et al. (2023), An introduction to Bayesian knowledge tracing with pyBKT, Psych 5(3), 770–786.
Pavlik, P. I., Cen, H. & Koedinger, K. R. (2009). Performance Factors Analysis — A New Alternative to Knowledge Tracing. AIED 2009. NOT RETRIEVED — pact.cs.cmu.edu returned 403 from the egress proxy.
Gervet et al. (2020) results table, PFA row (AUC 0.62–0.85 across eight datasets)

findings.implication: Do not model mastery as a binary latent state and do not ship a BKT. Every item's per-player state is continuous and decaying: (stability, difficulty, last_seen) for scheduling, plus the six counts for the logistic prediction. The UI must follow the model, not fight it — that means no "mastered" badge that can never be revoked, and no achievement that permanently certifies a character. Use the three-state chip (new / learning / solid) where SOLID can and does silently fall back to LEARNING when R decays below ~0.7, and show that as a gentle "3 characters need a refresh" nudge rather than as a demotion.
findings._topic: Scheduling, adaptivity and measurement for a co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA — spaced repetition algorithms, knowledge tracing, group-adaptive sequencing, vocabulary-gain measurement, cold start and adaptive-system failure modes

findings.claim: Signage is a function-word-free telegraphic register, so pure character-frequency ordering is at its LEAST useful exactly at the beginning of learning. The top of every Chinese frequency list is dominated by grammatical morphemes that essentially never carry meaning on a sign.
findings.detail: Jun Da's Modern Chinese Character Frequency List (~193M character corpus, 2004) and SUBTLEX-CH (Cai & Brysbaert 2010, ~47M characters of film/TV subtitles) both open with 的 一 是 了 我 不 人 在 他 有 这 个 上 们 来 到 时 大 地 为 子 中 你 说 生 国 年 着 就 那 和 要. Of the top 50, my estimate is that roughly 30 are function words, copulas, pronouns, aspect markers, or verbs of speech/cognition (的了是在和有就不也都而我你他们说想会能对之于所) which appear on public signage only inside longer set phrases, never as the load-bearing element. Signage drops function words the way headlines and telegrams do: 禁止吸烟, 小心地滑, 开往西直门方向, 保质期12个月 — no 的, no 了, no pronouns. Estimated yield: the first 50 characters by frequency give you perhaps 15-20 that change your behaviour on a sign; 50 characters chosen functionally give you ~50. That is a ~2.5-3x efficiency gap over the first 100 characters, converging with frequency ordering somewhere around 1,200-1,500 characters where the functional set is exhausted and only frequency remains as a guide. UNVERIFIED: I could not open either frequency list this session. Verification recipe: take Jun Da's top 300, tag each character for 'appears as the semantically load-bearing element of a public sign, menu line, or product label', and plot cumulative signage-yield against cumulative corpus frequency; the two curves should visibly diverge below rank 300 and re-converge above ~1,500.

sources.citation: Cai, Q., & Brysbaert, M. (2010). SUBTLEX-CH: Chinese word and character frequencies based on film subtitles. PLoS ONE, 5(6), e10729.
Da, Jun (2004). A corpus-based study of character and bigram frequencies in Chinese e-texts. Modern Chinese Character Frequency List, Middle Tennessee State University (~193M characters).
Xun, E., Rao, G., Xiao, X., & Zang, J. (2016). The construction of the BCC Corpus in the age of Big Data. Corpus Linguistics, 3(1). BLCU Corpus Center, ~15 billion characters.

findings.implication: Do NOT seed the item bank from a frequency list. Order the bank by functional payoff and use frequency only as a tie-breaker within a functional tier. Concretely: ship Tier 0 = 60 characters that change behaviour (出入口男女禁止小心危险开关推拉上下大小前后内外满空免费收费营业休息元角分斤克特价折满减号线站换乘辣麻素荤生冷热), Tier 1 = +120, Tier 2 = +200, total ~380 characters for functional literacy across all five domains. Store a `freqRank` field per item but never sort by it at the top level.
findings._topic: A corpus-grounded survival READING curriculum for China — what to learn first, ordered by real payoff, for a phone-first co-located multiplayer Mandarin reading PWA aimed at Dutch and English speakers. NOTE ON METHOD: this session had zero source-retrieval capability (WebSearch budget exhausted at 200/200 before this agent started; all outbound HTTPS to scholar.google.com, api.semanticscholar.org, arxiv.org, aclanthology.org, eric.ed.gov, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, frontiersin.org, cambridge.org, lingua.mtsu.edu and every institutional repository returned 403 policy denials from the egress proxy). ZERO papers were read. Every citation below is from model knowledge and is UNVERIFIED in this session; the `access` field is deliberately omitted from all sources rather than falsely claiming full-text or abstract access. Evidence grades reflect my confidence in the literature as I know it, discounted for the fact that I could not check anything. Treat every numeric claim as a hypothesis with a stated verification recipe, not as a measurement. The lexical lists are a different matter: they are practitioner/domain knowledge, are the substance of the deliverable, and are stated as such.

findings.claim: The linguistic-landscape research tradition cannot supply the corpus this product needs. LL studies code signs by LANGUAGE, script, and top-down/bottom-up authorship — they almost never publish a character or lexeme frequency distribution. There is, to my knowledge, no published character-frequency corpus of Chinese urban signage.
findings.detail: The field's founding paper (Landry & Bourhis 1997, n=2,010 Francophone students) defines the linguistic landscape as the visibility of languages on public signs and measures ethnolinguistic vitality, not lexis. Ben-Rafael, Shohamy, Amara & Trumper-Hecht (2006) introduced the top-down (government) vs bottom-up (private) coding that most subsequent work uses. Backhaus (2007) — the methodological benchmark, 2,444 multilingual signs across 28 survey areas on Tokyo's Yamanote line — counts sign tokens by language combination. Chinese-context LL work (Shang Guowen & Zhao Shouhui's review in 外语教学与研究, 2014, introduced the paradigm to Chinese scholarship; the Shohamy & Gorter 2009 edited volume contains Chinese cases) follows the same coding scheme: it will tell you what proportion of Shenzhen shop signs are Chinese-only vs Chinese-English, and nothing about which characters recur. That is the wrong axis for a reading curriculum. UNVERIFIED: none of these retrieved. The honest conclusion is a negative finding, and it is the single most consequential one in this report — the item bank CANNOT be corpus-derived from published work and must be either practitioner-derived (declared as such) or derived from a bespoke photo corpus you build yourself.

findings.implication: Architecture: build the corpus as a product feature. Ship a `capture` mode where a player photographs a real sign, the photo is stored locally with GPS + city + domain tag, and the characters they could not read are queued as candidate items. Store: `{imageBlob, lat, lng, city, domainTag, ocrText[], unknownChars[], capturedAt}`. Sync captures peer-to-peer at the end of a co-located session so a group of four travellers pools one corpus. After ~5,000 captures you own the dataset nobody has published, and the item bank stops being practitioner-derived. Until then, label every item in the bank with `provenance: 'practitioner' | 'corpus' | 'capture'` and surface it in the app's about screen.

findings.claim: Transit is the LOWEST-payoff of the five domains, not the highest, because Chinese public transport signage is bilingual by national standard. Menus, supermarket labels and neighbourhood shopfronts are where English disappears and reading actually pays.
findings.detail: GB/T 30240 《公共服务领域英文译写规范》 (Guidelines for the Use of English in Public Service Areas), issued 2017 in 10 parts covering transport, tourism, culture, sport, education, medicine, post/telecom, catering, commerce and finance, standardised English translations across public service signage. In practice this means tier-1 and most tier-2 metro systems, high-speed rail stations and airports carry near-total English coverage: 出口/Exit, 换乘/Transfer, 安检/Security Check, 检票口/Ticket Gate. Airports and HSR are the most anglicised built environments in China. Meanwhile the catering part of the standard governs translated dish names on menus but is only advisory and is applied almost exclusively in tourist-facing restaurants; the neighbourhood 面馆 and the 干锅 place have a laminated Chinese-only sheet or a QR code that opens a Chinese-only mini-programme. Supermarket product labels are governed by GB 7718 (food labelling) which mandates CHINESE and permits but does not require foreign language, and requires that any foreign text be no larger than the corresponding Chinese — so labels are functionally Chinese-only. Shopfront fascias are unregulated for language and are overwhelmingly Chinese-only outside tourist strips. UNVERIFIED against the standard texts. Payoff ranking that follows: (1) supermarket/product labels — no English, high consequence (allergens, dates, price-per-catty), high frequency of use; (2) menus — little English away from tourist areas, highest emotional stakes, several times a day; (3) shopfronts — no English, needed to find the thing at all; (4) universal safety/instruction signage — partly pictographic, partly bilingual, but the residue is high-consequence; (5) transit — heavily bilingual, high pictogram support, lowest marginal payoff per character learned.

findings.implication: Reorder the five categories in the shuffled-bag draw. Do NOT give the five domains equal weight. Weight the bag: market/label 30%, menu 30%, street/shopfront 20%, safety/universal 15%, transit 5%. Put a one-line justification in the app ('the metro is already in English; the noodle shop is not') because the ordering is counter-intuitive and players will otherwise think the bank is broken. Keep transit in the bank at low weight for the 20% of the trip that is a small-city bus station where the standard has not reached.

findings.claim: China's safety signage is a four-category colour-and-shape system fixed by national standard. Teaching the four categories takes about 90 seconds and removes the need to read the characters at all in the highest-consequence situations.
findings.detail: GB 2894 《安全标志及其使用导则》 defines four sign classes: 禁止 (prohibition) = red circle with diagonal bar; 警告 (warning) = yellow equilateral triangle, black border; 指令 (mandatory) = blue filled circle; 提示 (notice/information) = green square. GB/T 10001 《公共信息图形符号》 governs the public information pictograms (toilets, lifts, exits). The emergency exit sign is green with a running figure and reads 安全出口, not 出口 — a distinction worth teaching, because 出口 on a blue or black plate is just the way out of the station, while green 安全出口 is the fire escape. The colour therefore delivers the illocutionary force — forbidden / beware / you must / here is — before a single character is decoded, which collapses a reading task into a two-bit classification plus a specific-content lookup. This is a genuine free lunch and belongs at the very front of the curriculum. UNVERIFIED against the standard texts; the colour-shape scheme itself is ISO 7010-aligned and I am confident in it.

findings.implication: UI: the safety/hazard card template must render the real GB 2894 geometry — #E60012-ish red circle+bar, #FFF100 yellow triangle with black border, #0075C2 blue disc, #00A040 green square — at correct proportions, and the first four items in the safety strand must be colour-only recognition with no characters shown at all ('what is this sign telling you to do?'). Only after those four does the app show characters inside the shapes. Never recolour these to fit the app's dark chrome; the colour IS the content.

findings.claim: The 'card is an object' design decision — rendering each item in the typography of the real-world thing — is defensible but carries a specific, documented risk: environmental-print recognition is logo-driven and does not reliably transfer to decontextualised reading.
findings.detail: Masonheimer, Drum & Ehri (1984), Journal of Reading Behavior 16(4), 257-271, n=102 preschoolers: children who confidently 'read' familiar environmental print (logos, packaging) largely failed to notice when a letter was altered — the classic manipulation being XEPSI for PEPSI — and their environmental-print skill did not predict decontextualised word reading. The mechanism is that the whole visual gestalt (colour, shape, script style, context) is the cue, not the letters. Applied here: a learner who has only ever met 出口 in enamel-blue Beijing-metro styling may be recognising the plate, not the characters, and may fail on 出口 in a red mall fascia or a black hotel corridor plate — and worse, may fail to recognise 出 in 出发, 出租, 出售, 支出. The literature on whether environmental print supports emergent literacy is genuinely contested (Neumann et al. and others report mixed or null incremental effects once general print knowledge is controlled), so grade this as a real risk, not a settled result. UNVERIFIED: not retrieved. The design response is not to abandon realistic rendering — it earns motivation and object-recognition, which is itself half of real reading — but to force transfer explicitly.

findings.implication: UX: every character must be met in at least three different object treatments before it can graduate. Add a `contexts: Set<TemplateId>` to each item's mastery record and gate graduation on `contexts.size >= 3`. Add a deliberate 'naked' probe — the character alone, system serif, on plain background, ~10-15% of presentations — and a 'wrong object' probe where 出口 appears in the fascia template instead of the transit plate. Also add an Xepsi-style foil: present a visually near-identical wrong character in the correct object styling (出 vs 山, 天 vs 夭, 士 vs 土, 未 vs 末, 己 vs 已, 干 vs 千, 人 vs 入, 大 vs 太) and require discrimination. If a player's naked-probe accuracy trails their in-object accuracy by more than ~20 points, the app is teaching plates, not characters, and should say so.

findings.claim: Environmental context-dependent memory is real but small, and it is smaller for recognition than for recall — which is the format this product uses. Do not over-invest in visual realism as a memory intervention; invest in it as a motivation and object-recognition intervention.
findings.detail: Smith & Vela (2001), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 8(2), 203-220, is the meta-analysis: environmental context-dependent memory effects are reliable across ~75 studies but modest, and are attenuated or eliminated by 'outshining' — when strong internal or semantic cues are available, the incidental environment contributes little. Godden & Baddeley's diver studies are the canonical demonstration and the canonical caveat: the 1975 study (n=18) found a substantial context effect for free RECALL, and the 1980 follow-up found essentially none for RECOGNITION. Reading a sign in the wild is a recognition task, and the app's four-option format is a recognition task, so the context-reinstatement argument for photorealistic sign rendering is weaker than it intuitively feels. UNVERIFIED: not retrieved; both are well-known and I am reasonably confident in the recall/recognition dissociation. The design conclusion is a permission slip, not a prohibition: realism is worth it for the other reasons in this report, but do not spend engineering budget chasing photographic fidelity on the expectation of a memory payoff.

findings.claim: Vocabulary-coverage thresholds derived from running text (95-98%) systematically over-predict comprehension of signage, because signs are short, unforgiving and dominated by a small closed set plus proper nouns. On a six-character sign, 98% coverage is meaningless — you either know the operative character or you don't.
findings.detail: The coverage literature: Hu & Nation (2000), Reading in a Foreign Language 13(1), n=66, found ~98% lexical coverage needed for unassisted comprehension of fiction, with 95% giving only partial comprehension; Laufer & Ravenhorst-Kalovski (2010), Reading in a Foreign Language 22(1), position 95% as a minimal and 98% as an optimal threshold; Nation (2006), Canadian Modern Language Review 63(1), estimates 8,000-9,000 word families for novels. For Chinese the widely-repeated character-coverage figures from Jun Da's corpus are roughly: top 1,000 characters ≈ 89% of running text, top 2,000 ≈ 97%, top 3,000 ≈ 99%. UNVERIFIED — I could not open the list and these numbers are cited from memory; treat the exact percentages as approximate. The reason they mislead here is statistical: coverage thresholds assume redundancy — a long text lets you infer around gaps. A sign has no redundancy. 保质期12个月 is four content characters; missing 质 or 期 loses the whole message. Signage comprehension is closer to all-or-nothing per sign than to a graded function of coverage. The right metric for this product is therefore not percentage coverage but SIGN COMPLETION RATE: the proportion of real signs in a held-out photo set that the learner can act on correctly.

findings.implication: Architecture + UI: make the progress metric 'signs you can act on', not 'characters known'. Store a held-out validation set of ~120 real composite signs (each a full sign, not a single character) tagged with the character set they require, and compute `signsActionable = |{s : requiredChars(s) ⊆ masteredChars}|`. The home screen shows '43 of 120 real signs' with a photo strip, never '187 characters'. This also makes the curriculum self-ordering: greedily pick the next character that unlocks the most unactionable signs — a set-cover heuristic — which will automatically surface 期, 质, 净, 含 ahead of higher-frequency but sign-inert characters.

findings.claim: Pinyin support builds phonology, not orthography. For a pure READING product, the bet ladder's pinyin tier is pedagogically inverted: it makes the item easier in a way that does not build the representation the player needs.
findings.detail: Guan, Liu, Chan, Ye & Perfetti (2011), Journal of Educational Psychology 103(3), 509-522: handwriting practice strengthens orthographic representations of Chinese characters, whereas alphabetic (pinyin) coding strengthens phonological representations — the two routes are dissociable, and the pinyin route does not deliver the orthographic knowledge that character recognition depends on. Related work (Shen 2005, System 33(1), n=95, on character learning strategies; Shen & Ke 2007, Modern Language Journal, on orthographic knowledge development in CFL) supports the general picture that orthographic-component awareness is the thing that separates learners who can recognise novel characters from those who cannot. UNVERIFIED: not retrieved. The consequence for this product is sharp. The current ladder is: +1/-1 shows pinyin; +5/-3 hides pinyin; +15/-10 hides pinyin and makes all four options Chinese. The pinyin at the low tier is a phonological crutch that does nothing for the reading goal — a Dutch player will read 'chū kǒu', feel supported, and learn a sound they will never need to produce. The better low-tier scaffold for a reading goal is a SEMANTIC-COMPONENT hint (the radical and what it means: 辶 = motion, 疒 = illness, 氵 = water, 钅 = metal, 忄 = heart, 月 = flesh/body-part, 灬 = fire, 饣 = food, 讠 = speech, 车 = vehicle, 门 = gate) or an object-context hint, not a pronunciation.

findings.implication: UX: change the +1/-1 tier's scaffold from 'pinyin shown' to 'semantic component highlighted and glossed'. findings.claim: Four-option multiple choice is the format-appropriate test here, and making all four options plausible Chinese signs is not just harder, it produces measurably better learning than easy distractors.
findings.detail: Two lines converge. First, transfer-appropriate processing (Morris, Bransford & Franks 1977, Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior 16(5)) says learning transfers to the extent that study processing matches test processing — and reading a sign in the wild IS a forced-choice recognition against the small set of things that sign could plausibly say. So multiple choice is not a compromise here; it is the criterion task. Second, Little & Bjork (2015), Memory & Cognition, and related work by Little, Bjork, Bjork & Angello (Psychological Science 2012) show that multiple-choice tests with COMPETITIVE, plausible alternatives produce retention benefits for the information tested AND for information related to the incorrect alternatives, because the learner must retrieve evidence about why each wrong option is wrong. Easy distractors lose this entirely. The +15/-10 tier where all four options are real Chinese signs you would plausibly confuse is therefore the tier doing the actual teaching, and the design should say so out loud. UNVERIFIED: not retrieved. Countervailing evidence in the next finding.

Morris, C. D., Bransford, J. D., & Franks, J. J. (1977). Levels of processing versus transfer appropriate processing. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 16(5), 519-533.

findings.implication: Content: author distractors as a first-class field, never generate them randomly from the bank. Every item needs `distractors: [{hanzi, whyPlausible}]` drawn from one of four confusion families — (a) visually similar characters (出/山, 天/夭, 未/末, 己/已, 干/千, 人/入, 大/太, 士/土, 日/曰, 微/徽), (b) same-radical semantic neighbours (肠/肚/肝/肺/肾), (c) real signs from the same object class that mean something dangerously different (出口 vs 入口, 推 vs 拉, 冷藏 vs 冷冻, 生产日期 vs 保质期, 禁止 vs 请勿, 男 vs 女), (d) same-first-character compounds (安检 / 安全 / 安装; 特价 / 特色 / 特产). Family (c) is the highest-value and should be at least 40% of distractors.

findings.claim: Multiple choice also implants false knowledge from the lures. Every reveal must gloss all four options, not just mark the right one.
findings.detail: Roediger & Marsh (2005), Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition 31(5), 1155-1159: taking a multiple-choice test increases correct answers on a later test but ALSO increases the production of the multiple-choice lures as answers — a negative testing effect that scales with the number of alternatives. Butler & Roediger (2008), Memory & Cognition, showed that immediate corrective feedback substantially reduces or eliminates this lure-persistence. The interaction with the previous finding is the design constraint: plausible distractors maximise learning AND maximise false-knowledge risk, and feedback is what separates the two. In a signage app the failure mode is concrete and awful — a player who saw 冷冻 as a lure on the 冷藏 item and is now unsure which is 'refrigerate'. UNVERIFIED: not retrieved; the Roediger & Marsh result is well-replicated.

findings.implication: UI: the reveal screen must show a four-row table, not a green tick. Each row: the option's hanzi at ≥32px, its pinyin, its English AND Dutch gloss, and a one-clause note on where you would actually meet it ('冷冻 = vriezer, staat op diepvriesproducten — niet hetzelfde als 冷藏'). Correct row gets the accent bar; wrong rows stay fully legible, never greyed to the point of being skimmed past. Minimum reveal dwell time of 2,000 ms before the Next button enables — in a co-located game the acting team wants to move on and the reveal is the only moment the other three players learn anything.

findings.claim: Optimal spacing gap is roughly 10-20% of the intended retention interval, and for this product the retention interval is a known date: the flight. That turns a generic SRS into a trip-anchored scheduler, which is a real and unusual product advantage.
findings.detail: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted & Rohrer (2006), Psychological Bulletin 132(3), 354-380, meta-analysed 254 distributed-practice studies (839 comparisons, 14,594 participants) and established the spacing benefit robustly. Cepeda, Vul, Rohrer, Wixted & Pashler (2008), Psychological Science 19(11), 1095-1102, n=1,354 across gaps from minutes to months and retention intervals up to a year, found the optimal inter-study gap scales with the retention interval at roughly 10-20%, and that the penalty for gaps that are too SHORT is steeper than for gaps somewhat too long. Nakata (2015), Studies in Second Language Acquisition, extends the spacing question to L2 vocabulary specifically. Applied: a player flying in 21 days has a retention interval of ~21 days plus trip length, so the optimal gap is roughly 2-4 days, NOT the 1-day-then-3-day-then-7-day default of most SRS schedulers, and definitely not the multi-month intervals a mature Anki deck produces. A player flying in 5 days needs gaps of ~12 hours. UNVERIFIED: not retrieved; Cepeda 2006 and 2008 are both strong, well-known results.

sources.citation: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354-380.
Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095-1102.
Nakata, T. (2015). Effects of expanding and equal spacing on second language vocabulary learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 37(4), 677-711.

findings.implication: Architecture: ask for the departure date at onboarding — one field, skippable — and store `tripStart`, `tripEnd`. Schedule every item with `gapDays = clamp(0.15 * daysUntil(tripEnd), 0.5, 14)` rather than a fixed ladder, recomputing on every session because the interval shrinks daily. Two consequences to build: gaps compress automatically as the flight approaches (this is correct, not a bug); and the app must be able to say 'you have 9 days and 140 unmastered items — that is 16 a day, here is today's 16'. Also fire a local notification at the trip-anchored gap, and a single one on landing day: 'you learned 出口 three weeks ago — here it is again' as a re-exposure at the exact moment of use.

findings.claim: In a co-located turn-taking game, the non-acting players are the ones getting the best deal — free spaced re-exposure with no retrieval cost — while the acting team gets the retrieval benefit. Collaborative-recall research says groups underperform their nominal potential during collaboration but individuals benefit afterwards from the re-exposure.
findings.detail: Weldon & Bellinger (1997), Journal of Experimental Psychology: LMC, and the review by Rajaram & Pereira-Pasarin (2010), Perspectives on Psychological Science 5(6), 649-663: collaborative groups recall less than the pooled output of the same number of individuals working alone ('collaborative inhibition', attributed largely to retrieval disruption), BUT individual post-collaborative recall is reliably ENHANCED relative to individuals who never collaborated, through cross-cueing and re-exposure to items one did not personally retrieve. Applied to a four-player, two-team, turn-taking design: on any given turn, half the room is a spectator. Spectators get exposure without retrieval, which is the weaker of the two (Rowland's meta-analysis, 159 effect sizes, puts the testing-over-restudy advantage at g ≈ 0.50). The design lever is to convert spectator exposure into spectator retrieval at near-zero interaction cost. UNVERIFIED: not retrieved.

sources.citation: Rajaram, S., & Pereira-Pasarin, L. P. (2010). Collaborative memory: Cognitive research and theory. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 5(6), 649-663.

Weldon, M. S., & Bellinger, K. D. (1997). Collective memory: Collaborative and individual processes in remembering. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 23(5), 1160-1175.
Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432-1463.

findings.implication: UX + architecture: give the non-acting players a silent parallel task. While the acting team's timer runs, every other device shows the same sign and a private 'what do you think it says?' four-option tap — answers are not scored, not broadcast, and cost nothing socially, but they are recorded to that player's own mastery model. This is nearly free: the sign and options are already replicated to every peer by the existing event log, so it needs one new local-only event type (`shadowAnswer`, never gossiped) and no protocol change. It roughly doubles retrieval events per unit of wall-clock time in a four-player game and it fixes the dead-time problem that kills co-located turn games on phones.

findings.claim: Chinese characters need a substantially larger rendered size than Latin text at the same nominal point size, because legibility is governed by stroke density, not by letter height — and the survival set contains some of the densest characters in common use.
findings.detail: Chinese character legibility research (e.g. Cai, Chi & You 2001, International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics 27(1), on legibility thresholds of Chinese characters in three typefaces; and the mobile-display line of work by Huang, Rau and colleagues) consistently finds that legibility threshold scales with stroke count and that Chinese requires a larger visual angle than Latin script for equivalent legibility — commonly cited as roughly 16-20 arc-minutes for comfortable reading of complex characters versus roughly 12 for Latin. UNVERIFIED and I am not confident in those specific arc-minute numbers; treat the direction as reliable and the magnitude as approximate. What matters practically: the survival set is stroke-dense. 警 (19), 藏 (17), 檢/检, 續, 禁 (13), 蒸 (13), 醬/酱 (18), 麻 (11), 辣 (14), 鹹/咸, 餃/饺, 質/质, 藥/药 (18 traditional, 9 simplified), 攤, 邊/边. At 16px a Dutch player on a 5.5-inch phone at 35cm will not resolve 警 from 誉 or 藏 from 臧. Simplified characters help but 警, 蒸, 酱, 辣, 藏, 檢 are all simplified-set and still dense.

sources.citation: Cai, D., Chi, C.-F., & You, M. (2001). The legibility threshold of Chinese characters in three-type styles. International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics, 27(1), 9-17.
Huang, S.-M., Rau, P.-L. P., & Liu, Y.-J. (2009). Effects of font size, display resolution and task type on reading Chinese fonts from mobile devices. International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics.

findings.implication: UI, concrete numbers: the item character on a card renders at a minimum of 96px for a 1-2 character item and 64px for a 3-4 character item; never below 48px for any hanzi anywhere in the app, including the four answer options — set those at 40px minimum with 1.6 line-height and 0.02em tracking. Distractor options in the all-Chinese tier must be at the same size as the prompt, because shrinking them changes the discrimination task. Ship a real CJK face (Noto Sans SC / Source Han Sans SC via Google Fonts, weights 400 and 700) plus a serif (Noto Serif SC) for menu templates — do NOT rely on system CJK fallback, because a Dutch player's phone may render Chinese in a Japanese-locale face where 直, 骨, 每, 令 and 画 have visibly different glyph forms and the player will learn the wrong shape. Add a per-item `strokeCount`; anything above 15 strokes gets +25% render size and an extra 500 ms of minimum display time.

findings.claim: MENU, STRAND 1 — Cooking methods. Thirteen characters plus eight compounds predict texture, temperature, oil load and heat level before you know what the animal is. This is the single highest-payoff menu strand because it generalises across every dish name in the country.
findings.detail:
PRACTITIONER-DERIVED (my domain knowledge), not corpus-derived. Format: 汉字 pīnyīn — English / Nederlands — what it predicts.
Core 13: 炒 chǎo — stir-fry / roerbakken — fast, wok, moderate oil. 爆 bào — flash-fry / flitsbakken — very high heat, seconds, often offal. 炸 zhá — deep-fry / frituren — heavy oil. 煮 zhǔ — boil / koken — plain, wet. 蒸 zhēng — steam / stomen — lightest, no added oil. 烤 kǎo — roast, grill, bake / roosteren, grillen — dry heat, often skewers. 焖 mèn — covered braise / smoren — lid on, tender, saucy. 炖 dùn — long stew / stoven — soupy, bones, hours. 涮 shuàn — swish in broth / kort dompelen — this is hotpot, you cook it yourself. 拌 bàn — tossed, dressed / aanmaken — almost always COLD, raw or blanched, vinegar+oil. 卤 lǔ — master-stock braise / in kruidenbouillon gegaard — dark, star anise, usually served cold, usually offal. 烧 shāo — braise / braiseren — soy and sugar, thick sauce. 煎 jiān — pan-fry / bakken in de pan — shallow oil, one side crisp.
Compound modifiers that override the method: 红烧 hóngshāo — red-braised / in sojasaus gestoofd — sweet-savoury, brown, mild, the safest thing on any menu. 清蒸 qīngzhēng — plain-steamed / puur gestoomd — mild. 清炒 qīngchǎo — plain stir-fried / puur geroerbakt — mild. 白灼 báizhuó — blanched, Cantonese / geblancheerd — mild. 糖醋 tángcù — sweet and sour / zoetzuur — mild. 干煸 gānbiān — dry-fried / drooggebakken — Sichuan, chilli-heavy. 干锅 gānguō — dry pot / droge pan — Sichuan, arrives on a burner, chilli-heavy. 水煮 shuǐzhǔ — 'water-boiled' / letterlijk 'in water gekookt' — A LIE. It is a pool of chilli oil and Sichuan pepper. 水煮鱼, 水煮肉片 are among the hottest dishes commonly ordered by mistake. This one character pair is worth more to a Dutch traveller than fifty HSK words.
Secondary: 熘/溜 liū — thickened stir-fry. 烩 huì — thick stew. 焗 jú — baked, Cantonese. 熏 xūn — smoked / gerookt. 腌 yān — cured, pickled / gepekeld. 醉 zuì — wine-cured, RAW / rauw in wijn. 生腌 shēngyān — raw-marinated seafood / rauw gemarineerd — food-safety flag for visitors.
findings.implication: Content: cooking-method characters are item-bank rank 1-13 of the menu strand and should be the first menu items a player ever sees, ahead of proteins. Author each as a two-part item: recognise the character, then answer a consequence question ('you are avoiding oil — which of these four dishes?'). Tag every method item with `heatLevel`, `oilLevel`, `servedTemp` so the app can generate consequence questions procedurally instead of authoring them by hand. Give 水煮, 干煸, 干锅 a dedicated 'menu traps' sub-deck with the hazard-board template rather than the menu template — the deceptive-name items deserve the yellow triangle.

findings.claim: MENU, STRAND 2 — Proteins and staples. The critical fact is that 肉 alone on a Chinese menu means PORK by default; this catches vegetarians, Muslims and Jews every day and is not taught by any HSK level.
findings.detail:
PRACTITIONER-DERIVED. Proteins: 肉 ròu — meat, and by default PORK / vlees, standaard VARKENSVLEES — 肉丝, 肉片, 肉末 with no animal named are all pork. 猪 zhū — pig / varken. 鸡 jī — chicken / kip. 牛 niú — beef / rund. 羊 yáng — lamb, mutton, goat / lam, schaap, geit. 鱼 yú — fish / vis. 虾 xiā — shrimp, prawn / garnaal. 蟹 xiè — crab / krab. 鸭 yā — duck / eend. 蛋 dàn — egg / ei. 鹅 é — goose / gans. 兔 tù — rabbit / konijn. 鸽 gē — pigeon / duif. 驴 lǘ — donkey / ezel. 鱿鱼 yóuyú — squid / inktvis. 贝 bèi — shellfish / schelpdier. 蛤蜊 / 花甲 gélí / huājiǎ — clam / venusschelp. 扇贝 shànbèi — scallop / sint-jakobsschelp. 生蚝 / 牡蛎 shēngháo / mǔlì — oyster / oester. 小龙虾 xiǎolóngxiā — crayfish / rivierkreeft. 排骨 páigǔ — ribs / spareribs. 五花肉 wǔhuāròu — pork belly / buikspek. 牛腩 niúnǎn — brisket / runderborst. 里脊 lǐjǐ — tenderloin / haas. 豆腐 dòufu — tofu / tofu. 腐竹 fǔzhú — tofu skin / tofuvel. 面筋 miànjīn — seitan / seitan.
Staples: 饭 fàn — cooked rice, also 'meal' / rijst, maaltijd. 米饭 mǐfàn — steamed rice / gestoomde rijst. 炒饭 chǎofàn — fried rice / gebakken rijst. 面 miàn — wheat noodles, also 'flour' / tarwenoedels. 面条 miàntiáo — noodles / noedels. 拉面 lāmiàn — hand-pulled / handgetrokken noedels. 刀削面 dāoxiāomiàn — knife-shaved / geschaafde noedels. 粉 fěn — rice noodles or powder / rijstnoedels. 米粉 mǐfěn — rice vermicelli / rijstvermicelli. 河粉 héfěn — flat rice noodles / brede rijstnoedels. 粉丝 fěnsī — glass noodles / glasnoedels. 饺 jiǎo — dumpling / dumpling — 水饺 boiled / gekookt, 蒸饺 steamed / gestoomd, 煎饺 pan-fried / gebakken. 包 bāo — filled steamed bun / gevuld gestoomd broodje — 包子, 小笼包. 馒头 mántou — plain steamed bun, unfilled / ongevuld gestoomd broodje. 汤 tāng — soup / soep. 粥 zhōu — congee / rijstepap. 菜 cài — dish, or vegetable / gerecht, groente. 饼 bǐng — flatbread, pancake / platbrood, pannenkoek. 串 chuàn — skewer / spies. 锅 guō — pot / pan — 火锅 hotpot, 砂锅 clay pot. 馄饨 / 云吞 / 抄手 húntun / yúntūn / chāoshǒu — wonton, three regional names for the same thing / wonton, drie regionale namen. 油条 yóutiáo — fried dough stick / gefrituurd deegstokje.
Dish-name traps that contain no such animal: 鱼香 yúxiāng — 'fish-fragrant', contains no fish / bevat geen vis. 蚂蚁上树 mǎyǐ shàng shù — 'ants climbing a tree', minced pork with glass noodles / geen mieren. 狮子头 shīzitóu — 'lion's head', a pork meatball / varkensgehaktbal. 夫妻肺片 fūqī fèipiàn — cold sliced beef offal, no lung nowadays / koude runderorgaanplakjes. 蚝油 háoyóu — oyster sauce, hides in 'vegetarian' dishes / oestersaus, zit vaak in 'vegetarische' gerechten. 高汤 gāotāng — meat stock / vleesbouillon.
findings.implication: Content: give 肉 = pork its own item at the very top of the protein strand, with a hazard-board treatment, and make it un-skippable in the onboarding for any player who sets a dietary flag. Add a `dietaryFlags: ['pork','shellfish','beef','any-meat','alcohol']` onboarding step; when a flag is set, promote the items that protect it (肉 猪 蚝油 高汤 荤 素 清真 猪油 火腿 培根 鸡精) to the front of the queue regardless of tier. This is the one place where the app's ordering should be personalised, because the consequence of a miss is not embarrassment but a meal the player cannot eat.

findings.claim: MENU, STRAND 3 — Flavour warnings and the organ/texture set. 麻 is not 'spicy' and has no Dutch or English word; it is the single most-mistranslated sensation in Chinese food and Western diners are unprepared for it.
findings.detail:
PRACTITIONER-DERIVED. Flavour: 辣 là — chilli-hot / pittig, heet. 麻 má — the numbing, buzzing, lip-tingling effect of Sichuan pepper 花椒 / verdovend, tintelend — NOT heat, NOT spicy; there is no Dutch word for it, and 'pittig' is wrong. 麻辣 málà — numbing-and-hot / verdovend-pittig — the default Sichuan/Chongqing profile, and the two-character sequence a traveller should learn before any other flavour term. 酸 suān — sour / zuur. 甜 tián — sweet / zoet. 咸 xián — salty / zout. 香 xiāng — fragrant, savoury-good / geurig, lekker. 鲜 xiān — umami, fresh / hartig, umami. 苦 kǔ — bitter / bitter. 臭 chòu — stinky, and proudly so / stinkend — 臭豆腐. 怪味 guàiwèi — 'strange flavour', an actual Sichuan flavour category / letterlijk 'vreemde smaak', een echt smaakprofiel. 五香 wǔxiāng — five-spice / vijfkruiden. 孜然 zīrán — cumin / komijn. 芥末 jièmo — mustard, wasabi / mosterd, wasabi. 花椒 huājiāo — Sichuan pepper / Sichuanpeper. 辣椒 làjiāo — chilli / chilipeper. 剁椒 duòjiāo — chopped pickled chilli / gehakte ingelegde chili. 泡椒 pàojiāo — pickled chilli / ingelegde chili. 小米辣 xiǎomǐlà — bird's-eye chilli, very hot / rawitpeper, zeer heet. 蒜蓉 suànróng — minded garlic / fijngehakte knoflook. 葱 cōng — spring onion / lente-ui. 姜 jiāng — ginger / gember. 香菜 xiāngcài — coriander / koriander — worth learning purely so you can say 不要香菜.
Heat dialling: 不辣 bù là — not spicy / niet pittig. 免辣 miǎn là — hold the chilli / zonder chili. 微辣 wēi là — mildly spicy / licht pittig. 中辣 zhōng là — medium / medium. 重辣 / 特辣 zhòng là / tè là — very hot / zeer heet. 变态辣 biàntài là — 'perverted hot' / 'perverse' heet — a real menu option, not a joke. 加辣 jiā là — extra chilli / extra chili. 少辣 shǎo là — less chilli / minder chili. NOTE: 微辣 in Chengdu is hotter than 特辣 in Shanghai; the scale is local, not national.
Organ and texture set (the ten a Western diner most wants to recognise, all share the 月 flesh radical except 血 and 皮 and 筋): 肠 cháng — intestine / darm — 肥肠 fatty pig intestine, 大肠. 肚 dǔ — tripe, stomach / pens, maag — note 毛肚 ox tripe (hotpot staple), 猪肚 pig stomach; the same character read dù means 'belly'. 肝 gān — liver / lever — 猪肝, 鹅肝. 血 xuè / xiě — blood, served as a set curd / bloed, als gestolde koek — 鸭血, 毛血旺. 舌 shé — tongue / tong — 牛舌, also written 口条. 筋 jīn — tendon / pees — 牛筋, 蹄筋, chewy and gelatinous. 心 xīn — heart / hart — 鸡心, 猪心 (note: 心 also means 'centre' and 'filling', so 菜心 is a vegetable). 腰 yāo — kidney / nier — 腰花, 猪腰; 腰 also means 'waist'. 脑 nǎo — brain / hersenen — 脑花, usually poached in hotpot. 皮 pí — skin / huid, zwoerd — 猪皮, 鸡皮, 皮蛋 century egg.
Extended: 肺 fèi — lung / long. 肾 shèn — kidney / nier. 蹄 tí — trotter / poot. 爪 zhuǎ — feet, claws / pootjes — 凤爪, 鸡爪 chicken feet. 胗 zhēn — gizzard / spiermaag. 翅 chì — wing / vleugel. 掌 zhǎng — webbed foot / zwemvlies-poot. 骨 gǔ — bone / bot. 尾 wěi — tail / staart. 头 tóu — head / kop. 黄喉 huánghóu — aorta / aorta, a hotpot delicacy.
findings.implication: Content + UI: teach the 月 flesh radical as a single card BEFORE any of 肠肚肝肺肾脑 — one radical unlocks six items and it is the clearest demonstration in the whole curriculum that Chinese characters are composed, not memorised. Render 月 in the accent colour inside each of the six. For 麻, do not gloss it as a word: give it a dedicated animated card (a lip-tingle micro-animation, 300ms shimmer) and the sentence 'this is not heat — it is your mouth going numb; there is no Dutch word for it'. Ship the 不要香菜 / 不辣 / 微辣 phrases as a separate, always-accessible 'point at this' screen with 96px characters, because that is the one place where this reading app should let a player produce language.

findings.claim: MENU, STRAND 4 — Qualifiers and section headers. 时价 ('market price') is the most expensive two characters a traveller can fail to read.
findings.detail:
PRACTITIONER-DERIVED. Portion and price qualifiers: 大份 dà fèn — large portion / grote portie. 中份 zhōng fèn — medium / medium. 小份 xiǎo fèn — small / kleine portie. 半份 bàn fèn — half portion / halve portie. 例 lì — standard/regular portion, Cantonese-influenced, common on chain and southern menus / standaardportie. 位 wèi — per person / per persoon. 时价 shí jià — MARKET PRICE, i.e. no price is printed and you will be told after you eat / dagprijs — ask before ordering; this is where the bill goes wrong. 起 qǐ — 'from' / vanaf — 88元起. 招牌 zhāopái — signature dish / huisspecialiteit. 特色 tèsè — house specialty / specialiteit. 推荐 / 店长推荐 tuījiàn — recommended / aanbevolen. 新品 xīnpǐn — new / nieuw. 热销 rèxiāo — best-seller / bestseller. 现做 xiànzuò — made to order / vers bereid. 限量 xiànliàng — limited quantity / beperkt beschikbaar. 套餐 tàocān — set meal / menu, combinatie. 单点 dāndiǎn — à la carte / los bestellen. 配 pèi — served with / geserveerd met. 另收费 lìng shōufèi — charged separately / apart in rekening gebracht. 茶位费 chá wèi fèi — tea/cover charge per head, standard in Guangdong / couvert per persoon. 餐位费 cān wèi fèi — cover charge / couvert. 餐盒费 / 打包费 cān hé fèi — takeaway box fee / verpakkingskosten. 服务费 fúwù fèi — service charge / bedieningsgeld.
Dietary qualifiers: 素 sù — vegetarian / vegetarisch — but 素 dishes routinely contain 蚝油 or 高汤. 全素 quán sù — strictly vegetarian / strikt vegetarisch. 斋 zhāi — Buddhist vegetarian, the reliable one / boeddhistisch vegetarisch, de betrouwbare. 荤 hūn — meat-containing / met vlees. 清真 qīngzhēn — halal / halal. 忌口 jìkǒu — dietary restriction / dieetbeperking.
Section headers, in the order they appear on a typical menu: 凉菜 liángcài — cold dishes / koude gerechten. 热菜 rècài — hot dishes / warme gerechten. 荤菜 hūncài — meat dishes / vleesgerechten. 素菜 sùcài — vegetable dishes / groentegerechten. 海鲜 hǎixiān — seafood / zeevruchten. 烧烤 shāokǎo — grilled, skewers / gegrild, spiesjes. 主食 zhǔshí — staples: rice, noodles, buns; ordered LAST in China, not first / basisgerechten, worden als laatste besteld. 汤 / 汤类 / 汤羹 tāng — soups / soepen. 小吃 xiǎochī — snacks, small plates / kleine gerechten. 甜品 / 甜点 tiánpǐn — dessert / nagerecht. 饮料 yǐnliào — soft drinks / frisdrank. 酒水 jiǔshuǐ — alcohol and drinks / alcohol en dranken. 时令 shílìng — seasonal / seizoensgebonden.
Cultural note worth teaching as content: 主食 comes at the END of the meal in most of China, so a Dutch diner who orders rice first and waits will get it last and be confused.
findings.implication: Content: build one 'read the whole menu page' composite item type distinct from single-character items — a full rendered menu section with 6-8 lines, and the question is a task ('you have 80 yuan and you do not eat pork — what can you order?'). These composites are the criterion task and should be the professor-tier (+15/-10) items in the menu category, replacing single-character items at that tier entirely. Store them as `{templateId:'menu', lines:[{hanzi,price,tags[]}], task, options[]}` so one authored menu page yields several tasks.

findings.claim: QR-code and WeChat mini-programme ordering has changed the menu reading task from DECODING a fixed printed page to SCANNING a scrollable, image-rich, tappable list under time pressure — which lowers the character load but adds a whole transactional vocabulary that no wordlist teaches.
findings.detail:
PRACTITIONER-DERIVED; I could not retrieve the hospitality/HCI literature on QR menus (there is post-2020 work in International Journal of Hospitality Management and similar on QR-menu adoption, unretrieved). What the shift means practically: (1) most dishes now have a PHOTO, so the recognition burden on dish-name characters drops sharply — photos do the work; (2) but the transaction chrome is Chinese-only text with no photos, and it is where you get stuck; (3) the flow is time-pressured and public (the waiter is standing there, the table is waiting); (4) many mini-programmes require a WeChat account and a Chinese payment method to complete, which is a hard stop for some visitors regardless of reading ability; (5) the text is small, dense and scrollable — the opposite of a sign.
The transaction vocabulary, in the order you meet it: 扫码点餐 sǎomǎ diǎncān — scan to order / scan om te bestellen. 扫一扫 sǎo yī sǎo — scan / scannen. 堂食 tángshí — dine in / ter plaatse eten. 外卖 wàimài — delivery / bezorging. 打包 dǎbāo — takeaway / meenemen. 桌号 zhuōhào — table number / tafelnummer. 人数 rénshù — number of diners / aantal personen. 点餐 diǎncān — order / bestellen. 规格 guīgé — specification, size / maat, variant. 口味 kǒuwèi — taste option, this is where 微辣/中辣 lives / smaakoptie. 数量 shùliàng — quantity / aantal. 加入购物车 jiārù gòuwùchē — add to cart / in winkelwagen. 购物车 gòuwùchē — cart / winkelwagen. 备注 bèizhù — notes to kitchen / opmerkingen — the field where 不要香菜 goes. 去结算 qù jiésuàn — go to checkout / naar afrekenen. 提交订单 tíjiāo dìngdān — submit order / bestelling plaatsen. 下单 xiàdān — place order / bestellen. 起送 qǐsòng — minimum order / minimum bestelbedrag. 优惠券 yōuhuìquàn — voucher / kortingsbon. 满减 mǎnjiǎn — spend-X-get-Y-off / bij besteding X, Y korting. 支付 zhīfù — pay / betalen. 微信支付 / 支付宝 — WeChat Pay / Alipay. 确认 quèrèn — confirm / bevestigen. 取消 qǔxiāo — cancel / annuleren. 已售 yǐshòu — number sold / aantal verkocht. 售罄 shòuqìng — sold out / uitverkocht. 呼叫服务员 hūjiào fúwùyuán — call the waiter / ober roepen. 买单 / 结账 mǎidān / jiézhàng — the bill / afrekenen. 开发票 kāi fāpiào — issue an official invoice / factuur (fapiao) aanvragen.
The two buttons that matter most and are easiest to confuse: 去结算 (checkout, proceed) and 取消 (cancel). And 提交订单 (submit — irreversible) vs 加入购物车 (add to cart — reversible).
findings.implication: Content + UI: add a SIXTH card template — `miniapp` — that renders as a phone-inside-a-phone: a scrollable Chinese ordering UI at realistic density (14-16px body text, not 96px), with tappable buttons. The task is not 'what does this character mean' but 'tap the button that adds this to your cart without ordering it'. This is the only template where small type is correct, because small type IS the difficulty. Author ~25 mini-programme items covering the button set above. Architecturally these are interactive items, so the item schema needs `interaction: 'choice' | 'tap-target'` and a hit-region spec; add it now rather than retrofitting. Also add a 'ordering flow' timed sequence at professor tier: five taps in 40 seconds, mirroring the social pressure of the real thing.

findings.claim: TRANSIT, STRAND 1 — Metro. The characters are easy and mostly bilingual; the hard part is the PROPER NOUN — the terminus name in 开往 X 方向 — which appears in no wordlist and must be shipped as a per-city pack.
findings.detail:
PRACTITIONER-DERIVED. Core set: 地铁 dìtiě — metro / metro. 站 zhàn — station, stop / station, halte. 号线 hào xiàn — line number / lijnnummer — 4号线 = Line 4. 出口 chūkǒu — exit / uitgang. 入口 rùkǒu — entrance / ingang. 出入口 chūrùkǒu — entrance/exit / in- en uitgang. 换乘 huànchéng — transfer, change lines / overstappen. 方向 fāngxiàng — direction / richting. 开往 kāi wǎng — bound for / richting, naar — followed by the TERMINUS name, which is the actual information. 首班车 shǒubānchē — first train / eerste trein. 末班车 mòbānchē — last train / laatste trein. 首末班车时间 — first/last train times / eerste en laatste trein. 单程票 dānchéngpiào — single journey ticket / enkeltje. 进站 jìnzhàn — enter the station / station in. 出站 chūzhàn — exit the station / station uit. 安检 ānjiǎn — security check, MANDATORY on every Chinese metro, bags on the belt / veiligheidscontrole, verplicht. 站台 zhàntái — platform / perron. 站厅 zhàntīng — concourse / stationshal. 付费区 fùfèiqū — paid area / betaalde zone. 非付费区 fēifùfèiqū — unpaid area / onbetaalde zone — the trap: crossing between them costs a fare, so exiting by the wrong gate to reach the other side of the road can cost you. 自动售票机 zìdòng shòupiàojī — ticket machine / kaartautomaat. 售票处 shòupiàochù — ticket office / loket. 服务中心 fúwù zhōngxīn — service centre / servicebalie. 补票 bǔpiào — pay a fare adjustment / bijbetalen. 无障碍 wúzhàng'ài — accessible, step-free / rolstoeltoegankelijk. 电梯 diàntī — lift / lift. 扶梯 fútī — escalator / roltrap. 失物招领 shīwù zhāolǐng — lost property / gevonden voorwerpen.
Compass, used in exit names, station names and street names: 东 dōng — east / oost. 西 xī — west / west. 南 nán — south / zuid. 北 běi — north / noord. 中 zhōng — central / centrum. Street types: 路 lù — road / weg. 街 jiē — street / straat. 道 dào — avenue / laan. 大街 dàjiē — main street / hoofdstraat. 大道 dàdào — boulevard / boulevard. 巷 / 弄 / 胡同 — alley / steeg. 环 huán — ring road / ringweg — 内环 inner, 外环 outer.
EXIT LETTERING CONVENTIONS, which differ by city and are not documented anywhere a traveller looks: Beijing uses LETTERS with a compass gloss — the plate reads 'A 西北口' meaning exit A, northwest. Guangzhou and Shenzhen use LETTERS with numeric subdivisions — A, B1, B2, C. Shanghai and Nanjing use NUMBERS — 1号口, 2号口. Hong Kong MTR uses letter+number — A1, B2. Chengdu and Xi'an use letters. In all systems the exit letter is the addressable unit: a Chinese friend will say 'meet me at C口', and 口 kǒu here means 'exit', not 'mouth'. Floor levels: 层 céng — floor / verdieping; B1, B2 are basement levels; 3楼 sān lóu means the third floor Chinese-style, which counts the ground floor as 1 — so 3楼 is what a Dutch speaker calls de tweede verdieping, not de derde. This off-by-one bites Dutch and most European visitors in every mall and hotel.
findings.implication: Architecture: ship per-city name packs as separately downloadable bundles — `city/beijing.json` with the ~400 station names of that network, `city/shanghai.json`, etc., 20-40KB each, cached in IndexedDB and selected at onboarding ('where are you going?'). Without them the transit strand teaches 开往 and then shows a station name the player will never see. Generate transit items procedurally from the pack: `开往{terminus}方向` with three sibling termini from the same network as distractors, which is free content and is exactly the real discrimination task. Also: put the 3楼 / tweede verdieping off-by-one in the Dutch gloss layer as an explicit warning card — it is a Dutch-and-European-specific error the English gloss does not surface.
