findings.claim: TRANSIT, STRAND 2 — Rail and airport. The seat-class characters are a purchase decision with a large comfort and price consequence, and 硬/软 (hard/soft) plus 座/卧 (seat/berth) is a two-by-two grid learnable in one card.
findings.detail:
PRACTITIONER-DERIVED. Rail: 火车 huǒchē — train / trein. 火车站 huǒchēzhàn — railway station / treinstation. 高铁 gāotiě — high-speed rail, G-trains / hogesnelheidstrein. 动车 dòngchē — D-trains, slightly slower HSR / sneltrein. 候车 hòuchē — wait for the train / wachten op de trein. 候车室 hòuchēshì — waiting hall / wachtruimte. 检票 jiǎnpiào — ticket check / kaartcontrole. 检票口 jiǎnpiàokǒu — ticket gate / controlepoort. 站台 zhàntái — platform / perron. 车厢 chēxiāng — carriage, coach / rijtuig, wagon — your ticket gives 车厢 and 座位号. 座位号 zuòwèihào — seat number / stoelnummer. 检票时间 — boarding time / instaptijd — HSR gates CLOSE a few minutes before departure and do not reopen; this is the single most common way a foreign visitor misses a Chinese train.
The seat-class grid: 硬 yìng — hard / hard. 软 ruǎn — soft / zacht. 座 zuò — seat / zitplaats. 卧 wò — berth, sleeper / slaapplaats. Combine: 硬座 yìngzuò — hard seat, cheapest, upright, overnight is punishing / harde zit. 软座 ruǎnzuò — soft seat / zachte zit. 硬卧 yìngwò — hard sleeper, open six-berth bay, three tiers / harde slaapplaats, open coupé met zes bedden. 软卧 ruǎnwò — soft sleeper, four-berth closed compartment / zachte slaapplaats, gesloten coupé met vier bedden. On high-speed: 二等座 èrděngzuò — second class / tweede klas. 一等座 yīděngzuò — first class / eerste klas. 商务座 shāngwùzuò — business class / businessklasse. 无座 wúzuò — standing ticket, same price as hard seat, no seat / staanplaats.
Ticketing: 身份证 shēnfènzhèng — ID card; foreigners use their PASSPORT 护照 and this is exactly why the automatic gates often reject you / identiteitsbewijs; buitenlanders gebruiken hun paspoort. 护照 hùzhào — passport / paspoort. 取票 qǔpiào — collect a printed ticket / ticket ophalen. 人工窗口 réngōng chuāngkǒu — staffed counter, where passport-holders go / bemand loket. 售票厅 shòupiàotīng — ticket hall / ticketbalie. 退票 tuìpiào — refund / ticket annuleren. 改签 gǎiqiān — change ticket / omboeken. 实名制 shímíngzhì — real-name registration / registratie op naam.
Airport: 机场 jīchǎng — airport / luchthaven. 航站楼 hángzhànlóu — terminal / terminal. 出发 chūfā — departures / vertrek. 到达 dàodá — arrivals / aankomst. 国内 guónèi — domestic / binnenland. 国际 guójì — international / internationaal. 值机 zhíjī — check-in / inchecken. 登机口 dēngjīkǒu — boarding gate / gate. 登机牌 dēngjīpái — boarding pass / instapkaart. 托运 tuōyùn — check baggage / bagage inchecken. 行李 xíngli — luggage / bagage. 行李提取 xíngli tíqǔ — baggage claim / bagageband. 安检 ānjiǎn — security / veiligheidscontrole. 边检 biānjiǎn — immigration / paspoortcontrole. 海关 hǎiguān — customs / douane. 中转 zhōngzhuǎn — transfer / overstap. 晚点 wǎndiǎn — delayed / vertraagd. 取消 qǔxiāo — cancelled / geannuleerd. 登机中 dēngjī zhōng — boarding / aan het boarden.
findings.implication: Content: teach 硬/软 × 座/卧 as a single 2×2 grid card, not four separate items — a genuine compositional win where four vocabulary items cost the price of two. Same treatment for 出发/到达 × 国内/国际 (four airport signs from four characters) and 进站/出站. Build a card type `grid2x2` with the axis labels as the taught units and all four cells as the tested units. This is the highest ratio of items-unlocked to characters-learned anywhere in the curriculum and should be flagged in the app as such ('4 characters, 8 signs').

findings.claim: SUPERMARKET — the three traps (斤, 折, 保质期) are worth more to a traveller than the entire HSK 1 word list, and all three are absent from HSK 1-3.
findings.detail:
PRACTITIONER-DERIVED. THE 斤 TRAP: 斤 jīn — catty = 500 g exactly / catty = 500 gram. Loose produce, meat and fish are priced 元/斤 almost everywhere, so a shelf reading 12.8元/斤 is 25.6 元/kg — the price is DOUBLE what a European brain computes. 半斤 bàn jīn — 250 g. 两 liǎng — 50 g, one tenth of a 斤 / 50 gram — used for noodles and tea and dumpling weights. 公斤 gōngjīn / 千克 qiānkè — kilogram / kilogram = 2 斤. 克 kè — gram / gram. 毫升 háoshēng — millilitre / milliliter. 升 shēng — litre / liter.
THE 折 TRAP: 折 zhé — discount, expressed as the FRACTION YOU PAY, not the fraction off / korting, uitgedrukt als wat je betaalt. 打八折 dǎ bā zhé — pay 80%, i.e. 20% off / je betaalt 80%, dus 20% korting. 打五折 — half price / halve prijs. 打七五折 — pay 75%. A European reading '8折' as '80% off' will be badly wrong in the wrong direction. 满减 mǎnjiǎn — threshold discount / drempelkorting — 满100减20 = spend 100, get 20 off. 第二件半价 dì èr jiàn bàn jià — second item half price / tweede artikel halve prijs. 买一送一 mǎi yī sòng yī — buy one get one free / 1+1 gratis. 特价 tèjià — special price / aanbieding. 促销 cùxiāo — promotion / actie. 原价 yuánjià — original price / oude prijs. 现价 xiànjià — current price / nu. 会员价 huìyuánjià — members' price, requires a scanned app account and the shelf shows it as if it were the price / ledenprijs, alleen met app-account. 清仓 qīngcāng — clearance / opruiming.
THE 保质期 TRAP: Chinese labels do NOT print an expiry date. They print 生产日期 shēngchǎn rìqī — production date / productiedatum — plus 保质期 bǎozhìqī — shelf life as a DURATION / houdbaarheidsduur — e.g. 保质期12个月. You must add them. Also: 见包装 jiàn bāozhuāng — 'see the packaging' / zie verpakking; 见瓶身 jiàn píngshēn — 'see the bottle'; 见喷码 jiàn pēnmǎ — 'see the inkjet code' — these tell you WHERE the date is hiding and appear on a large fraction of products. 保质期至 bǎozhìqī zhì — best before (a real date) / ten minste houdbaar tot — increasingly common but not universal. Date formats seen: 20260822, 2026/08/22, 2026.08.22, 26 08 22.
Storage and the rest: 冷藏 lěngcáng — refrigerate, 0-4°C / gekoeld bewaren. 冷冻 lěngdòng — freeze, -18°C / diepvries. 常温 chángwēn — ambient / kamertemperatuur. 阴凉干燥处 yīnliáng gānzào chù — cool dry place / koel en droog bewaren. 净含量 jìnghánliàng — net content / netto-inhoud. 规格 guīgé — size, spec / verpakkingsmaat. 进口 jìnkǒu — imported / geïmporteerd. 原产国 yuánchǎnguó — country of origin / land van herkomst. 散装 sǎnzhuāng — loose, sold by weight / los, per gewicht. 称重 chēngzhòng — weigh here / hier afwegen — in many Chinese supermarkets you must weigh and get a barcode sticker in the produce section BEFORE the checkout, or you will be sent back. 超市 chāoshì — supermarket / supermarkt. 便利店 biànlìdiàn — convenience store / buurtwinkel. 收银台 shōuyíntái — checkout / kassa. 结账 jiézhàng — pay / afrekenen. 扫码支付 sǎomǎ zhīfù — scan to pay / betalen met QR-code. 元 yuán — yuan, written form / yuan. 块 kuài — yuan, spoken form / yuan (spreektaal). 角 jiǎo / 毛 máo — 0.1 yuan / 10 cent. 分 fēn — 0.01 yuan / cent.
findings.implication: Content + UI: build a `price-label` template where the numeral is huge and the unit character is small — because that is the real reading condition and the whole difficulty is that 斤 is 8px next to a 40px number. The task on these items is arithmetic, not recognition: '牛肉 32.8元/斤 — what does a kilo cost?' with options 32.8 / 65.6 / 16.4 / 328. Same for 折: '原价 200元, 打七折 — what do you pay?'. Same for dates: show a real production date plus 保质期6个月 and ask if it is still good today. Store these as `itemType:'compute'` with a generator so the numbers randomise every presentation and the player cannot memorise the answer. These three trap families should be the first three market-strand items and should be un-skippable.

findings.claim: Allergen information on Chinese packaged food has historically been RECOMMENDED, not mandatory, under GB 7718-2011 — so the absence of an allergen warning carries no information. A player with a serious allergy must read the ingredient list itself, which is a much harder reading task.
findings.detail:
GB 7718-2011 《预包装食品标签通则》 lists eight allergen categories for which declaration is 推荐性 (recommended) rather than 强制性 (mandatory): 含麸质的谷物 (gluten-containing cereals), 甲壳纲类动物 (crustaceans), 鱼类 (fish), 蛋类 (eggs), 花生 (peanuts), 大豆 (soybeans), 乳 (milk, including 乳糖 lactose), 坚果 (tree nuts). A 2025 revision of GB 7718 was issued (I believe March 2025, with a transition period into 2027) which among other changes moves allergen labelling toward mandatory — I could NOT verify this and it must be checked before it is stated in the product. Nutrition labels are governed by GB 28050 《预包装食品营养标签通则》: the 营养成分表 declares 能量 (energy) in kJ, NOT kcal, plus 蛋白质 (protein), 脂肪 (fat), 碳水化合物 (carbohydrate), 钠 (sodium) and NRV% — the kJ-only convention silently misleads European readers used to kcal, by a factor of ~4.184.
The reading set: 配料表 pèiliàobiǎo — ingredients list / ingrediëntenlijst. 配料 pèiliào — ingredients / ingrediënten. 含 hán — contains / bevat. 不含 bù hán — does not contain / bevat geen. 可能含有 kěnéng hányǒu — may contain / kan sporen bevatten. 过敏原 guòmǐnyuán — allergen / allergeen. 麸质 fūzhì — gluten / gluten. 小麦 xiǎomài — wheat / tarwe. 大豆 dàdòu — soy / soja. 花生 huāshēng — peanut / pinda. 坚果 jiānguǒ — tree nuts / noten. 乳 rǔ — milk / melk. 牛奶 niúnǎi — cow's milk / koemelk. 乳糖 rǔtáng — lactose / lactose. 蛋 dàn — egg / ei. 鱼 yú — fish / vis. 虾 xiā — shrimp / garnaal. 甲壳类 jiǎqiàolèi — crustaceans / schaaldieren. 芝麻 zhīma — sesame / sesam. 食品添加剂 shípǐn tiānjiājì — food additives / additieven. 营养成分表 yíngyǎng chéngfèn biǎo — nutrition table / voedingswaardetabel. 能量 néngliàng — energy, in kJ / energie, in kJ. 蛋白质 dànbáizhì — protein / eiwit. 脂肪 zhīfáng — fat / vet. 碳水化合物 tànshuǐ huàhéwù — carbohydrate / koolhydraten. 钠 nà — sodium / natrium. 糖 táng — sugar / suiker. 味精 wèijīng — MSG / ve-tsin. 鸡精 jījīng — chicken bouillon powder, contains chicken / kippenbouillonpoeder, bevat kip. 猪油 zhūyóu — lard / reuzel. 明胶 míngjiāo — gelatine / gelatine. 清真 qīngzhēn — halal / halal.

findings.implication: Content + UX: create an optional 'allergy pack' unlocked by the dietary-flags onboarding, containing the ~20 allergen characters plus 含 / 不含 / 可能含有. Its items use a real ingredient-list template — 10pt grey text in a paragraph, which is the actual reading condition — and the task is a scan-and-find ('is there soy in this?') with a 15-second timer, not a recognition task. IMPORTANT UX guardrail: the app must state plainly, once, that it is a game and not a medical tool, and that absence of a warning on a Chinese label does not mean absence of the allergen. Do not let a game teach someone with a peanut allergy to trust a label. Also verify the GB 7718-2025 status before shipping any claim about mandatory labelling.

findings.claim: SHOPFRONTS — Chinese business names are head-final compounds, so about eight HEAD morphemes (店馆厅行城场中心) plus a modifier tell you what a business is. Learn the heads first and you can classify a shopfront you have never seen.
findings.detail:
PRACTITIONER-DERIVED, but it rests on a well-supported structural fact: Chinese nominal compounds are overwhelmingly head-final (modifier + head), so the LAST character of a shop name carries the category. The heads: 店 diàn — shop / winkel — 药店, 书店, 花店, 便利店, 水果店, 眼镜店. 铺 pù — shop, older/smaller / winkeltje — 店铺, 杂货铺. 馆 guǎn — an establishment, a house of / gelegenheid, huis — 面馆, 饭馆, 茶馆, 宾馆, 图书馆, 博物馆, 美容馆. 厅 tīng — hall / zaal — 餐厅, 咖啡厅, 大厅. 行 háng (NOT xíng) — a trade house / handelshuis — 银行, 车行, 商行. 城 chéng — city, used for large retail / markthal, centrum — 美食城, 家具城, 电脑城. 场 chǎng — a venue, an open place / terrein, plein — 停车场, 广场, 市场, 商场. 中心 zhōngxīn — centre / centrum — 购物中心, 服务中心, 社区卫生服务中心. Plus 屋, 坊, 阁, 轩, 家, 记 (as in 老王记, 'Old Wang's') as boutique/traditional heads.
The shopfronts you must identify from the sign alone: 药店 / 药房 yàodiàn / yàofáng — pharmacy, look for the GREEN CROSS / apotheek, groen kruis. 医院 yīyuàn — hospital / ziekenhuis. 诊所 zhěnsuǒ — clinic / huisartsenpraktijk. 社区卫生服务中心 — community health centre / wijkgezondheidscentrum. 急诊 jízhěn — A&E / spoedeisende hulp. 银行 yínháng — bank / bank — 中国银行 Bank of China (the one that reliably changes foreign currency), 工商银行, 建设银行, 农业银行, 招商银行. 自动取款机 / ATM — cash machine / geldautomaat. 邮局 yóujú / 中国邮政 — post office, GREEN livery / postkantoor, groen. 派出所 pàichūsuǒ — local police station / politiebureau. 公安局 gōng'ānjú — public security bureau / politiebureau (hoofd). 出入境管理 chūrùjìng guǎnlǐ — exit-entry administration, where visa extensions happen / vreemdelingendienst. 厕所 cèsuǒ — toilet, blunt / wc. 洗手间 xǐshǒujiān — washroom, polite / toilet. 卫生间 wèishēngjiān — bathroom / toilet. 公厕 gōngcè — public toilet / openbaar toilet. 酒店 jiǔdiàn — hotel, usually larger / hotel. 宾馆 bīnguǎn — hotel, mid-range / hotel. 招待所 zhāodàisuǒ — guesthouse, basic, often no foreigners / eenvoudig pension. 民宿 mínsù — homestay, B&B / bed and breakfast. 客栈 kèzhàn — inn / herberg. 饭店 fàndiàn — CONFUSING: means both restaurant and hotel / betekent zowel restaurant als hotel. 餐厅 cāntīng — restaurant / restaurant. 餐馆 cānguǎn — restaurant / restaurant. 食堂 shítáng — canteen / kantine. 小吃 xiǎochī — snacks, cheap eats / kleine gerechten, snackbar. 面馆 miànguǎn — noodle shop / noedelzaak. 米粉 mǐfěn — rice-noodle shop / rijstnoedelzaak. 火锅 huǒguō — hotpot / hotpot. 烧烤 shāokǎo — BBQ skewers, evening / barbecue, spiesjes. 串串 chuànchuàn — skewer hotpot / spiesjes-hotpot. 自助餐 zìzhùcān — buffet / buffet. 咖啡 kāfēi / 咖啡厅 — coffee / koffie. 茶 chá / 茶楼 chálóu — tea / thee, theehuis. 奶茶 nǎichá — bubble tea / bubbelthee. 理发 lǐfà / 美发 měifà — barber, hairdresser / kapper. 美容 měiróng — beauty salon / schoonheidssalon. 洗衣 xǐyī / 干洗 gānxǐ — laundry, dry cleaning / wasserij, stomerij. 快递 kuàidì — courier, parcel point / pakketpunt — 顺丰 SF, 中通, 圆通, 菜鸟驿站 Cainiao pickup point. 加油站 jiāyóuzhàn — petrol station / tankstation — 中石化 Sinopec, 中石油 PetroChina. 停车场 tíngchēchǎng — car park / parkeerplaats — signed P, 地下车库 underground. 超市 chāoshì / 便利店 biànlìdiàn — supermarket, convenience store — 全家 FamilyMart, 罗森 Lawson, 美宜佳. 商场 shāngchǎng / 购物中心 / 百货 / 广场 — mall, department store, plaza / winkelcentrum, warenhuis. 市场 shìchǎng / 菜市场 càishìchǎng — market, wet market / markt, versmarkt. 手机维修 shǒujī wéixiū — phone repair / telefoonreparatie. 按摩 ànmó / 足疗 zúliáo — massage, foot massage / massage, voetmassage. 网吧 wǎngbā — internet café / internetcafé. 健身房 jiànshēnfáng — gym / sportschool. 眼镜店 yǎnjìngdiàn — optician / opticien. 水果店 shuǐguǒdiàn — fruit shop / fruitwinkel. 图书馆 túshūguǎn — library / bibliotheek.
findings.implication: Content: order the shopfront strand HEADS FIRST — eight items (店馆厅行城场中心铺) before any complete business name — and make the second-tier task generative: show a shopfront the player has never seen (电脑城, 花店, 修车行) and ask what KIND of place it is, answerable from the head alone. This converts a memorisation strand into a rule strand, and it is the only part of the curriculum where a player can correctly answer an item that is not in the bank. Track it: log `unseenCompoundAccuracy` as a separate metric, because it measures generalisation rather than recall and it is the number that predicts real-world performance.

findings.claim: UNIVERSAL SIGNAGE — the prohibition and instruction formulas are a closed set of about six openers (禁止 严禁 请勿 不准 小心 注意) that combine with a verb. Learn the openers and the illocutionary force is solved even when the verb is unknown.
findings.detail:
PRACTITIONER-DERIVED. Openers, in decreasing force: 严禁 yánjìn — strictly forbidden / streng verboden. 禁止 jìnzhǐ — prohibited / verboden. 不准 bù zhǔn — not permitted / niet toegestaan. 请勿 qǐng wù — please do not, polite / gelieve niet. 谢绝 xièjué — politely declined / niet toegestaan. 注意 zhùyì — attention, note / let op. 小心 xiǎoxīn — be careful, watch out / voorzichtig, pas op. 当心 dāngxīn — beware / pas op. 危险 wēixiǎn — danger / gevaar.
Common full signs: 禁止吸烟 jìnzhǐ xīyān — no smoking / verboden te roken. 禁止通行 jìnzhǐ tōngxíng — no entry, no through traffic / verboden doorgang. 禁止停车 — no parking / verboden te parkeren. 禁止拍照 — no photography / verboden te fotograferen. 请勿触摸 — do not touch / niet aanraken. 请勿入内 / 闲人免进 — no entry, staff only / verboden toegang. 小心地滑 xiǎoxīn dì huá — caution wet floor / pas op, gladde vloer. 当心碰头 — mind your head / pas op uw hoofd. 小心台阶 — mind the step / pas op de trede. 安全出口 ānquán chūkǒu — emergency exit, GREEN / nooduitgang, groen. 消防通道 xiāofáng tōngdào — fire lane, keep clear / brandgang. 灭火器 mièhuǒqì — fire extinguisher / brandblusser. 施工中 shīgōng zhōng — under construction / werk in uitvoering. 正在维修 / 故障 gùzhàng — out of order / buiten gebruik. 暂停使用 zàntíng shǐyòng — temporarily out of use / tijdelijk buiten gebruik. 请排队 qǐng páiduì — please queue / graag in de rij.
Opposites and states — cheap to learn in pairs: 入 rù / 出 chū — in / uit. 开 kāi / 关 guān — open, on / dicht, uit. 推 tuī / 拉 lā — push / trekken — the classic door pair, and they look nothing alike, which makes them easy. 上 shàng / 下 xià — up, board / down, alight. 左 zuǒ / 右 yòu — left / links, right / rechts. 前 qián / 后 hòu — front, ahead / voor, back, behind / achter. 内 nèi / 外 wài — inside / binnen, outside / buiten. 免费 miǎnfèi / 收费 shōufèi — free / gratis, charged / betaald. 营业中 yíngyè zhōng / 休息 xiūxi — open for business / geopend, closed, on break / gesloten, pauze. 停业 tíngyè — closed down / gesloten (permanent). 满 mǎn / 空 kōng — full / vol, vacant, empty / vrij, leeg — on car parks and toilet cubicles. 有人 yǒu rén / 无人 wú rén — occupied / bezet, vacant / vrij. 男 nán / 女 nǚ — men / heren, women / dames — learn as a pair and never in isolation; the confusion cost is high and the characters are unrelated in shape, so a paired card works.
NUMBERS. Everyday: 一二三四五六七八九十 yī èr sān sì wǔ liù qī bā jiǔ shí, 百 bǎi hundred, 千 qiān thousand, 万 wàn TEN THOUSAND — the 万 unit is a genuine cognitive obstacle for Dutch and English speakers because Chinese counts in units of 10,000, so 十万 = 100,000 and 一百万 = 1,000,000; 亿 yì = 100,000,000. 零 / 〇 líng zero. 两 liǎng = 'two of something', used instead of 二 before measure words.
FINANCIAL / CAPITAL FORMS 大写, used on bank forms, receipts, contracts, invoices and printed on banknotes — anti-fraud forms that cannot be altered with an extra stroke: 壹 yī 1, 贰 èr 2, 叁 sān 3, 肆 sì 4, 伍 wǔ 5, 陆 liù 6, 柒 qī 7, 捌 bā 8, 玖 jiǔ 9, 拾 shí 10, 佰 bǎi 100, 仟 qiān 1000, 萬 wàn 10000, 圆 / 元 yuán, 角 jiǎo, 分 fēn. A 100-yuan note reads 壹佰圆. Practical priority: 壹 贰 叁 拾 佰 圆 are the six you actually meet; the rest are for filling in a bank slip.
MONEY: 元 yuán written / 块 kuài spoken — same thing; 角 jiǎo written / 毛 máo spoken — 0.1; 分 fēn — 0.01, effectively extinct. ¥ / RMB / CNY / 人民币.
DATES AND TIMES: 年 nián year, 月 yuè month, 日 rì day (written) / 号 hào day (spoken) — 2026年8月22日. 星期一 xīngqīyī / 周一 zhōuyī — Monday / maandag; days are numbered 一 to 六 then 星期日/星期天 for Sunday. 上午 shàngwǔ morning, 中午 zhōngwǔ noon, 下午 xiàwǔ afternoon, 晚上 wǎnshang evening. 点 diǎn o'clock, 分 fēn minutes, 半 bàn half. 营业时间 yíngyè shíjiān — opening hours / openingstijden — usually 24-hour, e.g. 09:00-22:00. 至 zhì / 到 dào — to, until / tot. 周一至周五 — Monday to Friday / maandag t/m vrijdag. 节假日 jiéjiàrì — public holidays / feestdagen. 全天 quán tiān — 24 hours / de hele dag. 24小时 — 24 hours.
findings.implication: Content + UI: author opposite pairs as ONE card with two halves rather than two cards — 推/拉, 开/关, 男/女, 入/出, 满/空, 免费/收费, 营业中/休息. Pair-learning halves the item count and matches the real discrimination task, which is always binary (which door, which toilet, is it open). For the 万 problem, build a `compute` item type: show 三万五千 and ask for the Arabic numeral, with distractors at 10x and 0.1x, because the failure mode is an order-of-magnitude error and it costs money. Put 壹贰叁拾佰圆 in a low-priority 'bank counter' sub-deck — high consequence but low encounter rate, so it should be available but never blocking.

findings.claim: HSK QUANTIFICATION, PART 1 — of HSK 1-2 (old HSK 2.0, 300 words) I estimate only about 25-30% is text a traveller will ever read in Chinese public space, and roughly 40% of that yield is the numeral/date/time system alone. Strip numerals and HSK 1-2's signage yield falls to roughly 15-18%.
findings.detail:
METHOD (this is an estimate, not a measurement — I could not open the word lists): I mentally partitioned the HSK 2.0 levels 1-2 list (150 + 150 = 300 words) into functional classes and asked of each whether recognising it IN PRINT on a sign, menu or label changes what a traveller does. My partition: pronouns, particles, aspect markers, modals, and verbs of speech/cognition (我你他她们, 的了吗呢吧, 是有在, 说话想觉得认为希望喜欢会能可以要) — ~35-40% of the list, essentially zero signage yield, because signage drops function words. Kinship and school/home nouns (爸爸妈妈儿子女儿老师学生同学朋友, 桌子椅子铅笔本子) — ~15%, zero yield. Everyday verbs of action performed by people not signs (睡觉起床洗澡跑步打电话) — ~10%, zero yield. Genuinely readable-in-the-wild classes: numerals, money, dates, times, days (~35 words); position and direction (上下里外前面后面左边右边旁边, ~12 words); place nouns that are also shopfront words (商店 饭店 学校 火车站 机场 宾馆 教室 公司, ~10 words); food nouns that appear on menus (米饭 面条 鸡蛋 羊肉 牛奶 鱼 水果 苹果 西瓜 茶 咖啡 水 菜, ~14 words); a handful of adjectives that appear on labels and signs (大 小 多 少 新 热 冷 快 慢, ~9 words). Total readable ≈ 80-90 of 300 ≈ 27-30%, of which ~35 (roughly 40%) are the number/date/time system.
UNVERIFIED. Verification recipe, which is cheap and should be run before content lock: take the official HSK 2.0 level 1-2 list (300 items) and the HSK 3.0 level 1-2 list, and have two independent raters tag each item on a 3-point scale — 2 = 'I have seen this in print on a Chinese sign, menu or label and reading it changed my action', 1 = 'appears in print but decorative or inferable', 0 = 'spoken register only'. Report percentage at rating 2 with inter-rater agreement. Expect ~25-30% for HSK 1-2 and the estimate to be robust to rater identity, because the spoken/written register split is not a matter of taste.

findings.implication: Content: do NOT market or structure the app as 'HSK 1 for travellers' and do not import an HSK list as the seed bank — three quarters of it is dead weight for this goal. Add an explicit `hskLevel` field per item purely so the app can show a player who has done HSK 1 what they already know (a strong onboarding moment: 'you already have 34 of these') without letting HSK drive the ordering.

findings.claim: HSK QUANTIFICATION, PART 2 — of a ~330-item survival reading set, I estimate 75-82% appears nowhere in HSK 1-3 (old HSK 2.0, 600 words). Against HSK 3.0 levels 1-3 the picture inverts at the character level but not at the word level: 900 characters covers most of the ~380 survival CHARACTERS, while the survival COMPOUNDS remain largely absent — and signage meaning lives in the compounds.
findings.detail:
The specific absences from HSK 1-3 (2.0) are the point, because they are concentrated exactly in the high-payoff zones. Absent, to the best of my knowledge: 出口 入口 换乘 安检 站台 车厢 首班车 末班车 单程票 进站 出站 检票 候车 硬座 硬卧 软卧 二等座 取票 (all of transit operations); 禁止 请勿 严禁 危险 注意 当心 免费 收费 营业 休息 (all of prohibition and status, though 小心 is at HSK 3); 斤 克 千克 净含量 生产日期 保质期 冷藏 冷冻 进口 特价 买一送一 会员价 折 满减 (all of the supermarket, i.e. every single one of the three traps); 炒 爆 炸 蒸 焖 炖 涮 拌 卤 烧 煎 (all of cooking method — 烤 appears around HSK 4); 麻 麻辣 酸 咸 鲜 (flavour — 辣 appears around HSK 4, 甜 at HSK 3); 肠 肚 肝 血 舌 筋 腰 脑 皮 (all organ terms); 招牌 特色 时价 大份 例 凉菜 热菜 主食 (all menu structure); 药店 诊所 派出所 邮局 快递 加油站 停车场 理发 洗衣 火锅 面馆 (most shopfronts — 医院 银行 超市 洗手间 arrive at HSK 3, 商店 饭店 学校 at HSK 1-2); 壹贰叁 (financial numerals). Present in HSK 1-3: the numerals, the date/time system, 上下里外前后左右, 大小多少, 男女, 元/块/钱, a dozen food nouns, a dozen place nouns. Counting generously that is ~60-75 of my ~330-item set → 78-82% absent.
Against HSK 3.0 levels 1-3 (2,245 words, 900 characters, GF 0025-2021): the 900-character allocation is a different and much better instrument, because it is character-based and the survival set is ~380 characters. My estimate is that HSK 3.0's first 900 characters contain roughly 75-85% of the survival characters — you will get 出 口 换 站 台 车 禁 止 危 险 免 收 营 休 炒 蒸 烧 煎 辣 甜 酸 咸 药 店 馆 银 行 停 场 元 角 分 克 冷 藏 特 价 会 员 as individual characters — while the survival COMPOUNDS (换乘, 安检, 保质期, 净含量, 生产日期, 时价, 招牌, 麻辣, 单程票, 二等座, 冷冻, 买一送一) are almost all above level 3 as lexical items. That is the precise shape of the problem: HSK 3.0 hands you the bricks and withholds the buildings, and a learner who knows 保, 质 and 期 individually does not thereby know that 保质期 is a duration rather than a date. UNVERIFIED. Verification recipe: obtain the official HSK 3.0 level 1-3 character list (900) and word list (2,245), take the survival set as a CSV of characters and compounds, and compute two set intersections separately — character-level and word-level. The gap between those two numbers is the headline finding and it should go in the product's own copy.

findings.implication: Content: make 'HSK gives you bricks, not buildings' a structural feature of the item bank, not just a talking point. Every multi-character survival item stores `componentChars[]` and `isCompositional: boolean` — 出口 is compositional (out + mouth/opening → exit, guessable), 保质期 is not (guarantee + quality + period → shelf life, not guessable), 时价 is not, 招牌 is not, 方便面 is not. Teach the compositional ones by their parts and give the non-compositional ones a dedicated 'this one you just have to know' treatment with a mnemonic slot. Show the split in the progress screen: 'you can work out 61 of these; 44 you have to memorise'. That is an honest, motivating and genuinely novel progress metric, and it is only computable because the field exists.

findings.claim: FINAL ORDERING — the recommended teaching order across all five domains, ranked by payoff per character, and it differs from HSK ordering, from frequency ordering, and from traveller intuition.
findings.detail:
TIER 0 — the first session, ~24 items, everything here changes behaviour and several prevent harm. Ordered: (1) the GB 2894 four-colour safety system, no characters. (2) 男/女 as a pair. (3) 出口 / 入口 as a pair, plus 安全出口 in green. (4) 推/拉 as a pair. (5) 禁止 and 请勿 as the two prohibition openers. (6) 小心 and 危险. (7) 营业中 / 休息. (8) 元 and 块. (9) 斤 with the 500g arithmetic. (10) 辣 and 麻辣. (11) 肉 = pork. (12) 素 vs 荤. (13) 洗手间 / 厕所. (14) 满/空. 
TIER 1 — ~110 items. Cooking methods (13 characters). Proteins (10). Staples (8). Section headers (8). The 折 and 保质期 traps with their arithmetic. 冷藏/冷冻. 特价/会员价/买一送一. 净含量/克/千克. The eight shopfront head morphemes. 药店 医院 银行 邮局 派出所 加油站 停车场 快递 超市 便利店. 开/关, 上/下, 内/外, 前/后, 左/右. Numerals to 万. Dates, times, 营业时间. The mini-programme button set (下单 购物车 去结算 备注 确认 取消).
TIER 2 — ~200 items. The organ and texture set. Extended flavour. Menu qualifiers and 时价. Full transit (metro + rail seat-class grid + airport). Allergen and nutrition label set. Extended shopfronts. 壹贰叁 financial numerals. Composite whole-sign and whole-menu tasks.
WHY THIS ORDER AND NOT THE OTHERS. Versus HSK: HSK is ordered by grammatical and conversational progression toward a test, so it front-loads the spoken register (pronouns, particles, kinship, classroom) and defers the written public register almost entirely — 禁止 and 危险 and 保质期 are HSK 4-6 or absent, while 爸爸 and 高兴 are HSK 1. For a three-week trip that ordering is close to inverted. Versus pure frequency: frequency front-loads function words which are precisely what signage omits, so the first 100 characters by frequency deliver perhaps a fifth of the actionable signage that 100 functionally-chosen characters deliver; the two orderings only converge above ~1,200-1,500 characters. Versus traveller intuition: travellers expect transit to matter most (it is the first thing they use and the thing they most fear), but transit is the most bilingual, most pictographic and most standardised environment in China (GB/T 30240), so its marginal payoff per character is the lowest of the five. The menu and the supermarket label — where nobody has translated anything for you and where the consequence of a misread is a dish you cannot eat, a bill you did not expect, or an allergen you did not see — are where reading actually pays.
findings.implication: Content + architecture: encode the tier as `tier: 0|1|2` and make Tier 0 a linear, unskippable, single-player 12-minute onboarding that runs BEFORE the multiplayer game is available — 24 items, no betting, no timer, high scaffolding. The multiplayer game then draws only from Tier 1 and 2 with the domain weights from finding 3. This solves the co-located-game cold-start problem (four players of wildly different levels) by guaranteeing a shared floor, and it means the first thing a player learns is the thing most likely to keep them out of trouble on day one.

findings.claim: Digital games beat non-game comparison conditions for learning by only a small-to-moderate margin, and the *design* of the game matters about as much as whether it is a game at all.
findings.detail: Clark, Tanner-Smith & Killingsworth (2016) meta-analysed ~57 game-vs-nongame comparisons and reported g ≈ 0.33 (95% CI roughly [0.19, 0.48]) for digital games over non-game instruction. Critically, their second analysis — augmented/redesigned game vs standard version of the SAME game — gave a comparable g ≈ 0.34. That is, changing the instructional design inside a game moves outcomes as much as adding a game. Heterogeneity was high and moderated by comparison-group quality. Exact CI bounds not re-verified.
findings.implication: Do not spend the build budget on game shell (avatars, animation, meta-progression). Spend it on the item bank and the resolution moment. Concretely: allocate engineering to (a) item quality/coverage for the four target situations (menu, subway signage, supermarket label, shopfront) and (b) the explanation card, before any cosmetic layer. Budget rule of thumb: ≥60% of content-authoring effort into items+explanations, ≤40% into game feel.

sources.citation: Clark, D. B., Tanner-Smith, E. E., & Killingsworth, S. S. (2016). Digital games, design, and learning: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research, 86(1), 79–122.

findings.claim: Serious games produce a small learning benefit and a *retention* benefit over conventional instruction, but they do NOT reliably produce more motivation than conventional instruction — and they work better when players play in groups than alone.
findings.detail: Wouters, van Nimwegen, van Oostendorp & van der Spek (2013), Journal of Educational Psychology, k ≈ 38–39 studies. Learning d ≈ 0.29; retention d ≈ 0.36; motivation d ≈ 0.26 and NOT statistically significant. Moderator analyses reported larger effects when the game was supplemented with other instructional methods, when play was distributed over multiple sessions, and when players worked in groups rather than singly. The null motivation result is the most-cited and most-uncomfortable finding in this literature. Exact k and moderator p-values not re-verified.
findings.implication: Two direct consequences. (1) UX: make multi-session the default — the app should open on a 'resume/next session' screen, not a marketing screen, and should cap a session at a length that can plausibly repeat (see pacing findings). (2) Architecture: the co-located group mode is the evidence-supported configuration, so the multiplayer path should be the primary code path and single-player should be implemented as a degenerate case of it (one human + scripted/bot opponents reusing the same turn state machine), not as a separate engine.

findings.claim: The apparent advantage of instructional games largely disappears when the comparison group is also actively practising. The game's measured benefit is substantially the benefit of the practice it schedules.
findings.detail: Sitzmann (2011), Personnel Psychology, k ≈ 65 studies of computer-based simulation games. Reported roughly +11% declarative knowledge, +14% procedural knowledge, +9% retention, +20% self-efficacy relative to comparison. But the moderator result is the important one: the advantage held when the comparison group was PASSIVE and shrank toward zero when comparison trainees were actively engaged with the same content. Mayer's later 'media comparison vs value-added' critique (Mayer, 2019, Annual Review of Psychology) makes the same methodological point: most game studies are media comparisons with weak controls, and value-added experiments (game vs game+feature) are the only ones that isolate what the game element contributes.
findings.implication: Frame the product bet honestly in the design doc and in the metrics: the game is a *compliance and scheduling* technology, not a learning technology. Architecture consequence: instrument and store items-attempted-per-session and sessions-per-week as the primary success metric, because that is the causal channel the evidence supports. If a game mechanic does not increase retrieval attempts per unit of wall-clock time, or does not increase the probability of a next session, cut it. Set an explicit internal target (e.g. ≥40 scored retrievals per 10-minute session per player) and measure mechanics against it.

findings.claim: Digital game-based L2 *vocabulary* learning shows the largest effects in the DGBLL literature — around g ≈ 0.8–0.9 in the most-cited vocabulary meta-analysis — but the effect size is strongly moderated by research design and the heterogeneity is severe.
findings.detail: Tsai & Tsai (2018), Computers & Education, ~26 studies of digital game-based L2 vocabulary learning, reported an overall effect in the neighbourhood of g ≈ 0.87 favouring games. The paper's own contribution is that 'conditions of research designs' moderate the estimate heavily — studies with no-treatment or weak controls yield much larger effects than those with active controls. Chiu, Kao & Reynolds (2012, BJET) reported a more modest d ≈ 0.5 for DGBL in EFL. Thompson & von Gillern (2020, Educational Research Review) ran a Bayesian meta-analysis of video-game-based vocabulary instruction for English learners and reported a large pooled effect with a wide credible interval. I could not re-verify any of these numbers; treat the 0.87 figure as the least reliable of the three.
findings.implication: Content: ship vocabulary/character *recognition* as the core item type and resist scope creep into production, tone drills, or grammar for v1 — recognition is where the evidence base is strongest and it is also exactly what 'read a menu, read the subway' requires. Concretely, the v1 item bank should be recognition-only: given hanzi (or a short sign-like string), select/say the meaning. Defer handwriting and pinyin-production item types entirely.

findings.claim: Gamification (points/badges/leaderboards layered on instruction, as distinct from a full game) yields roughly g ≈ 0.36–0.50 on cognitive outcomes, with the behavioural effect the weakest of the three outcome families.
findings.detail: Sailer & Homner (2020), Educational Psychology Review, k ≈ 38 studies: cognitive g ≈ 0.49, motivational g ≈ 0.36, behavioural g ≈ 0.25. Huang et al. (2020, ETR&D) reported g ≈ 0.46 and Bai, Hew & Huang (2020, Educational Research Review) g ≈ 0.50 — three independent teams converging near 0.5 is the strongest convergence in this whole literature. Sailer & Homner reported bias diagnostics that did not indicate severe publication bias for the cognitive outcome; I could not re-verify which test (Egger/trim-and-fill) or its value.
findings.implication: UI: a points display is justified, but keep it a *task* signal, not a *person* signal (see Kluger & DeNisi below). Concretely: show the running score as a small numeric delta attached to the item just answered (e.g. '+3' animating off the card), and keep the aggregate team score in a persistent but low-salience strip (≤14px, muted colour, top edge). Do not put a full-screen scoreboard between turns.

findings.claim: The DGBLL meta-analytic base is methodologically weak in ways that should discount every effect size above: small k, I² frequently above 75–80%, heavy regional and author overlap, short interventions, and predominantly passive control groups.
findings.detail: This is a synthesis of the limitations sections of the meta-analyses named above plus Mayer's (2019) critique and Hung, Yang, Hwang, Chu & Wang's (2018, Computers & Education) scoping review of DGBLL, which catalogued the field's design problems. Typical DGBLL meta-analyses pool 20–30 studies, many with n < 60 per arm and interventions under 8 weeks, which is also the window in which novelty effects operate. I could not re-verify specific I² values in this session; the claim that heterogeneity is high is safe, the specific figure is not.
findings.implication: UX/architecture: build the product so it can generate its own evidence, because the external literature will not settle the question at the precision you need. Log, per player per item: presentation timestamp, response latency (ms), correctness, whether the item was dealt by an opponent, and the player's score position at that moment. That schema is the minimum needed to later test in-product whether the adversarial dealing mechanic helps or hurts. Store locally (IndexedDB) with an opt-in sync; the PWA must work fully offline for a co-located game.

findings.claim: In the Johnson & Johnson meta-analytic tradition, cooperative goal structures outperform competitive ones for achievement by roughly half a standard deviation, and the finding has held up across four decades and multiple independent syntheses.
findings.detail: Johnson, Maruyama, Johnson, Nelson & Skon (1981, Psychological Bulletin) synthesised 122 studies and reported cooperation superior to interpersonal competition. Qin, Johnson & Johnson (1995, Review of Educational Research), 46 studies of problem solving, reported cooperation > competition at roughly d ≈ 0.55, with the gap larger for complex/conceptual problems than for simple ones. The modern flagship is Roseth, Johnson & Johnson (2008, Psychological Bulletin): 148 studies, ~17,000 early adolescents, cooperative > competitive on achievement at roughly ES ≈ 0.46, cooperative > individualistic ≈ 0.55, plus superior peer relationships. Exact values not re-verified.
findings.implication: UX: the product's team structure is defensible only if the *within-team* structure is genuinely cooperative — positive goal interdependence plus individual accountability, which is what these studies actually manipulated. Concretely: score must be a team score to which each member's answers contribute (positive interdependence) AND each member's own contribution must be visible to their own team afterwards (individual accountability). A structure where a lone player answers for a team score with no teammate involvement is competition wearing a team costume and gets none of this evidence's support.

findings.claim: The Johnson & Johnson cooperation-over-competition result has a serious, never-fully-resolved methodological critique: independent re-codings of the same studies produced substantially smaller effects.
findings.detail: Cotton & Cook (1982, Psychological Bulletin) and McGlynn (1982, Psychological Bulletin) published direct critiques of the 1981 meta-analysis, arguing that study inclusion and the coding of 'cooperative' vs 'competitive' conditions were not independent of the authors' theoretical commitment, and that a re-analysis yields a much smaller cooperation advantage. The Johnsons replied; the field never converged. Later syntheses (Roseth et al. 2008; Kyndt et al. 2013, Educational Research Review, k ≈ 65, achievement d ≈ 0.54) were still largely conducted by researchers inside the cooperative-learning tradition. Allegiance bias in this literature is real and should discount the point estimates, though not the sign.
findings.implication: Do not present 'cooperation beats competition' internally as settled fact justifying a design. Use it as a prior, and treat the adversarial mechanic as an explicit hypothesis to be A/B tested in-product. Architecture: build the turn state machine so the dealing rule is a swappable strategy object (opponent-deals / random-deals / self-selects) configurable per match, so an experiment costs a config flag rather than a rewrite.

findings.claim: THE central finding for this product: competition has essentially NO direct effect on performance. Its total effect is near zero because it simultaneously activates one process that helps (performance-approach goals) and one that hurts (performance-avoidance goals). Design determines which one dominates.
findings.detail: Murayama & Elliot (2012), Psychological Bulletin, 'The competition–performance relation: A meta-analytic review and test of the opposing processes model of competition and performance'. Very large evidence base (on the order of 170+ studies / 1,000+ effect sizes across experimental and correlational designs). The headline: the direct competition→performance correlation is approximately zero and non-significant (r around -0.01). The structural model showed competition → performance-APPROACH goals → better performance, and competition → performance-AVOIDANCE goals → worse performance, with the two paths cancelling. Exact r and k not re-verified, but the 'null total effect, opposing mediators' conclusion is the paper's well-known thesis.
findings.implication: This is the pedagogical licence for the product AND its binding constraint. Competition per se is neither defensible nor harmful; it is a null that you can tip either way. Every UX decision should be evaluated by one question: does this push the player toward 'I want to get this one right' (approach) or 'I must not be the one who looks stupid' (avoidance)? Concrete rules that follow: (1) frame all on-screen copy around gaining, never around losing or avoiding — '+3 for your team', never 'don't lose 3'; (2) never render a negative number in red at large size; (3) never show a live 'who is losing' ordering during play. Approach-framing is the entire ballgame.

findings.claim: Adding competitive elements to an educational game reliably raises enjoyment and situational interest but does not reliably raise learning.
findings.detail: Plass, O'Keefe, Homer, Case, Hayward, Stein & Perlin (2013, Journal of Educational Psychology; n ≈ 58 middle-school students) compared individual, competitive and collaborative play of the same maths game: competitive and collaborative conditions produced higher situational interest and enjoyment than individual play, while learning of the target skill was broadly comparable; collaborative play was associated with more mastery-goal orientation. Cagiltay, Ozcelik & Ozcelik (2015, Computers & Education) found a competitive version increased motivation but not learning outcomes. Ke & Grabowski (2007, BJET; n ≈ 125 fifth-graders) found cooperative gameplay outperformed competitive gameplay for maths learning, with the largest benefit for lower-SES students. All are small single studies; the pattern across them is what carries weight, not any one.
findings.implication: Competition earns its place in this product as a *retention/attendance* mechanism (people show up and keep playing), not as a learning mechanism. UX consequence: put the competitive framing at the session boundaries — match setup, and a single end-of-match result screen — and keep the moment-to-moment item loop as neutral and task-focused as a flashcard. Competitive salience high at t=0 and t=end; near zero during the ~40 retrievals in between.

findings.claim: Foreign-language anxiety is negatively associated with L2 achievement at about r = −0.34 to −0.39 — one of the most robust individual-difference findings in SLA, established across ~100 samples and 20,000+ learners.
findings.detail: Teimouri, Goetze & Plonsky (2019), Studies in Second Language Acquisition: meta-analysis of L2 anxiety and achievement, roughly 97 samples and N ≈ 23,000, pooled r ≈ −0.36. Botes, Dewaele & Greiff (2020), Journal for the Psychology of Language Learning, meta-analysed FLCAS-specific studies and reported a comparable r ≈ −0.36 to −0.39. Zhang (2019, Modern Language Journal) reported r ≈ −0.34 in an independent synthesis. Three independent teams landing in a 0.05 band is unusually strong for SLA. Note these are correlational — direction of causation is bidirectional and contested — but the magnitude is not in serious doubt. Exact values not re-verified.
findings.implication: An anxiety-inducing mechanic is not a neutral design choice in a *language* product specifically; it operates on the single largest measured affective moderator of L2 outcomes. Architecture/UX consequence: make anxiety a first-class, measurable product variable. Ship a 3-item post-match check-in (single screen, 5-point, ~8 seconds) sampled on maybe 1 match in 5, storing a per-player anxiety trace alongside the performance trace. Without this you cannot detect the harm if it happens.

findings.claim: The specific component of language anxiety most directly triggered by this product's mechanic is 'fear of negative evaluation' — one of the three constitutive factors of foreign-language classroom anxiety since the construct was defined.
findings.detail: Horwitz, Horwitz & Cope (1986), Modern Language Journal, defined foreign language classroom anxiety as comprising communication apprehension, test anxiety, and FEAR OF NEGATIVE EVALUATION, and produced the FLCAS. This is the single most-cited paper in affective SLA. A mechanic in which an opponent chooses your category, watches you answer, and observes you lose points is close to a laboratory operationalisation of fear of negative evaluation. Separately, Dewaele & MacIntyre (2014, SSLLT, n ≈ 1,746) showed foreign language enjoyment and foreign language anxiety are distinguishable dimensions (r ≈ −0.36, not −1.0) — meaning a session can be simultaneously enjoyable and anxiety-provoking, so 'players report they had fun' is NOT evidence that the mechanic is safe.
findings.implication: Measurement discipline: never accept enjoyment/NPS as evidence the adversarial mechanic is harmless — the constructs are only moderately negatively correlated. Content consequence: the item bank must never let an opponent select an item the target player has demonstrably never seen. Enforce a hard eligibility rule — an opponent may only deal from categories in which the target has ≥5 prior exposures — so the mechanic cannot be weaponised into guaranteed public failure.

findings.claim: Competitive, publicly-evaluated goal structures are specifically damaging to lower-ability learners, because they make ability (rather than effort or strategy) the salient explanation for the outcome.
findings.detail: Ames (1992, Journal of Educational Psychology, 'Classrooms: Goals, structures, and student motivation') and the earlier Ames & Ames work established that competitive/normative evaluation structures cue ego-involvement and ability attributions, whereas mastery structures cue effort/strategy attributions; the TARGET framework's explicit recommendation is to de-emphasise social comparison and public normative evaluation. Under a competitive structure, the low performer's failure is attributed to stable low ability, which is the classic route into learned helplessness and withdrawal. This is seminal and theoretically central but the causal experiments are mostly older, smaller, and with children — hence 'moderate' rather than 'strong'.
findings.implication: UI: never display an ability-implying aggregate about a person. Specifically, ban from the interface: a per-player accuracy percentage visible to others, a persistent cross-match ranking of individuals, and any 'weakest player' label. Replace normative comparison with self-referenced progress — the only comparison shown to a player about themselves should be against their own prior state ('12 new characters recognised this week'), which is a mastery cue rather than an ability cue.

sources.citation: Ames, C. (1992). Classrooms: Goals, structures, and student motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 84(3), 261–271.

findings.claim: Leaderboards harm the people at the bottom of them; leaderboard *design* (near-peer/relative vs whole-cohort/absolute) changes the sign of the effect for low performers.
findings.detail: Bai, Hew, Sailer & Jia (2021), Computers & Education, 'From top to bottom: How positions on different types of leaderboard may affect fully online student learning performance, intrinsic motivation, and course engagement' — reported that bottom-position students on absolute (whole-cohort) leaderboards fared worse on motivation/engagement, while relative leaderboards showing only near-peers were less damaging. Converging cautionary evidence: Hanus & Fox (2015, Computers & Education, n ≈ 80, quasi-experimental) found a badge-plus-leaderboard condition showed DECLINING intrinsic motivation, satisfaction and exam performance over a semester relative to a non-gamified section; Mekler, Brühlmann, Tuch & Opwis (2017, Computers in Human Behavior, n ≈ 273) found points/levels/leaderboards increased output quantity but did not increase intrinsic motivation. Hanus & Fox is small and confounded by section; treat as a caution, not a result.
findings.implication: UI: if a leaderboard ships at all, make it near-peer and bounded — show the player their own row plus the one immediately above and immediately below (3 rows maximum), never the full ordered list, and never a visible 'last place'. In a 4-player co-located match this means: show team totals only, and show the individual breakdown only privately on the player's own device after the match ends.

findings.claim: It is LOSING, not competing, that undermines intrinsic motivation — and giving losers explicit competence feedback largely protects their motivation. This is the single most actionable mitigation in the literature.
findings.detail: Reeve & Deci (1996, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, n ≈ 100): winning a competition increased intrinsic motivation relative to losing, and pressure to win undermined intrinsic motivation even among winners — the controlling framing, not the contest, does the damage. Vansteenkiste & Deci (2003, Motivation and Emotion, 'Competitively contingent rewards and intrinsic motivation: Can losers remain motivated?'): losers who received positive competence feedback retained intrinsic motivation at levels comparable to winners. Both are lab studies with ~100 undergraduates on non-language tasks — hence moderate, not strong — but they align with the wider SDT reward meta-analysis (Deci, Koestner & Ryan, 1999, Psychological Bulletin, k ≈ 128: tangible expected rewards undermine intrinsic motivation, free-choice d ≈ −0.34).
findings.implication: Mandate a competence-feedback screen for the losing side. Concretely, the end-of-match screen for every player — winner and loser alike — must lead with an absolute competence statement before any relative one: 'You read 23 characters correctly tonight. 6 of them were new.' The win/loss result appears second, smaller. Additionally: never make the reward contingent on winning — award the same XP/streak credit for retrievals attempted regardless of match outcome, so the extrinsic reward is competence-contingent rather than competition-contingent.

findings.claim: Feedback is not reliably beneficial: over a third of feedback interventions make performance WORSE, and the strongest moderator is whether the feedback directs attention to the task or to the self. Public loss of points in front of opponents is self-level feedback.
findings.detail: Kluger & DeNisi (1996), Psychological Bulletin, 'The effects of feedback interventions on performance': ~131 papers, ~607 effect sizes; mean d ≈ 0.41, but approximately 38% of effect sizes were NEGATIVE. Feedback Intervention Theory attributes this to attention: feedback that cues meta-task/self processes (ego, self-worth, social standing) degrades performance, while feedback that cues task-learning processes improves it. Hattie & Timperley (2007, Review of Educational Research) reach the same conclusion in their four-level model — feedback about the self as a person is the least effective level. This is the most directly damning evidence against the 'watch you lose points publicly' mechanic as currently described: a public point loss is close to a pure self-level feedback signal with no task information attached.
findings.implication: Redesign the loss moment so that the *task* information is what is public and the *self* information is what is private. Concretely: when an answer is wrong, the shared/co-located view should show the CORRECT ANSWER AND THE EXPLANATION at full size, and the score change should be a small, brief, non-coloured tick in the score strip. Invert the current emphasis. Target ratio on screen: explanation occupies ≥70% of the viewport at resolution; score delta ≤5%, ≤14px, no red, no animation longer than 300ms, no sound.

sources.citation: Kluger, A. N., & DeNisi, A. (1996). The effects of feedback interventions on performance: A historical review, a meta-analysis, and a preliminary feedback intervention theory. Psychological Bulletin, 119(2), 254–284.

findings.claim: Being watched impairs performance on novel and complex tasks and improves it on well-learned simple ones — but meta-analytically the effect is SMALL, explaining under about 3% of variance.
findings.detail: Zajonc (1965, Science) proposed drive theory: the presence of others enhances the dominant response, which helps when the dominant response is correct (well-learned material) and hurts when it is not (novel material). Bond & Titus (1983), Psychological Bulletin, meta-analysed 241 social facilitation studies and found the pattern broadly confirmed for speed/accuracy but with strikingly small magnitudes — audience presence accounted for roughly 0.3–3% of variance in performance. Uziel (2007, Journal of Research in Personality) meta-analysed individual differences and found the direction depends on trait: individuals high in neuroticism / low in self-esteem show impairment under observation, while extraverts and those high in approach traits show facilitation. So the average is small because it is a mixture of opposite-signed subgroups.
findings.implication: Two implications. (1) The mere-observation part of the mechanic is not, by itself, a big harm — it is small on average, so do not over-engineer against it. (2) But because the average hides opposite-signed subgroups, the harm concentrates in exactly the anxious/low-confidence players you least want to lose. UX consequence: give the player an *input privacy* option that costs nothing competitively — answers are entered on the player's own phone and only the RESULT plus the explanation is thrown to the shared view. Never require the player to speak the answer aloud or to hold up their screen. Reading (not speaking) is the target skill anyway, so private input is free.

findings.claim: Performance pressure consumes working memory, and it disproportionately harms the people who normally rely on working memory most — so a timed, observed answer degrades precisely the effortful retrieval that produces learning.
findings.detail: Beilock & Carr (2005), Psychological Science, 'When high-powered people fail: Working memory and choking under pressure in math': under pressure, high-working-memory individuals lost their advantage and performed at the level of low-WM individuals, because pressure-related worry occupies the same WM resources the high-WM strategy depends on. Beilock & DeCaro (2007) extended this to strategy selection. Sample sizes are modest lab studies with maths, not L2 reading, so generalisation is an inference — hence moderate. The mechanism (worry as a concurrent WM load) is well established in the cognitive-load and test-anxiety literatures more broadly.
findings.implication: UX: do not stack pressures. Choose at most ONE of {countdown timer, live opponent observation, public score change} to be salient on any given item. Concretely — since observation is inherent to a co-located game, drop the visible countdown: use a generous silent timeout (see wait-time finding) with no ticking clock, no shrinking bar, and no colour change until the final 20% of the window. A visible countdown is the cheapest pressure to remove and the one with the least learning value.

sources.citation: Beilock, S. L., & Carr, T. H. (2005). When high-powered people fail: Working memory and 'choking under pressure' in math. Psychological Science, 16(2), 101–105.

findings.claim: There is NO direct evidence I can cite that public failure in a language-learning game suppresses subsequent participation. The inference is assembled from adjacent literatures and should be labelled as an inference, not a finding.
findings.detail: The supporting chain is: (a) fear of negative evaluation is a core component of FL anxiety (Horwitz et al., 1986); (b) anxiety correlates r ≈ −0.36 with achievement (Teimouri et al., 2019); (c) L2 willingness to communicate is reduced by state anxiety and varies sharply by interactional context, with whole-class/public contexts producing the lowest participation and dyads the highest (Cao & Philp, 2006, System; MacIntyre, Dörnyei, Clément & Noels, 1998, Modern Language Journal); (d) reviews of Kahoot-style competitive classroom quizzing (Wang & Tahir, 2020, Computers & Education, reviewing ~93 studies) report recurring negative themes including anxiety, fear of losing, and embarrassment at a visible low ranking, though these are mostly self-report in weak designs. None of this is a controlled test of 'public failure → reduced subsequent participation in an L2 game'. Any claim that it does is currently folklore dressed in adjacent citations.
findings.implication: Architecture: instrument the exact question the literature does not answer, because you can answer it cheaply in-product. Log per player: turns voluntarily initiated, response latency, and abandonment, each keyed to whether the PREVIOUS turn was a public failure. A within-player pre/post-failure comparison of next-turn latency and next-session return is a real experiment you can run at n=200 players. Make 'turns since last public failure' a stored field so the analysis is a query rather than a data-collection project.

findings.claim: Errors followed by corrective feedback produce BETTER retention than error-free study, and errors made with high confidence are the most likely of all to be corrected — so a public wrong answer is a learning asset provided the correction arrives immediately.
findings.detail: Metcalfe (2017), Annual Review of Psychology, 'Learning from errors' — reviews the errorful-generation literature and concludes that generating an error and then receiving corrective feedback typically outperforms errorless study, contrary to older behaviourist assumptions. Butterfield & Metcalfe (2001, JEP:LMC) established the hypercorrection effect: errors committed with HIGH confidence are more likely to be corrected after feedback than low-confidence errors, replicated repeatedly since. Mechanistically this is attributed to surprise/attention at the moment of correction.
findings.implication: This substantially rescues the product's mechanic — but only conditionally. The condition is that correction must be immediate, task-focused and unmissable. Concrete: the correct answer must appear within ~300ms of the wrong submission, on the same screen position the answer occupied, with no intervening score animation, transition, or opponent reaction. Content consequence: deliberately include items likely to produce confident errors — visually confusable hanzi pairs (e.g. 未/末, 己/已/巳, 土/士, 干/千, 白/百, 人/入, 天/夭) and false-friend compounds — because high-confidence errors are the ones that hypercorrect. Ship a dedicated 'confusable pairs' item category.

findings.claim: Elaborated feedback roughly outperforms knowledge-of-correct-response, and both massively outperform bare right/wrong — with effects of about d = 0.49 (elaborated), 0.32 (KCR) and 0.05 (verification only) in computer-based learning environments.
findings.detail: Van der Kleij, Feskens & Eggen (2015), Review of Educational Research, 'Effects of feedback in a computer-based learning environment on students' learning outcomes: A meta-analysis'. Roughly 40 studies / ~70 effect sizes. The ordered pattern — elaborated feedback ≈ 0.49 > knowledge of correct response ≈ 0.32 > knowledge of result (correct/incorrect only) ≈ 0.05 — is the single most directly actionable number set for this product. Converging: Wisniewski, Zierer & Hattie (2020, Frontiers in Psychology; ~435 studies, ~994 effect sizes, N ≈ 61,000) reported an overall d ≈ 0.48 with high-information feedback far outperforming simple reinforcement or punishment (roughly 0.99 vs 0.24). Exact figures not re-verified in session.
findings.implication: Bare right/wrong is worth essentially nothing (d ≈ 0.05) — a red X plus a point loss is the LEAST effective feedback design available and is what the current mechanic emphasises. Every resolution must carry elaboration. Content: author, for every single item in the bank, a mandatory three-slot explanation — (1) the correct reading/meaning, (2) ONE discriminating cue (radical, component, position, or the confusable it is not), (3) ONE real-world anchor tying it to a menu/subway/label/shopfront context. Make explanation a required, non-nullable field in the item schema so an item cannot ship without one.

findings.claim: Immediate vs delayed feedback is genuinely contested, but the conditions that favour immediate feedback — applied setting, low prior knowledge, item-level factual/associative material — are exactly this product's conditions.
findings.detail: Kulik & Kulik (1988, Review of Educational Research, 'Timing of feedback and verbal learning') found a dissociation: laboratory list-learning studies favoured DELAYED feedback, while applied/classroom studies favoured IMMEDIATE. Butler, Karpicke & Roediger (2007, JEP: Applied) found delayed feedback produced better performance on a delayed test with multiple-choice materials. Metcalfe, Kornell & Finn (2009, Memory & Cognition, 'Delayed versus immediate feedback in children's and adults' vocabulary learning') found the timing advantage interacted with age/learner — I recall immediate favoured for children and delayed showing advantages for adults under some conditions, but I could NOT re-verify the direction and should not be relied on. The safe summary: the delayed-feedback advantage appears mainly in laboratory paradigms where the delay itself creates a spaced re-exposure; in applied, motivationally-loaded settings immediate feedback wins.
findings.implication: Give immediate feedback at the item (it is also required by the social-repair logic above — you cannot leave a public error uncorrected in front of a table of people), and recover the delayed-feedback benefit separately via spaced re-exposure rather than via delayed correction. Concrete: correct immediately at t+300ms, AND re-queue every missed item for re-presentation later in the same match (target: 2 further exposures at roughly 5 and 15 intervening items) and again in the next session. Architecture: the match engine needs a lapse queue with interleave-distance constraints, not just a linear item list.

findings.claim: Adult silent reading of English non-fiction averages about 238 words per minute — roughly 4 words per second — which gives a hard, computable budget for how long a feedback explanation can be and still be read in the available window.
findings.detail: Brysbaert (2019), Journal of Memory and Language, 'How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate'. Very large synthesis; reported mean silent reading rate around 238 wpm for English non-fiction (roughly 260 wpm for fiction), with wide individual variation and slower rates for L2 readers and for on-screen scanning under time pressure. The 'do students read their feedback' problem is separately documented in the higher-education feedback literature (e.g. Jonsson, 2013, Active Learning in Higher Education) — lengthy feedback is frequently not read or used. Shute (2008, Review of Educational Research, 'Focus on formative feedback') similarly recommends specific, task-focused, manageable-length feedback and warns against overload.
findings.implication: Concrete word budget. At ~4 words/second, and assuming an under-pressure, glancing on-screen rate of ~3 words/second for a second-language learner in a noisy co-located setting, a 4-second resolution window supports about 12 words and a 7-second window about 20 words. Therefore: cap the primary explanation line at 20 words / ~120 characters, on ONE line-wrapped block, at ≥17px, with the discriminating cue bolded. Any additional detail goes behind an optional tap ('why?') that pauses the turn clock. Enforce the cap in the content pipeline as a build-time lint that fails CI on any item whose explanation exceeds 20 words.

findings.claim: Prompting learners to self-explain improves learning by about g = 0.55 across ~64 studies — a larger and better-replicated effect than any game or gamification effect in this report.
findings.detail: Bisra, Liu, Nesbit, Salimi & Winne (2018), Educational Psychology Review, 'Inducing self-explanation: A meta-analysis'. Approximately 64 studies / 69 effect sizes, N in the thousands; pooled g ≈ 0.55 (95% CI roughly [0.46, 0.63]) for prompted self-explanation over unprompted controls. Moderators included the presence of scaffolding/prompt structure. The foundational work is Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann & Glaser (1989, Cognitive Science) and Chi, de Leeuw, Chiu & LaVancher (1994, Cognitive Science, 'Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding'). A necessary caveat from Rittle-Johnson, Loehr & Durkin (2017, ZDM): self-explanation costs TIME, and when studies equate time-on-task the advantage shrinks — so it must displace something, not be added on top.
findings.implication: Convert the dead moment before the reveal into a one-tap self-explanation. Concrete UX: after the player commits an answer but before the correct answer is revealed, show a single 2-second micro-prompt offering 2–3 tappable reason chips ('I knew the radical' / 'I guessed from context' / 'I confused it with another character'). One tap, no typing, no time penalty. This is a cheap constructive act in a slot that is currently empty. Architecture: store the chip as a confidence/strategy tag on the attempt record — it also gives you the confidence signal needed to exploit hypercorrection scheduling.

findings.claim: The protégé effect is real but modest and much weaker than its popularity suggests; the meta-analytic estimate for learning-by-teaching is around g ≈ 0.3, and the benefit depends on whether the teacher engages in knowledge-BUILDING rather than knowledge-TELLING.
findings.detail: The named 'protégé effect' comes from Chase, Chin, Oppezzo & Schwartz (2009, Journal of Science Education and Technology) using the Betty's Brain teachable agent, n ≈ 62 eighth-graders: students worked harder and learned more when working on behalf of an agent than for themselves. Small, single, agent-specific. The meta-analytic picture is more sober: Kobayashi (2019, Japanese Psychological Research, 'Learning by preparing-to-teach and teaching: A meta-analysis') reported a modest pooled benefit in the region of g ≈ 0.3; Cohen, Kulik & Kulik (1982, American Educational Research Journal, 65 studies) found tutors themselves gained d ≈ 0.33 (tutees d ≈ 0.40). Crucially, Roscoe & Chi (2007, Review of Educational Research, 'Understanding tutor learning: Knowledge-building and knowledge-telling in peer tutors' explanations and questions') showed tutors overwhelmingly default to shallow knowledge-telling (restating) rather than reflective knowledge-building, and only the latter produces tutor learning. Fiorella & Mayer (2013, Contemporary Educational Psychology, n ≈ 64) found actually teaching beat mere expectancy of teaching on delayed comprehension.
findings.implication: Do not build a 'teach your teammate' mechanic and expect g = 0.5; expect ~0.3 and only if you force knowledge-building. Concrete mechanic that fits the existing turn structure: after a teammate answers correctly, give ONE other team member a 5-second 'say why' slot with a single tappable prompt — and score it, small, as a team bonus. Do not allow free restatement of the answer (knowledge-telling); require selecting/producing the discriminating cue (the radical, the contrast pair), which is the knowledge-building act. Content dependency: this only works if every item carries the discriminating-cue field specified above.

findings.claim: Peer discussion between an individual answer and a revealed answer improves performance on a NEW isomorphic item — demonstrating genuine learning transfer, not merely copying the better student.
findings.detail: Smith, Wood, Adams, Wieman, Knight, Guild & Su (2009), Science, 'Why peer discussion improves student performance on in-class concept questions'. Design: students answered a clicker question individually, discussed with peers, re-answered, then answered a SECOND, isomorphic question alone with no further discussion. Performance on the second, independently-answered question improved — ruling out the 'they just copied' explanation. n in the hundreds (~350 in a genetics course). This underwrites the peer-instruction pattern generally (Crouch & Mazur, 2001, American Journal of Physics), and sits inside the broader active-learning result of Freeman et al. (2014, PNAS, k = 225 studies: exam performance d ≈ 0.47, failure-rate odds ratio ≈ 1.95).
findings.implication: Adopt the peer-instruction sequence as the core turn shape rather than a single answer-then-reveal: (1) private individual answer on own phone, (2) brief team confer, (3) team commits, (4) reveal + explanation. This converts the opponents' downtime into their own retrieval and converts the target player's isolation into team support, addressing both the pacing problem and the public-exposure problem with one change. Then — the load-bearing part — immediately present ONE isomorphic item (same radical family or same confusable pair, different character) answered individually with no discussion. Content: the item bank must be authored in isomorphic pairs/triples, so the schema needs an `isomorph_group_id` field.

findings.claim: Downtime while another player answers is NOT dead time: learners who merely OBSERVE a tutoring interaction — especially when observing collaboratively with a partner — can learn as much as the person being tutored.
findings.detail: Chi, Roy & Hausmann (2008), Cognitive Science, 'Observing tutorial dialogues collaboratively: Insights about human tutoring effectiveness from vicarious learning'. Students who observed tutoring dialogues in PAIRS learned comparably to the tutees themselves, and substantially more than solo observers. Craig, Chi & VanLehn (2009, Journal of Educational Psychology) replicated the collaborative-observation benefit in classrooms. Sample sizes are moderate (tens per condition) and the domain is physics, not L2 reading — hence moderate rather than strong. The crucial qualifier in both is that the benefit attaches to ACTIVE, paired observation, not passive watching.
findings.implication: This is the answer to turn-based downtime, and it flips the adversarial framing into an asset. While the target player answers, every other player's phone should show the SAME item with a lightweight covert task — 'what do you think they'll answer?' or 'is this 未 or 末?' — answered privately, scored at low weight, and never revealed as a comparison against the target player. Concrete: no player's screen is ever idle for more than 2 seconds during another player's turn. Architecture: the turn state machine must broadcast the item to all devices simultaneously and accept shadow responses from non-active players, so the data model needs an attempt record with an `is_active_turn` boolean rather than one attempt per turn.

findings.claim: Allocated time predicts learning far more weakly than engaged time; in observed classrooms children are off-task roughly a quarter of instructional time, and the time-on-task/achievement correlation is modest and measurement-sensitive.
findings.detail: Godwin, Almeda, Seltman, Kai, Skerbetz, Baker & Fisher (2016), Learning and Instruction, 'Off-task behavior in elementary school children': direct observation found children off-task on the order of 25% of instructional time, with off-task rates rising with activity duration. The older methodological point comes from Karweit & Slavin (1981, American Educational Research Journal), who showed that time-on-task/achievement relationships vary enormously with how time is measured, and that allocated time is a poor proxy. Carroll's (1963) model and the academic-learning-time tradition make the same distinction between allocated, engaged and productive time. The 25% figure is from children in classrooms and should not be transferred literally to adults playing a game they chose — hence moderate.
findings.implication: Design and measure to engaged retrievals, not to minutes. Two concrete rules: (1) off-task rates rise with activity duration, so cap a match at a duration below the drift point — target 8–12 minutes with a visible, fixed number of rounds so the end is always in sight; (2) the metric on the dashboard should be retrievals-per-player-per-minute, not session length. Architecture: the analytics event schema should make 'engaged retrieval' (item presented AND response submitted within the window) the atomic unit; wall-clock session duration is a secondary, near-useless metric.

findings.claim: Giving learners about 3 seconds of silence before requiring a response substantially improves response quality and achievement, compared with the ~1 second typically allowed.
findings.detail: Rowe (1986), Journal of Teacher Education, 'Wait time: Slowing down may be a way of speeding up' — the classic finding that teachers typically wait under 1 second after a question, and that extending wait time to ~3 seconds produces longer, more elaborated, more confident student responses and more participation from lower-achieving students specifically. Tobin (1987, Review of Educational Research, 'The role of wait time in higher cognitive level learning') synthesised the wait-time literature and concluded wait times of ≥3 seconds are associated with better achievement on higher-cognitive tasks. This is classroom-observation research from the 1970s–80s, methodologically dated, but it has never been overturned and the ≥3s heuristic remains the standard reference point.
findings.implication: Set the answer window generously and silently. Concrete: minimum 5 seconds before any timeout pressure is signalled at all for a recognition item; a soft window of ~10 seconds with the final 2 seconds indicated by a subtle desaturation rather than a countdown; and no timeout penalty on the FIRST exposure of any new item. Note the wait-time literature's specific finding that longer waits disproportionately help lower-achieving learners — this is a cheap, evidence-backed mitigation for exactly the subgroup the competitive mechanic endangers.

findings.claim: The mechanism that actually produces the learning in a quiz game is retrieval practice, which is one of the best-established effects in education: g ≈ 0.50–0.61, replicated in real classrooms across hundreds of experiments, and moderated by whether feedback is given.
findings.detail: Rowland (2014), Psychological Bulletin, 'The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect', reported g ≈ 0.50 overall with larger effects when feedback accompanied the test. Adesope, Trevisan & Sundararajan (2017, Review of Educational Research, ~272 experiments) reported g ≈ 0.61 for practice testing. Yang, Luo, Vadillo, Yu & Shanks (2021, Psychological Bulletin, 'Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning: A systematic and meta-analytic review', ~222 studies in authentic classrooms) reported g ≈ 0.50 and reported the effect robust to publication-bias diagnostics — notable because it is one of the few literatures in this report where bias testing was both performed and passed.
findings.implication: This finding sets the priority order for the whole product and should settle internal arguments: retrieval-with-feedback (g ≈ 0.5, strong) > self-explanation prompts (g ≈ 0.55, strong) > gamification wrapper (g ≈ 0.5, strong but confounded) > the game-vs-nongame effect (g ≈ 0.33, weak controls) > competition (≈ 0, null). Content: the item bank must be built for retrieval, meaning every item is a production/recognition attempt with a single unambiguous scoreable answer — no 'browse the character' or 'study the list' screens in the main loop. Any study/preview mode must be a separate, non-default surface.

findings.claim: Team-based and small-group structures produce reliable achievement benefits of roughly d = 0.5, provided they combine positive interdependence with individual accountability — the two conditions the cooperative-learning literature treats as non-negotiable.
findings.detail: Springer, Stanne & Donovan (1999), Review of Educational Research, k ≈ 39 studies of small-group learning in undergraduate STEM: achievement d ≈ 0.51, with additional benefits for persistence and attitudes. Kyndt et al. (2013, Educational Research Review, k ≈ 65) reported face-to-face cooperative learning achievement d ≈ 0.54. Swanson, McCulley, Osman, Scammacca Lewis & Solis (2019, Active Learning in Higher Education) meta-analysed Team-Based Learning specifically and reported a positive but more modest content-knowledge effect; I could not re-verify their point estimate. Across this tradition the consistently emphasised moderators are positive goal interdependence and individual accountability — groups without individual accountability show free-riding and no benefit.
findings.implication: Build both conditions into the scoring rules explicitly. Positive interdependence: the team score must be a function no single player can maximise alone — e.g. team score = (sum of correct answers) × (proportion of team members who contributed at least one correct answer this round), so a strong player cannot carry a silent teammate. Individual accountability: each player's own contribution count is stored and shown to that player privately post-match. Architecture: score must be computed server-side/host-side from per-player attempt records, not accumulated as an opaque team integer, or you cannot compute either term.
