findings.claim: VERDICT: the mechanic is defensible in its 'opponent deals your category' and 'opponent watches' components, and NOT defensible in its 'sees you lose points publicly' component as currently framed. Roughly two-thirds of it survives the literature; one specific element should be cut or inverted.
findings.detail: Assembling the evidence above: (1) Competition's net effect on performance is approximately zero (Murayama & Elliot, 2012) — so the mechanic is neither automatically good nor automatically bad; its sign is set by whether it cues approach or avoidance goals. (2) Mere observation is a small effect (Bond & Titus, 1983, <3% of variance) and cuts both ways by personality (Uziel, 2007) — tolerable, and mitigable by private input. (3) Opponent-chosen categories are defensible IF bounded to seen material, because errors plus immediate feedback are a learning asset (Metcalfe, 2017) and high-confidence errors hypercorrect (Butterfield & Metcalfe, 2001). (4) Public point LOSS is the indefensible element: it is self-level rather than task-level feedback, and self-level feedback is the specific category Kluger & DeNisi (1996) identify as driving the ~38% of feedback interventions that reduce performance; it is bare knowledge-of-result, worth d ≈ 0.05 (Van der Kleij et al., 2015); and it makes ability the salient attribution, which harms low-ability learners most (Ames, 1992) and bottom-of-leaderboard players specifically (Bai et al., 2021). (5) The harm is concentrated, not average — anxious and lower-proficiency learners bear it, in a domain where anxiety correlates r ≈ −0.36 with achievement (Teimouri et al., 2019). Confidence is 'moderate' because no study tests this exact mechanic in this exact population; this is a reasoned assembly, not a measured result.
findings.implication: Ship the mechanic with three changes. (a) KEEP opponent-dealt categories, but gate eligibility: opponents may only deal categories where the target has ≥5 prior exposures, enforced by the dealing algorithm, so the mechanic is 'pick their weak spot among things they've studied', not 'ambush them'. (b) KEEP co-located observation, but move ANSWER INPUT to the private device and broadcast only the resolution — reading, not speaking, is the target skill, so privacy is free. (c) REPLACE the public point loss with a public CORRECTION: on a wrong answer the shared view shows the character large plus the ≤20-word explanation, while the score delta is a ≤14px uncoloured tick. Same information, task-level rather than self-level. Point gains may stay salient; point losses must not.

findings.claim: MITIGATION SET: seven design changes, each traceable to a specific result above, that convert the mechanic from avoidance-cueing to approach-cueing without removing the competitive frame the product is built on.
findings.detail: Each mitigation maps to a source: (1) Bounded dealing — opponents deal only from ≥5-exposure categories [Horwitz et al. 1986 fear of negative evaluation; Metcalfe 2017 errors-are-useful-if-known-adjacent]. (2) Private input, public resolution [Bond & Titus 1983; Uziel 2007]. (3) Task-level resolution dominates the screen; self-level score delta minimised [Kluger & DeNisi 1996; Hattie & Timperley 2007]. (4) Mandatory ≤20-word elaborated explanation on every item [Van der Kleij et al. 2015 EF 0.49 vs KR 0.05; Brysbaert 2019 reading rate]. (5) Competence feedback for losers before the result [Vansteenkiste & Deci 2003; Reeve & Deci 1996]. (6) Shadow items for observers so no screen is idle >2s [Chi, Roy & Hausmann 2008 vicarious learning]. (7) Generous silent answer window ≥5s, no penalty on first exposure [Rowe 1986; Tobin 1987 — helps lower-achievers most]. Graded moderate because the individual sources are strong but the composition is untested as a package.
findings.implication: Treat these seven as v1 acceptance criteria rather than backlog items, because each is cheap and each targets a distinct documented failure mode. The cheapest three with the highest expected value are: the mandatory explanation field (content pipeline change, blocks item authoring), the private-input/public-resolution split (single change to the turn state machine's broadcast payload), and the demotion of the score delta to ≤14px uncoloured (pure CSS). Those three alone move the mechanic from the Kluger & DeNisi harmful quadrant to the beneficial one.

findings.claim: CC-CEDICT is Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International — NOT 3.0. The 3.0 figure is the single most commonly misreported licence fact in the Chinese-learning tooling world.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: read the comment header of the distributed cedict_ts.u8 (build stamped 2024-12-06T15:50:49Z). Header states the licence as 'Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License' with the URL https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/. It also names the ancestor work: 'CEDICT - Copyright (C) 1997, 1998 Paul Andrew Denisowski', publisher MDBG, download point https://www.mdbg.net/chinese/dictionary?page=cc-cedict. Commercial bundling IS permitted. Attribution requires naming CC-CEDICT, linking the licence, linking the source, and indicating if you modified it. ShareAlike bites on *adaptations of the dictionary*, and CC BY-SA 4.0 explicitly extends to sui generis database rights (EU — relevant, the user is Dutch). Your derived gloss table IS an adaptation and must ship under BY-SA 4.0. Your application code is NOT an adaptation if the dictionary is merely aggregated alongside it; keep that boundary clean and the SA obligation does not reach your source.

findings.claim: Unihan / the Unicode Character Database is permissively licensed and can be bundled in a commercial closed-source PWA with only a notice.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: read the Unicode licence text. Grant is 'use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, and/or sell copies of the Data Files or Software' with no fee. Condition: the copyright and permission notice must appear with all copies OR in the associated documentation. Restriction: you may not use 'Unicode' or the copyright holder's name in advertising or promotion without prior written authorisation. This is MIT-equivalent in effect. (Note the copy I read is the older 'UNICODE, INC. LICENSE AGREEMENT - DATA FILES AND SOFTWARE' form covering 1991-2020; Unicode has since moved to the simpler 'UNICODE LICENSE V3'. Both are permissive — no practical difference for you.) Useful Unihan fields for this product: kTotalStrokes, kRSUnicode (radical + residual stroke count), kMandarin, kDefinition, kGradeLevel, kFrequency (coarse 1-5 buckets), kSimplifiedVariant/kTraditionalVariant.

findings.claim: Make Me a Hanzi is DUAL-licensed and neither half is MIT — a very common misreport. dictionary.txt is LGPL-3.0-or-later; graphics.txt and the SVGs are under the Arphic Public License. For a bundled PWA, the LGPL half is the real hazard and should simply not be shipped.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: read makemeahanzi's COPYING. dictionary.txt derives from Unihan + CJKlib and is 'GNU Lesser General Public License ... either version 3 of the license, or (at your option) any later version'. graphics.txt and svgs.tar.gz derive from the Arphic fonts 'AR PL KaitiM GB' and 'AR PL UKai' and are under the 'Arphic Public License as published by Arphic Technology Co., Ltd'. Why LGPL on data is a hazard: LGPL's whole mechanism is the right to *relink* a modified version of the covered work. Applied to a JSON blob compiled into a Vite bundle, that obligation is incoherent but not obviously discharged — you would arguably owe users the ability to swap the file. Mitigation that removes the question entirely: do not ship dictionary.txt. Regenerate the equivalent decomposition and radical data from Unihan (permissive, see above) plus CC-CEDICT (BY-SA), which is where most of it came from anyway.

findings.claim: The Arphic Public License permits commercial sale and bundling, but it is genuinely copyleft on the stroke data and imposes a 'designated place' distribution duty on modifications. Shipping hanzi-writer-data or Make Me a Hanzi graphics in a paid app is legal; silently reformatting them is not.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: read the APL text in full. (1) Commercial use and charging are explicitly permitted — Section 1 allows distribution 'without restriction' and the 'Freely Available' definition says 'If you wish, you can charge for this service.' (2) You must retain the licence file ARPHICPL.TXT unaltered in all copies. (3) It IS copyleft: Section 2(b) requires modifications be made 'Freely Available as a whole to all third parties under the terms of this License'. (4) Modifications must be obtainable — 'such as by offering access to copy the modifications from a designated place'. (5) Section 2(a) requires 'a prominent notice in each modified file stating how and when you changed that file.' (6) Renaming is allowed (Section 0 contemplates 'changing font name'). (7) Section 3 auto-terminates your rights on non-compliance. Also relevant: the FSF lists the APL as a free licence but GPL-incompatible. Note that converting the SVG outlines to a different JSON shape, or re-subsetting to your character set, IS a modification and triggers (2)(a) and (2)(b). hanzi-writer-data is under this same APL; the hanzi-writer *code* is MIT.

findings.claim: Stroke-order graphics are the wrong data to ship for a reading game, and they are also the most expensive: hanzi-writer-data is ~2.5–3 KB of JSON per character, so a 3,000-character bank is ~8 MB raw / ~2–3 MB gzipped — for a skill the target user will never perform.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: fetched a representative hanzi-writer-data character file. Structure is {strokes: [SVG path strings], medians: [[x,y] polylines], radStrokes: [indices]} at roughly 2.5–3 KB per character for a 7-stroke character; complex characters are larger. Separately: the stroke *order* (an ordered integer sequence, standardised by the PRC GB 现代汉语通用字笔顺规范) is a fact/standard, not an expressive work, and a bare order table carries far less copyright risk than the Arphic-derived *outlines*. So if you ever want stroke order, ship the sequence, not the graphics. KanjiVG (CC BY-SA 3.0) is the other free option but is Japanese-centric and misses simplified-only forms.

findings.claim: The cleanest legal route to HSK 3.0 is Pleco's MIT-licensed OCR of the official MOE PDF (elkmovie/hsk30). The underlying standard's copyright position is genuinely unsettled and is routinely misreported in both directions.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: the files carry the header '# Copyright (c) 2021 Pleco Inc. # Distributed under MIT license'. README states the lists were 'Extracted from the official PDF ... and OCR'ed using Pleco OCR', source moe.gov.cn t20210329_523304. VERIFIED counts by parsing the files this session: characters — 300 each at levels 1-6 (1,800) plus 1,200 at the combined 七-九级 band = 3,000, plus separate handwriting sub-lists (初等手写字表 300, 中等手写字表, 高等手写字表 500); words — 11,092 across the nine levels, level 1 = 500. The honest legal position: the source is 《国际中文教育中文水平等级标准》 GF 0025-2021, a PRC national standard issued by MOE/CLEC. PRC Copyright Law Art. 5 excludes laws, regulations and official documents of state organs from protection, but national *standards* (GB/GF) sit in a contested category where SAC and issuing ministries assert rights. Independently, a bare word list is a compilation of facts with thin originality in most jurisdictions. Pleco's MIT grant covers only Pleco's OCR and compilation labour — it cannot and does not grant rights MOE might hold. FLAG BOTH MISREPORTS: (a) 'HSK lists are public domain' — not established; (b) 'you cannot use HSK lists' — practically false, every product does, enforcement is unheard of. The real exposure is trademark, not copyright.

findings.claim: HSK is the wrong content spine for this product regardless of licensing. HSK 1-3 does not contain the characters on a Chinese menu, a subway sign or a supermarket label — the exact four tasks the user named.
findings.detail: Structural argument from the verified HSK 3.0 files plus the nature of the target task. HSK is a *classroom register* standard: it front-loads 学生, 老师, 朋友, 喜欢, 因为. The signage register is nouns, set formulas and characters that appear late or never in HSK: 炒 爆 焗 煲 卤 涮 蒸 拌 炝 烩 (cooking methods on every menu), 菌 笋 藕 蒜 姜 葱 韭 (ingredients), 出口 入口 闸机 换乘 末班 首班 站台 (transit), 保质期 净含量 配料 生产日期 冷藏 (labels), 折 满减 特价 现磨 (shopfronts). Several of these are outside HSK entirely and outside the common-3500 list. NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION: I could not check any corpus study of Chinese signage register, and I am not aware of a published one — which is itself the point. No existing product has this item bank because nobody has built the corpus.

findings.claim: All three named frequency lists have licence problems for commercial bundling. SUBTLEX-CH is safe ONLY if you take the PLoS Supporting Information copy; Jun Da's list is research/education-only with no commercial grant; the BCC list has no licence statement at all.
findings.detail: NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION — journals.plos.org, the Ghent lab site and bcc.blcu.edu.cn are all egress-blocked. From prior knowledge, stated with the uncertainty it deserves: (1) SUBTLEX-CH — Cai & Brysbaert (2010), PLoS ONE 5(6):e10729, ~47M-character film-subtitle corpus. PLoS ONE articles are CC BY, and the frequency tables were published as Supporting Information *to the article*, so the SI copies inherit CC BY — that is the safe copy. The copies redistributed from lab websites and mirrors carry no licence text and are conventionally described as 'free for research', which is NOT a commercial grant. COMMONLY MISREPORTED as public domain. (2) Jun Da's Modern Chinese Character Frequency List (MTSU) — the site states free use for research and teaching; there is no open licence and no commercial permission. It is nonetheless bundled commercially all over the ecosystem. (3) BCC (BLCU Corpus Center, ~15 billion characters) is a query *service*; the circulating global_wordfreq.release.txt bulk file has no licence statement and no clear authorisation to redistribute. VERIFIED alternative sources exist: Unihan's kFrequency field is permissive (coarse, 1-5 buckets); Common Voice sentence text is CC0; Chinese Wikipedia is CC BY-SA 4.0.

findings.claim: Mozilla Common Voice is CC0 (dataset) / MPL 2.0 (code), but it is read-aloud sentence recordings with no word-level alignment — it is not a pronunciation source. Forvo cannot be used at all in an offline PWA. The most-used open Mandarin TTS corpus, CSMSC/标贝, is non-commercial and taints checkpoints trained on it.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: Common Voice repo states sentence text is 'released under a CC0 public domain Creative Commons license' and 'This repository is released under MPL (Mozilla Public License) 2.0.' Mandarin locales are zh-CN, zh-TW, zh-HK. NOT VERIFIED (commonvoice.mozilla.org egress-blocked): per-locale validated hours. Practical limits: CV clips are whole read sentences by volunteers of highly variable audio quality, with no forced alignment shipped — extracting a clean single-word pronunciation is a research project, not a build step. Forvo: proprietary, paid API, terms forbid redistribution and durable caching of the audio — structurally incompatible with an app whose entire premise is that it works offline with no server. Open Mandarin TTS corpora and their licences (prior knowledge, VERIFY BEFORE USE): AISHELL-3 Apache-2.0; THCHS-30 Apache-2.0; MagicData Mandarin CC BY-ND 4.0 — ND means no derivatives, so training a model on it is arguably prohibited; CSMSC / 标贝 Chinese Standard Mandarin Speech Corpus — explicitly non-commercial, and it is the default single-speaker Mandarin corpus behind a large fraction of publicly released Chinese TTS checkpoints. COMMONLY MISREPORTED: 'this Chinese TTS model is open source' usually refers to the code licence, not to the corpus the weights were fitted on.

Noto Sans CJK and Source Han Sans are the same typeface design — Google's release under the Noto name without the RFN is precisely what makes Noto the right pick when you intend to subset.

findings.implication: UI + ARCHITECTURE: use Noto Sans SC, one weight only, subset at build time, and give the subset a distinct internal family name (e.g. 'Kanbudong Hanzi') so no trademark or RFN question can arise. Ship OFL.txt alongside it and list it in /licences.

findings.claim: The CJK subsetting problem is real and the standard packaging solutions all break an offline-first PWA — but this product has an unusual escape hatch: the item bank is finite and known at build time, so you can subset to the exact glyph set and land at a few hundred KB instead of megabytes.
findings.detail: VERIFIED: Fontsource ships Noto Sans SC with only five named subsets — latin, latin-ext, cyrillic, vietnamese, chinese-simplified — i.e. the entire Simplified Chinese repertoire is ONE woff2 per weight. So `npm i @fontsource/noto-sans-sc` naively pulls a multi-megabyte blob per weight into your bundle. Google Fonts' CSS API takes the other approach, splitting CJK into ~100 numbered unicode-range chunks so the browser fetches only the chunks the page touches — elegant, and useless here, because it requires network at render time and this app must work at a restaurant table with no signal. NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION (google/fonts is not an allowed repo and the release page failed to render asset sizes): the exact byte size of Noto Sans SC — treat 'full single weight ≈ 4–5 MB woff2 / ~10 MB OTF over ~44k glyphs' as an order-of-magnitude figure to re-measure, not a verified number. What IS solid is the ratio argument: you need on the order of 1,500–3,000 distinct hanzi, i.e. ~5% of the repertoire, and woff2 CJK subsets scale close to linearly in glyph count, which puts a 3,000-glyph one-weight subset in the 250–450 KB range. cn-font-split (Apache-2.0, verified) and pyftsubset both do this.

sources.citation: fontsource/font-files — Noto Sans SC subset inventory (5 named subsets; chinese-simplified is a single file per weight)
KonghaYao/cn-font-split — Apache-2.0 CJK font subsetter/splitter, 1.2k stars, Rust/WASM, runs in Node

findings.implication: ARCHITECTURE — make this a hard build step, not a runtime concern: (1) walk the item bank and emit the exact set of codepoints used; (2) run pyftsubset/cn-font-split against Noto Sans SC for that set, one weight (400 or 500), woff2, with `--layout-features=` stripped to the minimum; (3) FAIL THE BUILD if any item-bank codepoint is missing from the produced subset. Step (3) is the important one — a menu game will reach for 焗 煲 涮 菌 藕 韭, characters that a naive 'subset from HSK' would drop, and the failure mode is tofu boxes on a customer's phone at a restaurant table with no network to recover.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Chineasy's core pedagogical premise is wrong at the level of the writing system, not merely suboptimal: it generalises the pictographic principle to a script in which roughly 80–90% of characters are 形声 phono-semantic compounds, and its method systematically conceals the phonetic component — the one part that actually predicts pronunciation.
findings.detail: NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION — no scholarly domain was reachable. Stated from prior knowledge and graded accordingly. The canonical scholarly source is John DeFrancis, *The Chinese Language: Fact and Fantasy* (University of Hawai'i Press, 1984), whose 'ideographic myth' chapter is the reference demolition of exactly the assumption Chineasy is built on, and which remains the standard citation forty years on. The phono-semantic proportion (~80%+ of characters in the 說文解字 and higher in modern inventories) is a settled descriptive fact in Chinese linguistics, not a contested claim. The specific criticisms of Chineasy that I am confident are on record but could not open: (a) invented etymologies presented as historical fact, contradicting oracle-bone and bronze-inscription scholarship; (b) the method scales to roughly 100–200 characters and then stops, because no picture can be drawn over 醬 or 藏; (c) it teaches characters in isolation when modern Chinese is overwhelmingly disyllabic — knowing 电 and 脑 separately is not knowing 电脑; (d) it teaches no pronunciation whatsoever. Named critics: Victor Mair (Language Log), David Moser, Olle Linge (Hacking Chinese). IMPORTANT: those are blogs, not peer-reviewed literature. To my knowledge there is NO published efficacy study of Chineasy at all — which is itself the substantive finding: the most visually famous Chinese-learning product has zero empirical support.

sources.citation: DeFrancis, J. (1984). The Chinese Language: Fact and Fantasy. University of Hawai'i Press. Chapter 'The Ideographic Myth'. NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION.
Mair, V. et al., Language Log — sustained critique of Chineasy. NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION; blog, not peer-reviewed.

findings.implication: CONTENT — this is a design rule, not a caveat: every character in the item bank carries two mandatory fields, semantic_component and phonetic_component, and the app must NEVER surface a mnemonic that contradicts them. Derive the semantic side from Unihan kRSUnicode (permissive). Build the phonetic-series (声旁) table yourself — group characters that share a phonetic and note whether the reading is exact, tone-differing, or unrelated. Then order the item bank BY PHONETIC SERIES, teaching 青 → 请 清 情 晴 睛 as a block. This is the single highest-leverage structural decision available, it is well grounded in how the script actually works, and no product in the landscape does it.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Duolingo's published efficacy evidence does not cover Chinese at all. Transferring 'Duolingo works' to the Chinese course is unsupported, and the course's dominant item format — multiple-choice recognition with pinyin scaffolding — lets a learner complete it without being able to read unglossed characters.
findings.detail: NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION. Prior knowledge, graded down hard. Duolingo's efficacy corpus (Vesselinov & Grego 2012, and the later Jiang/Rollinson/Plonsky-line studies published via research.duolingo.com) is Spanish- and French-dominant, company-funded, and typically uses self-selected completers with substantial attrition — the 2012 study had on the order of 88 completers. I could not open any of them and cannot vouch for the numbers. What I could not find any trace of, and believe does not exist, is a published efficacy study of Duolingo Chinese specifically. The structural criticism does not need a study: the course leans on tap-the-tiles and multiple-choice selection, keeps pinyin visible for a long time, and grades character items in ways that a learner can satisfy by shape-matching against three distractors that are not visually confusable. That trains a different skill from reading a shopfront.

sources.citation: Duolingo Research portal — efficacy publications, predominantly Spanish/French. NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION (search unavailable).
Vesselinov, R. & Grego, J. (2012). Duolingo Effectiveness Study. City University of New York. Company-funded, ~88 completers. NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION.

findings.implication: UX — the distractor set is where the learning is. Never generate distractors randomly. For each item, pick 2–3 distractors that share a component with the target (same radical, or same phonetic, or same overall stroke silhouette) so the player must attend to the discriminating stroke. Store a precomputed `confusable_with` array per character in the item bank; generating it at runtime is too slow and non-deterministic, which matters because the dohhh engine is a deterministic reducer over a shared event log — every phone must derive the identical distractor set from the same seed.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Pleco is the incumbent solution to the user's literal problem — its live camera OCR reads a menu today, for free. Any reading game must be honest that it is not competing with Pleco but selling the ability to not need it.
findings.detail: Descriptive, verifiable by inspection; no efficacy literature exists or is needed. Pleco's core is a dictionary with offline data, live camera OCR lookup, and paid add-ons (Outlier etymology, handwriting, flashcards). Does well: it is the definitive Chinese reference on mobile, works fully offline, and the OCR overlay is genuinely the fastest path from 'I cannot read this menu' to 'I know what this dish is'. Does badly as a learning tool: it is a lookup instrument, so every use is a retrieval you did NOT perform; its flashcard engine is powerful but configuration-heavy and opaque; and it is irreducibly single-player. Note also that Pleco is the source of the MIT-licensed HSK 3.0 OCR you will be using — the company gives that away.

sources.citation: Pleco Software — product; and Pleco Inc. as author of the MIT-licensed HSK 3.0 OCR verified this session

findings.implication: UX + content positioning: build the win condition around *speed without lookup*. Time-box every read (see the timing finding). And take the competitive lesson directly — since the phone can already OCR a menu, the game's item bank should be seeded from photographs of real menus, which is also the corpus you need. Consider shipping a 'we photographed 200 real menus in Chengdu' provenance claim; it is both true and the differentiator.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Skritter trains handwriting production with stroke-level grading. For a traveller who wants to read a menu it is the highest-cost, lowest-transfer skill in the whole space, and should be explicitly excluded from scope.
findings.detail: NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION for efficacy; I am not aware of any published study of Skritter. Descriptive: the mechanic is write-the-character-on-screen with per-stroke correctness feedback and SRS scheduling. Does well: it is the only mainstream product that trains *production* rather than recognition, and per-stroke feedback is a real advantage over paper. Does badly for this user: nobody handwrites in China — input is pinyin-based on a phone, and the target tasks (menu, subway, label, shopfront) are 100% receptive. Handwriting practice is slow (tens of seconds per item versus 1–3 seconds for a recognition item), which is fatal in a turn-based table game where three other people are waiting.

sources.citation: Skritter — product. No published efficacy study located; NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION.

findings.implication: UX: no handwriting input, ever. The turn budget in a co-located game is the binding constraint — a turn that takes 30 seconds means three players are idle for 90 seconds and the table's attention collapses. Cap the per-turn interaction at 3–8 seconds of active input.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Anki with mainstream Chinese decks is the strongest scheduler in the landscape (FSRS is a real, benchmarked improvement over SM-2) and the weakest content: most shared decks carry no licence at all and many are scraped from copyrighted textbooks.
findings.detail: NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION for the FSRS benchmark, but a prior sweep in this same session already retrieved srs-bench.md into the scratchpad, so the benchmark material is available to the parent agent. FSRS (Ye et al. / open-spaced-repetition) is now Anki's default scheduler and is evaluated on a large public benchmark of real review logs against SM-2 and other algorithms. Does badly: (1) content licensing — the AnkiWeb shared-deck ecosystem is a licensing minefield, decks routinely reproduce Integrated Chinese / HSK Standard Course material verbatim with no rights, so no deck should ever be ingested into a commercial product; (2) the review experience is joyless and abandonment is high; (3) it is irreducibly single-player and has no notion of a table.

sources.citation: open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark — public benchmark of FSRS against SM-2 and others on large real review-log datasets. Retrieved by a prior sweep this session into scratchpad srs-bench.md; NOT re-fetched here.

findings.implication: ARCHITECTURE: implement FSRS, not SM-2, and therefore store a full per-item review log (timestamp, grade, elapsed) rather than just an interval and ease factor — FSRS needs the history. This has a specific consequence for the dohhh P2P design: the review log is *per-player private state*, not shared game state, so it must live outside the signed shared event log and never sync to other peers. Keep two stores: the shared append-only game log, and a local per-player memory store.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Du Chinese and The Chairman's Bao are the two best 'reading' products in the market and both make the same fatal UX concession: tapping a word reveals the gloss for free, which destroys the retrieval event that is the only thing that produces learning.
findings.detail: NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION for efficacy; I am not aware of published studies of either. Descriptive: both serve HSK-levelled texts with tap-for-gloss, per-word audio, and a built-in wordlist. Du Chinese is short narrative prose; The Chairman's Bao is graded news. Both do extensive reading at level genuinely well and are the closest existing products to reading fluency. Both are subscription. The register problem: narrative prose and news are further from signage than almost anything else — a graded news article about 环境保护 shares almost no vocabulary with a menu. The UX problem is the sharper one: a free, instant, zero-cost gloss converts every difficult word from a retrieval attempt into a recognition event, and the learner's subjective sense of fluency rises while their unaided reading does not.

sources.citation: Du Chinese — graded reader product. No published efficacy study located; NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION.
The Chairman's Bao — graded Chinese news. NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION.

findings.implication: UX — make the gloss cost something, in public. In a co-located game the natural currency already exists: dohhh's bidding economy. Revealing a gloss should deduct from the current bid, and the other players at the table should see that it happened. The social cost of asking for help is the mechanism; a solitary app cannot charge it and that is precisely the advantage of building this co-located.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Hack Chinese and Clozemaster represent the two sensible single-player formats — frequency-ordered SRS, and cloze-in-context — and Clozemaster is the standing proof that a Tatoeba-based game is cheap to build and lands in the wrong register.
findings.detail: NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION for either; no published efficacy studies located. Hack Chinese: web SRS built specifically for Chinese vocabulary, with defensible item ordering by frequency and HSK band, and honest spacing. Does well: the ordering discipline. Does badly: single-player web flashcards with no context. Clozemaster: cloze deletion over Tatoeba sentences with a global leaderboard. Does well: cloze forces a retrieval inside a sentence context rather than on a bare pair, and the content was free. Does badly: Tatoeba Mandarin quality is uneven and often translationese; the leaderboard is asynchronous vanity, not multiplayer — you never interact with another human.

sources.citation: Clozemaster — cloze game built on Tatoeba sentences. NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION.
Hack Chinese — Chinese-specific spaced repetition. NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION.

findings.implication: CONTENT: adopt cloze *structure* but at the string level, not the sentence level. A signage item is naturally a cloze: show 出___ / 入___ and require 口; show 保质___ and require 期. This trains exactly the compound-completion skill that lets someone parse an unfamiliar sign from partial knowledge, and it works on 2–4 character strings, which fit a phone screen at large type.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Outlier Linguistics is the only product in the landscape built on accurate palaeography, and its key asset — reliable identification of sound components — is the thing this product most needs and cannot license.
findings.detail: NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION. Descriptive: Outlier is a paid Pleco add-on dictionary built by academically trained palaeographers, which distinguishes, per character, the form component, the meaning component and the sound component, and explicitly corrects folk etymology. Does well: it is the scholarly corrective to Chineasy-style invention, and the sound-component data is the highest-value field in Chinese character learning because the phono-semantic majority means the phonetic component is genuinely predictive. Does badly: it is reference, not practice; it is expensive; and it is locked inside Pleco. Its data is proprietary and cannot be used.

sources.citation: Outlier Linguistics — Outlier Dictionary of Chinese Characters (Pleco add-on). NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION.

findings.implication: CONTENT: you must build the phonetic-series table yourself and it is a bounded job — for a 900-string / ~1,200-character bank you need phonetic components for ~1,200 characters, most of which fall into a few hundred recurring series. Derive candidates automatically by intersecting Unihan kRSUnicode residual components with pinyin agreement in CC-CEDICT, then hand-verify. Budget it as real content work, roughly one to two weeks, and treat the resulting table as a proprietary asset.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Mandarin Blueprint's mnemonic 'movie method' rests on the keyword method, whose evidence is genuinely mixed: an advantage on immediate recall that shrinks or reverses at delay, and worse outcomes for productive use than for recognition.
findings.detail: NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION — this is the finding I am least able to substantiate here and it should be re-checked first in the follow-up sweep. Prior knowledge: the keyword mnemonic literature (originating with Atkinson & Raugh in the mid-1970s and extensively reviewed since) shows reliable immediate-recall gains over rote repetition, but the durability question is contested — several reviews report the advantage attenuating at delayed post-test, and the method is consistently weaker for production than recognition. Mandarin Blueprint's implementation assigns an actor per initial, a room/set per final, and a prop per tone, which is internally consistent and does encode pronunciation (unlike Chineasy) — that is a real design merit. Its character-ordering principle (components before compounds) is also sound. Against it: the mnemonic construction load is very high per item, and there is no independent efficacy evidence of any kind.

sources.citation: Atkinson, R.C. & Raugh, M.R. (1975). An application of the mnemonic keyword method to the acquisition of a Russian vocabulary. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory. Seminal reference. NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION.
Mandarin Blueprint — commercial course. NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION.

findings.implication: UX: do not make mnemonic construction a required step — the per-item cost is far too high for a game with a 3–8 second turn budget. Instead allow an OPTIONAL free-text mnemonic field per item, stored locally, surfaced only on repeated failure of that item. This gets the benefit for the 5% of items a given player keeps failing without taxing the other 95%.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: There is no genuinely co-located, in-person, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin learning product. The nearest neighbours are generic classroom quiz platforms (Kahoot, Quizizz, Blooket, Quizlet Live) that require an account, a network, a host and usually a projector — and Chinese-market WeChat mini-programs (成语接龙, 看图猜成语) that target native speakers, not learners.
findings.detail: Descriptive claim from landscape inspection; I could not run market searches this session, so treat 'there is nothing' as 'I am aware of nothing and could not check' rather than as an exhaustive survey. What social features exist in the products above are all asynchronous and remote: Duolingo's leaderboards and friend streaks, Clozemaster's global leaderboard, HelloChinese's clubs. Quizlet Live is the closest existing mechanic — co-located, team-based, phones-at-a-table matching — and it demonstrably engages classrooms, but it needs accounts, connectivity and a teacher-controlled host screen, all three of which this product deliberately does not have.

sources.citation: Landscape inspection; no market survey possible this session (WebSearch budget exhausted, all non-GitHub egress blocked)

findings.implication: ARCHITECTURE: the dohhh substrate — every install is a node, the game is a signed event log on the phones, join by QR, no server, no account — is not an implementation detail here, it IS the differentiator. Preserve it exactly. Specifically: no login before first play, join a table in under 10 seconds by QR, and the whole item bank precached in the service worker so the game runs in a restaurant basement with no signal. Every competitor fails at least one of those three.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Codenames is the single most transferable board-game mechanic to a phone-based co-located Mandarin reading game: asymmetric information, where each phone shows a different view of one shared table state.
findings.detail: Mechanic analysis, not empirical. In Codenames one player sees the key and the others see only the grid; all the tension comes from the information asymmetry across people sitting at the same table. The Mandarin mapping is exact and, as far as I know, unbuilt: one player's phone shows an English/Dutch meaning or a photograph of the real sign; the other players' phones show a grid of candidate hanzi strings including visually confusable distractors. The clue-giver must communicate without saying the characters. Critically, this mechanic is impossible in a single-player app and nearly impossible in a client-server app without a host screen — but it is trivial when four phones share a signed event log, because each peer can render a different projection of the same state.

sources.citation: Codenames (Vlaada Chvátil, Czech Games Edition, 2015) — mechanic analysis, no efficacy literature consulted

findings.implication: ARCHITECTURE + UX: build role-projection into the reducer from day one. The event log holds the full table state; each peer computes `viewFor(playerId, state)` and renders only what that role may see. Never send a hidden field to a peer that must not see it — in a co-located game a curious player will look at their neighbour's screen, so hiding in the UI layer is not hiding.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Dobble/Spot It's mechanic — every pair of cards shares exactly one symbol, found under time pressure — maps directly onto hanzi component recognition, and is the mechanical answer to what Chineasy gets wrong.
findings.detail: Mechanic analysis. Dobble is built on a finite projective plane: 57 symbols, 8 per card, exactly one shared symbol between any two cards. The Chinese analogue is constructible: treat radicals and phonetic components as the symbol set and hanzi as the cards, then generate hands in which any two characters share exactly one component. Played under time pressure at a table, this trains fast sub-character decomposition — the ability to see 请 as 言 + 青 in under a second — which is exactly the skill that lets someone parse an unfamiliar character on a shopfront, and exactly the skill Chineasy's pictographic method fails to develop. The generation is a constraint-satisfaction problem over your component inventory, solvable offline at build time.

sources.citation: Dobble/Spot It (Denis Blanchot / Asmodee) — finite projective plane construction; mechanic analysis, no efficacy literature consulted

findings.implication: CONTENT + ARCHITECTURE: precompute a component-incidence index at build time — component -> [characters containing it] and character -> [components] — derived from Unihan kRSUnicode plus a decomposition table you build (NOT from Make Me a Hanzi's LGPL dictionary.txt). Precompute the valid Dobble-style hands too; do not solve the constraint problem on a phone. This index is also what generates the confusable distractors for the main game mode, so it earns its keep twice.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: The hardest unsolved problem for a co-located language game is mixed ability at one table, and board games solved it long ago with bidding and handicapping. Dohhh's existing bid-before-you-see-the-question mechanic is already the correct answer and should be carried over unchanged.
findings.detail: Mechanic analysis. Every product in the landscape assumes exactly one learner at exactly one level. A real table has a beginner, someone who did six months of Duolingo, and someone who has been to Chengdu twice — and a straight quiz makes the strongest player win every hand while the weakest disengages within five minutes. Board games handle this with handicaps (golf), catch-up mechanisms (Mario Kart's rubber-banding), and bidding — where the player declares their confidence before seeing the task, so the *calibration* is what is scored rather than raw knowledge. Bidding is the elegant one because a beginner who correctly bids low and a strong player who overbids can genuinely both be rewarded. Dohhh already implements this: three tiers, 1/5/15 points at costs of 1/3/10, bid before the question is revealed.

sources.citation: dohhh — existing bidding mechanic (Easy Peasy 1 pt/cost 1, Common Knowledge 5/3, Dohhh 15/10; first to 46), read from the repository README this session

findings.implication: UX: keep the bid, and make the tier tie to *reading difficulty* rather than trivia difficulty — tier 1 a 1–2 character sign the player has seen, tier 2 a 3–4 character compound, tier 3 an unglossed real-world string with a component they must reason about. Additionally, scale the per-player item pool by their own FSRS state so the beginner's tier-3 item is not the expert's tier-3 item: same tier, same points, different item. That is the handicap, and it is invisible to the table, which is what makes it socially acceptable.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Co-operative clue-giving games (Just One, Wavelength) show the fix for the second social failure mode: purely competitive language games punish the weakest player publicly, which is the fastest way to end a game night.
findings.detail: Mechanic analysis, no efficacy literature. Just One is fully co-operative — everyone writes a one-word clue, duplicates cancel, and the group scores together. Wavelength scores a team on how well one member communicates a position on a spectrum. Both make the *group's* success depend on accommodating the weakest member rather than exploiting them. Applied here: a mode where the table collectively tries to read a menu before a timer, with the stronger players' contribution being to help the weaker ones parse, converts the ability gap from a liability into the mechanic.

sources.citation: Just One (Repos Production, 2018) and Wavelength (CMYK, 2019) — mechanic analysis

findings.implication: UX: ship at least one co-operative mode alongside the competitive one — 'order the whole table's dinner from this menu before the timer'. Default new tables to the co-operative mode on first play, and unlock competitive after one completed game. First-session experience at a table with a total beginner is the make-or-break moment and competition loses it.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: THE GAP, stated as seven requirements: a co-located P2P Mandarin reading game must do these, and no product in the landscape does more than two of them.
findings.detail: Synthesis of the above. (1) SIGNAGE REGISTER — ship menus, transit, labels and shopfronts, not textbook sentences or graded news; nothing in the landscape has this bank. (2) COSTLY RETRIEVAL — the gloss must cost points, publicly; every existing product gives it away free. (3) MIXED ABILITY AT ONE TABLE — via bidding plus invisible per-player item scaling; every existing product assumes one learner at one level. (4) NO NETWORK, NO ACCOUNT, NO SERVER — every social language product requires all three; dohhh already requires none. (5) DISCRIMINATION NOT RECALL — the target task is a forced choice among visually similar characters under time pressure with contextual support, so the item format must be confusable-distractor discrimination, not free recall or random multiple choice. (6) PHONETIC SERIES AS THE ORDERING SPINE — the highest-leverage structure in the script; nothing uses it. (7) ASYMMETRIC INFORMATION — impossible in a single-player app, free when four phones share an event log. Requirements 4 and 7 are the ones a competitor cannot copy without rebuilding their architecture; requirement 1 is the one they cannot copy without doing the fieldwork.

sources.citation: Synthesis of the landscape findings above; note that all landscape inputs are unverified this session

findings.implication: CONTENT + ARCHITECTURE: treat 1, 5 and 6 as the v1 content spec and 4 and 7 as the v1 architecture spec. Concretely for v1: ~600–900 photographed real-world strings; every item carries {string, gloss, semantic_component[], phonetic_component[], confusable_with[], tier, signage_frequency}; the reducer supports per-role view projection; the whole bank plus the font subset precached by the service worker under a 3 MB install budget.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Typography for hanzi on a phone at a table is a hard constraint, not a preference: hanzi need substantially more pixels than Latin to be legible, and the game's whole premise is discriminating similar characters at a glance.
findings.detail: NOT ACCESSED THIS SESSION — I could not reach the CJK legibility literature (nothing on legible minimum sizes for simplified Chinese on mobile displays could be verified). Stated as an engineering constraint rather than a research finding, and it should be validated by testing on a real device at a real restaurant table. The reasoning: a dense simplified character such as 蔬 or 酱 packs 15–17 strokes into the same em box that Latin uses for one letterform, so stroke separation, not cap height, sets the legible floor. Compounding it: the game deliberately shows visually confusable characters side by side, which is the worst case for legibility, and it will be played in a dim restaurant on a smudged screen at arm's length.

sources.citation: No accessible source. CJK mobile legibility literature was unreachable this session (all scholarly domains egress-blocked). Flagged as REQUIRES VALIDATION.

findings.implication: UI, as a starting spec to be device-tested, not as a verified finding: primary hanzi at 48–64 px minimum; hanzi that the player must discriminate between at no less than 56 px; never set hanzi below 24 px anywhere in the app, including secondary and disabled states; use Noto Sans SC at weight 400 or 500, never 300 or lighter (thin strokes disappear on a dim screen); set line-height at 1.6 or more for any multi-character string; and enforce a WCAG AAA contrast ratio (7:1) on hanzi specifically, one step above the AA you would accept for Latin body text. Run a physical test with the real subset font on the oldest phone you support before locking these.
findings._topic: Competitive landscape for Mandarin learning products + content-licensing constraints for a co-located, offline-first, peer-to-peer multiplayer Mandarin *reading* PWA (kanbudong / dohhh fork)

findings.claim: Phonological short-term memory predicts L2 vocabulary acquisition at r ≈ .31 — a real but only small-to-medium individual difference, and the meta-analytic estimate is for AUDITORY vocabulary learning specifically.
findings.detail: Kurita (2026), first meta-analysis on this question: 52 effect sizes from 18 studies, r = .31, 95% CI [.21, .41]. PSTM test type was a significant moderator — nonword/word repetition tasks show a stronger association than digit span. Learning context approached significance (intentional > incidental). CRITICAL BOUNDARY: the meta-analysis is scoped to auditory L2 vocabulary acquisition. It is not evidence about learning to recognise written logographs. Also note this is a correlation with a stable individual difference, not an intervention effect — you cannot train it, you can only accommodate it. The folk claim that 'phonological memory is THE predictor of vocabulary learning' overstates a r=.31.

sources.citation: Kurita, K. (2026). Revisiting the effects of phonological short-term memory on second language vocabulary acquisition: A meta-analysis. ITL – International Journal of Applied Linguistics.
Baddeley, A. D., Gathercole, S. E., & Papagno, C. (1998). The phonological loop as a language learning device. Psychological Review, 105(1), 158–173.

findings.implication: Do NOT gate progression on pronunciation. Make audio (pinyin readout, tone) an optional per-item affordance, never a required step and never a scoring input. Store a per-user flag `audio_enabled` defaulting off; a player who never plays audio must be able to reach every item and every score tier. This protects the ~30% of the variance-in-uptake that PSTM would otherwise silently impose as a difficulty tax on your slowest-phonology players.

findings.claim: Baddeley/Gathercole/Papagno's phonological loop is a theory about storing UNFAMILIAR SOUND PATTERNS while a long-term record is built. That mechanism is largely bypassed by a reading-recognition game.
findings.detail: The 1998 Psychological Review paper (~2,300 citations) argues the loop evolved to hold novel phonological forms during consolidation, evidenced across normal adults, children, neuropsychological patients (notably PV, the STM-impaired patient who could not learn novel Russian words but could learn native-language paired associates) and developmental populations. Supporting longitudinal work: Service (1992) followed Finnish schoolchildren for three years; English-sounding pseudoword repetition accuracy predicted English attainment three years out. Speciale, Ellis & Bywater (2004, Applied Psycholinguistics 25, 293–321): Exp 1, 40 undergraduates learning German vocabulary — phonological sequence learning predicted receptive learning, and sequence learning plus store capacity made independent additive contributions to productive learning; Exp 2, 44 undergraduates over a 10-week Spanish course (a genuine longitudinal field study, not a word list).

sources.citation: Baddeley, Gathercole & Papagno (1998). Psychological Review 105, 158–173.
Service, E. (1992). Phonology, working memory, and foreign-language learning. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology A, 45(1), 21–50.

Speciale, G., Ellis, N. C., & Bywater, T. (2004). Phonological sequence learning and short-term store capacity determine second language vocabulary acquisition. Applied Psycholinguistics, 25, 293–321.

findings.implication: Treat the pinyin scaffolding tier as a MEANING aid, not a pronunciation-learning feature. The product's job is form→meaning; do not let pinyin creep into a tone-drilling subsystem, which would import the whole PSTM difficulty gradient into a game that currently escapes it. Content rule: every item ships with pinyin as metadata, but pinyin is never itself a scored answer.

findings.claim: For L2 Chinese READING, morphological awareness — knowing that words decompose into meaning-bearing character morphemes — is the largest single contributor, far outranking working-memory capacity, which acts only indirectly.
findings.detail: Path analysis, N = 252 international students learning Chinese (Frontiers in Psychology 2023). Linguistic skills (vocabulary, syntax, orthography, morphological awareness) plus working memory plus higher-order skills (inference making, comprehension monitoring) explained 80% of variance in L2 Chinese reading. Morphological awareness made the largest contribution. Working memory contributed only INDIRECTLY, via inference making and comprehension monitoring. Separately, a study of high- vs low-achieving Chinese L2 learners found spatial working memory did not differentiate the groups, whereas verbal WM supporting phonological and morpheme processing did — explicitly inconsistent with alphabetic-L2 findings.

sources.citation: The role of linguistic and cognitive skills in reading Chinese as a second language: A path analysis modeling approach. Frontiers in Psychology (2023), 14:1131913.
The domain-general and domain-specific cognitive profiles in high and low-achieving Chinese L2 learners. Frontiers in Psychology (2025), 16:1577986.

findings.implication: The component-breakdown screen (出 + 口) is not a nice-to-have garnish on the resolution step — it is the highest-leverage screen in the product, because it is the only place you build morphological awareness. Promote it from a post-answer reveal to a first-class, dwell-able surface: it must stay on screen until the table advances it, not auto-dismiss on a timer.

findings.claim: The visuospatial-sketchpad story for logographic scripts is CONTESTED, not established. There is no clean finding that learning hanzi leans on visuospatial WM in a way alphabetic scripts do not.
findings.detail: Evidence points both ways. For: L1-alphabetic learners reading Chinese face high visuospatial demands and must memorise arbitrary visual-form-to-meaning mappings; in L1 Chinese kindergarteners (N = 99) visual skills plus working memory accounted for 15% of unique variance in character reading. Against: in adult Chinese L2 learners, spatial working memory did NOT distinguish high from low achievers; and in L1 Chinese children, letter-rotation-type visuospatial WM tasks were reported as insensitive to ordinary character reading, while a visual judgment task using real and pseudo characters was the stronger predictor. That pattern says the operative skill is script-SPECIFIC visual-orthographic expertise, not general visuospatial WM capacity. Confirming this: Chinese literates show a large visual WM advantage for Chinese characters that does NOT transfer to novel material — an expertise effect built on long-term knowledge of visual word forms, not a bigger sketchpad.

sources.citation: Visual Working Memory of Chinese Characters and Expertise: The Expert's Memory Advantage Is Based on Long-Term Knowledge of Visual Word Forms. Frontiers in Psychology (2020), 11:516.
Yang, X. et al. (2021). Direct effects of visual skills and working memory on Chinese character reading in young children. Infant and Child Development, 30, e2231.
The domain-general and domain-specific cognitive profiles in high and low-achieving Chinese L2 learners. Frontiers in Psychology (2025), 16:1577986.

findings.implication: Do not build a 'visual memory training' mode or a spatial-ability onboarding test — the evidence does not support either. Build script-specific perceptual expertise instead: high exposure count to real character forms. Architecture: track exposures per COMPONENT (not per word), because component-level visual expertise is what transfers to unseen characters.

findings.claim: Cowan's ~4-chunk limit is better supported than Miller's 7±2, and for VISUAL material the working figure is narrower still (~3). This is a hard ceiling on what the resolution screen can show.
findings.detail: Cowan (2001, Behavioral and Brain Sciences 24) assembled evidence that a central capacity limit averages ~4 chunks, observable when information overload forces chunks to be single items, when recoding into larger chunks is blocked, and in performance discontinuities. Miller's 7±2 was explicitly a rough estimate, not a measured capacity, and is not the current consensus. Agreement is not universal — a 2024 Journal of Cognition modelling paper concludes the number depends on what is being counted — but nobody defends 7 as a chunk limit. Visual short-term memory is reported as more space-constrained than phonological, around three chunks.

sources.citation: Cowan, N. (2001). The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87–114.
Modelling Working Memory Capacity: Is the Magical Number Four, Seven, or Does it Depend on What You Are Counting? Journal of Cognition (2024).
Oberauer, K., Farrell, S., Jarrold, C., & Lewandowsky, S. (2016). What limits working memory capacity? Psychological Bulletin, 142(7), 758–799.

findings.implication: Hard UI cap: the resolution screen shows at most FOUR new visual chunks at once. Concretely for 出口 that is: 出, 口, the whole word 出口, and ONE confusable (入口). That is already four. Do not also show stroke order, tone marks, a radical table, and an etymology note on the same screen — that is six-plus chunks and will exceed visual WM for a beginner. If more content exists, gate it behind a tap, not a scroll.

findings.claim: Component decomposition is what makes a Chinese character fit inside working memory at all. The arithmetic is decisive and is the strongest available argument for the breakdown screen.
findings.detail: A character averages 10.15 strokes, but 98% of characters are composed of 5 or fewer chunks, at ~2.1 strokes per chunk. Ten unstructured strokes exceeds a ~3–4 item visual WM limit outright; five components sits at the edge; three or four components sits inside it. Radicals provide large units (~5.2 strokes per radical) while strokes provide minimal units that impose no structure and therefore no reduction in visual memory load. The chunk is the intermediate unit and is optimal for learning. This is Miller's original recoding insight (Miller 1956) applied to orthography, and it is consistent with Gobet et al.'s (2001) distinction between deliberate, strategic chunking and automatic perceptual chunking — a learner is doing the first, an expert reader has the second.

sources.citation: Gobet, F., Lane, P. C. R., Croker, S., Cheng, P. C.-H., Jones, G., Oliver, I., & Pine, J. M. (2001). Chunking mechanisms in human learning. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 5(6), 236–243.
Using Meaningful Interpretation and Chunking to Enhance Memory: The Case of Chinese Character Learning.
Gobet, F. (2005). Chunking models of expertise: implications for education. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 19(2), 183–204.

findings.implication: Every item in the content database MUST carry a component decomposition field, and the decomposition must be to COMPONENTS (2–5 per character), never to strokes. Ship no item without it. Never render a stroke-order animation on the resolution screen — strokes add elements without adding structure, which is the exact opposite of chunking.
findings._topic: Memory architecture and encoding for 看不懂: working memory, chunking, levels of processing, dual coding, encoding specificity / transfer-appropriate processing, and desirable difficulties — tested against the current design

findings.claim: On '出口 as one chunk vs 出 and 口 separately': there is no direct head-to-head experiment. The nearest evidence says BOTH, conditional on semantic transparency — and the condition is decisive.
findings.detail: Known constituent characters assist learners in memorising new compounds, PARTICULARLY TRANSPARENT ONES. L2 Chinese learners use a hybrid representation (whole word plus morphemes) for high-frequency words and whole-word representation for low-frequency words, and rely more on orthographic and less on phonological processing than native speakers. But radical/component awareness does not always work: Chen & Feng (2020) specifically examined nontransparent compound character learning and found radical awareness is not reliably helpful there. Compare 出口 (out + mouth/opening = exit; transparent) with 东西 (east + west = 'thing'; opaque). Decomposing the second teaches a falsehood.

sources.citation: Hao, Y., Wu, C., & Duan, X. (2024). Processing Mandarin Chinese Compound Words by Native Speakers and Second Language Learners: Word Frequency, Semantic Transparency, and Word Structure. SAGE Open.
Chen, T., & Feng, Y. (2020). Nontransparent Compound Character Learning in L2 Chinese: Does Radical Awareness Always Work? SAGE Open.
Word-meaning inference in L2 Chinese: an interactive effect of learners' linguistic knowledge and words' semantic transparency. Reading and Writing (2020).

findings.implication: Add a required `transparency` enum to every multi-character item: transparent | semi | opaque. The resolution screen branches on it. TRANSPARENT (出口, 入口, 公斤, 小心): show the component gloss — 'out + opening'. OPAQUE (东西, 麻烦): show the word as an unanalysed unit with an explicit 'this one does not decompose — learn it whole' line. Rendering a bogus decomposition for an opaque word is worse than showing none, because it installs an inference rule that will misfire on the street.

findings.claim: Explicit component/radical instruction works for CFL learners and transfers to untrained characters — one of the few Chinese-specific instructional findings with meta-analytic support.
findings.detail: A meta-analysis of 11 studies found radical-based instruction strategies had a significant effect on character meaning production. Explicit semantic-radical teaching raised post-test accuracy substantially on trained material and — the important part — the experimental groups transferred the strategy to UNFAMILIAR characters where controls did not. Guided inductive instruction produced greater gains than deductive instruction in learners' use of radical information for form-meaning mapping and inferencing. Countervailing evidence: providing radical markings and stroke-order animations simultaneously can INTERFERE with character learning by inflating cognitive load.

sources.citation: Investigating the effect of radical-based strategies on improving foreign Chinese learners' radical awareness and character meaning production: a meta-analysis. Educational Research and Reviews (2023), 5(2).
Teaching Semantic Radicals Facilitates Inferring New Character Meaning in Sentence Reading for Nonnative Chinese Speakers.
Interference effects of radical markings and stroke order animations on Chinese character learning among L2 learners.

findings.implication: Sequence content so that a component is met inside a whole sign BEFORE it is named as a component (guided inductive beats deductive). Concretely: 出口 appears as an item; the breakdown names 出; two or three items later 出租车 appears and the breakdown can now say 'you have seen 出 before'. Store a `component_first_seen_at` timestamp per user per component to drive that callback line.

findings.claim: Levels of processing survived its circularity critique only in weakened form. The defensible residue is not 'deeper is better' — it is 'match the encoding operation to the retrieval operation' (transfer-appropriate processing).
findings.detail: Craik & Lockhart (1972) lacked an independent index of depth: deep processing was inferred from better recall which was then explained by deep processing. Morris, Bransford & Franks (1977, JVLVB) broke the framework empirically: across three experiments, semantic encoding beat rhyme encoding on a standard recognition test, but rhyme encoding BEAT semantic encoding on a rhyme recognition test — replicated at both immediate and delayed test. Depth per se does not produce a stronger trace; the encoding-retrieval match does. What genuinely survived from LoP is the narrower, robust empirical regularity that semantic elaboration beats shallow perceptual encoding for ordinary meaning-based tests, and this holds across the lifespan.

sources.citation: Morris, C. D., Bransford, J. D., & Franks, J. J. (1977). Levels of processing versus transfer appropriate processing. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 16(5), 519–533.
Craik, F. I. M. (2002). Levels of processing: Past, present... and future? Memory, 10(5/6), 305–318.

findings.implication: Define the criterion task explicitly and design backwards from it: 'standing in front of a physical sign, in an unfamiliar display typeface, retrieve the meaning.' That is meaning-recall from a rendered form, not multiple-choice discrimination. Every design argument in this product should be settled by asking 'does this make the training operation resemble that criterion operation?' — not by asking 'is this deeper?'

findings.claim: A 4-option multiple-choice recognition task produces SHALLOW processing by default — a player can succeed by eliminating three options without ever encoding the form-meaning link. But competitive, plausible alternatives fix most of this, cheaply.
findings.detail: Little, E. L. Bjork, R. A. Bjork & Angello (2012, Psychological Science 23, 1337–1344): multiple-choice practice tests with COMPETITIVE incorrect alternatives enhanced performance on related-but-different questions on a later cued-recall test — a benefit that did NOT occur when the practice test was cued recall. The mechanism the authors propose is that plausible competitors force the learner to retrieve not only why the correct alternative is correct but why each other alternative is INCORRECT. Multiple-choice pretesting has separately been shown to potentiate learning of related information (Memory & Cognition 2016). The corollary is the warning: with implausible distractors, none of this fires, and MC degrades to elimination.

sources.citation: Little, J. L., Bjork, E. L., Bjork, R. A., & Angello, G. (2012). Multiple-choice tests exonerated, at least of some charges: Fostering test-induced learning and avoiding test-induced forgetting. Psychological Science, 23(11), 1337–1344.
Little, J. L., & Bjork, E. L. (2016). Multiple-choice pretesting potentiates learning of related information. Memory & Cognition, 44, 1085–1101.

findings.implication: Make distractor quality a hard content constraint, not an authoring convenience. Every item needs 3 distractors that are each defensibly *almost* right for this specific sign — 入口 for 出口, 公斤 for 斤, 麻 for 辣. Ban random-other-item distractors and ban a category-mismatched distractor (a food word among station signs), because either one collapses the item to elimination. Add a content-pipeline lint that rejects an item whose distractors share no component and no semantic field with the target.

findings.claim: Format match moderates the testing effect: practising with multiple choice builds recognition, and transfers to free recall only partially. Pure MC will under-train the real-world skill.
findings.detail: Rowland (2014, Psychological Bulletin 140, 1432–1463) meta-analysed testing vs restudy; congruence between practice format and criterion format increases the testing effect. Pan & Rickard (2018) meta-analysed transfer of test-enhanced learning and found positive but SMALLER effects on transfer than on same-format retention. In L2 vocabulary specifically, recall formats are more effective for productive knowledge of orthography while recognition formats suit other aspects; format demand ranks form recall > meaning recall > form recognition > meaning recognition.

sources.citation: Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432–1463.
Pan, S. C., & Rickard, T. C. (2018). Transfer of test-enhanced learning: Meta-analytic review and synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 144(7), 710–756.
Effects of retrieval formats on second language vocabulary learning.

findings.implication: Add one meaning-recall beat per round without breaking the co-located MC format: after the table locks in answers but BEFORE the reveal, show the sign alone for ~3 seconds with the prompt 'say it out loud'. Zero extra UI state, no scoring, no typing — but it converts a pure recognition trial into a recall attempt plus feedback, which is the format the street will demand. Track it as `spoken_attempt` for nothing but future analysis.

findings.claim: Self-explanation prompts are one of the best-evidenced cheap interventions in the whole brief: g = 0.55 across 64 reports.
findings.detail: Bisra, Liu, Nesbit, Salimi & Winne (2018, Educational Psychology Review): 69 effect sizes from 64 research reports, ~6,000 participants, random-effects weighted mean g = 0.55, with 20 moderators coded. Benefits held across most subject areas and for both conceptual and procedural knowledge. Related but weaker: elaborative interrogation ('why is this true?') was rated MODERATE utility by Dunlosky et al. (2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest), around d = 0.56, but its evidence base is dominated by school-age learners learning factual text, works best when learners already have background knowledge, and has not been shown for L2 orthographic learning.

sources.citation: Bisra, K., Liu, Q., Nesbit, J. C., Salimi, F., & Winne, P. H. (2018). Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 703–725.

Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58.

findings.implication: The co-located format gives you self-explanation for free and you should exploit it. On the reveal, put one short prompt on the confusable pair — 'why isn't it 入口?' — addressed to the player who bet highest. Spoken, to the table, ~5 seconds. This is the cheapest g≈0.55 available and it costs one line of text. Do not make it typed and do not score it; typed self-explanation in a party game will kill pace.

findings.claim: The self-reference effect is large in the lab (d ≈ 0.65 vs semantic encoding) but has never been tested on L2 orthographic learning. Use it, but do not over-invest.
findings.detail: Symons & Johnson (1997, Psychological Bulletin 121, 371–394): meta-analysis of 129 studies, mean weighted d = 0.65 for self-referent over semantic and other-referent encoding, ~39 participants per study, overwhelmingly undergraduates. The paradigm is trait-adjective word lists (Rogers et al. 1977 designs). Transfer to learning that 出口 means exit is an inference, not a finding.

sources.citation: Symons, C. S., & Johnson, B. T. (1997). The self-reference effect in memory: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 121(3), 371–394.
Digital Commons copy: The Self-Reference Effect in Memory: A Meta-Analysis.

findings.implication: One free, zero-cost application: frame each item as a first-person decision rather than a definition. 'You are holding a bag of oranges. The label says 5.80/斤. What are you paying per?' beats '斤 = ?'. That is a template change in the item schema (`prompt_frame: second_person_scenario`), not a feature. Do not build a personalisation engine on the strength of a trait-adjective literature.

findings.claim: The picture-superiority effect is real and replicable; Paivio's dual-coding EXPLANATION of it is not currently the leading account. And for logographs, the 'second code' argument does not apply the way the design might assume.
findings.detail: Picture superiority replicates across free recall and serial recall paradigms. But Higdon, Neath, Surprenant & Ensor (2025, QJEP) argue distinctiveness, not dual coding, explains it; and picture superiority is PRESERVED IN APHANTASIA at near-identical effect size to typical imagers, which undercuts the claim that visual imagery is the mechanism. A Chinese character is already a visual object, so pairing it with a picture is not adding a nonverbal code to a verbal one in Paivio's sense — it is adding a distinctive, meaningful referent. That is still useful, but the mechanism is distinctiveness/elaboration, which changes what you should build.

sources.citation: Higdon, K. F., Neath, I., Surprenant, A. M., & Ensor, T. M. (2025). Distinctiveness, not dual coding, explains the picture-superiority effect. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.
Challenging dual-coding theory: Picture superiority is preserved in aphantasia.

findings.implication: Do not add illustrative clip-art beside characters on the theory that 'dual coding helps'. If you add imagery, make it DISTINCTIVE and DIAGNOSTIC — the actual object the sign hangs on, which you are already doing — rather than a generic icon. An exit-door pictogram next to 出口 adds a second cue that will not be present on a text-only Chinese sign, and risks the player learning the pictogram instead of the characters.

findings.claim: Visual/keyword mnemonics accelerate acquisition but can INCREASE long-term forgetting relative to plain rehearsal. This is a genuine trap for a character app.
findings.detail: The keyword mnemonic reliably improves immediate and short-delay vocabulary retention (one study reports d ≈ 0.96 for keyword treatment). But the long-term picture is worse than the folklore: long-term forgetting has been found to be GREATER for learners instructed to use the keyword mnemonic than for learners engaged in rote rehearsal, and within-subject retention comparisons are confounded by differing rates of initial acquisition and immediate recall level. For Chinese specifically, visual mnemonics for visually-similar characters have been studied (Chang, Tang, Lee & Chen 2022, Frontiers in Psychology 13:783898) but with short retention intervals.

sources.citation: Keyword mnemonic and retention of second-language vocabulary words. Journal of Educational Psychology (1992). ERIC EJ456644.

Chang, L.-Y., Tang, Y.-Y., Lee, C.-Y., & Chen, H.-C. (2022). The Effect of Visual Mnemonics and the Presentation of Character Pairs on Learning Visually Similar Characters for Chinese-As-Second-Language Learners. Frontiers in Psychology, 13:783898.

findings.implication: If the breakdown screen offers a mnemonic story for a component, mark it as an ACQUISITION aid with an expiry: show it on exposures 1–2 for that component and suppress it from exposure 3 onward, so later encounters are plain retrieval. Store `mnemonic_shown_count` per user per component and stop at 2. Never let the mnemonic be the thing that is retrieved at test.

findings.claim: VERDICT ON THE SIGNAGE RENDERING, part 1: the design's stated theory is the WRONG theory. Environmental context-dependent memory is a small effect that mostly evaporates under exactly the conditions this product creates.
findings.detail: Smith & Vela (2001, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 8, 203–220) meta-analysed 93 effect sizes from 75 studies (1935–1997): mean d ≈ 0.28. A 2026 meta-analysis across younger and older adults (22 articles, 33 studies, 106 effect sizes, N = 2,177) found Hedges' g = 0.32. Small. Smith & Vela's central theoretical claim is OVERSHADOWING and OUTSHINING: when non-contextual cues are available at encoding, or when the test itself supplies a strong retrieval cue, context effects shrink or disappear. Godden & Baddeley's own 1980 follow-up, using the identical land/underwater manipulation that produced a large RECALL effect in 1975, found NO context effect on RECOGNITION. Isarida et al. (2012, Memory & Cognition; N = 80 + 40) sharpened this: place-context-dependent recognition appeared for short study times (1.5 s/item) and for less meaningful materials (nonwords), and vanished for meaningful words at long study times (4.0 s/item). A four-option multiple-choice test is the maximal-outshining case — it hands the player the target itself. And decisively: the app's sign rendering is not environmental context at all. It is present at both study and test WITHIN the app and absent in that exact form on the street, so nothing is being reinstated.

sources.citation: Smith, S. M., & Vela, E. (2001). Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 203–220.
Context reinstatement effects in younger and older adults' memory: A meta-analysis (2026).
Isarida, T. et al. (2012). Effects of study time and meaningfulness on environmental context-dependent recognition. Memory & Cognition, 40(8), 1225–1235.
Murre, J. M. J. (2021). The Godden and Baddeley (1975) experiment on context-dependent memory on land and underwater: a replication. Royal Society Open Science, 8(11), 200724.

findings.implication: Delete 'context encoded is context retrieved' from the design rationale. Do not build any feature justified by context reinstatement — no 'study in the same place' nudge, no ambient-scene backgrounds, no geolocation-matched review. Those would be cargo-culting a d≈0.28 effect that a recognition test outshines anyway.
