findings.claim: VERDICT ON THE SIGNAGE RENDERING, part 2: the rendering IS doing real work — but as transfer-appropriate PERCEPTUAL training, and the direct evidence for that is a Chinese-character typeface experiment.
findings.detail: High-variability orthographic training (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, March 2025): n = 190 participants with no prior Chinese learned 24 characters, either in a single typeface or across three. Result: compared with single-typeface training, variable-typeface training produced SLOWER responses for characters tested in the FAMILIAR typeface but FASTER responses in a NOVEL typeface. That is a textbook desirable difficulty with both halves measured — a cost during acquisition, a gain in generalisation. This is the mechanism by which real signage earns its place: a station plate, a shopfront fascia and a shelf-edge label carry genuinely different display typefaces, weights, colours and contrast, and the criterion task is reading characters in typefaces the learner has never seen. Convergent general finding: variability in training unlocks generalisation in visual perceptual learning through invariant representations (Current Biology 2023).

sources.citation: High variability orthographic training: Learning words in a logographic script through training with multiple typefaces. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (2025).
Variability in training unlocks generalization in visual perceptual learning through invariant representations. Current Biology (2023).

findings.implication: This reframes the signage from decoration to core mechanic — but only if you enforce typeface variety deliberately. Add a required `typeface` field per rendered item and a constraint that any given word must appear in at least THREE distinct typefaces across its exposure schedule (e.g. a heavy sans station plate, a condensed shop fascia, a thin supermarket label). Do not render every item in one house font, however handsome — that is the single-typeface condition, and the study says it buys speed you cannot use and costs generalisation you need.

findings.claim: VERDICT ON THE SIGNAGE RENDERING, part 3: the rendering also earns its place by making the meaning EVALUABLE — but only the parts of it that constrain meaning. Everything else is a seductive detail and measurably harms retention.
findings.detail: Yanagisawa & Webb (2021, Language Learning 71(2), 487–536): 398 effect sizes from 42 studies, N = 4,628. The Involvement Load Hypothesis significantly predicted learning, explaining 15.0% of variance on immediate and 5.1% on delayed post-tests. The EVALUATION component — comparing a word against a context to decide whether it fits — contributed the most, NEED second, and SEARCH contributed nothing. A price label that makes 斤 a unit of weight, or a station plate that makes 出口 a direction, supplies evaluation. Against this: Rey (2012) meta-analysed the seductive detail effect and found negative effects on retention (small-to-medium) and transfer (medium), with attentional distraction the best-supported mechanism and effects STRONGER under LIMITED study time; a 2020 Educational Psychology Review meta-analysis ('Keep it Coherent') confirms. This game is timed and socially pressured — the limited-study-time condition where seductive details bite hardest.

sources.citation: Yanagisawa, A., & Webb, S. (2021). To What Extent Does the Involvement Load Hypothesis Predict Incidental L2 Vocabulary Learning? A Meta-Analysis. Language Learning, 71(2), 487–536.
Rey, G. D. (2012). A review and meta-analysis of the seductive detail effect. Educational Research Review, 7(3), 216–237.
Sundararajan, N., & Adesope, O. (2020). Keep it Coherent: A Meta-Analysis of the Seductive Details Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 707–734.

findings.implication: Adopt a one-line test for every pixel of the sign rendering: does it constrain the meaning of the target? The ¥ symbol and the number on a price label pass (they make 斤 a unit). The station plate's arrow passes. A photographic Chinese street scene behind the card FAILS and must be cut. Steam curling off a bowl next to 麻辣 FAILS. Render the physical object as a flat, high-contrast, information-bearing rectangle — the plate, the label, the fascia — with no environmental photography, no atmospheric gradient, and no ambient clutter.

findings.claim: Encoding specificity (Tulving & Thomson 1973) does support the design — but the cue it licenses is the CHARACTER FORM AS IT WILL BE MET, not the surrounding scene.
findings.detail: Tulving & Thomson (1973, Psychological Review; ~5,400 citations) showed that a cue is effective only if it was encoded with the target, and demonstrated recognition failure of recallable words: participants failed to recognise a target word presented in isolation yet later recalled it given the cue it had been studied with. The principle is about which specific features got bound into the trace. Applied here: if the learner only ever encodes 出口 as clean black Song-font on white, then black-Song-on-white is the effective cue, and a white-on-green backlit station plate is a different stimulus. This is the same conclusion the typeface-variability experiment reaches from the perceptual side.

sources.citation: Tulving, E., & Thomson, D. M. (1973). Encoding specificity and retrieval processes in episodic memory. Psychological Review, 80(5), 352–373.

findings.implication: Content sourcing rule: items must be photographed-from-life or faithfully reconstructed sign renderings, including the real colour inversion (white-on-green for Chinese station exit signage, white-on-red for hazard boards, black-on-yellow price tags). Do not normalise every item to one card style for visual consistency — visual consistency is here in direct tension with the criterion task, and the criterion task wins.

findings.claim: Split attention is a real and measured cost in Chinese character learning specifically: WHERE you put the pinyin changes the learning outcome.
findings.detail: Lee & Kalyuga (2011, Language Learning 61(4), 1099–1118, UNSW): compared vertical and horizontal layouts of characters, pinyin and English translations. Significant advantage for the VERTICAL format, attributed to eliminating split attention by placing each pinyin syllable exactly below its matching character. The authors warn that the commonly used horizontal layout may impose high cognitive load and hinder character learning. Converging eye-tracking evidence (Michigan State doctoral study, learners' fixations on characters vs pinyin vs English): the ADJACENT format led to better learning outcomes and promoted attention to the CHARACTERS, versus horizontal and vertical-separated formats. General principle: the split-attention/spatial-contiguity effect is large for high-element-interactivity material and disappears for low-element-interactivity material.

sources.citation: Lee, C. H., & Kalyuga, S. (2011). Effectiveness of Different Pinyin Presentation Formats in Learning Chinese Characters: A Cognitive Load Perspective. Language Learning, 61(4), 1099–1118.
Working memory, presentation formats, and attention: an eye-tracking study on learning L2 Chinese characters in a computer-assisted self-study environment. Michigan State University.

findings.implication: Concrete UI spec for the pinyin scaffolding tier: render pinyin as per-character syllables directly BELOW each character, baseline-aligned to that character's box — chū under 出, kǒu under 口. Do NOT render 'chūkǒu' as a single romanised string beside or beneath the word, which is the horizontal layout the study found worse. Same rule for the English gloss: attach it to the whole word directly under the pinyin row, not off to the side.

findings.claim: Pairing a deliberately chosen confusable (入口 beside 出口) is well supported — by discriminative contrast, not by 'more exposure'. The juxtaposition itself is the active ingredient.
findings.detail: Kornell & Bjork (2008) found interleaving exemplars of different categories enhances inductive learning; Kang & Pashler (2012) showed the benefit tracks JUXTAPOSITION rather than temporal spacing — interleaving helped, temporal spacing alone did not. Follow-up work found temporal spacing was HARMFUL when it interrupted the juxtaposition of interleaved categories, even with total spacing held constant. Countervailing risk, real and Chinese-specific: learning related items simultaneously can produce interference and cross-item confusion from the start, and Chinese characters are unusually susceptible because they share components. Chang et al. (2022) tested exactly this — visually similar vs dissimilar character pair presentation, 30 compound characters — but I could not read the result, so the direction for VISUALLY similar (as opposed to semantically contrastive) pairs is unresolved.

sources.citation: Birnbaum, M. S., Kornell, N., Bjork, E. L., & Bjork, R. A. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402.
Kang, S. H. K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Learning painting styles: Spacing is advantageous when it promotes discriminative contrast. Applied Cognitive Psychology.
Chang, L.-Y., Tang, Y.-Y., Lee, C.-Y., & Chen, H.-C. (2022). Frontiers in Psychology, 13:783898.

findings.implication: Show the confusable pair SIMULTANEOUSLY and side by side on the reveal, with the discriminating component visually marked (出 vs 入 highlighted, the shared 口 left plain). Do not show the confusable as a 'next item' a few turns later — the evidence says temporal separation destroys the discriminative contrast that makes this work. And show the contrast only AFTER the answer resolves, never among the options before the answer, so the pair is a discrimination lesson rather than an interference source at first encoding.

findings.claim: The betting mechanic has no direct evidential support as a memory intervention — but it earns its place indirectly through confidence elicitation, and the hypercorrection literature tells you exactly what to do with the confidence signal.
findings.detail: On wagering itself: the literature is thin and largely correlational (confidence wagering correlates with metacognitive alignment and summative performance in a gamified SQL practice study); there is no experiment showing betting improves retention. Grade that folklore. But betting FORCES an explicit pre-answer confidence judgement, and that is a well-studied lever. The hypercorrection effect (Metcalfe & Finn 2011, JEP:LMC; Butler, Fazio & Marsh 2011): errors committed with HIGH confidence are corrected MORE readily following feedback than low-confidence errors, and the effect persists at a one-week delay. The critical operational detail: high-confidence errors do NOT return at a delay IF a test intervenes after the corrective feedback, but they DO return if no test intervenes. Caveat: later work found memory for the feedback and for the original response, not confidence or surprise per se, were the significant predictors of correction.

sources.citation: Metcalfe, J., & Finn, B. (2011). People's hypercorrection of high-confidence errors: Did they know it all along? Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition.
Butler, A. C., Fazio, L. K., & Marsh, E. J. (2011). The hypercorrection effect persists over a week, but high-confidence errors return. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 18, 1238–1244.
Beyond hypercorrection: remembering corrective feedback for low-confidence errors (2017).

findings.implication: Persist the bet as a confidence value on every attempt (`bet_tier`, `was_correct`), then act on it: any item missed at the HIGHEST bet tier must be re-tested before the session ends — not merely scheduled for tomorrow. That single rule is what converts a one-off correction into a durable one, per Butler et al. Cheap implementation: a `high_confidence_miss` queue drained in the session's final round.
findings._topic: Memory architecture and encoding for 看不懂: working memory, chunking, levels of processing, dual coding, encoding specificity / transfer-appropriate processing, and desirable difficulties — tested against the current design

findings.claim: Betting before seeing the item is a PRETEST, and prequestion benefits are large but strictly item-specific — they do not spread to material the question did not target.
findings.detail: A multilevel meta-analysis of prequestions found g = 0.66 for learning of the information specifically targeted by the prequestion, and NO evidence of a general benefit for other, non-prequestioned information present in the same activity. The broader pretesting literature (Richland, Kornell & Kao 2009; Pan & Carpenter 2023 review) shows that unsuccessful retrieval attempts before study improve later memory relative to equal-time reading, PROVIDED corrective feedback follows. Mechanisms proposed include generation of semantic mediators, search-set activation, error-correction signals and attentional focusing.

sources.citation: The Effect of Prequestions on Learning: A Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2025).
Pan, S. C., & Carpenter, S. K. (2023). Prequestioning and Pretesting Effects: A Review of Empirical Research, Theoretical Perspectives, and Applications. Educational Psychology Review.
Richland, L. E., Kornell, N., & Kao, L. S. (2009). The pretesting effect: Do unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance learning? JEP: Applied.

findings.implication: Narrow the category the opposing team deals. 'Transport' is too broad to function as a prequestion — the item-specificity finding says the anticipation must target roughly what will be asked. Deal categories at the granularity of 'signs on a subway platform' or 'weight and price on a market label', so the pre-bet moment actually activates the right search set. Corollary: always show the correct answer on resolution — a pretest without corrective feedback forfeits the effect entirely.

findings.claim: Curiosity states enhance memory for BOTH the anticipated item and incidental material encountered during the anticipation window — a direct neural warrant for the bet-then-reveal structure.
findings.detail: Gruber, Gelman & Ranganath (2014, Neuron 84(2), 486–496): participants showed improved memory both for information they were curious about AND for incidental, unrelated material encountered during high-curiosity states, at IMMEDIATE and ONE-DAY-DELAYED test. Midbrain and nucleus accumbens activity was elevated during high curiosity, and the memory benefit depended on midbrain–hippocampus interactions, consistent with dopaminergic modulation of hippocampal encoding during anticipation.

sources.citation: Gruber, M. J., Gelman, B. D., & Ranganath, C. (2014). States of Curiosity Modulate Hippocampus-Dependent Learning via the Dopaminergic Circuit. Neuron, 84(2), 486–496.
PubMed record.

findings.implication: Protect and lengthen the anticipation gap. After the bet is locked and before the sign is revealed, hold a deliberate beat (~1.5–2 s) with the category named and the stake visible. Do not optimise this away for pace. The incidental-memory finding also means the component breakdown shown during that high-curiosity window will stick better than the same breakdown shown in a flat review screen — so put the breakdown on the reveal, not in a separate 'study' tab.

findings.claim: 'The whole table watches' is defensible: observers gain from others' retrieval, and collaborative retrieval improves later INDIVIDUAL memory even though the group recalls less in the moment.
findings.detail: Collaborative recall shows collaborative inhibition — a group recalls less than the pooled output of the same people working alone — but post-collaborative individual recall is improved: when re-exposure occurs during collaboration, its benefit shows up in the recipient's later individual memory, and hearing an item recalled functions as a second learning opportunity. Computationally, listeners use others' recalls as external retrieval cues that update their own mental context. Collaborative retrieval practice has also been shown to reduce mind-wandering during learning.

sources.citation: Rajaram, S., Greeley, G., & Peña, M. (2024). Collaborative memory: A selective review.
A context-based model of collaborative inhibition during memory search. Scientific Reports (2024).
Collaborative Retrieval Practice Reduces Mind-Wandering During Learning.

findings.implication: Credit exposure to spectators, not just the answering player. Architecture: when an item resolves, write an exposure record for EVERY player at the table, flagged `role: observer` vs `role: answerer`, and let observer exposures advance that player's scheduling state at a discounted weight. Without this, a player who watches thirty items and answers six is modelled as having seen six — and will be re-shown material the whole table already discussed.

findings.claim: Desirable difficulties are real for the five canonical manipulations, but the slogan overreaches in two documented ways: difficulties REVERSE for high-element-interactivity material, and they reverse with expertise.
findings.detail: The well-evidenced five are spacing, interleaving, retrieval practice, generation and varied practice (Bjork & Bjork). Against the slogan: Chen, Castro-Alonso, Paas & Sweller (2018, Frontiers in Psychology 9:1483) document UNDESIRABLE difficulty effects — failures to obtain expected benefits and outright reversals — attributed to the element interactivity of the learning material, with testing and generation effects interacting differently with material complexity. Separately, the expertise reversal effect (Kalyuga; Chen, Kalyuga & Sweller argue it is a variant of the general element-interactivity effect): detailed guidance that helps novices becomes redundant and harmful for more knowledgeable learners, who must reconcile external explanation with existing schemas. The boundary condition is that a difficulty is desirable only if the learner can actually execute the effortful process.

sources.citation: Chen, O., Castro-Alonso, J. C., Paas, F., & Sweller, J. (2018). Undesirable Difficulty Effects in the Learning of High-Element Interactivity Materials. Frontiers in Psychology, 9:1483.
Chen, O., Kalyuga, S., & Sweller, J. (2017). The Expertise Reversal Effect is a Variant of the More General Element Interactivity Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 393–405.
Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2020). Desirable difficulties in theory and practice. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition.

findings.implication: The bet-as-scaffolding-removal is the right SHAPE but must be bounded by competence, not just courage. Gate the top tier (Chinese-only options): a player may only bet it on a category where they already hold some component knowledge — e.g. at least N prior correct exposures to components appearing in that category. Otherwise the top bet is not a desirable difficulty, it is a coin flip, and a coin flip teaches nothing. Store per-user per-category `component_mastery` and use it to grey out (not hide) unearned bet tiers with an explicit 'unlock by…' line.

findings.claim: Difficulty has a documented MOTIVATIONAL cost that the retention literature routinely omits — and for a product that can lose a player mid-session, this is a first-order risk, not a footnote.
findings.detail: Learners frequently choose not to use desirable-difficulty strategies, or disengage when they are imposed. Retrieval practice specifically confronts learners with evidence of their own non-mastery, which induces negative affect; learners are unlikely to discover retrieval practice's effectiveness from their own experience because the in-the-moment signal (I got it wrong, this feels bad) is opposite to the long-term outcome. The applied literature on why language learners quit converges on inability to perceive progress: difficulty is motivating when progress feels legible, and demotivating when the learner cannot answer 'what can I do now that I couldn't before?'. I found no RCT quantifying dropout as a function of difficulty in a language app — this is an evidence gap, and the practitioner literature filling it (Duolingo case studies and gamification blogs) is folklore, not evidence.

sources.citation: Motivational Strategies to Engage Learners in Desirable Difficulties. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition (2020).
How task difficulty and academic self-efficacy impact retrieval practice guidance.

findings.implication: Make progress legible in the product's own currency — signs, not points. End every session with a single screen: 'you can now read these 7 signs' rendered as the actual signs, at real size, in their real typefaces. That directly answers the 'what can I do now?' question the demotivation literature identifies, and it costs one screen. Second, protect the social floor: never surface a per-player accuracy leaderboard at the table — a co-located game makes non-mastery public, which is exactly the affect the retrieval-practice literature warns about. Score the TABLE against the item bank, and let bets be the only individual number on screen.

findings.claim: The meta-analytic case for the method of loci is a case about immediate SERIAL RECALL of word lists, and nothing else is well evidenced. Outside serial recall the evidence is graded low to very low quality.
findings.detail: Ondřej et al. (2025, Br J Psychol 116:930–986) is the current systematic review + meta-analysis (GRADE + RoBMA). Headline: strong evidence for a large effect on IMMEDIATE SERIAL RECALL vs rehearsal, d = 0.88, 95% CI [0.47, 1.25], BF = 161.94. For everything else the review reports low-to-very-low quality evidence; ~80% of included experiments were rated high risk of bias (insufficient randomisation reporting, missing data, absence of valid control groups). Twomey & Kroneisen (2021, QJEP) pooled 13 RCTs, mostly university settings: g = 0.65 [0.45, 0.85], I² = 45.5%, robust to publication-bias adjustment — again overwhelmingly list-recall outcomes. Material: laboratory word lists. Retention interval: immediate in the pooled estimate. I could not read either full text (both hosts blocked), so I could not extract a recognition-specific or paired-associate-specific subgroup estimate — but neither abstract reports one, which is itself informative.
findings.implication: Do not build a memory-palace feature, and do not order content on the assumption that players recall items in sequence. The one thing MoL is proven to do — put N items back in order — is a capability 看不懂 never asks for. Reallocate that design budget to the component-breakdown and confusable-pair panels (findings below), which are evidenced for the task the app actually runs.

sources.citation: Ondřej, J. et al. (2025). The method of loci in the context of psychological research: A systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Psychology, 116(4), 930–986. doi:10.1111/bjop.12799
Twomey, C., & Kroneisen, M. (2021). The effectiveness of the loci method as a mnemonic device: Meta-analysis. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 74(8). doi:10.1177/1747021821993457

findings.claim: Roediger's classic head-to-head shows mnemonics buy you ORDER, not quantity — the loci/peg advantage is largest under a strict positional scoring criterion and much smaller for unordered recall. This is the wrong currency for sign reading.
findings.detail: Roediger (1980, JEP: Human Learning & Memory 6(5), 558–567), N = 150 undergraduates, four mnemonics (imagery, link, peg, loci) vs control, 20-word lists. All mnemonic groups beat control on unordered recall, but the largest differences appeared under strict positional scoring, with peg and loci best; the stated conclusion is that mnemonic devices have greater effects on the ordering of recall than on the number of words recalled. Lab word lists; immediate test. Full text (Washington University repository PDF) was blocked; details from the indexed abstract and record.
findings.implication: Kill any instinct to make the game a 'chain' or 'journey' through a set of signs. Items should be independently addressable and independently scheduled — a random-access item pool, not an ordered route. Concretely: item selection at deal time should be free to draw any item from the category, with no adjacency constraint.

sources.citation: Roediger, H. L. (1980). The effectiveness of four mnemonics in ordering recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 6(5), 558–567.

findings._topic: Mnemonics and spatial memory for 看不懂 — method of loci, keyword method, Chinese-character mnemonic systems, gesture/embodiment, and the distinctiveness family (survival, picture superiority, bizarreness, production) — evaluated specifically against the task the app trains: four-option recognition of a written Chinese form seen on a real object.

findings.claim: The deepest reason mnemonics are aimed at the wrong direction here: recognition is driven primarily by ITEM-SPECIFIC processing, whereas the method of loci (and story/link mnemonics generally) supply RELATIONAL processing. The dissociation is one of the better-replicated principles in memory research.
findings.detail: Hunt & Einstein's relational vs item-specific framework: free recall benefits when BOTH relational and item-specific information are encoded; recognition is affected primarily by item-specific processing, and orienting tasks that elicit item-specific processing beat those eliciting relational processing on recognition. A memory palace is a relational/organisational device — it links items to each other via a route. Four-option multiple choice on a written form is a recognition test that additionally requires discriminating the target from three lures, which is an item-specific, form-level demand. Lab word-list literature; the framework is textbook-level and heavily cited, but I could not read the primary Hunt & Einstein (1981, JVLVB) paper (host blocked).
findings.implication: Design the resolution screen around item-specific difference, not narrative linkage. For 出口 vs 入口 the payload should be the ONE discriminating feature rendered large and isolated (the 出 vs 入 glyph, stroke-diffed), not a story that ties both into a scene. Rule of thumb for content authoring: every resolution card must name a feature that is TRUE OF THIS ITEM AND FALSE OF ITS PAIRED LURE.

sources.citation: Hunt, R. R., & Einstein, G. O. (1981). Relational and item-specific information in memory. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 20(5), 497–514.
Hunt, R. R., & Worthen, J. B. (eds.) Distinctiveness and Memory. Oxford University Press.

findings.claim: The spatial scaffold is probably not the active ingredient of the method of loci at all. Navigation knowledge and spatial ability barely predict MoL success; the method behaves like a peg system that happens to use places.
findings.detail: Caplan, Legge, Cheng & Madan (2019, QJEP). Participants trained on three virtual environments deliberately varying in navigational structure (an apartment, an open field, a radial-arm maze) and used each as the basis for MoL on five 11-word lists. Conclusion as stated: navigation-relevant knowledge and ability were not major determinants of success in verbal memory, even among participants verified to be complying with the strategy; imagined navigation is unlikely to be directly responsible for effectiveness; MoL may be best viewed as a variant of peg methods. Legge et al. (2012, Acta Psychologica 141:380–390, N = 142, ten 11-word lists) similarly found spatial familiarity dispensable — a five-minute virtual environment worked as well as a lifelong familiar one.
findings.implication: Strip 'spatial memory' from the design rationale entirely. In particular, do NOT justify rendering items as physical objects (station plate, shelf-edge label) on spatial-memory grounds — that justification is unsupported. There is a good reason to render them as physical objects, but it is perceptual/transfer-appropriate (see the typeface-variability and outshining findings), and framing it correctly changes what you build: you need VARIED real substrates, not a consistent navigable 'place'.

sources.citation: Caplan, J. B., Legge, E. L. G., Cheng, B., & Madan, C. R. (2019). Effectiveness of the method of loci is only minimally related to factors that should influence imagined navigation. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 72(10). doi:10.1177/1747021819858041

Legge, E. L. G., Madan, C. R., Ng, E. T., & Caplan, J. B. (2012). Building a memory palace in minutes: Equivalent memory performance using virtual versus conventional environments with the Method of Loci. Acta Psychologica, 141(3), 380–390.

findings.claim: On the specific question you asked — does the spatial scaffold survive being on a screen — yes, it does. Virtual memory palaces match conventional ones, and the operative component is explicit binding of an item to a location. But this is demonstrated for free recall of words and 3D objects, never for recognition of an orthographic form.
findings.detail: Legge et al. (2012): N = 142, a briefly-studied (≈5 min) virtual apartment/school/warehouse worked as well as a highly familiar real environment, across ten 11-word lists. Reggente, Essoe & Rissman (2020, Journal of Cognitive Enhancement, doi:10.1007/s41465-019-00141-8): N = 60 (30 experimental / 30 control) in VR, 15 3D objects at 20 s each; the group able to CLICK each object to lock it into place recalled 28% more objects than the group without that affordance, and spatial memory for objects/landmarks correlated strongly with verbal recall strength. Outcome measure throughout: free recall. No recognition-memory outcome reported in either abstract.
findings.implication: If a memory-palace mode is ever built, a screen is not the obstacle — but it is still the wrong tool, because every demonstration is free recall. Concretely: do not spend engineering on a 3D/spatial layer. If you want the one transferable lesson from Reggente, it is that an explicit, deliberate BINDING ACTION at encoding is what pays. The app's cheap analogue is the bet: forcing a commitment before the item is revealed is an explicit act, not passive viewing. Keep the bet mandatory and before reveal.

sources.citation: Reggente, N., Essoe, J. K.-Y., Baek, H. Y., & Rissman, J. (2020). The Method of Loci in Virtual Reality: Explicit binding of objects to spatial contexts enhances subsequent memory recall. Journal of Cognitive Enhancement, 4, 12–30.
Legge, E. L. G., Madan, C. R., Ng, E. T., & Caplan, J. B. (2012). Acta Psychologica, 141(3), 380–390.

findings.claim: The construction cost of the method of loci is 30 minutes a day for six weeks before the benefit appears. That is roughly 20 hours of pure overhead, and the payoff is durable free recall of word lists.
findings.detail: Dresler et al. (2017, Neuron 93:1227–1235): N = 51 mnemonics-naive men (24 ± 3.0 yrs) randomised to 6 weeks daily ~30-min online MoL training, working-memory training, or no training, plus 23 of the world's top memory athletes. Trained novices went from ~26/72 words recalled to ~62/72 after ~40 days of daily 30-min sessions; recall probed at 20 min and 24 h, retested at 4 months with a fresh 72-word list, and performance remained high. Wagner et al. (2021, Science Advances 7:eabc7606) reports the same cohort's fMRI story plus 'durable, longer-lasting memories' at 4 months. This is the single strongest MoL result in existence, and it is 72 unrelated words in free recall after 20 hours of training.
findings.implication: The cost is categorically incompatible with a co-located party game whose session is minutes long and whose players are Dutch and English adults preparing for a trip. Do not ship any training arm, tutorial, or onboarding that asks the player to construct or rehearse loci. Budget onboarding at under 60 seconds total and spend it on the bet mechanic and the scaffolding ladder instead.

sources.citation: Dresler, M. et al. (2017). Mnemonic training reshapes brain networks to support superior memory. Neuron, 93(5), 1227–1235. doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2017.02.003
Wagner, I. C. et al. (2021). Durable memories and efficient neural coding through mnemonic training using the method of loci. Science Advances, 7(10), eabc7606.

findings.claim: Mnemonic training does not reliably transfer to untrained paired-associate tasks — which is what vocabulary is. Transfer of strategy training to non-trained associative tasks is explicitly described in the literature as a rare finding.
findings.detail: Sandberg, Boraxbekk, Zogaj & Nyberg (2021, J Gerontol B 76(4):681–691), N = 359 adults across the lifespan, MoL delivered in a smartphone app. The study explicitly measured transfer via three paired-associate cued-recall tests — face/name, face/occupation, scene/object. The abstract-level material I could reach reports usage, training gains and age moderation but does not report a positive transfer result; I could not read the results section (Oxford Academic and PMC both blocked), so I am recording this as 'transfer was tested and is not headlined', not as a confirmed null. Separately, a 2023 J Cognitive Enhancement paper on associative mnemonic training describes near transfer to non-trained associative tasks as 'a rare finding in strategy training research', which is the field's own characterisation of the base rate.
findings.implication: Do not build a 'mnemonic gym' side mode on the theory that general memory training will lift sign reading. Train the target task directly. Architecturally this means the scheduler should track per-item recognition state (item id → last seen, last outcome, scaffolding level at which it was answered), not a per-player 'memory skill' score, because there is no evidence a general score would predict anything.

findings.claim: The founding citation for the memory palace — Bower (1970) — is a narrative article in a general-interest science magazine, not a controlled trial. It should be cited as history, not as evidence.
findings.detail: Bower, G. H. (1970). Analysis of a mnemonic device. American Scientist, 58, 496–510. American Scientist is a general-science magazine, not a peer-reviewed experimental journal. The article surveys anecdotal and experimental evidence for loci, peg, rhyme, analytic substitution and keyword systems. I could not access the text (all hosting domains blocked) and could extract no design, N, or effect size from it. Nearly every popular claim about memory palaces traces back through this paper.
findings.implication: Content/comms discipline: never cite Bower 1970 in the app's own copy, marketing, or design documentation as evidence that memory palaces work. If a 'why this works' page ships, cite Ondřej et al. 2025 and Twomey & Kroneisen 2021 with their actual scope (immediate serial recall) stated.

sources.citation: Bower, G. H. (1970). Analysis of a mnemonic device. American Scientist, 58(5), 496–510.

findings.claim: The keyword method's retention-interval story is the opposite of the folklore: it wins at immediate cued recall and LOSES at delay. Keyword learners forgot roughly twice as many items as rote learners at a two-day delay.
findings.detail: Wang & Thomas, across a programme of studies (incl. Thomas & Wang, 'Learning by the keyword mnemonic: Looking for long-term benefits', and Bulletin of the Psychonomic Society work on long-term retention under intentional learning). Reported pattern: on delayed cued recall at 2 days, keyword learners had forgotten almost twice the number of items as participants who rehearsed the same material by rote; the keyword advantage is confined to immediate cued recall and reverses after a delay. Keyword self-generation did not attenuate the forgetting; providing PICTURES of the keyword and the translation referent during study did improve long-term retention. Materials: foreign vocabulary paired associates, i.e. genuine L2 material, not nonsense syllables — which makes this more damning, not less. Retention intervals: immediate, 2 days, 1 week.
findings.implication: Do not make an invented keyword story the primary encoding for any item. If the app ships mnemonic flavour text at resolution, treat it as engagement decoration and schedule the item as if it had NO mnemonic support — i.e. do not lengthen the interval to the second exposure because 'they got a good story'. Concretely: item difficulty/interval should be computed from the player's actual recognition outcome at reveal, never from whether a mnemonic was displayed.

sources.citation: Thomas, M. H., & Wang, A. Y. (1996). Learning by the keyword mnemonic: Looking for long-term benefits. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 2(4), 330–342.

findings.claim: This has been tested on Chinese characters specifically, and the answer is the same: imagery-based mnemonics gave no advantage over rote beyond the immediate test — in no instance across two experiments.
findings.detail: Wang, A. Y., & Thomas, M. H. (1992). The effect of imagery-based mnemonics on the long-term retention of Chinese characters. Language Learning, 42(3), 359–376. Two experiments, 2×2 between-subjects factorial (learning condition: mnemonic vs rote × time: immediate vs delayed), cued recall of English translations of Chinese characters. Study 1 held total exposure time constant, tested immediately and at 2 days. Study 2 INCREASED rote exposure time so that immediate performance was matched, and extended the delay to one week. Stated conclusion: in no instance was there any indication that imagery-based mnemonics conferred an advantage beyond the immediate test of recall. This is the single most directly on-point study for 看不懂's content strategy and it is a null-to-negative result. Caveat: the outcome was cued recall of MEANING from the character, not four-option recognition, and the retention ceiling is 1 week.
findings.implication: Do not ship a Heisig-style or Mandarin-Blueprint-style invented story per character as the app's teaching payload. Ship instead: (a) the true component decomposition, (b) the paired confusable, (c) repeated spaced exposure. If you want a one-line memorable gloss for flavour, cap it at one line and derive it from the actual components (出 = a foot leaving an enclosure) rather than inventing a scene with props and actors.

findings.claim: With experienced foreign-language learners, rote rehearsal OUTPERFORMED the keyword method outright. With inexperienced learners the two were equal on accuracy, but keyword learners were SLOWER to retrieve.
findings.detail: van Hell, J. G., & Mahn, A. C. (1997). Keyword mnemonics versus rote rehearsal. Language Learning, 47(3), 507–546. Experiment 1: 36 experienced Dutch learners of foreign languages, naive to Spanish. Experiment 2: 40 Americans, inexperienced FL learners, learning Dutch words. Concreteness of the novel words and keyword quality (meaningfully related vs semantically unrelated keyword) were manipulated. Results as reported: in experienced FL learners, rote learners' performance exceeded keyword learners'; in inexperienced learners, rote and keyword recalled the same proportion of words but keyword learners had LONGER RETRIEVAL TIMES. Keyword imagery did not impede abstract-word learning; meaningfully related keywords were better cues than unrelated ones. Note this cohort is a close match to 看不懂's audience: Dutch adults who already speak a second language.
findings.implication: Two things. (1) Your Dutch and English-speaking adult audience is, by definition, experienced FL learners — the subgroup for whom keyword was WORSE than rote. Weight the content strategy accordingly. (2) Latency matters: reading a station sign is a two-second task, and a mnemonic that adds a retrieval hop is a real cost. Instrument response time on every answer, surface it in the UI (a per-item speed indicator on the resolution card), and use a latency threshold — not just correctness — to decide whether an item has been learned and can be retired to a long interval.

sources.citation: van Hell, J. G., & Mahn, A. C. (1997). Keyword mnemonics versus rote rehearsal: Learning concrete and abstract foreign words by experienced and inexperienced learners. Language Learning, 47(3), 507–546.

findings.claim: The keyword method structurally cannot attach to a Chinese character read cold, because the keyword is a PHONOLOGICAL bridge and the character's written form does not give you its sound. For reading, keyword adds a hop rather than removing one.
findings.detail: The keyword method is defined as a two-stage procedure: (1) form a stable acoustic link between the unfamiliar L2 word and a familiar L1 word that sounds like a salient part of it; (2) encode an interactive image between that keyword and the meaning (Pressley, Levin & Delaney, 1982, Review of Educational Research 52(1), 61–91). Stage 1 requires access to the L2 word's phonology. In Chinese the visual-to-phonological mapping is 'rather arbitrary and depends on learning and experience', unlike alphabetic systems; orthography plays the dominant role in Chinese word recognition and phonology a weaker, more limited one. Phonetic components exist in the large majority of compound characters but are unreliable and are of no use to a learner who does not already know the component's reading. So a keyword can only be hung off the PINYIN, which the reader of a sign does not have. I could not read Pressley et al. 1982 (host blocked); its scope statement — that the method has been investigated most extensively for recall of definitions from vocabulary words, 'particularly for immediate recall' — is from the indexed record.
findings.implication: This is a direct argument for the bet ladder you already have. The highest-scaffolding rung (pinyin shown) is the ONLY rung on which keyword-style phonological mnemonics are even applicable; the no-pinyin rungs are pure orthography-to-meaning. Therefore: attach any sound-based mnemonic content ONLY to the pinyin-shown presentation, and make the no-pinyin rungs' resolution card purely form-based (components + confusable). Do not show the same mnemonic text at every rung — it is meaningless at the top rung.

sources.citation: Pressley, M., Levin, J. R., & Delaney, H. D. (1982). The mnemonic keyword method. Review of Educational Research, 52(1), 61–91.
Cheng, Y. Different phonographic L1 effects in processing L2 Chinese (dissertation, U. Mississippi) — on arbitrariness of Chinese visual-phonological mapping and phonogram statistics.

findings.claim: Where the keyword method does help, the benefit is RECEPTIVE (L2 form → L1 meaning) — which is the app's direction — but it does not extend to production, and combining keyword with retrieval practice benefits the receptive side only.
findings.detail: Recent work on combining the keyword mnemonic with retrieval practice in L2 vocabulary reports significant benefits 'but only for the receptive aspect'. The wider retrieval-direction literature is consistent: backward translation (L2→L1) preferentially builds meaning recall; forward translation (L1→L2) preferentially builds form recall; treatment direction determines which knowledge type you get. Practically: recognising 出口 on a plate is receptive meaning recall, so the app is on the favourable side of the keyword literature — but 'favourable side' here means 'the side where keyword sometimes helps at short delay', not 'the side where it survives a week'.
findings.implication: Do not add a production mode (type the character, write the character, produce the pinyin from the meaning). It trains a different knowledge type, costs session time, and none of the mnemonic evidence supports it for this goal. Every item in the schema should have exactly one tested direction: rendered_form → meaning. Store the item without a production field so the temptation never arises.

sources.citation: The facilitative effect of the keyword mnemonic on L2 vocabulary retrieval practice. (2024). Acta Psychologica / ScienceDirect S240584402401243X.
Studying the effect of retrieval direction during reading on productive and receptive knowledge of vocabulary.

findings.claim: If any mnemonic ships, it must be AUTHORED, not player-generated, and it must include the picture. Provided keywords beat self-generated ones for weaker learners, and provided pictures — not self-generation — are what rescued long-term retention in the keyword literature.
findings.detail: Two convergent strands. (a) Keyword-generation method matters: for students with academic difficulties, learning improved more when keywords were PROVIDED than when learners created them; the efficiency of the keyword method relative to self-generation increases when students are given pictures. Countervailing evidence exists that self-generation avoids coder mismatch, and one study found a peer-generated-keyword group best for high-vividness words — so this is genuinely mixed. (b) From the Wang/Thomas programme: keyword self-generation did NOT attenuate long-term forgetting, whereas provision of pictures of the keyword and translation referent during study DID improve long-term retention. Keyword mnemonics work for high-image-vividness words and not for low-vividness ones.
findings.implication: Never ask the table to invent mnemonics — it is slow, it is uneven in quality, and the one manipulation that fixed long-term forgetting was a supplied picture, not learner effort. Concretely: mnemonic content is authored, ships in the item bundle, and always pairs text with an image. And apply the vividness filter at authoring time: only items with a concrete, depictable referent (出口, 麻辣, 公斤) get mnemonic treatment; abstract or functional items get component breakdown only.

sources.citation: The importance of the keyword-generation method in keyword mnemonics. Experimental Psychology, 51(2), 125–. doi:10.1027/1618-3169.51.2.125
Presentation of keywords by means of interactive drawings. The Spanish Journal of Psychology.

findings.claim: The best controlled test of story-mnemonics vs form-focused instruction for Chinese characters found that ALL strategies were equally effective for READING. The mnemonic advantage appeared only on WRITING, and only for visually similar pairs.
findings.detail: Chang, L.-Y., Tang, Y.-Y., Lee, C.-Y., & Chen, H.-C. (2022). Frontiers in Psychology 13:783898. N = 66 non-beginning learners of Chinese, randomly assigned; each learned ten characters via three strategies differing in how much they promote interrelated attention to form and meaning: (1) Stroke Sequence — form only; (2) Key-images — form + meaning, visual code; (3) Pithy Formulas with Key-images — form + meaning, visual + verbal code. Crossed with whether characters were presented in visually SIMILAR pairs or DISSIMILAR pairs, plus testing time. Reported outcome: all strategies were effective for reading; learners' subjective experience ratings favoured the two form+meaning strategies; the advantage of Pithy Formulas + Key-images over Key-images alone was on WRITING and was specific to participants who learned with visually similar pairs. I could not read the results section (Frontiers blocked), so I do not have the effect sizes or the exact retention intervals.
findings.implication: This is the finding that should settle the app's content spec. 看不懂 tests reading only. On reading, elaborate mnemonics bought nothing over plain form instruction — but learners LIKED them more. So: use mnemonic flavour as motivational garnish (one line, at resolution, after the answer), and spend the actual instructional real estate on the component breakdown and the confusable pair. Budget: component breakdown gets the largest block on the resolution card; mnemonic line gets one line or is omitted.

sources.citation: Chang, L.-Y., Tang, Y.-Y., Lee, C.-Y., & Chen, H.-C. (2022). The effect of visual mnemonics and the presentation of character pairs on learning visually similar characters for Chinese-as-second-language learners. Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 783898. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2022.783898

findings.claim: The deliberately paired confusable is the best-evidenced element in the whole design. Simultaneous paired presentation of visually similar characters improved discrimination — and colour-coding the differing parts made things WORSE.
findings.detail: Li, Shi & Wang (2025). Languages 10(10), 260. N = 183 non-tonal native speakers with no prior Chinese character experience. 2×2×2 design: colour coding (with/without) × presentation style (single vs PAIRED characters) × stroke similarity (identical strokes, e.g. 人/入, vs one extra stroke, e.g. 日/白). Results: (1) characters differing by an added stroke were learned more easily than identical-stroke pairs; (2) SIMULTANEOUS character presentation enhanced discrimination of subtle stroke differences; (3) COLOUR CODING SLOWED REACTION TIMES, interpreted as visual overload. Stated pedagogical conclusion: support paired character presentation, caution against excessive visual enhancement. Reinforced by Chang et al. 2022, where the mnemonic advantage existed only in the visually-similar-pair condition.
findings.implication: Keep the paired confusable — 入口 beside 出口, 公斤 beside 斤, 麻 beside 辣 — and show BOTH MEMBERS SIMULTANEOUSLY, side by side at the same size, not sequentially and not one-then-reveal. Do NOT colour-code the differing stroke or the differing component: it costs recognition speed, which is the thing you care about. Use position, size and whitespace to draw the contrast instead. Also: prioritise identical-stroke and near-identical pairs in the confusable table, because those are where the discrimination help is most needed (the added-stroke pairs are learned easily anyway).

sources.citation: Li, Shi & Wang (2025). Learning Chinese characters of visual similarity: The effects of presentation style and color coding. Languages, 10(10), 260. doi:10.3390/languages10100260
Chang, L.-Y. et al. (2022). Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 783898.

findings.claim: Component/radical instruction — the 出 + 口 breakdown — has direct experimental support with adult CFL learners, including transfer to inferring the meaning of NEW characters in running text.
findings.detail: (a) A radical-derived character e-learning intervention with N = 129 Chinese-American CFL learners (69 experimental, 60 comparison), nonequivalent pretest–posttest quasi-experiment, three-week course covering orthographic knowledge and at least seven phonetic/semantic radicals plus their derivative characters per week. Experimental group significantly better on radical recognition, semantic radical awareness and phonetic radical awareness. (b) Teaching semantic radicals facilitated inferring NEW character meanings during sentence reading for nonnative Chinese speakers — i.e. genuine generalisation beyond taught items. (c) Shen (2005, System 33(1)), N = 95 non-native learners across levels, 30 strategies identified; factor analysis showed orthographic-knowledge-based cognitive strategies are the most commonly used. Design quality is quasi-experimental, not RCT, so this is moderate rather than strong.
findings.implication: The component breakdown at resolution is not decoration — it is the app's transfer engine, and it is the only element with evidence for generalising to unseen items. Make it structural: store each item with an explicit component tree (character → components → each component's semantic gloss and, where genuine, its phonetic role), and render the tree, not a flat string. Then exploit it: after a player has seen 口 in 出口, the scheduler should be able to surface 入口, 门口, 窗口 as related items. That component index is a first-class piece of the data model, not a display field.

sources.citation: Using a radical-derived character e-learning platform to increase learner knowledge of Chinese characters. Language Learning & Technology / ScholarSpace, U. Hawaii.
Teaching semantic radicals facilitates inferring new character meaning in sentence reading for nonnative Chinese speakers.
Shen, H. H. (2005). An investigation of Chinese-character learning strategies among non-native speakers of Chinese. System, 33(1), 49–68.

findings.claim: Heisig, Mandarin Blueprint and Outlier have no controlled evidence behind them. Chineasy has been criticised on record by Chinese-language faculty as not teaching reading at all. The comparison you asked about — story mnemonics vs component-structure instruction — is essentially untested outside Chang et al. 2022.
findings.detail: Heisig's Remembering the Kanji / Remembering the Hanzi teaches 'primitives' plus invented 'imaginative memory' scenes; I found no peer-reviewed empirical evaluation of it, and the review literature on character teaching methods does not report one. Outlier Linguistics is founded by Ash Henson, who holds a PhD from NTNU and has published peer-reviewed work on Chinese paleography and phonology — so its ETYMOLOGY is scholarly, but there is no published evaluation of the course's learning outcomes. Mandarin Blueprint returned no academic literature at all. Chineasy: Language Log (Victor Mair's blog, hosted at UPenn LDC — not peer review, but authored by Sinologists) carries sustained criticism, including a Chinese Language Program director quoted saying 'what she is teaching is not reading' and that at best it enables recognition of a few pictographic characters in isolation. Zhang's review (Chinese as a Second Language, 2024) synthesised 22 articles from 1952 onward and identified six categories among 39 instructional methods — and flags the lack of curriculum-level comparative research as a weakness.
findings.implication: Ship etymologically defensible component glosses and explicitly do NOT adopt a proprietary story system's vocabulary of props, actors and scenes. Practical content rule: each component gloss must be checkable against a scholarly source (Outlier's dictionary or equivalent paleographic reference) and must be marked in the data as either 'etymological' or 'mnemonic-only' where the historical story is unhelpful or unknown. Surfacing that distinction is cheap and protects you from the Chineasy failure mode of teaching charming falsehoods.

sources.citation: Mair, V. et al. Chineasy? Not / Chineasy2. Language Log, University of Pennsylvania LDC.
Zhang (2024). Effective character teaching methods for L1 English Chinese-as-a-foreign-language learners: A review of empirical research. Chinese as a Second Language. doi:10.1075/csl.00033.zha
Remembering the Kanji and Remembering the Hanzi (overview of the Heisig method).

findings.claim: Rendering the same character across MULTIPLE real typefaces is the strongest evidence-backed reason to render items as physical objects — and it is a perceptual-generalisation argument, not a spatial-memory one. Single-typeface training was faster on the trained typeface but MUCH slower on novel ones.
findings.detail: High variability orthographic training: learning words in a logographic script through training with multiple typefaces. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (2025), doi:10.3758/s13423-025-02646-0. N = 190 participants with no previous Chinese experience learned 24 Chinese characters, each seen six times and associated with an English definition, in either a Single-Typeface group (one of three Chinese typefaces) or a Variable-Typeface group (all three). Results: single-typeface training produced faster responses for the FAMILIAR typeface but much slower responses for NOVEL typefaces; variable-typeface training produced better generalisation to novel typefaces. This is a recognition-speed outcome on Chinese characters in adult naive learners — an unusually good match to 看不懂's task. Sits inside the broader perceptual-variability literature (Psychon Bull Rev, doi:10.3758/s13423-020-01780-1).
findings.implication: Make typeface variability a hard content requirement, not an art-direction preference. Every item that appears more than once must be rendered in a DIFFERENT face/substrate on its later exposures: a Song/Ming serif station plate, a bold sans shopfront fascia, a condensed grotesque shelf label, a handwritten-brush menu board, a stencilled hazard board. Store a typeface/substrate id per exposure on the item's schedule and forbid repeating the same one. This is also the reason to resist a single beautiful house style for all cards — the aesthetic consistency would actively cost you real-world transfer.

sources.citation: High variability orthographic training: Learning words in a logographic script through training with multiple typefaces. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (2025). doi:10.3758/s13423-025-02646-0
Perceptual variability: Implications for learning and generalization. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (2020). doi:10.3758/s13423-020-01780-1

findings.claim: Do not justify the physical-object rendering as environmental context reinstatement. Context-dependent memory effects are reliable overall but are reduced or eliminated for RECOGNITION tests — the outshining effect.
findings.detail: Smith, S. M., & Vela, E. (2001). Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 203–220. Across studies environmental context effects were reliable, BUT: use of noncontextual cues during learning (overshadowing) and at test (outshining), and mental reinstatement of context at test, all reduce the effect. Smith, Glenberg & Bjork (1978) found context manipulations did not affect recognition memory even where they reliably affected recall — because a recognition test supplies abundant noncontextual cues (the item itself, plus the other tested items) that outshine the ambient context. Lab word lists.
findings.implication: Keep the physical-object rendering — but change the reason it exists in the design doc, because the reason determines the spec. It is NOT there to reinstate a context at retrieval; it is there so the trained percept matches the real percept (transfer-appropriate processing) and so the player sees the character under real-world typographic and layout variability. Spec consequence: fidelity of the SIGN (typeface, stroke weight, spacing, contrast, plate/enamel/backlit substrate, grime) matters a great deal; fidelity of the SURROUNDING SCENE (the street, the crowd, the station hall) buys nothing measurable and can be dropped. Spend art budget on the plate, not the platform.

findings.claim: The enactment effect is enormous (g = 1.23) and, unusually, is NOT moderated by test format or retention interval — but it applies to enactable action phrases, not to written characters on a sign. The transfer to this app is close to zero.
findings.detail: Roberts, B. R. T. et al. (2022). The enactment effect: A systematic review and meta-analysis of behavioral, neuroimaging, and patient studies. Psychological Bulletin. 145 behavioural studies, 7 neuroimaging, 31 neurological patient studies (183 total). Average enactment effect across behavioural studies g = 1.23 (large). Reported moderator picture: study design and comparison task reliably influence effect size, whereas TEST FORMAT, learning-instruction type, RETENTION INTERVAL, and presence of objects at encoding likely do not. That last clause is the good news — the effect isn't a recall-only or short-delay artefact. The bad news is the material: the paradigm is subject-performed tasks, i.e. verb-object phrases like 'lift the pen' that can be physically performed. 出口 is not an action phrase. There is no study applying enactment to recognition of an orthographic form.
findings.implication: Do not build a gesture or charades layer on the strength of the enactment literature. The effect size is real and the material mismatch is total. If you want a physical action at the table, the defensible one is speech (see the production effect), not pantomime — speech is the one motor act that can be performed on an arbitrary written form.

sources.citation: Roberts, B. R. T., MacLeod, C. M., & Fernandes, M. A. (2022). The enactment effect: A systematic review and meta-analysis of behavioral, neuroimaging, and patient studies. Psychological Bulletin.

findings.claim: Gesture research in L2 vocabulary is about learning SPOKEN words, not written forms — and even within it, watching a gesture works as well as performing one. So the phone-at-a-table format does not lose much, because there was nothing here for reading in the first place.
findings.detail: Oppici, L., Mathias, B., Narciss, S., & Proske, A. (2023). Benefits of enacting and observing gestures on foreign language vocabulary learning: A systematic review and meta-analysis. 7 studies, N = 309. Finding: gesture OBSERVATION was just as effective as self-enactment across free recall, cued L2 recognition, and cued L1 recognition — with large dispersion of true effect across studies. Underlying primary work: Macedonia (2014, Mind Brain & Education), classroom training with 36 words, audio-visual vs gestural condition, retention measured out to 14 months; Kelly, McDevitt & Esch (2009, Language & Cognitive Processes 24(2), 313–334), novel Japanese verbs, memory tests at 5 minutes, 2 days and 1 week, with the largest gains where gesture conveyed redundant imagistic information to speech. Every one of these trains an auditory word form. Related: observing gesture at learning enhances later phonological and semantic processing of L2 words (N400 study, Brain & Language 2023); pitch gestures improved English speakers' discrimination of Mandarin tone meanings, while semantic gestures HINDERED tone identification. Nothing addresses recognition of a character.
findings.implication: Be honest in the design doc: gesture does not transfer to this format, because the app trains reading and gesture research trains listening. The one narrowly usable crumb — observation equals enactment — means that IF you ever add a spoken/tone layer, a short looping animation the whole table watches is as good as making people move, at a fraction of the UX cost. Do not add gesture to the reading loop. And note the tone warning: if you ever animate a tone contour, use a pitch-shaped motion, never a meaning-miming one.

findings.claim: The one embodied manipulation with a plausible orthographic payoff is HANDWRITING, and it dissociates cleanly: handwriting strengthens orthography→meaning mapping and orthographic recognition; typing strengthens orthography→sound mapping.
findings.detail: A synthetic review of typing vs handwriting in Chinese-language learning (Journal of Second Language Writing / ScienceDirect S0883035521000100) reports three findings: typing enhances phonology recognition and phonological-semantic mapping; handwriting enhances orthography recognition and orthographic-semantic mapping; learner preference favours typing but writing-performance effects are mixed. A more recent study (Shi, Foreign Language Annals 2026) reports the typing group outperforming on character recognition and dictation while the handwriting group scored higher on MEANING recognition — consistent with handwriting building orthography→meaning links. Mechanistic account: handwriting builds long-term motor memory that strengthens the orthographic representation and helps extract the visuospatial information character recognition needs. Caveat: none of this is established for finger-tracing on a phone as opposed to pen on paper, and none of it is established under the time pressure of a party game.
findings.implication: If you want one embodied element, make it an OPTIONAL single-component finger trace on the resolution screen — trace 口 once, not the whole character, and never in the timed round. Gate it behind a per-player setting and never make it block the table. Given the app's target is meaning recognition (orthography→meaning), handwriting is directionally the right motor act; but treat it as an unproven experiment in this form factor and instrument it (A/B on items where trace was and was not performed) rather than assuming it works.

sources.citation: Comparison studies of typing and handwriting in Chinese language learning: A synthetic review. Journal of Second Language Writing (2021). ScienceDirect S0883035521000100
Shi (2026). Orthography-sound vs. orthography-meaning mapping in Chinese character learning: Evidence on typing and handwriting. Foreign Language Annals. doi:10.1111/flan.70053

findings.claim: The production effect is the one distinctiveness effect that survives everything the app does to it: it works in PURE-LIST between-subject designs, it works specifically for RECOGNITION, it is LARGER in a second language than a first, and it endures to at least a week. Making every player say the item aloud is the highest-value cheap intervention available.
findings.detail: Fawcett (2013, Acta Psychologica, meta-analysis): production improves recognition when varied BETWEEN subjects, g = 0.37 — small-to-moderate but 'surprisingly consistent'. The design detail matters enormously: for FREE RECALL a within-list effect is consistently found and a between-lists effect consistently ABSENT, whereas for RECOGNITION a between-list (pure-list) effect is reliably present, though smaller than the within-list effect. Updated meta-analysis: Fawcett, J. M. et al. (2023), Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology, 77(1), 35–44 — 'Production improves recognition and reduces intrusions in between-subject designs'. Durability: production benefits endure and improve memory for text, with a production effect observed at a 1-week retention interval (MacLeod et al./Ozubko et al.). L2 amplification: bilinguals showed a pronounced production effect in both languages but GREATER in the second language than the first, attributed to increased phonological encoding/effort when reading aloud in L2. Social boundary: Forrin & MacLeod (2018, Memory 26(4)) found a gradient — speaking > hearing oneself (recorded) > hearing someone else speak > reading silently; self-production gave a substantially larger benefit than hearing another person say the word.
findings.implication: Build it in, and build it so EVERY player produces. Concretely: at reveal, the resolution card shows the item plus its pinyin and prompts the WHOLE TABLE to say it aloud in unison (a 2-3 second beat with a visible countdown), not one nominated reader. Forrin & MacLeod is explicit that listening to someone else delivers far less than speaking. This is the rare case where the pure-list problem does not bite — the recognition between-subject effect survives everything being produced — so you do not need to make production intermittent. Two corollaries: (1) the effect is bigger in L2, so this is a better bet here than in a native-language quiz; (2) production aids memory, not comprehension, which is exactly the app's goal.

sources.citation: Fawcett, J. M. (2013). The production effect benefits performance in between-subject designs: A meta-analysis. Acta Psychologica, 142(1), 1–5.

Fawcett, J. M., Baldwin, M. M., Whitridge, J. W., et al. (2023). Production improves recognition and reduces intrusions in between-subject designs: An updated meta-analysis. Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology, 77(1), 35–44.

Production benefits on encoding are modulated by language experience: Less experience may help. (2024).

findings.claim: The bizarreness effect will not work in this app, and trying to use it will backfire. It requires mixed lists and within-subject manipulation, it is absent in cued recall, and it is unreliable in recognition. If everything is bizarre, nothing is.
findings.detail: Convergent boundary conditions from the McDaniel & Worthen programme: bizarreness effects in free recall emerge only if bizarreness is manipulated WITHIN subjects using MIXED lists, and disappear under between-subjects designs with pure lists. Across a set of experiments, NONE produced a bizarreness effect for CUED RECALL, although bizarre noun pairs beat common pairs for free recall in two of them. Effects depend on (a) within- vs between-list manipulation, (b) intervening learning, (c) test task (recall vs recognition). McDaniel & Einstein (1995, 'The bizarreness effect: It's not surprising, it's complex') is the canonical statement of the complexity. More recent work finds visual imagery plays little role (concurrent visuospatial distractor tasks don't disturb it), further undercutting the 'make a vivid weird picture' folk theory.
findings.implication: Do not adopt a house style of weird mnemonics. If a bizarre gloss ships for an item, it must be the exception in its deck — bizarreness is a relative-distinctiveness effect and is destroyed by uniformity. Practical authoring rule: cap bizarre/absurd mnemonic glosses at a small minority of items in any category deck (roughly one in five or fewer), and reserve them for the items with the worst measured accuracy. Add a per-item 'tone' field so the authoring pipeline can enforce the ratio rather than leaving it to whoever writes the deck.

sources.citation: McDaniel, M. A., & Einstein, G. O. (1995). The bizarreness effect: It's not surprising, it's complex. Journal of Experimental Psychology: LMC.
Worthen, J. B. et al. The bizarreness effect: Evidence for the critical influence of retrieval processes. Memory & Cognition. doi:10.3758/s13421-013-0335-4

findings.claim: Survival processing is the wrong tool twice over: the advantage does not appear in cued recall, it is weaker or reversed for recognition of pictures, and it fails outright in a second language.
findings.detail: Scofield, Buchanan & Kostic (2018, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review) meta-analysis, bias-corrected: ηp² ≈ .06–.09 between-subjects, .15–.18 within-subjects — so the raw effect is real but modest, and the analysis used p-curve, p-uniform, trim-and-fill, PET-PEESE and selection models. But the boundary conditions are fatal here. (1) Test type: 'the survival effect has been well established in explicit free recall and recognition tests, but has not been evident in implicit memory tests or in cued explicit tests' — Nairne & Pandeirada's account is that restricting retrieval to a specific cue removes the benefit of multiple retrieval routes. (2) Pictures: in a 2023 Memory study, survival participants recalled more verbal labels, but correct RECOGNITION was highest in the pleasantness condition and LOWEST in the survival condition. (3) Language: 'Surviving in a second language' (Cognition and Emotion, 2021, 35(2)) replicated the survival processing effect in L1 but NOT in L2; Kazanas, Wilck & Altarriba (2022) similarly found the advantage in Spanish (L1) but not English (L2) in 127 Spanish–English bilinguals. Note one contrary datapoint: a Memory & Cognition (2019) paired-associate study did report a survival advantage across three cued-recall tasks — which cuts against (1) and makes this genuinely contested rather than settled.
findings.implication: Do not frame the game around survival/danger scenarios ('you must find the exit before the train leaves'). It is the wrong test type, the wrong stimulus type, and — decisively — it fails in L2, which is the only language state your players are in. Frame item categories functionally instead (station, menu, supermarket, hazard). The hazard board deck is fine to ship because hazard signs are genuinely useful content, not because danger framing helps memory.

findings.claim: Picture superiority is robust in recognition — which is the app's test — but recent work says the mechanism is DISTINCTIVENESS, not dual coding. A deck of forty visually interchangeable station plates would destroy the effect it is meant to exploit.
findings.detail: Picture superiority: items studied as pictures are better remembered than items studied as words, even when targets are presented as words at test — a robust adult recognition finding, developmentally graded (absent at 7 years, largest in young adults). Dual coding (Paivio) is the traditional explanation. But Higdon, Neath, Surprenant & Ensor (2025, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, doi:10.1177/17470218241235520) report that the picture memory advantage was ELIMINATED in both recognition and free recall when distinctiveness was reduced for images and heightened for words — 'Distinctiveness, not dual coding, explains the picture-superiority effect'. A 2026 study finds picture superiority persists in aphantasia, further undercutting the imagery-based account.
findings.implication: The photorealistic sign rendering earns its keep only if items are visually DISTINCT FROM EACH OTHER within a session. Design consequence: within any one deal/category, no two items may share the same substrate template. Vary plate vs fascia vs shelf label vs menu board vs hazard board across consecutive items, and vary colour ground, mounting and wear. Concretely, add a 'substrate template id' to the item schema and have the dealer enforce non-repetition within a round. A uniform card design — the obvious, tidy choice — is the one that costs you the effect.

sources.citation: Higdon, K. F., Neath, I., Surprenant, A. M., & Ensor, T. M. (2025). Distinctiveness, not dual coding, explains the picture-superiority effect. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology. doi:10.1177/17470218241235520

findings.claim: Direct answer to the brief's recurring question: of every mnemonic technique reviewed, exactly one — the production effect — is evidenced for RECOGNITION under the design constraints this app actually operates under. Everything else is evidenced for recall of a meaning or a sound, or for ordered recall.
findings.detail: Summary of the direction audit. Method of loci: ordered/serial recall of lists; recognition never tested; relational not item-specific, so theoretically misaligned. Keyword method: cued recall of MEANING from a word, receptive direction, wins immediately and loses at delay; requires phonology the reader of a character does not have. Story mnemonics for characters: no advantage over form-focused instruction on READING (Chang et al. 2022); advantage confined to writing. Enactment/gesture: recall and recognition of spoken/enactable material; no orthographic-recognition evidence. Survival processing: free recall, fails in cued recall and in L2. Bizarreness: free recall only, mixed lists only, absent in cued recall, unreliable in recognition. Picture superiority: recognition yes, but conditional on within-set distinctiveness. Production effect: recognition specifically, in pure-list between-subject designs, larger in L2, durable to a week. Paired-confusable presentation and component instruction are not 'mnemonics' at all — they are form instruction — and they are the two best-evidenced elements for this task.
findings.implication: Write the ranked intervention list into the design doc in this order and build in this order: (1) simultaneous paired-confusable presentation, (2) component/radical decomposition stored as a tree and used for related-item surfacing, (3) whole-table say-it-aloud at reveal, (4) typeface and substrate variability across repeat exposures, (5) within-round substrate distinctiveness. Then, and only then, optional single-component finger trace. Explicitly deprioritise: memory palaces, keyword stories, invented character narratives, gesture, survival framing, uniformly bizarre mnemonics, colour-coded components.

sources.citation: Synthesis across the sources cited in the preceding findings; anchor citations: Ondřej et al. 2025 (Br J Psychol); Chang et al. 2022 (Front Psychol); Fawcett et al. 2023 (Can J Exp Psychol); Li, Shi & Wang 2025 (Languages); Wang & Thomas 1992 (Language Learning).

findings.claim: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve replicates, but the real shape is shallower and lumpier than the folklore version, and it has a discontinuity around 24 hours rather than a smooth exponential decay.
findings.detail: Murre & Dros (2015), PLOS ONE 10(7):e0120644. Design: N = 1 (single dedicated subject, ~70 hours of learning), method of savings, nonsense-syllable lists, relearned at 20 min, 1 h, 9 h, 1 day, 2 days, 6 days, 31 days. Reported savings at 1 day ≈ 31.7% (31.22 repetitions to learn initially vs 21.33 to relearn); most intervals cluster around the 20% savings range; the 31-day point is 4.1% raw and 13.7% after the authors' correction. The authors explicitly conclude the curve 'is not completely smooth but most probably shows a jump upwards starting at the 24 hour data point' — i.e. retention at 24 h is no worse (and by some measures better) than at 9 h, which is where the overnight sleep interval falls. Retention intervals: 20 min to 31 days. Caveat: single subject, nonsense syllables, savings (relearning) rather than free recall — the weakest possible material for generalising to meaningful L2 signs.

sources.citation: Murre, J. M. J., & Dros, J. (2015). Replication and Analysis of Ebbinghaus' Forgetting Curve. PLOS ONE, 10(7), e0120644.

findings.implication: Do not hard-code a smooth exponential decay into the scheduler, and do not model the first 24 hours as continuous. Architecture: store per-item review events with wall-clock timestamps AND a boolean 'crossed a sleep period', and treat the first overnight boundary as a scheduling landmark rather than just N hours elapsed. An item reviewed at 22:00 and again at 08:00 the next morning has crossed a consolidation boundary; the same 10-hour gap inside one waking day has not.

findings.claim: The widely repeated 'you forget 50% within an hour and 70% within 24 hours' figure is folklore when applied to meaningful language material.
findings.detail: The percentages circulating in learning-app marketing are read off Ebbinghaus's 1885 nonsense-syllable savings curve for a single subject and then reported as retention of meaningful content. The modern replication (Murre & Dros 2015) is a savings measure on nonsense syllables by one highly practised participant. Bahrick's real-L2 data (below) show a completely different function for actual vocabulary. There is no meta-analytic forgetting function for L2 vocabulary that resembles the folklore curve.

sources.citation: Murre, J. M. J., & Dros, J. (2015). PLOS ONE, 10(7), e0120644.
Bahrick, H. P. (1984). Semantic memory content in permastore: Fifty years of memory for Spanish learned in school. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 113(1), 1–29.

findings.implication: Content/copy: never show the user a forgetting-curve graphic or a 'you'll forget 70% by tomorrow' nudge. It is not true for this material and it makes the product's factual claims indefensible. If you want a retention visual, drive it from the user's own observed relearning cost, not from a textbook curve.
