findings.claim: Real L2 vocabulary does not decay exponentially to zero. It declines for roughly 3–6 years after instruction stops and then plateaus for decades ('permastore'), and the size of the plateau is set by the amount of original training, not by rehearsal during the interval.
findings.detail: Bahrick (1984), JEP: General 113(1). N = 733 individuals, retention intervals up to 50 years after school Spanish, tested on reading comprehension, recall and recognition vocabulary, and grammar, with a questionnaire capturing original training level, grades, and rehearsal. Curves decline exponentially for the first 3–6 years, then remain essentially unchanged for up to 30 years before a final decline. Retention across the whole 50 years was predicted by level of original training; the great majority of participants rehearsed so little that no significant rehearsal effect was detectable. Cross-sectional rather than longitudinal, which is the main limitation.

sources.citation: Bahrick, H. P. (1984). Semantic memory content in permastore: Fifty years of memory for Spanish learned in school. JEP: General, 113(1), 1–29.

findings.implication: Architecture: make the primary mastery variable 'number of distinct days on which this item was successfully retrieved', not a recency-weighted decay score. The design target is to push each sign over a training threshold and then stop paying attention to it, rather than to keep topping up against a daily decay. Practically: retire an item from the active deck after ~4 successful cross-day retrievals and re-audit it once at a long interval (months), rather than keeping it in a perpetual SRS rotation.

findings.claim: Savings on relearning is the right progress metric, and long inter-session gaps buy disproportionate long-term retention at almost no extra acquisition cost.
findings.detail: Bahrick & Phelps (1987), JEP:LMC. 50 Spanish–English word pairs, adult learners, relearning sessions spaced at 30 days vs 1 day vs all massed on one day, same number of sessions. Eight-year retention test: 15% recalled (30-day spacing) vs 8% (1-day spacing) vs less for massed. The 30-day group needed only slightly longer acquisition sessions to reach the same criterion. Bahrick, Bahrick, Bahrick & Bahrick (1993, Psychological Science) extended this to 13 relearning sessions over 5 years with 14/28/56-day intervals, with the longest interval best. Design: quasi-experimental longitudinal, small samples, but the retention interval (8 years, 5 years) is unmatched anywhere else in this literature.

sources.citation: Bahrick, H. P., & Phelps, E. (1987). Retention of Spanish vocabulary over 8 years. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 13(2), 344–349.
Bahrick, H. P., Bahrick, L. E., Bahrick, A. S., & Bahrick, P. E. (1993). Maintenance of foreign language vocabulary and the spacing effect. Psychological Science, 4(5), 316–321.

findings.implication: Architecture + UX: record trials-to-correct per item per session and surface the delta ('this sign took you three looks last month; one today'). That is a savings measure and it is both the scientifically correct progress signal and a better game stat than a streak. Schedule the third and fourth encounters of a sign weeks apart, not days — a 30-day gap is not a failure state to be punished by the scheduler.

findings.claim: The optimal gap between two study episodes is roughly 10–20% of the target retention interval for horizons of weeks, dropping to ~5% for a one-year horizon.
findings.detail: Cepeda, Vul, Rohrer, Wixted & Pashler (2008), Psychological Science 19(11), 1095–1102. N > 1350, factual material, inter-study gaps up to 3.5 months, final test delays up to 1 year. At any given retention interval, increasing the inter-study gap first increases and then gradually reduces final performance; the optimum gap is ~20% of the test delay at delays of a few weeks, falling to ~5% at one year. Material is trivia facts, not L2 words, and the tests are lab tests — but the sample is large and the retention intervals are long.

sources.citation: Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095–1102.

findings.implication: UX + architecture: ask for the trip date at onboarding and derive intervals from it rather than from a generic SRS curve. For a 6-week horizon, the second exposure of a sign should land ~4–8 days out; for a 1-week horizon, ~1 day out; for a 6-month horizon, ~2–4 weeks out. Store target_date on the user profile and compute gap = 0.15 × (target_date − now), clamped to at least one overnight.

findings.claim: Word learning proceeds in two stages with different neural substrates: fast hippocampal familiarisation within a session, then slow neocortical lexicalisation offline. 'Recognised in session' and 'integrated into the lexicon' are different states.
findings.detail: Davis & Gaskell (2009), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 364(1536), 3773–3800 — a theoretical review synthesising complementary learning systems (McClelland, McNaughton & O'Reilly 1995) with behavioural and neuroimaging word-learning data. Rapid initial acquisition is supported by medial temporal/hippocampal learning; slower neocortical learning is achieved by offline consolidation of already-acquired information. The operational marker of the second stage is the new word's ability to compete with phonological/orthographic neighbours during recognition — a marker that is absent immediately after learning even when explicit recall is already good. This is a framework, not a single effect; its strength is that it makes a falsifiable dissociation (recall vs competition) that has repeatedly been observed.

sources.citation: Davis, M. H., & Gaskell, M. G. (2009). A complementary systems account of word learning: neural and behavioural evidence. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 364(1536), 3773–3800.

findings.implication: Architecture: give each item a two-bit state, not a single score — 'acquired' (correct within the introducing session) and 'consolidated' (correct on a retrieval that happened after at least one intervening night). Gate downstream behaviour on the second bit: an item may not be used as a distractor for a confusable sibling, and may not be counted toward a mastery total, until it is consolidated. This single rule implements most of the interference verdict below.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Sleep reliably benefits novel word learning relative to an equivalent period of wakefulness, with a moderate meta-analytic effect.
findings.detail: Schimke, Angwin, Cheng & Copland (2021), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. Systematic review and meta-analysis: 25 unique studies, 42 outcome measures, 29 between-group comparisons, N = 1,396 healthy adults. Omnibus effect g = 0.50 favouring sleep over wake; recall g = 0.57; recognition g = 0.52. Materials are almost entirely novel/pseudo words in laboratory paradigms with retention intervals of 12–24 hours (some up to a week). This is a meta-analysis of lab word learning, NOT of classroom L2 acquisition over weeks — no equivalent meta-analysis exists for the latter.

sources.citation: Schimke, E. A. E., Angwin, A. J., Cheng, B. B. Y., & Copland, D. A. (2021). The effect of sleep on novel word learning in healthy adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 28, 1811–1838.

findings.implication: UX: it is defensible to default the daily reminder to the evening and to end a session with 'that's a good place to stop for tonight'. It is not defensible to make claims about how much more the user will remember. Keep the nudge soft and unquantified.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Lexical integration specifically — the new word starting to compete with existing similar words — requires sleep rather than merely elapsed time.
findings.detail: Dumay & Gaskell (2007), Psychological Science 18(1), 35–39. Novel spoken words overlapping real words (e.g. 'cathedruke'/'cathedral'). Words learned at 8 p.m. produced no competition effect immediately, produced competition after a 12-hour interval containing sleep, and continued at 24 h. Words learned at 8 a.m. produced no effect immediately and none after 12 hours of wakefulness, but did after 24 h — i.e. after a night had intervened. Small-N lab study on spoken pseudowords; the crossover design is what makes it persuasive, because it dissociates sleep from elapsed time. It does not dissociate sleep from circadian phase completely (see the failure/boundary finding below).

sources.citation: Dumay, N., & Gaskell, M. G. (2007). Sleep-associated changes in the mental representation of spoken words. Psychological Science, 18(1), 35–39.

findings.implication: UX: the second exposure of any newly introduced sign should be scheduled to fall on a different calendar day, never later the same evening. Concretely, the scheduler's minimum inter-exposure gap should be 'next session after the next sleep', not 'N hours'. This matters most for exactly the items the app cares about — the ones with confusable neighbours, since competition is the thing that consolidates late.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Overnight integration tracks sleep spindle activity, and it dissociates from raw recall gains — the two things consolidate on different schedules.
findings.detail: Tamminen, Payne, Stickgold, Wamsley & Gaskell (2010), Journal of Neuroscience 30(43), 14356–14360. Participants learned novel spoken words phonologically overlapping familiar words; polysomnography during the retention night. Spindle activity was associated with overnight lexical integration (competition with the existing neighbour) but NOT with gains in recall rate or in recognition speed of the novel words themselves. Single study, correlational EEG, small N.

sources.citation: Tamminen, J., Payne, J. D., Stickgold, R., Wamsley, E. J., & Gaskell, M. G. (2010). Sleep spindle activity is associated with the integration of new memories and existing knowledge. Journal of Neuroscience, 30(43), 14356–14360.

findings.implication: Architecture: measure two separate things per item and do not average them. (1) recall accuracy — did the player pick the right meaning; (2) discrimination — did the player pick the right meaning when the confusable sibling was among the four options. These improve at different rates, so a single mastery scalar will systematically overrate items whose siblings are not yet in the option pool.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: The sleep-consolidation effect for words is not universal: it fails for contextually learned words, and the classic 12-hour sleep/wake design confounds sleep with circadian phase.
findings.detail: Schimke, Copland, Gomersall & Angwin (2024), Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology — 'To sleep or not to sleep? No effect of sleep on contextual word learning in younger adults': a null result from the same group that produced the positive meta-analysis. Separately, the standard design (learn 8 p.m., test 8 a.m. vs learn 8 a.m., test 8 p.m.) confounds circadian phase with sleep at both encoding and test, so an apparent sleep benefit can partly be a time-of-day effect on retrieval. Studies that hold circadian phase constant (nocturnal sleep vs nocturnal wake) generally still find a sleep benefit, so the effect survives, but at reduced and less certain magnitude.

sources.citation: Schimke, E. A. E., Copland, D. A., Gomersall, S. R., & Angwin, A. J. (2024). To sleep or not to sleep? No effect of sleep on contextual word learning in younger adults. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 77(3).

findings.implication: UX: do not build a feature whose value depends on the size of the sleep effect (no 'sleep score', no 'consolidation window' countdown, no bedtime-gated content). The only robust consequence to bake in is ordinal: exposures should straddle nights. Everything beyond that is over-fitting to a contested effect.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Consolidation of newly learned word forms generalises across modality — a form learned in one modality competes in the other after ~24 hours — which makes the overnight rule plausibly applicable to written/orthographic forms, though never tested on a logographic L2.
findings.detail: Bakker, Takashima, van Hell, Janzen & McQueen (2014), Journal of Memory and Language — auditorily acquired novel words entered into competition in both the spoken and the written modality after a 24-hour consolidation period. Separately, 'Bedding down new words: Sleep promotes the emergence of lexical competition in visual word recognition' (Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2017) shows the sleep-dependent competition effect directly in visual word recognition. All of this is alphabetic; I found no study running the consolidation/competition paradigm on Chinese characters for L2 learners.

sources.citation: Bakker, I., Takashima, A., van Hell, J. G., Janzen, G., & McQueen, J. M. (2014). Competition from unseen or unheard novel words: Lexical consolidation across modalities. Journal of Memory and Language, 73, 116–130.
Bedding down new words: Sleep promotes the emergence of lexical competition in visual word recognition. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (2017), 24, 625–631.

findings.implication: Architecture: apply the same overnight-gating rule to character/sign items as you would to spoken words — there is no reason from the evidence to treat orthographic items as exempt. But flag this in your own docs as an extrapolation, not a demonstrated result for Chinese.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Targeted memory reactivation (playing vocabulary cues during sleep) works in controlled lab conditions but is fragile, timing-sensitive, and can actively harm memory in unsupervised home use.
findings.detail: Schreiner & Rasch (2015) showed re-exposure to Dutch–German vocabulary cues during sleep improved recall in the lab. Göldi & Rasch (2019) found no effect when cueing began 30 minutes after sleep onset. Göldi & Rasch / Schechtman-line at-home work (npj Science of Learning 2019) found unsupervised multi-night home TMR benefited overall scores only in the subgroup reporting no sleep disturbance from the cues; participants reporting general sleep disturbance showed no benefit, and a third subgroup showed impaired memory. Salfi et al. (2025), Journal of Sleep Research, attempted closed-loop at-home TMR. Effects depend on cue timing relative to sleep stage, which a phone app cannot reliably determine.

sources.citation: Effects of targeted memory reactivation during sleep at home depend on sleep disturbances and habituation. npj Science of Learning (2019), 4, 5.
Schreiner, T., & Rasch, B. (2017). The beneficial role of memory reactivation for language learning during sleep: A review. Brain and Language, 167, 94–105.
Salfi, F., et al. (2025). Promoting vocabulary learning during sleep at home using closed-loop targeted memory reactivation. Journal of Sleep Research.

findings.implication: Explicit negative recommendation. Do not ship a sleep-audio / overnight-playback feature. The evidence shows a subgroup gets worse, the app cannot detect sleep stage well enough to time cues, and the downside (disturbed sleep) falls on the user. Remove it from the backlog rather than parking it.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: 'Study just before bed and you retain 20–30% more' is folklore. The best adolescent study found afternoon training beat evening training at 24 hours and found no difference at 7 days.
findings.detail: The circulating figure traces to popular write-ups and to Duolingo usage-data journalism, not to a retention experiment. Against it: Holz et al. (2012), PLOS ONE 7(7):e40963, 'The timing of learning before night-time sleep differentially affects declarative and procedural long-term memory consolidation in adolescents' — subjects trained in the afternoon showed significantly higher retention of word pairs at 24 hours than subjects trained in the evening, and the difference had disappeared at 7 days. Gais et al. (2006, Learning & Memory) do report enhanced vocabulary consolidation when sleep directly follows acquisition, so the literature is genuinely mixed; the point is that no defensible number exists, and at the 1-week horizon the timing effect washes out.

sources.citation: Holz, J., et al. (2012). The timing of learning before night-time sleep differentially affects declarative and procedural long-term memory consolidation in adolescents. PLOS ONE, 7(7), e40963.
Gais, S., Lucas, B., & Born, J. (2006). Sleep after learning aids memory recall. Learning & Memory, 13(3), 259–262.

findings.implication: UX/content: do not build a 'best time to play' feature or make time-of-day claims in copy. Let the user choose their reminder time. The only timing rule the evidence supports is about the gap between sessions (must cross a night), not about the hour of the session.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Classical interference theory predicts maximum damage exactly for the app's confusable structure: shared cue, different and antagonistic responses.
findings.detail: Osgood's (1949) transfer surface plots transfer as a joint function of stimulus and response similarity: interference is greatest when cues are the same and targets differ, and rises sharply to maximum as responses approach antagonism (antonyms). Higa (1963), Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior — six paired-associate lists varying the relationship among response members (antonyms, coordinates, strong free associates, shared-associate words, connotatively+denotatively similar, connotatively similar only); intralist similarity increased learning difficulty, with antonyms among the worst. 入口/出口 is literally the antonym-plus-shared-cue case (shared 口, shared 'doorway' semantic frame, opposed meanings); 麻/辣 is a coordinate pair in the same semantic field. These are the two worst cells of the classical surface. Caveat: all of this is nonsense-syllable and English-word paired-associate work with short retention intervals, and it describes learning two new associations, not discriminating one new item from an established one.

sources.citation: Higa, M. (1963). Interference effects of intralist word relationships in verbal learning. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 2(2), 170–175.
Osgood, C. E. (1949). The similarity paradox in human learning: A resolution. Psychological Review, 56(3), 132–143. (transfer surface; summary at Kihlstrom, Berkeley)

findings.implication: Content: the pairing rule must be asymmetric in time. Never enter both members of a confusable pair into the deck as new items in the same session — that is the Osgood worst case. Introduce one, and make the sibling eligible only once the first is consolidated (see the two-bit item state above).
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: The L2 'don't teach semantically related words together' advice is genuinely contested, not settled: roughly six studies negative, two conditionally negative, four positive out of thirteen.
findings.detail: The tally is reported in Nakata & Suzuki (2019, SSLA): negative — Erten & Tekin (2008), Finkbeiner & Nicol, Tinkham (1993, 1997), Waring (1997), Wilcox & Medina; conditionally negative — Higa, Papathanasiou (2009); positive — Hashemi & Gowdasiaei (2005), Hoshino, Schneider et al. The prescriptive advice is Nation (2000), TESOL Journal 9(2), 6–10, 'Learning vocabulary in lexical sets: dangers and guidelines', which lumps together antonyms (rich–poor), near-synonyms (fast–rapid), synforms (soup–soap), free associates (bed–sleep) and lexical sets (vegetables, clothes) as prone to confusion. Note that Nation's list mixes formal confusables (synforms) with semantic ones, and the evidence below suggests those two behave very differently. Most studies in the tally use pseudowords or short retention intervals and differ substantially in how vocabulary knowledge was measured, which is the standard explanation for the inconsistency.

sources.citation: Nation, P. (2000). Learning vocabulary in lexical sets: dangers and guidelines. TESOL Journal, 9(2), 6–10.
Tinkham, T. (1997). The effects of semantic and thematic clustering on the learning of second language vocabulary. Second Language Research, 13(2), 138–163.
Nakata, T., & Suzuki, Y. (2019). Effects of massing and spacing on the learning of semantically related and unrelated words. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 41(2), 287–311.

findings.implication: Content: do not adopt 'never show related words together' as a design principle on Nation's authority — the evidence does not carry it. But do split Nation's list: treat formal confusables (synforms) as the real hazard and semantic sets as a much weaker one. The app's pairs are mostly both at once, which is why they need care.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: The best-controlled test says the damage comes from FORM similarity, not semantic relatedness. When physical similarity is controlled out, semantically related sets are no harder than unrelated ones.
findings.detail: Ishii (2015), Language Teaching Research 19(6), 712–722, 'Semantic connection or visual connection: Investigating the true source of confusion'. Compared learning of (1) unrelated, (2) semantically related sets controlled for physical relatedness, and (3) physically related sets. Physically related sets were harder to learn and produced more confusion errors at a 20-minute test. Semantically related sets, once form-controlled, were neither harder nor easier than unrelated sets, though some confusion appeared during learning. The author's conclusion is that the repeatedly reported semantic-clustering penalty may be partly an artefact of visual features shared between the referents of semantically similar words. Major caveat: the retention interval is 20 minutes, which is not evidence about learning a language.

sources.citation: Ishii, T. (2015). Semantic connection or visual connection: Investigating the true source of confusion. Language Teaching Research, 19(6), 712–722.

findings.implication: Content: audit your confusable pairs and label each as form-confusable, meaning-confusable, or both. 入口/出口 = both (share 口, opposed meanings). 公斤/斤 = form-confusable (containment). 麻/辣 = meaning-confusable but visually distinct. The three deserve different treatment: the form-confusable ones need staged introduction; 麻/辣 can be shown together freely. Store a `confusion_type` enum on the pair, not a single `confusable` boolean.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Form similarity always increases confusion errors in L2 vocabulary learning; semantic relatedness helps or hurts depending on test direction, and it helps in the comprehension direction the app actually uses.
findings.detail: Kemp (2021), Language Learning 71(3). L1-English speakers learned a fixed set of L2 vocabulary on lists formed by crossing semantic relatedness (unrelated vs related) with L2 orthographic form similarity (not similar vs similar); half studied L2→L1 and half L1→L2, with both directions tested immediately and at delay. Results: form similarity usually hurt accuracy and ALWAYS increased confusion errors. Semantic relatedness in the absence of form similarity improved accuracy when the first test taken was L2→L1, and tended to hurt when the first test was L1→L2, sometimes increasing confusion errors. Best long-term performance came from L1→L2 study direction combined with the favourable semantic and form conditions. A clean factorial with a delayed test — one of the better-designed studies in this literature.

sources.citation: Kemp, J. (2021). Second language vocabulary acquisition: The effects of semantic relatedness, form similarity, and translation direction. Language Learning, 71(3), 730–770.

findings.implication: This is load-bearing for 看不懂 and it is good news for the concept. The game is sign→meaning, i.e. L2→L1 comprehension, which is exactly the direction in which semantic relatedness among options helps rather than hurts. Design rule: keep the task recognition/comprehension (which meaning is this sign?) and resist any temptation to add a production mode (write/type the Chinese for 'exit'), which is the L1→L2 direction where relatedness turns harmful. UI: it is fine for the four options to be semantically related meanings; it is not fine for the four options to be four orthographically near-identical signs during a sign's first appearance.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Semantic relatedness can leave overall accuracy unchanged while still installing confusion — the harm shows up in error type, not in score.
findings.detail: Nakata & Suzuki (2019), SSLA 41(2), 287–311. N = 133 Japanese university students, 48 real English–Japanese word pairs, half semantically related and half unrelated, studied massed vs spaced, tested at 1 week. Result: no significant difference between semantically related and unrelated items in posttest SCORES, but semantically related items produced significantly more interference errors (choosing/producing the sibling's meaning). Spacing beat massing 1.6× at 1 week (massed 16.87%, spaced 26.62%), and spacing benefited unrelated items more than related ones. Real L2 words, real learners, 1-week retention interval — the strongest material/interval combination in the semantic-clustering literature.

sources.citation: Nakata, T., & Suzuki, Y. (2019). Effects of massing and spacing on the learning of semantically related and unrelated words. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 41(2), 287–311.

findings.implication: Architecture — the single most actionable item in this sweep. Log WHICH distractor was chosen on every wrong answer, not just correct/incorrect. Maintain a per-user confusion matrix keyed on (target_item, chosen_item). Drive scheduling from it: when confusion[入口][出口] exceeds a threshold, stop presenting them as co-options and re-teach the distinguishing component in isolation. A plain accuracy score will show a healthy curve while the pair is quietly being cross-associated.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Interleaving similar exemplars beats blocking for inductive category learning, and learners reliably believe the opposite.
findings.detail: Kornell & Bjork (2008), Psychological Science 19(6), 585–592. Six paintings by each of 12 artists, artist name shown below; half the artists blocked, half interleaved. On classifying PREVIOUSLY UNSEEN paintings by the same artists, interleaved 59% vs blocked 36%. Participants reported that they had learned better in the blocked condition — a straight metacognitive reversal. Birnbaum, Kornell, E. Bjork & R. Bjork (2013), Memory & Cognition 41, 392–402, decomposed the effect: the benefit comes from discrimination (juxtaposing exemplars of different categories) rather than from spacing per se. Lab, visual categories, tests within-session to short delay.

sources.citation: Kornell, N., & Bjork, R. A. (2008). Learning concepts and categories: Is spacing the 'enemy of induction'? Psychological Science, 19(6), 585–592.
Birnbaum, M. S., Kornell, N., Bjork, E. L., & Bjork, R. A. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41(3), 392–402.

findings.implication: UX: expect the confusable panel to feel unpleasant and expect players to rate it as making things harder. Do not remove it on the basis of self-report or a satisfaction metric; A/B it on delayed discrimination accuracy at ≥1 week instead. Also: test transfer, not repetition — the payoff of contrast is classifying a sign the player has not seen in that exact rendering, so the item bank must hold multiple physical renderings per sign.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Whether contrast helps depends on how similar the categories are: interleaving helps HIGH-similarity categories, blocking helps LOW-similarity ones. This reconciles the interference and discrimination traditions.
findings.detail: Carvalho & Goldstone (2014), Memory & Cognition 42, 481–495, 'Putting category learning in order: Category structure and temporal arrangement affect the benefit of interleaved over blocked study' — interleaved sequences improved classification of novel items for high-similarity categories, whereas blocked sequences improved it for low-similarity categories. Meagher, Carvalho, Goldstone & Nosofsky (2017), Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 24, 1987–1994, 'Organized simultaneous displays facilitate learning of complex natural science categories' — simultaneous displays during learning improved both acquisition and generalisation over purely sequential study, for rock categories with dispersed similarity structure. Lab category learning, short intervals, non-linguistic material.

sources.citation: Carvalho, P. F., & Goldstone, R. L. (2014). Putting category learning in order: Category structure and temporal arrangement affect the benefit of interleaved over blocked study. Memory & Cognition, 42(3), 481–495.

Meagher, B. J., Carvalho, P. F., Goldstone, R. L., & Nosofsky, R. M. (2017). Organized simultaneous displays facilitate learning of complex natural science categories. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 24(6), 1987–1994.

findings.implication: Content sequencing: interleave WITHIN a confusable family (入口 / 出口 / 进口 / 门口) once its members are individually consolidated, and block/space ACROSS unrelated families (don't mix station signage with supermarket weight labels in the same drill run). Architecture: give each item a `family_id`; the session builder should draw a block of unrelated families and interleave within the one family currently under discrimination training.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: The interleaving benefit reverses for word learning. Meta-analytically, blocking beats interleaving when the material is words.
findings.detail: Brunmair & Richter (2019), Psychological Bulletin 145(11), 1029–1052, 'Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators'. 59 studies, 238 effect sizes nested in 158 samples. Overall interleaving effect Hedges' g = 0.42. By material: paintings g = 0.67; mathematics g = 0.34; expository texts and tastes non-significant; WORDS g = −0.39, i.e. a reliable advantage for BLOCKING. The authors' conclusion is that interleaving fosters inductive learning but that setting and material type must be considered, specifically flagging texts and words as exceptions. This is the strongest single constraint on generalising the Kornell & Bjork result to vocabulary.

sources.citation: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin, 145(11), 1029–1052.

findings.implication: This is the hinge of the verdict, and it forces a split in the app. A 看不懂 item is two things at once: a VISUAL CATEGORY (the shape of 出 vs 入 — interleave and contrast, g ≈ +0.67 territory) and a WORD (the form→meaning mapping for 出口 — block and space, g ≈ −0.39 territory). Design accordingly: contrast the character forms freely, but never run the two form→meaning mappings as competing to-be-learned associations in the same acquisition session. Concretely — the component-breakdown panel may show 出 beside 入 from day one; the four answer options may not contain both 入口 and 出口 as candidate meanings until one of them is consolidated.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: For Chinese characters specifically, simultaneous paired presentation improves discrimination of subtle stroke differences in absolute beginners — and colour-coding the difference makes things worse.
findings.detail: Li, Shi & Wang (2025), Languages 10(10), 260, 'Learning Chinese Characters of Visual Similarity: The Effects of Presentation Style and Color Coding'. N = 183 native speakers of non-tonal languages with NO prior experience of Chinese characters. 2 × 2 × 2 design: colour coding (with vs without) × presentation style (single vs paired) × stroke similarity (identical strokes, e.g. 人/入, vs one extra stroke, e.g. 日/白). Results: (1) characters differing by an added stroke were learned more easily than identical-stroke pairs; (2) simultaneous character presentation ENHANCED discrimination of subtle stroke differences; (3) colour coding slowed reaction times, interpreted as visual overload. Authors' recommendation: use paired presentation, avoid excessive visual enhancement. Single recent study, beginners, short retention interval not established from the abstract.

sources.citation: Li, J., Shi, M., & Wang, X. (2025). Learning Chinese Characters of Visual Similarity: The Effects of Presentation Style and Color Coding. Languages, 10(10), 260.

findings.implication: UI, and it cuts against a design instinct: keep the side-by-side confusable panel, but do NOT colour-highlight the differing stroke or component. Render both characters in the same neutral ink at the same size, side by side, and let the visual system do the differencing. If you need to direct attention, use spatial arrangement (aligned, same baseline, same optical size) and a brief motion/reveal, not colour. Also: prioritise added-stroke pairs (日/白, 斤/斥) over identical-stroke pairs (人/入, 己/已) in early content — the latter are measurably harder.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Pairing visually similar Chinese characters only pays off if the distinguishing component is given meaning; a purely structural breakdown is not enough.
findings.detail: Chang, Tang, Lee & Chen (2022), Frontiers in Psychology 13:783898. N = 66 non-beginning CSL learners. Pretest–posttest equivalent-group design crossing learning strategy — Stroke Sequence (form only), Key-images (form+meaning, visual code), Pithy Formulas with Key-images (form+meaning, visual + verbal code) — with presentation of character pairs (visually similar vs dissimilar). Immediate and 1-week delayed posttests on reading and writing. Both form+meaning strategies beat Stroke Sequence for writing accuracy; crucially, the advantage of Pithy Formulas with Key-images over Key-images alone was SPECIFIC to participants who learned with visually similar pairs. All strategies worked for reading; learners preferred the form+meaning strategies.

sources.citation: Chang, L.-Y., Tang, Y.-Y., Lee, C.-Y., & Chen, H.-C. (2022). The effect of visual mnemonics and the presentation of character pairs on learning visually similar characters for Chinese-as-second-language learners. Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 783898.

findings.implication: Content: the component-breakdown panel must be semantic, not just decompositional. '出 + 口' is not sufficient. It must carry a short meaning-bearing formula — 出 = coming out (feet stepping out of an enclosure), 入 = going in (a wedge entering) — and that formula is what makes the side-by-side pairing productive rather than merely confusing. Budget authoring time for one written mnemonic formula per distinguishing component, and treat it as required content for any item that has a form-confusable sibling, not as optional flavour text.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Retrieving one member of a competing pair measurably suppresses the other — around 9 percentage points — and the effect depends on the competitor actually competing.
findings.detail: Murayama, Miyatsu, Buchli & Storm (2014), Psychological Bulletin 140(5), 1383–1409, 'Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: a meta-analytic review of retrieval-induced forgetting'. Average RIF effect ≈ 8.7%. The effect is competition-dependent: non-practised items (Rp−) are impaired only if they actually compete for retrieval access during practice, with larger RIF when competitors are stronger or more accessible. The meta-analysis supports inhibition as a contributor while concluding that non-inhibitory processes (strength-based competition, blocking) also contribute — the mechanism remains contested; the phenomenon does not. Lab word-list paradigms, mostly category–exemplar materials, retention intervals typically minutes to a day.

sources.citation: Murayama, K., Miyatsu, T., Buchli, D., & Storm, B. C. (2014). Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: A meta-analytic review of retrieval-induced forgetting. Psychological Bulletin, 140(5), 1383–1409.

findings.implication: Architecture: enforce pair-balanced testing. If a confusable family is in the active deck, every member must be tested within the same rotation window — a deck that repeatedly quizzes 出口 and never 入口 is actively degrading 入口 by roughly the RIF magnitude. Implement as a constraint in the session builder: when selecting item X, mark all members of X.family_id as due-soon rather than letting them drift.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Four-option multiple choice with genuinely competitive distractors is the format that AVOIDS retrieval-induced forgetting and instead strengthens the distractors — which converts the app's core mechanic into the intervention rather than the hazard.
findings.detail: Little, J. L., Bjork, E. L., Bjork, R. A., & Angello, G. (2012), Psychological Science 23(11), 1337–1344, 'Multiple-choice tests exonerated, at least of some charges: Fostering test-induced learning and avoiding test-induced forgetting'. Two experiments. Multiple-choice practice tests with competitive, plausible incorrect alternatives enhanced later cued-recall performance on questions about those ALTERNATIVES, apparently because test-takers spontaneously retrieve why the correct option is correct and why the others are not. Cued-recall practice produced retrieval-induced forgetting of related non-tested material; competitive multiple choice did not. See also Little & Bjork (2015), 'Optimizing multiple-choice tests as tools for learning', Memory & Cognition. Material is facts/prose, not L2 vocabulary; retention intervals are within-session to short delay. The mechanism depends entirely on the distractors being plausible enough to invite rejection reasoning.

sources.citation: Little, J. L., Bjork, E. L., Bjork, R. A., & Angello, G. (2012). Multiple-choice tests exonerated, at least of some charges: Fostering test-induced learning and avoiding test-induced forgetting. Psychological Science, 23(11), 1337–1344.
Little, J. L., & Bjork, E. L. (2015/2014). Optimizing multiple-choice tests as tools for learning. Memory & Cognition.

findings.implication: UI/UX, and this reframes the whole design question. The confusable belongs in the FOUR OPTIONS at test time, not only in a post-hoc panel. Distractor policy: every option must be a real, defensible candidate the player could argue for — pull them from the item's confusable family and from the same physical context (other things that appear on station plates). Ban random unrelated distractors: they forfeit the entire benefit and make the item a two-way guess. Architecture: distractor selection should be a function over the confusion graph, not a random sample of the deck.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Committing to an answer before seeing the correct one (the app's betting mechanic) is a generation/pretesting manipulation that helps item memory, but the evidence that it helps the form–meaning association is contested.
findings.detail: Potts & Shanks (2014), JEP: General — participants learning definitions of rare English words and Euskara nouns did better when they guessed (and almost always erred) before feedback than when they simply studied; errorful generation with immediate corrective feedback beat errorless reading. Seabrooke et al. (2019) failed to replicate using a cued-recall test, concluding that experiencing errors with semantically unrelated material improves memory for targets and cues in isolation but not for the ASSOCIATION between them. Burgess et al. (2023, Neuropsychological Rehabilitation) found errorful learning improved recognition memory for new vocabulary in a brain-injury population. Lab word lists, short intervals.

sources.citation: Potts, R., & Shanks, D. R. (2014). The benefit of generating errors during learning. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 143(2), 644–667. (and Seabrooke et al. 2019 replication failure, Journal of Memory and Language)
Burgess, et al. (2023). Errorful learning improves recognition memory for new vocabulary... Neuropsychological Rehabilitation.

findings.implication: UX: keep the bet — it is a commitment-before-feedback structure with defensible support and strong game value — but make the feedback immediate, unavoidable and adjacent to the committed answer. Do not batch feedback to end-of-round: the association-learning benefit is the contested part, and delayed feedback removes what support there is. Show the chosen option and the correct option in the same visual frame at resolution.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: For confusable contrasts, identification training with feedback beats same/different discrimination training, and learners fail to encode a confusable contrast into new items unless attention is explicitly directed to the critical difference during learning.
findings.detail: From the L2 speech-perception training literature, which is the most developed body of work on training confusable contrasts. Identification and discrimination training improve discrimination about equally, but identification training produces substantially greater gains in identification — attributed to the type and amount of feedback available in identification regimes. Separately, learners do not establish a phonological contrast between confusable sounds in newly learned words unless their attention is directed to the critical difference during word learning; form-focused training gives an initial benefit for learning confusable L2 words. Different modality (auditory) from the app, so this is an analogy, not a direct result.

sources.citation: Differential effects of identification and discrimination training tasks on L2 vowel identification and discrimination. Studies in Second Language Acquisition.
From meaning to sound: how word learning shapes non-native speech perception. (2025).

findings.implication: UX: keep the task as identification ('which of these four is 出口?' / 'what does this sign say?') and never add a same/different mode ('are these two signs the same word?'). And at resolution, the differing component must be explicitly named and attended to in words, not merely rendered adjacent — a silent side-by-side does not direct attention. One sentence: 'the difference is the top: 出 has the extra stroke pushing out.'
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: L1 retrieval interferes with L2 access, so the game's high-bet 'all options in Chinese, no pinyin' mode is defensible on interference grounds and not merely as a difficulty setting.
findings.detail: Levy, McVeigh, Marful & Anderson (2007), Psychological Science, 'Inhibiting your native language: The role of retrieval-induced forgetting during second-language acquisition' — naming pictures in L2 impaired subsequent recall of L1 translations, interpreted as domain-general inhibition. The converse has also been reported: in a Welsh word-learning study, participants showed significantly longer reaction times to items previously retrieved in L1, suggesting L1 retrieval perturbs L2 access during early L2 vocabulary acquisition. Small samples, reaction-time measures, short intervals.

sources.citation: Levy, B. J., McVeigh, N. D., Marful, A., & Anderson, M. C. (2007). Inhibiting your native language: The role of retrieval-induced forgetting during second-language acquisition. Psychological Science, 18(1), 29–34.
Retrieval induced forgetting and second language acquisition: Insights from a Welsh word-learning study.

findings.implication: UX/content: frame the highest bet tier (no pinyin, Chinese-only options) as the mode that trains reading rather than translation, and make it the default target state rather than an expert extra. Where possible, make the four options pictures or icons of the referent rather than Dutch/English words, so the player never routes through L1 at all — that removes the L1-retrieval interference entirely and matches the real-world task (see a sign, act).
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: The visual word form area is built by exposure to real written forms and recycles cortex weakly tuned to tools; reading expertise for a new script is a visual-statistical achievement, not a verbal one.
findings.detail: Dehaene-Lambertz, Monzalvo & Dehaene (2018), PLOS Biology — ten 6-year-olds scanned longitudinally 6–7 times with fMRI before and through the first year of school; voxels specific to written words and digits emerged at the VWFA location, encroaching on voxels initially weakly specialised for tools and adjacent to face-responsive cortex, while those voxels kept their original category selectivity and added a stronger word response. Literate/illiterate/ex-illiterate comparisons (Dehaene et al.; Nature Reviews Neuroscience 2015 review) show VWFA activation is the main correlate of reading ability, and that word recognition partly displaces face processing toward the right hemisphere. Children/adults, alphabetic scripts.

sources.citation: Dehaene-Lambertz, G., Monzalvo, K., & Dehaene, S. (2018). The emergence of the visual word form: Longitudinal evolution of category-specific ventral visual areas during reading acquisition. PLOS Biology, 16(3), e2004103.
Dehaene, S., Cohen, L., Morais, J., & Kolinsky, R. (2015). Illiterate to literate: behavioural and cerebral changes induced by reading acquisition. Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 16, 234–244.

findings.implication: Content: ship many physical renderings of the same sign — different fonts, materials, lighting, enamel plate vs LED vs hand-painted vs printed shelf label — rather than one canonical rendering per item. The design already renders signs as physical objects; the neuroscience says the VARIABILITY is the active ingredient, not the realism. Architecture: model an item as (sign_text → N renderings) and require at least 3 distinct renderings before an item can reach 'consolidated' state, so mastery is never certified on a single visual instance.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Chinese character reading recruits additional left middle frontal gyrus and bilateral/right ventral occipito-temporal cortex relative to alphabetic reading — usually attributed to analysis of the square, spatially configured character.
findings.detail: Wu, Ho & Chen (2012), NeuroImage 63(1), 381–391 — ALE meta-analysis of fMRI studies of Chinese orthographic, phonological and semantic processing; consolidates the finding of additional recruitment of left middle frontal gyrus and right fusiform gyrus for Chinese character processing relative to the alphabetic-derived universal reading network, with bilateral ventral occipito-temporal involvement for both phonological and semantic processing. Converges with Tan et al. (2005) meta-analysis of phonological processing in Chinese vs alphabetic words. Both are meta-analyses and agree on the anatomy; the FUNCTIONAL interpretation (LMFG as visuospatial/graphomotor addressing of the square configuration, vs as working-memory demand) is contested, and a later re-analysis explicitly reopens 'rethinking the function of brain regions for reading Chinese characters'.

sources.citation: Wu, C.-Y., Ho, M.-H. R., & Chen, S.-H. A. (2012). A meta-analysis of fMRI studies on Chinese orthographic, phonological, and semantic processing. NeuroImage, 63(1), 381–391.

Tan, L. H., Laird, A. R., Li, K., & Fox, P. T. (2005). Neuroanatomical correlates of phonological processing of Chinese characters and alphabetic words: A meta-analysis. Human Brain Mapping, 25(1), 83–91.

findings.implication: UI, with the interpretation caveat stated: the component breakdown should show WHERE components sit, not only WHICH they are. Render the breakdown as a spatial decomposition inside a square frame (left/right, top/bottom, enclosure) rather than as a linear list '出 + 口'. This is the one place the neuroimaging earns a UI change; do not over-read it beyond that.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Orthographic regularity in Chinese is acquired by statistical learning, in a fixed order — components first, then structure, then positional legality — and positional knowledge is implicit and hard to acquire.
findings.detail: Zhang et al. (2021), Language Awareness 30(3) — 213 CSL students in Hong Kong completed tasks measuring component knowledge, structural knowledge and position-regularity knowledge; the three developed non-synchronously, with component knowledge affecting position-regularity knowledge INDIRECTLY via structural knowledge. Knowledge of component positional constraints (what makes a string a legal character) is implicit and difficult to acquire. Native Chinese 5-year-olds are already sensitive to component distributional patterns. fMRI work shows left occipital cortex and VWFA respond more strongly at low positional consistency in pseudocharacters, i.e. implicit statistical learning of positional regularity.

sources.citation: How do Chinese as a second language (CSL) learners acquire orthographic knowledge: component, structure and position regularity. Language Awareness, 30(3), 2021.
Chinese children's statistical learning of orthographic regularities: Positional constraints and character structure.

findings.implication: Content ordering + architecture: tag every item with its components AND each component's position (left/right/top/bottom/enclosing). Order the content so that high-frequency components appear early and often across MANY different characters, and so that each component is seen in its legal position repeatedly before any item requires positional discrimination. Do not teach positional rules explicitly — the evidence says it is acquired implicitly from distributional exposure. Track per-user component×position exposure counts and use them to bias item selection, so the statistical learning actually gets the input it needs.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

findings.claim: Explicit semantic-radical instruction transfers to untaught characters, and the transfer was demonstrated using exactly a four-option contrastive format where options share one component and differ in the meaning-bearing one.
findings.detail: Nguyen, Zhang, Li, Wu & Cheng (2017), Frontiers in Psychology 8:1846. N = 54 Vietnamese undergraduates majoring in Chinese with ~1 year of study, two experimental groups receiving 'old-for-new' semantic radical teaching plus one control. Pre/post sentence cloze task in which participants chose the appropriate character from FOUR OPTIONS THAT SHARED THE SAME PHONETIC RADICAL BUT DIFFERED IN SEMANTIC RADICAL. Experimental groups improved significantly, control did not, and — the key result — the experimental groups transferred the strategy to infer meanings of unfamiliar characters containing semantic radicals that had NOT been taught. Small N, no long-delay posttest reported.

sources.citation: Nguyen, T. P., Zhang, J., Li, H., Wu, X., & Cheng, Y. (2017). Teaching semantic radicals facilitates inferring new character meaning in sentence reading for nonnative Chinese speakers. Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 1846.

findings.implication: Content, and it turns the interference problem into an asset. Construct at least one option-set generator that HOLDS ONE COMPONENT CONSTANT AND VARIES THE MEANING-BEARING COMPONENT (e.g. options all containing 口, or all containing 斤; or 麻/摩/磨 sharing 麻). This is the one confusable-pairing configuration with direct evidence of producing generalisable, transferable knowledge in CSL learners rather than item-specific memorisation. Ship it as a distinct card type — call it a component-contrast round — and reserve it for items already consolidated.
findings._topic: Consolidation, forgetting and interference between sessions — and whether 看不懂 should present confusable pairs (入口/出口, 公斤/斤, 麻/辣) side by side on resolution

added_by_critics.claim: Deep knowledge tracing does not reliably beat far simpler models, and for a cold-start PWA it is strictly worse. The published, deployed baseline for exactly this product shape is Half-Life Regression.
sources: Gervet, T., Koedinger, K., Schneider, J., & Mitchell, T. (2020). When is deep learning the best approach to knowledge tracing? Journal of Educational Data Mining, 12(3), 31-54.
Wilson, K. H., Karklin, Y., Han, B., & Ekanadham, C. (2016). Back to the basics: Bayesian extensions of IRT outperform neural networks for proficiency estimation. EDM 2016.
Xiong, X., Zhao, S., Van Inwegen, E., & Beck, J. (2016). Going deeper with deep knowledge tracing. EDM 2016.
Settles, B., & Meeder, B. (2016). A trainable spaced repetition model for language learning. ACL 2016, 1848-1858. https://aclanthology.org/P16-1174/
[All memory-sourced; NOT verified this session - academic egress fully blocked]
added_by_critics.implication: The brief specifies a hand-rolled Cepeda-ratio scheduler and never addresses learner modelling, which means someone will eventually propose a neural tracer. Pre-empt it. Gervet et al. found logistic-regression family models (IRT, DAS3H, best-LR) match or beat DKT, and win decisively when per-learner data is sparse - which is the permanent condition of a travel app used for four weeks before a trip. Settles & Meeder's Half-Life Regression is the right target: it is a spaced-repetition model trained on exactly this data shape (item features + lag + outcome), it beat Leitner and Pimsleur in production at Duolingo, it is a few dozen lines, it runs client-side, and its half-life output is directly interpretable as the `next_due_at` the brief already wants to persist. Recommend: ship fixed intervals in v1, HLR in v2 once the attempt log has volume, and put a written 'no neural knowledge tracing' decision in the architecture doc with these citations attached.

added_by_critics.claim: The 44px touch target is a platform convention, not an empirical finding, and the actual research supports a smaller number. WCAG's normative minimum is 24 CSS px.
sources: W3C (2023). WCAG 2.2, SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) - 24x24 CSS px, Level AA; SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) - 44x44 CSS px, Level AAA. https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
Parhi, P., Karlson, A. K., & Bederson, B. B. (2006). Target size study for one-handed thumb use on small touchscreen devices. MobileHCI 2006, 203-210.
Apple Human Interface Guidelines (44x44 pt) and Material Design (48x48 dp) - vendor conventions.
[Parhi et al. memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
added_by_critics.implication: The brief specifies FONT sizes (32-40px distractors) and never specifies a touch target, which in a 2x2 option grid with tight padding will produce sub-40px hit areas and misfires that the attempt log will record as genuine errors - poisoning both the learning KPI and the difficulty controller. Fix: specify hit areas separately from glyph sizes, at >=48x48 CSS px with >=8px spacing between adjacent options, and log a `tap_offset_from_center` field so accidental-tap errors can be filtered out of the accuracy signal. Do not cite '44px' as research; the empirical work (Parhi et al.: ~9.2mm discrete, ~9.6mm serial, roughly 34-36 CSS px) supports a smaller floor, and WCAG's normative AA requirement is 24px with 44px only at AAA. Meeting 48px is a good call for a thumb-driven game - just make it on ergonomic-margin grounds, not by miscrediting a convention to the literature.

added_by_critics.claim: Tone colour coding has essentially no controlled evidence of a learning benefit. The well-supported intervention for Mandarin tone is high-variability phonetic training with multiple talkers and immediate feedback.
sources: Wang, Y., Spence, M. M., Jongman, A., & Sereno, J. A. (1999). Training American listeners to perceive Mandarin tones. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 106(6), 3649-3658.
Sadakata, M., & McQueen, J. M. (2013). High-stimulus-variability training improves perception of Mandarin Chinese tones. JASA, 134(3).
Tone-colour schemes (Pleco/Hanping conventions, 'Chinese Through Tone and Color') are commercial conventions with no controlled trials I am aware of.
[All memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
added_by_critics.implication: Colour-coding tones is one of the most requested features in Mandarin apps and one of the least evidenced; it also carries a redundancy-effect cost (a second visual code competing with the orthographic form the app is trying to teach) and an accessibility cost for the ~8% of male users with red-green deficiency, since the standard four-tone palettes lean on red/green contrasts. If tones enter the product at all, the evidence-backed form is multi-talker audio with immediate feedback - HVPT generalises to new talkers and new words and has shown retention at months, which colour has never been shown to do. For a READING-first product the cleanest decision is to leave tone training out of v1 entirely and say so explicitly, so it does not get added later on aesthetic grounds.

added_by_critics.claim: 'Handwriting is essential for hanzi' is over-claimed, but the brief's flat 'never ask a beginner to write' is also unsupported. Writing reliably improves ORTHOGRAPHIC memory - which is exactly the brief's confusion-set problem - it is just expensive per unit time.
sources: Guan, C. Q., Liu, Y., Chan, D. H. L., Ye, F., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Writing strengthens orthography and alphabetic-coding strengthens phonology in learning to read Chinese. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 509-522.
Xu, Y., Chang, L.-Y., Zhang, J., & Perfetti, C. A. (2013). Reading, writing, and animation in character learning in Chinese as a foreign language. Foreign Language Annals, 46(3).
[Memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
added_by_critics.implication: Both the folk claim and the brief's rebuttal are too strong. The defensible position: writing practice builds form-level orthographic representations better than reading-only, which is precisely what is needed to keep 人/入, 千/干 and 木/本/末/未 apart - and the brief's own design has no other mechanism for building that representation, since a 4-alternative tap can be passed on partial visual cues. But writing is slow, and the brief's efficiency argument against it is sound. The design resolution neither the brief nor the folk claim reaches: get the orthographic attention without the motor cost. Build a component-assembly item type - show the meaning, present 6 components, the player taps the 2-3 that compose the character in the right positions. It costs ~6 seconds instead of ~30, produces the same forced attention to internal structure, and generates a clean retrieval event. Ship that instead of handwriting, and instead of nothing.

added_by_critics.claim: The co-located multiplayer premise is NOT untested territory, as the brief's gaps section says - it is well-studied in the collaborative-memory literature, which the brief never consults, and that literature yields three concrete and non-obvious design rules.
sources: Roediger, H. L., Meade, M. L., & Bergman, E. T. (2001). Social contagion of memory. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 365-371.
Weldon, M. S., & Bellinger, K. D. (1997). Collective memory: Collaborative and individual processes in remembering. JEP: LMC, 23(5), 1160-1175.
Basden, B. H., Basden, D. R., & Henry, S. (2000). Costs and benefits of collaborative remembering. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 14(6).
Rajaram, S., & Pereira-Pasarin, L. P. (2010). Collaborative memory: Cognitive research and theory. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 5(6), 649-663.
[All memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
added_by_critics.implication: This is the single largest gap in the brief and it fills cleanly. (1) SOCIAL CONTAGION: seeing another player's wrong answer implants it - participants later reproduce other people's errors as their own memories. This is a far stronger reason to hide per-player wrong answers than the anxiety argument the brief uses, and it upgrades that recommendation from a comfort feature to a correctness requirement. It also rules out a tempting mechanic: never show 'what everyone else picked' as a distribution bar. (2) COLLABORATIVE INHIBITION: groups recalling together retrieve less than the same people recalling separately, because hearing others' retrieval disrupts your own strategy. Simultaneous private answering - which the brief already specifies for a different reason - avoids this; any 'discuss it as a table' mechanic would incur it. (3) POST-COLLABORATIVE BENEFIT: individuals nonetheless show improved later recall after group sessions, via re-exposure to items they did not themselves retrieve. Capture it deliberately with a short solo re-test at the end of each co-located round covering items the player got wrong or did not answer. Together these say the brief's product shape is right, for reasons the brief did not have.

added_by_critics.claim: A real Chinese street-signage corpus already exists, is licensed for research, and is character-annotated - the brief's 'highest-leverage content decision' does not require photographing Beijing yourself.
sources: Yuan, T.-L., Zhu, Z., Xu, K., Li, C.-J., Mu, T.-J., & Hu, S.-M. (2019). A large Chinese text dataset in the wild (Chinese Text in the Wild, CTW). Journal of Computer Science and Technology, 34(3), 509-521.
ICDAR 2019 ReCTS: Reading Chinese Text on Signboards competition dataset (~25k signboard images).
ICDAR 2017 RCTW-17: Reading Chinese Text in the Wild.

Cai, Q., & Brysbaert, M. (2010). SUBTLEX-CH: Chinese word and character frequencies based on film subtitles. PLoS ONE, 5(6), e10729. - spoken-register frequency, a better prior than written-corpus frequency for travel language.
[All memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
added_by_critics.implication: CTW is roughly 32k street-view images with around a million annotated character instances across ~3,850 character classes - i.e. a character frequency distribution measured on actual Chinese street scenes, which is exactly the sub-corpus the brief proposes to build by hand and calls the project's highest-leverage decision. ReCTS is specifically SIGNBOARDS. Using these turns a multi-week manual corpus effort into a frequency query, and it gives you a defensible, citable basis for the coverage number you put in the UI - which is the thing the brief could not source and correctly flagged. Caveats to check before relying on it: CTW skews to street-view photography (shopfronts, banners) rather than metro interiors, menus or product labels, so menu and packaging vocabulary still needs a hand-built supplement; and licence terms are research-oriented, so verify commercial use. Pair it with SUBTLEX-CH rather than a written-text frequency list, since travel language is closer to the spoken register.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's proposed learning KPI measures learning the app, not learning Chinese. Recognition accuracy on the same stimulus in the same UI is the measure most inflated by context-dependent and item-specific learning.
sources: Godden, D. R., & Baddeley, A. D. (1975). Context-dependent memory in two natural environments. British Journal of Psychology, 66(3), 325-331.
Smith, S. M., & Vela, E. (2001). Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 203-220.
Soderstrom, N. C., & Bjork, R. A. (2015). Learning versus performance: An integrative review. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 10(2), 176-199. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25910388/
[Godden & Baddeley and Smith & Vela memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
added_by_critics.implication: The brief defines Learning KPI = 'accuracy on items at a >=7-day delay, computed from the attempt log'. That number will be systematically optimistic: same typeface, same card layout, same four distractors, same app context. The whole point of the product is recognition on a wall in Shanghai, and the learning/performance dissociation the brief itself endorses says the training-context measure is the one most likely to diverge from that. Build a held-out TRANSFER test: photographs of real signage the player has never seen in training, in display and handwritten typefaces, at oblique angles, with the target character embedded in a longer string. Run it at 7 and 28 days on a sample of users. It is a few hours of work and it is the only metric that can distinguish a product that teaches Chinese from a product that teaches its own card layout. Report both numbers side by side and expect a substantial gap; the size of that gap is your most valuable internal statistic.

added_by_critics.claim: Training every item in a single clean typeface will under-produce transfer to real signage, where display faces, neon, handwriting and vertical setting dominate. Perceptual variability during training is the cheap fix.
sources: Sanocki, T., & Dyson, M. C. (2012). Letter processing and font information during reading. Attention, Perception & Psychophysics, 74(1).
Schmidt, R. A., & Bjork, R. A. (1992). New conceptualizations of practice: Common principles in three paradigms suggest new concepts for training. Psychological Science, 3(4), 207-217.
Sadakata & McQueen (2013) on high-variability training - same principle in the auditory domain.
[All memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
added_by_critics.implication: This is the legitimate 'desirable difficulty' the brief was reaching for and rejected wholesale after correctly killing Sans Forgetica. Perceptual DISFLUENCY (degrading legibility) is a documented failure; perceptual VARIABILITY (multiple legible exemplars) is a different manipulation with a much better track record, and it is the one that maps onto the transfer problem. Design: render each item across at least three fully legible typefaces - a Song/serif, a Hei/sans, and a display or handwritten form - rotating across repetitions, plus at least one photographed real-world instance per high-value item. Keep every rendering at WCAG AA contrast as the brief demands. Add a `render_variant` field to the attempt record so you can measure whether variability-trained items outperform single-face items on the transfer test. Also cover the two signage facts the brief never mentions: vertical setting (still common on shopfronts and banners) and the fact that some mainland signage, especially older or decorative shopfronts and anything Hong Kong/Taiwan-adjacent, uses traditional forms.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief is a reading brief with no phonology at all, which is a substantive pedagogical gap rather than a scoping choice - and it also means the pinyin recall 'hard mode' it proposes has no supporting content model.
sources: Perfetti, C. A., & Tan, L. H. (1998). The time course of graphic, phonological, and semantic activation in Chinese character identification. JEP: LMC, 24(1).
Share, D. L. (1995). Phonological recoding and self-teaching: Sine qua non of reading acquisition. Cognition, 55(2), 151-218.
Guan, C. Q., Liu, Y., Chan, D. H. L., Ye, F., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 509-522.
[All memory-sourced; NOT verified this session]
added_by_critics.implication: The brief contains zero pinyin and zero tone marks anywhere across 30 findings - which is a clean record in the sense that there are no tone-mark errors to correct, but it also means the item bank as specified has no pronunciation field, while one finding casually proposes a 'type the pinyin' hard mode. Those are inconsistent. More substantively: phonological activation is automatic and early in Chinese character identification even for skilled readers, and having a spoken form to attach the graphic form to gives the learner a second retrieval route and a verbal rehearsal handle that a purely visual form-meaning pair lacks. It is also what makes a character usable in the actual travel scenario - reading 换乘 silently does not let you ask anyone about it. Recommend: add `pinyin` (with tone marks, not tone numbers) and `audio` to every item from day one even if v1 never surfaces them; the retrofit cost across 500 items later is exactly the argument the brief itself makes for the `semantic_transparency` and `stroke_count` fields.

added_by_critics.claim: Every effect size in this brief comes from a fully-blocked network and none of them has been checked against a source - not by the brief's author, and not by me. The brief discloses this; the risk is that the disclosure is buried in gaps[0] while the findings read as verified.
sources: Proxy status endpoint this session: 403 on CONNECT for pubmed, PMC, ERIC, arXiv, ACL Anthology, ACM DL, Springer, Wiley, Taylor & Francis, SAGE, Cambridge Core, ScienceDirect, Semantic Scholar (site and API), Crossref API, OpenAlex, Google Scholar, Frontiers, PsyArXiv, and every search engine tested.
WebSearch budget exhausted at 200/200 before this review began.
added_by_critics.implication: Two independent agents have now failed to read a single full text on this topic. That is a process finding, not a research finding, and it should be escalated rather than worked around. Concretely: (1) Move the access disclosure from gaps[0] to the top of the document, because a reader who skims findings will take 'evidence_strength: strong' at face value and none of these grades has been source-checked. (2) The four verification priorities are right but incomplete - add the Brunmair & Richter words-category composition (decision-critical, and now doubly so given the semantic-clustering literature that cuts against the brief's round design), the Sailer & Homner moderator analysis (the brief's narrative-over-points directive rests entirely on it), Ingendahl et al. (2025) which is a 2025 paper the brief grades 'strong' without reading, and the Nakata (2016) participant description which does not match that author's usual population. (3) Cheapest fix by far: one person with an unrestricted connection and a library login spends half a day resolving the ~35 DOIs and pasting abstracts into a shared doc. Until that happens, no engineering costing more than a day should be justified by this brief - which, to be fair, is close to what the brief itself says.

added_by_critics.claim: Interleaving confusable exemplars during practice is the single best-evidenced lever for building visual discrimination between similar categories — and it is exactly what a hanzi-recognition app needs. The brief has no interleaving finding at all, and one of its rules actively forbids it.
sources: Kornell N, Bjork RA (2008). Learning concepts and categories: Is spacing the 'enemy of induction'? Psychological Science 19(6):585-592
Birnbaum MS, Kornell N, Bjork EL, Bjork RA (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: the roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition 41:392-402
Rohrer D, Dedrick RF, Stershic S (2015). Interleaved practice improves mathematics learning. Journal of Educational Psychology 107(3):900-908
added_by_critics.implication: Kornell & Bjork found interleaved exposure to different artists' paintings beat blocked exposure for later classification of *new* examples, despite learners overwhelmingly believing blocking worked better — a metacognitive illusion that matters for a consumer app, because the better schedule will feel worse. Birnbaum et al. localised the mechanism to discrimination: interleaving juxtaposes confusable categories so their differences become salient. This is precisely the 人/入, 日/白, 未/末, 大/太/犬 problem. Concretely: build confusion-set clusters at bank-build time and schedule members of a cluster *close together but not adjacent* (5-15 intervening items) rather than blocking them or separating them across sessions. This directly contradicts the brief's Roediger-mitigation rule (a) forbidding a lure from being a correct answer elsewhere in the same session — that rule prohibits the intervention. It also refines the brief's spacing rule 'never show the same character twice within one session': showing a *neighbour* of a character within the same session is beneficial and different from showing the character itself. Finally, warn in-product: because interleaving feels harder, expect worse self-rated session satisfaction, and do not let an A/B on satisfaction kill it.

added_by_critics.claim: Adding a picture to a to-be-learned written form can impair learning of that form — the picture overshadows the orthography. This directly contradicts the brief's recommendation to pair every concrete-noun hanzi with a photograph on the reveal card.
sources: Samuels SJ (1967). Attentional process in reading: the effect of pictures on the acquisition of reading responses. Journal of Educational Psychology 58(6):337-342
Torcasio S, Sweller J (2010). The use of illustrations when learning to read: a cognitive load theory approach. Applied Cognitive Psychology 24(5):659-672
Solman RT, Wu HM (1995). Pictures as feedback in single word learning. Educational Psychology 15(3):227-244
added_by_critics.implication: This is a long-standing and repeatedly replicated finding in reading acquisition: when a picture accompanies a written word, learners attend to the picture — the easier and more informative cue — and encode the orthography less well, producing worse later performance on the word alone. Solman & Wu found the effect even when the picture appeared as *feedback* after the response, which is exactly the brief's proposed configuration. The brief reached its picture recommendation from the multimedia-gloss meta-analyses, but those measure *meaning* acquisition for words whose written form the learner can already decode; here the written form is the thing being learned, which flips the prediction. Repair: on the reveal card, show the hanzi alone first (roughly 800 ms, large, no other content), then reveal the gloss text and only then the image, so the glyph gets an unshared encoding window. Better still, A/B image-on-reveal against text-only-on-reveal with a delayed recognition test — this is cheap to run and the literature predicts the image condition loses. Note this also reconciles with the brief's own coherence and cognitive-load findings, which it had to argue against to justify the images.

added_by_critics.claim: Deep knowledge tracing does not reliably outperform simple logistic/IRT-style models, and several of its reported wins traced to data-set artifacts. This is a much stronger basis for the brief's 'do not build a complicated scheduler' recommendation than the spacing-schedule-shape argument it used — but it also implies the brief's fixed ladder is too simple in a different way.
sources: Gervet T, Koedinger K, Schneider J, Mitchell T (2020). When is Deep Learning the Best Approach to Knowledge Tracing? Journal of Educational Data Mining 12(3):31-54
Wilson KH, Karklin Y, Han B, Ekanadham C (2016). Back to the basics: Bayesian extensions of IRT outperform neural networks for proficiency estimation. EDM 2016 / arXiv:1604.02336
Xiong X, Zhao S, Van Inwegen E, Beck J (2016). Going deeper with deep knowledge tracing. EDM 2016
added_by_critics.implication: Gervet et al. compared DKT against logistic-regression baselines across nine datasets and found the simpler models competitive or better, with DKT's advantage depending on dataset size and on whether the data have strong temporal structure; Wilson et al. showed a plain hierarchical IRT extension beating DKT on proficiency estimation; Xiong et al. showed part of DKT's original reported advantage on ASSISTments came from duplicated records in the benchmark. For this product — a small bank, sparse per-user data, cold start on every new user — the simple model is not a compromise, it is the better-performing choice, and that can be said with evidence rather than as a v1 shortcut.
