The refinement the brief misses: the useful adaptivity is *per-item difficulty*, not schedule shape. A fixed 1/3/7/21/60-day ladder applied identically to 出口 and to 蒜蓉 wastes review on the easy item. A Leitner box or SM-2-style per-item interval is barely more code than a fixed ladder and captures nearly all the available gain; that is the right v1, not the ladder.

added_by_critics.claim: L2 learners from alphabetic backgrounds do not begin with component-level (radical) sensitivity — it develops over exposure. This contradicts the brief's scheduler rule that a compound may never be presented before its semantic radical has been seen twice.
sources: Wang M, Perfetti CA, Liu Y (2003). Alphabetic readers quickly acquire orthographic structure in learning to read Chinese. Scientific Studies of Reading 7(2):183-208
Shen HH, Ke C (2007). Radical awareness and word acquisition among nonnative learners of Chinese. Modern Language Journal 91(1):97-111
Taft M, Zhu X, Peng D (1999). Positional specificity of radicals in Chinese character recognition. Journal of Memory and Language 40(4):498-519
added_by_critics.implication: Early L2 learners process hanzi largely holistically and only gradually become sensitive to component structure and, importantly, to *positional* constraints on where a radical may legally appear. Shen & Ke found radical awareness — particularly semantic-radical awareness — developing with proficiency rather than being available from the start. This creates a sequencing tension with the brief's finding 14 (Nguyen et al., teaching semantic radicals transfers): radical instruction works, but it works for learners who already have some orthographic footing, so front-loading 40-60 radicals as the first item type may teach them as meaningless shapes. Repair the scheduler rule: allow whole-character recognition from item one for high-frequency signage targets (出口, 女, 男, 门), and introduce the radical layer as a *second pass* after ~50-100 characters of whole-form exposure, at which point the 'old-for-new' transfer effect has something to attach to. Store the radical fields from the start (they cost nothing); just do not let them gate the schedule at the beginning. Taft et al. also supply a free distractor-generation rule the brief lacks: pseudo-characters that place a real radical in an illegal position are strong lures precisely because positional sensitivity is late-developing.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief specifies a signage/menu item bank of '300-600 characters' with no corpus behind it, and cites no frequency or coverage statistic anywhere. General-purpose Chinese frequency lists — the obvious thing to reach for — are the wrong corpus for this product, because signage and menu registers have a heavy tail that general running-text frequency does not cover.
sources: 通用规范汉字表 (Table of General Standard Chinese Characters), State Council of the PRC, 2013: 8,105 characters total; Level 1 = 3,500, Level 2 = 3,000, Level 3 = 1,605
现代汉语常用字表 (1988): 2,500 常用字 + 1,000 次常用字
Jun Da, Modern Chinese Character Frequency List, derived from a ~258M-character corpus of modern written Chinese
《国际中文教育中文水平等级标准》 (Chinese Proficiency Grading Standards / HSK 3.0), 2021: 3,000 characters and 11,092 words across 9 levels
Xiao R, McEnery T. Lancaster Corpus of Mandarin Chinese (LCMC)
added_by_critics.implication: Two things follow. First, if you want a coverage argument at all, get it from a named corpus and state it: general written Chinese reaches roughly 90% running-text coverage at ~1,000 characters and ~99% at ~3,000, and the official Level 1 set of 3,500 is the state's own definition of general-purpose sufficiency. Those are the numbers to quote — and to quote *with* the corpus, which the brief's own review instructions demanded and it did not do. Second and more important: those figures do not transfer. Menu characters (焖, 煸, 蒜, 韭, 螺, 粿), transit characters (换乘, 闸机), and shop-category characters cluster outside the top 1,000 while being near-certain to appear in the target environment. So the bank must be built from a *domain* corpus you assemble — photograph or scrape menus, metro maps, shopfronts and packaging from the target cities — and ranked by frequency within that corpus, not by general frequency. This is the highest-value piece of unglamorous work in the project and the brief does not mention it. It also gives you the situational-distractor sets for free: characters co-occurring on the same real menu are the priority-2 distractors.

added_by_critics.claim: 'Handwriting is essential for learning hanzi' is the standard claim in this space and the brief neither asserts nor refutes it — leaving its MC-only design undefended against the most predictable objection. The evidence supports handwriting for *production* and for orthographic precision, but does not establish it as necessary for *recognition*, which is this product's only goal.
sources: Guan CQ, Liu Y, Chan DHL, Ye F, Perfetti CA (2011). Writing strengthens orthography and alphabetic-coding strengthens phonology in learning to read Chinese. Journal of Educational Psychology 103(3):509-522
Tan LH, Spinks JA, Eden GF, Perfetti CA, Siok WT (2005). Reading depends on writing, in Chinese. PNAS 102(24):8781-8785

Cao F, Vu M, Chan DHL, Lawrence JM, Harris LN, Guan Q, Xu Y, Perfetti CA (2013). Writing affects the brain network of reading in Chinese: a functional magnetic resonance imaging study. Human Brain Mapping 34(7):1670-1684
added_by_critics.implication: Guan et al. is the strongest pro-handwriting result and it is genuinely a good study: character-writing practice improved orthographic knowledge and reading outcomes relative to pinyin-typing practice, which instead improved phonological outcomes. Cao et al. show a corresponding neural effect. But Tan et al. (2005), the paper most often deployed as 'reading depends on writing', is a correlational study of Chinese *children*'s writing and reading skill — it does not license the inference that an adult L2 learner needs handwriting to recognise 出口 on a sign. The honest position for this product: handwriting buys orthographic precision, which is most valuable exactly where the brief already identifies risk (identical-stroke confusable pairs), and buys little elsewhere. Concrete recommendation, which is more defensible than either 'no handwriting' or 'add handwriting': keep MC as the loop, and offer optional tracing/writing *only* for characters an individual learner's confusion log shows they repeatedly mis-select against a visual neighbour. That targets the one outcome handwriting is best evidenced for, at a fraction of the interaction cost. Say this explicitly in the design doc, because 'why is there no writing practice' will be the first question asked.

added_by_critics.claim: Training on a single typeface risks failing the criterion task, because real Chinese signage is typographically far more variable than Latin signage — and the brief's own recommendation ('use a Hei face as the single hanzi face') optimises legibility at the cost of transfer. This is the specific untested risk the brief's own gaps section gestures at but does not resolve.
sources: Kornell N, Bjork RA (2008). Psychological Science 19(6):585-592 — variability of exemplars in inductive category learning
Gómez RL (2002). Variability and detection of invariant structure. Psychological Science 13(5):431-436
Dobres J, Chahine N, Reimer B, Gould D, Zhao N (2016). Displays 41:42-49 — establishes legibility differences across Chinese typefaces, i.e. the forms differ enough to matter perceptually
added_by_critics.implication: Mainland shopfronts, menus and packaging use 楷体, 隶书, 行书, 宋/明, condensed and expanded Hei, neon and hand-painted forms freely; only transit and road signage is standardised. The perceptual-learning principle that variability of training exemplars improves generalisation to novel exemplars is well established in category learning generally, and Dobres et al. establish that Chinese typefaces differ enough to be perceptually consequential — but I could locate no controlled test of font variability in hanzi acquisition, so this is a flagged risk, not a finding. The design consequence is cheap enough to adopt anyway: keep Hei for the *prompt* the learner must discriminate (legibility wins there), but vary the typeface across repeated exposures of the same item over time, and add a late-stage 'in the wild' review mode using photographs of real signage rather than rendered type. That mode is also the honest way to test whether the app's training transfers at all, which is the question no study in the brief answers. Treat font variability as the product's first A/B: variable-font exposure vs single-font, outcome measured on photographed real signage.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief contains no mobile-learning effect size at all despite being a specification for a mobile learning product, and misses the moderator that matters most to its own concept: whether learning is situated in the authentic context of use.
sources: Sung Y-T, Chang K-E, Liu T-C (2016). The effects of integrating mobile devices with teaching and learning on students' learning performance: a meta-analysis and research synthesis. Computers & Education 94:252-275
Burston J (2015). Twenty years of MALL project implementation: a meta-analysis of learning outcomes. ReCALL 27(1):4-20
Cho K, Lee S, Joo M-H, Becker BJ (2018). The effects of using mobile devices on student achievement in language learning: a meta-analysis. Education Sciences 8(3):105
added_by_critics.implication: Sung et al. found a moderate overall benefit for mobile-device-integrated learning (around g ≈ 0.5) across 110 experimental studies, with moderators including duration, setting and pedagogy. Burston's counterweight is important and is the kind of thing the brief should have included: he documents that the MALL outcomes literature is dominated by very short interventions with small samples and weak designs, so the aggregate effect is fragile — the same publication-bias story as gamification. The design consequence specific to this product: the moderator that repeatedly matters is whether learning happens in the authentic context of use, which is the one structural advantage this concept has over a flashcard app and which the brief never exploits. Build for in-situ use as a first-class mode — a scene-scoped session ('you are standing in a noodle shop') triggered by the user, with the bank filtered to that scene's real item set — rather than treating co-located multiplayer as the differentiator. Situated use is better evidenced than the co-located-multiplayer literature the brief leans on, which it itself grades weak and admits has no learning-outcome studies.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's accessibility coverage is one contrast ratio. For a Dutch-market consumer app aiming at public-sector or educational distribution, the binding constraint is the European Accessibility Act, which took effect in June 2025 and applies EN 301 549 / WCAG 2.1 AA to consumer e-commerce and digital services.
sources: Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act), applicable from 28 June 2025
EN 301 549 v3.2.1, the harmonised European accessibility standard, incorporating WCAG 2.1 Level AA
W3C WCAG 2.2 (October 2023): SC 1.4.1 Use of Color, 1.4.4 Resize Text, 1.4.12 Text Spacing, 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum)
Nederlandse overheid: Tijdelijk besluit digitale toegankelijkheid overheid (for public-sector distribution)
added_by_critics.implication: This converts several of the brief's discretionary recommendations into requirements and settles one of its open arguments. SC 1.4.1 (Use of Colour) independently prohibits colour as the only carrier of information — which decides the tone-colour and radical-colour question on legal grounds regardless of how the Godfroid and Skulmowski readings come out, and is a far more robust argument than either. SC 1.4.4 requires content to remain usable at 200% text scaling, which the brief's fixed --hanzi-base plus a single 1.25x toggle does not satisfy: the layout must survive OS-level font scaling, so use rem-relative sizing and test the answer-row layout at 200%. SC 1.4.12 sets text-spacing overrides the card layout must tolerate. SC 2.5.8 sets the 24×24 CSS px target floor. Add screen-reader handling the brief never mentions: every hanzi needs a lang="zh-Hans" attribute so VoiceOver and TalkBack select a Mandarin voice rather than attempting the glyph in Dutch, and the Latin gloss needs lang="nl" or lang="en" — get this wrong and the app is unusable with a screen reader and non-conformant. Also: the timed-round design engages SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable, which requires the user be able to turn off, adjust or extend a time limit; the brief's per-item deadline needs an accessible escape.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's one-item-per-screen recommendation is justified from a mobile-survey scrolling-versus-paging study, which is a weak analogue — but the correct supporting literature exists and is stronger, and it changes one of the brief's specific parameters.
sources: Bjork RA, Bjork EL (2011). Making things hard on yourself, but in a good way: creating desirable difficulties to enhance learning. In Psychology and the Real World
Roediger HL III, Karpicke JD (2006). Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science 17(3):249-255
Metcalfe J (2017). Learning from errors. Annual Review of Psychology 68:465-489
added_by_critics.implication: The reason to isolate one item per screen is not survey-completion economics; it is that adjacent items on screen provide retrieval support that reduces the difficulty of the retrieval attempt, and the retrieval-practice benefit scales with the effort of successful retrieval. That argument is stronger than the Mavletova & Couper transfer and it survives the coherence-effect-size correction above. It also revises a brief parameter: the brief predicts a 10-20% wall-clock penalty from paging and shrinks the round to 12 items to absorb it. That penalty is a survey-form artifact (page loads, navigation taps) that does not apply to a timed game where per-item time is set by the deadline anyway — the brief says this itself and then applies the penalty regardless. Drop the adjustment; size the round from the item deadline directly. Metcalfe's review adds a directly useful point the brief misses entirely: errors followed by corrective feedback produce *better* retention than errorless performance, so the brief's instinct to protect players from visible failure (batch reveal, 'characters you can now read' scoring) should not extend to suppressing the error itself. Show the wrong answer clearly, then correct it.

added_by_critics.claim: Co-located group retrieval suppresses individual recall — "collaborative inhibition" — so a pass-and-play or buzzer-style shared round will destroy the spaced-retrieval benefit for every player who is not answering. Groups recalling together retrieve less than the pooled total of the same people recalling alone, because exposure to others' retrievals disrupts each individual's own retrieval organisation. The compensating result is that *post*-collaborative individual recall is often improved via re-exposure.
sources: Weldon, M. S. & Bellinger, K. D. (1997). Collective memory: collaborative and individual processes in remembering. Journal of Experimental Psychology: LMC, 23(5).
Rajaram, S. & Pereira-Pasarin, L. P. (2010). Collaborative Memory: Cognitive Research and Theory. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 5(6).
Basden, B. H., Basden, D. R., Bryner, S. & Thomas, R. L. (1997). A comparison of group and individual remembering: does collaboration disrupt retrieval strategies? JEP:LMC, 23(5).

NOTE: cited from knowledge — this session's proxy refused every scholarly host (Scholar, Semantic Scholar, ACM DL, doi.org, Crossref, OpenAlex) and the WebSearch budget was exhausted at 200/200, so I could not re-verify. These are well-replicated, textbook-level findings; verify page-level details before quoting.
added_by_critics.implication: This is the central design constraint for a co-located multiplayer *learning* game and the brief's biggest miss — it flags the co-located evidence gap but treats it as merely unevidenced rather than as a known hazard. Concrete rule: every player must produce their own answer privately on their own phone before any answer is revealed to the room. Simultaneous private answer → then reveal → then social scoring. Never a buzzer, never turn-taking where three players watch one player retrieve. The social layer belongs in the reveal and scoring phase, which is where the re-exposure benefit lives, not in the retrieval phase, which is where the inhibition lives. This makes the brief's finding-17 requirement (every shared-session card writes back to that player's individual schedule) not just possible but coherent: each player has actually retrieved each item.

added_by_critics.claim: In much of urban mainland China the paper menu has been substantially replaced by a QR code and a WeChat mini-program ordering flow (请扫码点单 / 扫码点餐). The product's core scenario — standing in front of a printed menu decoding characters — is materially less common in exactly the tier-1 cities a Dutch or English visitor will be in, and the replacement surface is digital text on the user's own phone.
sources: Direct observation of mainland Chinese restaurant practice post-2020 (scan-to-order mini-programs); NOT verified against a published source in this session — every search and fetch path was blocked. This is a market-research claim that should be validated with a small field study, not a literature claim.
added_by_critics.implication: Two consequences the brief never considers. (1) Threat: the tier-1 promise ('read a real menu') may be aimed at a shrinking surface. Signage, transit, product labels and shopfronts are far more robust to this shift than menus are, so re-weight the domain corpus away from menus. (2) Opportunity, and it is a large one: a scan-to-order menu is *digital text*, which means the app can accept pasted or shared text and gloss it live — a far better product than photo-OCR, and it converts the phone from a study device into an in-situ reading aid. That is a different core loop than the one the brief scoped and it deserves a decision, not silence. Also add 请扫码点单, 扫码点餐, 支付宝, 微信支付, 扫码支付, 现金, 不收现金 to tier 1.

added_by_critics.claim: Tone sandhi means displayed citation-form pinyin systematically contradicts natural audio on high-frequency domain items, and it does so precisely on the T2/T3 boundary the brief identifies as the fragile one. Third-tone sandhi (T3+T3 → T2+T3) applies in 水饺 shuǐjiǎo→shuíjiǎo, 米粉 mǐfěn→mífěn, 老板 lǎobǎn→láobǎn, 两碗 liǎng wǎn→liáng wǎn, 九点 jiǔdiǎn→jiúdiǎn. 一 and 不 sandhi apply in 一个 yíge, 不要 búyào, 不是 búshì.
sources: Chen, M. Y. (2000). Tone Sandhi: Patterns across Chinese Dialects. Cambridge University Press.
Zhang, J. & Lai, Y. — work on the productivity of Mandarin third-tone sandhi.
This is a descriptive fact of Standard Mandarin, checkable in any reference grammar; citations given from knowledge, unverifiable in this session.
added_by_critics.implication: If the app renders per-character citation pinyin next to a natural recording, it will show a T3 while playing a T2 on exactly the items where the learner is already weakest — actively training the confusion finding 5 says to avoid. Schema fix: store `pinyin_citation` and `pinyin_surface` as separate fields per token, render surface form when audio is present, and add a `sandhi = true` flag so those items are excluded from any tone-scoring drill. Note this also further undermines the per-character pronunciation model in finding 16: sandhi, like heteronymy, is a property of the token in context.

added_by_critics.claim: Deep knowledge tracing does not reliably beat simple logistic/IRT models, and loses hardest in the small-data regime this product will live in. Well-featured logistic regression matches or beats DKT on most real datasets; a plain IRT model outperformed DKT on the original benchmarks; and part of DKT's headline advantage traced to duplicate-record preprocessing artifacts in the ASSISTments data.
sources: Gervet, T., Koedinger, K., Schneider, J. & Mitchell, T. (2020). When is Deep Learning the Best Approach to Knowledge Tracing? Journal of Educational Data Mining, 12(3).
Wilson, K. H., Karklin, Y., Han, B. & Ekanadham, C. (2016). Back to the Basics: Bayesian Extensions of IRT Outperform Neural Networks for Proficiency Estimation. EDM.
Xiong, X., Zhao, S., Van Inwegen, E. & Beck, J. (2016). Going Deeper with Deep Knowledge Tracing. EDM — documents the duplicate-record issue.
Cited from knowledge; ACM DL, arXiv and Semantic Scholar all refused in this session.
added_by_critics.implication: Pre-empt the inevitable 'let's add a transformer' proposal. A four-phone co-located game generates single-digit-thousands of events per user at best — the exact regime where DKT underperforms. Ship a simple, inspectable scheduler and spend the modelling budget on content instead.

added_by_critics.claim: Half-life regression and FSRS are better-evidenced schedulers than the SM-2-style (interval, ease, lapses) model the brief specifies. Half-life regression trained on ~12M Duolingo practice sessions beat Leitner and Pimsleur heuristics on recall prediction and improved engagement in a live A/B test; FSRS is the open successor with published benchmarks against SM-2 on large Anki review logs.
sources: Settles, B. & Meeder, B. (2016). A Trainable Spaced Repetition Model for Language Learning. ACL 2016 — ACL Anthology P16-1174.
FSRS (Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler) — published benchmark comparisons against SM-2 on Anki review-log datasets.
Cited from knowledge; aclanthology.org refused in this session. The brief was told to search ACL Anthology and did not.
added_by_critics.implication: Use FSRS (there are MIT-licensed JS/TS ports that run offline in a service worker) rather than hand-rolling SM-2 with an ease factor. Concretely relevant to the brief's finding 17: FSRS exposes an explicit retrievability estimate, which is exactly the quantity a co-located game needs in order to pick an item that is due for *several* players at once — the scheduling conflict at the heart of a shared multiplayer round, which the brief's last-write-wins sync design does not address at all.

added_by_critics.claim: The '44px touch target' is a platform guideline mis-transcribed from a different unit, not a research finding, and it is not the accessibility floor. Apple HIG specifies 44×44 pt; Android Material specifies 48×48 dp; WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (AA) requires only 24×24 CSS px with spacing exceptions, and 44×44 CSS px is the AAA criterion (2.5.5). The empirical mobile-touch literature supports roughly 9–10 mm for reliable discrete and serial tapping, which is not the same number as any of these.
sources: W3C WCAG 2.2 (Recommendation, October 2023), SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) and SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced).
Apple Human Interface Guidelines — 44×44 pt minimum.
Material Design — 48×48 dp minimum touch target.
Parhi, P., Karlson, A. K. & Bederson, B. B. (2006). Target size study for one-handed thumb use on small touchscreen devices. ACM MobileHCI.
Cited from knowledge; dl.acm.org refused in this session.
added_by_critics.implication: The brief specifies type sizes in detail (96 px hanzi, 40–48 px strings, 15–16 px gloss) and never specifies target size at all. For a 4-option forced-choice card tapped one-handed in a restaurant, the binding constraint is the thumb reach arc, not the target minimum: put the four options in the bottom half of the screen in a 2×2 grid, and put the hanzi hero element up top where nothing is tapped. Cite WCAG 2.2 AA (24 CSS px) as the floor and 44 CSS px as the target you actually ship, and stop repeating '44px' as though it were evidence.

added_by_critics.claim: Mandating a photograph on every item card (`image_url` non-null) risks cue overshadowing: when a highly salient visual cue is co-present with an orthographic form, learners can encode the picture–meaning association and never process the character form, producing knowledge that fails at the transfer target (a sign with no picture). This compounds the well-documented tendency of L2 Chinese learners to discriminate characters by partial, holistic visual features rather than full orthographic encoding.
sources: Cue competition / overshadowing in associative learning (Kamin; Rescorla–Wagner framework) as applied to paired-associate vocabulary learning.
Literature on L2 Chinese learners' reliance on holistic/partial visual cues rather than componential orthographic encoding.
Cited from knowledge; not verifiable in this session. Treat as a hypothesis to instrument rather than a settled result.
added_by_critics.implication: Two fixes, both cheap. (1) Put the photo on the *answer/reveal* side only, never co-present with the hanzi on the prompt side — this preserves dual coding at encoding-review while forcing orthographic processing at retrieval. (2) Do not mandate a photo for the large non-picturable share of the signage domain (禁止, 请勿, 优惠, 注意, 小心, 免费, 营业中, 暂停服务); for those, a photo *of the sign itself* turns the task into photo-to-photo matching, which will inflate in-app scores and not transfer. Add `picturable: bool` and allow text-only items. Also note a non-research blocker the brief treats as a mere pipeline cost: ~900 in-situ photographs of Chinese menus and shopfronts are third-party copyrighted works frequently containing identifiable people and trademarks. That is a legal review item before content authoring starts, not after.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's offline-in-China architecture has three platform-level failure modes it does not account for. (1) iOS Safari evicts script-writable storage — IndexedDB, Cache API, service-worker caches — after roughly seven days of non-use for sites not installed to the home screen, which directly destroys finding 2's requirement that a three-week gap must not reset progress. (2) Google Fonts and effectively all Western CDNs are unreachable from mainland China, so a Noto Sans SC face must be self-hosted and subsetted; a CJK face is multi-megabyte even subsetted, and a signage deck's character set is not the same as a standard subset. (3) Chinese Android builds routinely lack Google Play Services and terminate background service workers aggressively.
sources: WebKit storage policy — seven-day cap on script-writable storage for non-installed web apps (WebKit blog, ITP storage-eviction announcements).
Known mainland China network conditions: fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com unreachable.
Cited from platform documentation and knowledge; not re-verifiable in this session.
added_by_critics.implication: Finding 2's recommendation ('persist in IndexedDB with an export/restore path') is insufficient on iOS. Server-side sync must be the primary store with local as cache, not the reverse — and the sync must survive a Chinese network. Self-host the font subset generated from the actual item bank's character set. Test the seven-day eviction case explicitly in QA; it is the failure mode that silently deletes a returning user's entire history, which is the exact churn event finding 2 is trying to prevent.

added_by_critics.claim: The product's own success metric is not measurable by the format it ships. A 4-option forced choice has a 25% guess floor and measures recognition, which systematically and substantially overestimates the cued-recall knowledge that reading an unaided sign actually requires — the recognition/recall dissociation is among the oldest and most robust findings in memory research.
sources: Recognition–recall dissociation: standard result across the memory literature (e.g. Tulving's encoding-specificity and generation/recognition work; Mandler's dual-process account).
Cited from knowledge; unverifiable in this session, but this is textbook-level.
added_by_critics.implication: If the app displays 'you can read 340 signs' from 4-option performance, the number will be badly inflated relative to the street, and the moment the user stands in front of a real sign and fails is a high-risk churn event — the exact failure mode finding 2 says to architect against. Two fixes: (a) periodically calibrate with a harder recall-like format (a 12-option grid, or free typing of the meaning) and scale the displayed number by the measured recognition/recall ratio; (b) phrase the metric honestly — 'recognised in practice' rather than 'can read'. Also worth noting: the brief correctly avoided the two biggest traps in this genre — there is no Krashen input-hypothesis claim and no learning-styles claim anywhere in it. That is more than most briefs manage and is worth preserving as the bar for the next sweep.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief contains no memory-scheduling finding at all — no spacing effect, no retrieval practice, no interval scheduling — despite specifying a 'session scheduler' and 'per-route mastery'. This is the single largest omission, and it concerns the two interventions with the strongest evidence base in all of learning science.
sources: Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted & Rohrer (2006), Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: a review and quantitative synthesis, Psychological Bulletin 132(3) — NOT re-verified this session
Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Test-enhanced learning, Psychological Science 17(3)

Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan & Willingham (2013), Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1) — rates practice testing and distributed practice as the only two 'high utility' techniques of ten reviewed
added_by_critics.implication: Spacing and retrieval practice should be the backbone of the session scheduler, and they are cheap: they are scheduling policy, not content. Concretely — every item presentation must be a retrieval attempt (produce/choose before seeing the answer), never a study-then-recognise pass; intervals must expand across sessions with the gap scaled to the target retention horizon (the trip date is a natural, motivating deadline the brief never exploits); and per-attempt records need a timestamp plus outcome so intervals can be recomputed. This also interacts with the brief's handwriting conflict: Lu et al.'s opportunity-cost result is exactly a spacing/retrieval-density argument, so framing the tracing module as 'additive time' is the right call for the right reason.

added_by_critics.claim: Deep knowledge tracing does not reliably beat much simpler models, and would be a poor choice for this product.
sources: Piech et al. (2015), Deep Knowledge Tracing, NeurIPS — the original claim
Xiong, Zhao, Van Inwegen & Beck (2016), Going deeper with deep knowledge tracing, EDM — reports data leakage/preprocessing issues in the original DKT evaluation
Wilson, Karklin, Han & Ekanadham (2016), Back to the basics: Bayesian extensions of IRT outperform neural networks for proficiency estimation, EDM
Gervet, Koedinger, Schneider & Mitchell (2020), When is deep learning the best approach to knowledge tracing?, Journal of Educational Data Mining — all NOT re-verified this session
added_by_critics.implication: Do not build or buy a neural knowledge-tracing component. With a few hundred items, a few thousand players and a cold start, an Elo/IRT-style per-item difficulty plus per-player ability estimate, or a simple half-life/FSRS-style scheduler, will match or beat DKT while remaining debuggable and runnable offline in the PWA. Budget the saved effort into multi-talker audio (which the brief correctly prioritises) and telemetry.

added_by_critics.claim: Polyphonic characters (多音字) break the brief's item schema, and they are concentrated in exactly the highest-frequency band the product targets.
sources: Computed: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mozillazg/pinyin-data/master/pinyin.txt crossed with 通用规范汉字表 Tier 1
Computed: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/shengdoushi/common-standard-chinese-characters-table/master/level-1.txt
added_by_critics.implication: 1,378 of 3,500 Tier-1 characters (39.4%) carry more than one Unihan reading; 28.5% have more than one distinct segmental syllable and 10.9% differ by tone alone. The 39.4% is an upper bound (Unihan includes obsolete literary readings), but the practical head of the list is unavoidable: 的 de/dī/dí/dì, 了 le/liǎo, 地 dì/de, 着 zhe/zhāo/zháo/zhuó, 行 xíng/háng, 长 zhǎng/cháng, 重 zhòng/chóng, 得 dé/de/děi, 还 hái/huán, 为 wèi/wéi, 中 zhōng/zhòng, 分 fēn/fèn, 好 hǎo/hào, 发 fā/fà, 乐 lè/yuè, 教 jiào/jiāo, 调 diào/tiáo. The brief's 'sound (which pinyin+tone)' retrieval route and single per-route mastery flag are therefore ill-defined for a large minority of core items: a card showing 行 alone and asking 'which pinyin?' has two correct answers. Fix at schema level — reading must be a per-(character, word-context) value, not a per-character value, which is a further argument for the brief's own (correct) instinct to make the word the atomic item. Also exclude polyphones from any 'choose the pinyin' round unless the prompt supplies the word context.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's tone section omits the two obligatory sandhi rules that actually change the tone and that hit the highest-frequency characters in the language: 一 and 不.
sources: Computed frequency ranks: 一 = rank 1, 不 = rank 5, 个 = rank 16, 要 = 25, 点 = 172 (derived from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fxsjy/jieba/master/jieba/dict.txt)
Standard descriptive Mandarin phonology (Chao, Duanmu) — not a contested area
added_by_critics.implication: 不 bù → bú before a fourth tone (不是 búshì, 不要 búyào, 不对 búduì); 一 yī → yì before T1/T2/T3 and → yí before T4 (一点 yìdiǎn, 一起 yìqǐ, 一个 yíge). These are the #1 and #5 most frequent characters and they saturate travel speech (多少钱一个, 不要, 一点点). The brief's tone schema stores only citation vs post-T3-sandhi tone pairs, which does not represent 一/不 sandhi at all. Additionally, the brief's own example set is imprecise: 老板 lǎobǎn is genuine T3+T3→T2+T3 sandhi, but 好吃 hǎochī is T3+T1, where only allophonic half-third lowering applies — its stored 'surface tone pair' would be identical to citation, so it does not motivate the field it is cited to justify. Third omission: neutral tone. The brief uses 东西 as an opaque-compound example without noting that the 'thing' reading requires neutral tone (dōngxi), while dōngxī is 'east-west' — a neutral-tone minimal pair sitting inside the brief's own worked example. Store tone as a per-syllable surface value with an explicit neutral-tone state, and add 一/不 sandhi and neutral tone to the tone module.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief mandates visually-confusable multiple-choice distractors without addressing the well-documented risk that multiple-choice lures are later misremembered as correct.
sources: Roediger & Marsh (2005), The positive and negative consequences of multiple-choice testing, JEP:LMC 31(5)
Butler & Roediger (2008), Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing, Memory & Cognition 36(3) — both NOT re-verified this session
added_by_critics.implication: The negative suggestion effect is strongest exactly where lures are plausible — i.e. under the brief's own rule that distractors be drawn from the orthographic-neighbour list. The established mitigation is immediate corrective feedback, which reliably reduces or eliminates the effect and increases the net benefit of multiple choice. Product consequences: never end a round without showing the correct answer paired with the item; when a player picks a confusable neighbour, show the target and the chosen neighbour side by side with the discriminating component marked (this is also where the brief's paired-presentation finding applies); and prefer production/recall formats over recognition for high-confusability clusters. This directly qualifies the brief's 'distractor generation must be visual-first' recommendation — visual-first distractors are right, but only with mandatory feedback.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's typography recommendation and its offline-PWA requirement are in direct conflict, and it never costs the font.
sources: Google Noto CJK release documentation (Noto Sans SC static OTF is on the order of 8-10 MB per weight; full CJK families run to tens of MB)
Brief's own claim 22 requires the tone module to 'work fully offline in the PWA'; claim 28 requires 'Noto Sans SC Medium or heavier'
added_by_critics.implication: A co-located game in a restaurant with no network must cache its font, but a full Noto Sans SC weight is roughly 8-10 MB and two weights blow any reasonable PWA precache budget — while system CJK fallbacks differ across Android/iOS and will silently change glyph forms and stroke weights, breaking the brief's own stroke-count-driven sizing. The fix is cheap and should be a day-one architecture decision: subset the font to the actual item bank (a 1,000-2,000 character subset plus Latin/pinyin diacritics lands in the low hundreds of KB), precache the subset in the service worker, and regenerate the subset as part of the content build. Note also that pinyin tone marks need the Latin Extended ranges (ǖ ǘ ǚ ǜ ā á ǎ à) — these are routinely dropped by naive subsetting and are load-bearing for this product.

added_by_critics.claim: The 44px touch-target figure is a design convention, not an empirical optimum, and the empirical literature points larger — which matters for a phone passed between players.
sources: Apple Human Interface Guidelines (44x44 pt); Material Design (48x48 dp); WCAG 2.1 SC 2.5.5 Target Size (AAA, 44 CSS px); WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA, 24 CSS px)

Parhi, Karlson & Bederson (2006), Target size study for one-handed thumb use on small touchscreen devices, MobileHCI — reports ~9.2 mm (discrete) and ~9.6 mm (serial) thumb targets; NOT re-verified this session
added_by_critics.implication: The three 'standards' disagree by nearly 2x (24 to 48), which is itself evidence that none is an empirical result — they are platform conventions. The one empirical anchor points to ~9-10 mm for thumb use, which exceeds 44 px on most phones. For this product the relevant condition is worse than the lab: a device handed around a table, held at odd angles, possibly one-handed, under time pressure, by players who cannot yet read the labels. Size answer targets from the empirical thumb figure (~10 mm, i.e. comfortably above 48 px) rather than from the 44 px convention, keep generous inter-target spacing (mis-taps on confusable-character answers corrupt the very telemetry the brief wants to A/B on), and treat WCAG 2.2's 24 px as a floor for non-critical chrome only.

added_by_critics.claim: Gamification effect sizes in education are inflated by publication bias, short durations and novelty effects — relevant because the brief plans to justify game-format decisions with telemetry rather than literature, and will be tempted to import an effect size later.
sources: Sailer & Homner (2020), The gamification of learning: a meta-analysis, Educational Psychology Review 32 — small effects, high heterogeneity
Huang, Hew & Lo (2019/2020) and subsequent reviews noting short intervention durations

Hanus & Fox (2015), Assessing the effects of gamification in the classroom, Computers & Education — a longer-duration study finding declining motivation over a semester. All NOT re-verified this session
added_by_critics.implication: Treat published gamification effect sizes as unusable for planning. The pattern in that literature — small pooled effects, extreme heterogeneity, dominance of studies running a few weeks or less, and outcomes measured immediately — means a reported effect mostly indexes novelty. Two design consequences that survive regardless: (1) the brief's instinct to instrument and A/B is correct and should extend to the game shell, not just the tracing module; (2) measure retention at 7+ days and measure session-2 and session-5 return rates, because novelty effects show up precisely as strong first-session engagement followed by decay. Do not put a gamification effect size in any pitch or design doc.

added_by_critics.claim: Tone colour coding — the single most common design choice in Mandarin apps — has weak evidence and directly contradicts the brief's own no-colour-on-glyph rule, yet the brief never resolves the conflict.
sources: Brief's own claim 5 (Hou & Jiang 2022: radical colour markings increased RT and decreased accuracy) and claim 6 (Li, Shi & Wang 2025: colour coding slowed reaction times)
Chung (2007), Educational Psychology 27(1) — cited by the brief as finding colour-coded prompts helped, i.e. colour on the GLOSS, not the glyph

No controlled trial of Mandarin tone colour coding located; the widespread practice (Pleco, Hanping, Skritter, Dong Chinese) rests on convention, and the colour schemes are mutually incompatible across apps
added_by_critics.implication: The brief establishes 'keep hanzi in a single ink colour' and 'colour-code the gloss text, not the glyph', but never states the obvious corollary that tone colouring of characters — the default in most competing apps — falls on the wrong side of its own rule. Make this explicit, because it will otherwise be reintroduced by a designer as an industry norm. If tone needs a visual channel, put it on the pinyin or on a separate contour glyph (which the brief's T2/T3 turning-point recommendation already implies), never on the character. Also note colour-only tone encoding is an accessibility failure (WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color) and ~8% of male players cannot reliably use a red/green tone scheme — so a shape/contour channel is required regardless.

added_by_critics.claim: Real running-text character coverage — the statistic the brief flagged as its own unfilled gap — is far more favourable than its within-wordlist type coverage, and it also shows HSK's level-1 selection is not frequency-optimal.
sources: Computed 2026-08-22 over jieba's corpus-derived frequency dictionary (349,046 entries, ~100M frequency-weighted hanzi tokens, 12,010 distinct characters) — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fxsjy/jieba/master/jieba/dict.txt
Cross-tabulated against the GF0025-2021 cumulative character lists — https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30
added_by_critics.implication: Frequency-ranked coverage of running characters: top 300 → 60.3%, 600 → 76.8%, 900 → 85.2%, 1,200 → 90.0%, 1,500 → 93.1%, 1,800 → 95.1%, 2,500 → 97.6%, 3,000 → 98.5%; 50% is reached at 195 characters and 90% at 1,198. HSK cumulative sets do worse at equal size because they are pedagogically rather than frequency-ordered: HSK L1's 300 characters cover 43.3% (vs 60.3% for the frequency-matched 300 — 17 points given away), L1–3's 900 cover 79.4% (vs 85.2%), L1–6's 1,800 cover 93.3%, all 3,000 cover 97.8%. Two consequences. (1) This is direct, corpus-based support for the brief's 'do not order the bank by HSK level' conclusion — much stronger than its hand-built 125-item audit, and it should replace it. (2) It undercuts the brief's proposal to use the HSK 1–3 900-character set as the spine: at 79.4% of running characters, roughly one character in five on an unseen sign is still unknown, nowhere near the ~98% coverage conventionally treated as the threshold for unaided reading. Set the spine by frequency and treat HSK membership as metadata, exactly as the brief says — but size the spine at ~1,500–1,800 characters, not 900, and be honest in the UI that 900 characters is 'most of a sign', not 'a sign'. Caveat: dictionary frequencies are a proxy for a balanced written corpus, not for signage; a photographed signage corpus would shift the ranking toward menu and transit vocabulary.

added_by_critics.claim: Simplified vs traditional is a hard fork in the item bank that the brief never mentions once, and it cannot be papered over with a conversion step: 40% of HSK's reading characters change form and 230 of them are one-to-many.
sources: Computed 2026-08-22 by joining OpenCC's STCharacters.txt against the GF0025-2021 3,000-character reading list — https://github.com/BYVoid/OpenCC
https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30
added_by_critics.implication: Of the 3,000 HSK 3.0 reading characters: 1,790 are identical in traditional, 980 have exactly one different traditional form, and 230 map to more than one traditional character — 89 of those 230 fall inside the first 900 characters the brief proposes as the spine. The one-to-many cases cluster exactly in survival/menu vocabulary: 面 → 面/麪 (noodles), 干 → 幹/乾/干/榦 (dried, as on every 乾拌/乾貨 label), 发 → 發/髮, 后 → 後/后, 里 → 裏/里/哩, 表 → 表/錶, 系 → 系/係/繫, 只 → 只/隻. OpenCC's own phrase table renders 面条 as 麪條 and 收银台 as 收銀臺. Three design consequences the brief's architecture cannot absorb late: (1) the character-dependency graph is not isomorphic across scripts, so `component_char_ids[]` must be script-scoped, not shared; (2) a player's per-character FSRS state does not transfer — 面 and 麪 are two retrieval targets; (3) regional lexis diverges independently of script (mainland 换乘/单程票/充值 vs Taiwan usage), so 'convert on export' produces text no one has ever seen on a sign. Decide the target region in week one, build one script properly, and if both are wanted, model them as two banks sharing an abstract concept id rather than one bank with a conversion filter.

added_by_critics.claim: The proposed 60-item yes/no check-in cannot function as a learning-outcome metric: its 95% minimum detectable change between two sittings is about 27 percentage points.
sources: Computed 2026-08-22 from the brief's own specification (40 real items, 20 pseudowords, corrected score = hits/40 − false_alarms/20), binomial sampling error, assuming hit rate 0.75 and false-alarm rate 0.10
added_by_critics.implication: SE of the corrected score is sqrt(p_h(1−p_h)/40 + p_f(1−p_f)/20) ≈ 0.096, so a single score carries a 95% interval of roughly ±19 points, and the difference between two sittings has SE ≈ 0.136 — a minimum detectable change of ≈0.27. Even at a flattering hit rate of 0.90 and false-alarm rate of 0.05 the MDC is ≈0.19. Running it 'every 10 sessions' therefore produces a number that moves mostly at random, which is worse than no number, because the team will read the noise. To resolve a 10-point change you need ~284 real items + 142 pseudowords (426 items, roughly 10 minutes); for 5 points, ~1,700 items. Practical resolution: demote the check-in to a placement/onboarding instrument and a coarse band estimate (which is what 60 items can support), and take the actual outcome signal from the review log the brief is already storing — per-item first-session-correct rate, and n-th-session retention on items whose interval has crossed a fixed threshold, aggregated over hundreds of items per player. Those are free, continuous, and orders of magnitude better powered. If a discrete test is wanted for the 'hero number', run one long test (400+ items) twice a season rather than a short one ten times.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's own hard dependency constraint silently pins the whole group session to the weakest player, which defeats the response-format tiering it introduces two findings later.
sources: Computed 2026-08-22 by intersecting the cumulative-character/decodable-word curve derived from GF0025-2021 — https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30
added_by_critics.implication: The brief makes 'all component characters introduced for every player' a hard constraint on candidate selection. Combined with its own coverage curve, the eligible word set for a group equals the weakest player's set. A group whose weakest member knows 300 characters and whose strongest knows 1,200 has 1,451 eligible words rather than 7,330 — 80% of the strong player's readable vocabulary is excluded before the difficulty objective runs. At 600 vs 1,800 characters it is still 62% excluded. Varying the response format cannot recover this: a 4-alternative choice over a word the strong player finds trivial is still trivial. Fix by relaxing the constraint to be per-player rather than group-wide — the shared stimulus is a character or a short sign, and what differs per player is not only the response format but whether the item is scored for them at all (`role: exposure` for a player whose prerequisites are unmet, `role: co_committed` for the rest). That keeps the shared social moment, keeps the measurement honest, and removes the floor effect. Log `eligible_for` per round so the floor effect is visible in the data if it recurs.

added_by_critics.claim: A serverless co-located multiplayer PWA is not achievable on iPhones — there is no browser API for local peer discovery, and Web Bluetooth is unsupported in Safari on every current version.
sources: caniuse feature data read 2026-08-22: web-bluetooth — ios_saf 'n' through 26.5, safari 'n' through 27/TP; rtcpeerconnection — 'y' in ios_saf, safari, chrome, and_chr — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Fyrd/caniuse/main/features-json/web-bluetooth.json
added_by_critics.implication: The brief asserts 'no server', 'no backend', 'fully offline' repeatedly. That is true of the scheduler and the item bank; it is false of the multiplayer half. WebRTC data channels are universally supported but require out-of-band signalling — an exchange of SDP offers/answers that must happen over something. Web Bluetooth, the only realistic local-discovery alternative, is not implemented in Safari on iOS or macOS and is marked non-standard. So the options are: (a) a tiny signalling service (a few hundred lines, but it is a backend with uptime and privacy obligations); (b) QR-code SDP exchange between devices, which works offline but is fragile with more than two peers and needs camera permission; (c) single-device pass-the-phone or shared-screen-plus-one-device play, which removes the requirement entirely and is the only genuinely serverless option. Pick one now — it determines whether `review_duration` and the blind-commit window are even measurable per player, which the entire measurement design depends on. Also note the brief never mentions the Screen Wake Lock API (supported everywhere per the same data); a 30-round evening on a shared display needs it.

added_by_critics.claim: The closest published work to the brief's 'genuinely novel' group-selection layer is single-learner session-level item selection, and it has both an algorithm and a randomised field trial — neither of which the brief located.
sources: Networks-Learning/spaced-selection — 'a method for optimally selecting the items which the user should revise during a given session'; randomised trial run in the Swift driving-theory app; trial data released — https://github.com/Networks-Learning/spaced-selection
Networks-Learning/memorize — code and data for Tabibian et al., PNAS 116(10):3988–3993 (2019) — https://github.com/Networks-Learning/memorize

Upadhyay, Lancashire, Moser & Gomez-Rodriguez (2021), npj Science of Learning 6:26, doi 10.1038/s41539-021-00105-8 (paper not retrievable this session; existence, design and code confirmed from both repositories and from the FSRS project's Research-resources page)
added_by_critics.implication: The brief's framing — 'the group layer has no library, no benchmark and no paper to copy' — is right about the *group* part and wrong about the *selection* part. Memorize (PNAS 2019) chooses when to review by treating reviewing intensity as a stochastic-optimal-control problem; Spaced Selection (npj 2021) adapts it to the more product-shaped question of which items to serve in a session the learner initiated, and was evaluated in a randomised trial in a live commercial app against competitive baselines. Read both before writing `pickItem`: the single-learner objective they optimise is the thing the brief's squared-deviation heuristic is a hand-rolled substitute for, and their released trial data is the only public dataset I found where different session-level selection policies were randomised against each other. Then treat the group extension — N learners, one stimulus, one screen — as the genuinely open part, which it is. I could not run database searches (see verdict), so I still cannot say whether a co-located multi-learner selection literature exists; that search remains unrun.

added_by_critics.claim: The yes/no test's pseudoword machinery is on shakier ground in Chinese than the brief allows, and its worked example is a bad stimulus.
sources: Reasoned from the brief's own specification plus verified HSK data (票 and 冷 are both level-1 characters — https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30); the Chinese word-segmentation and lexical-decision literature could not be retrieved this session
added_by_critics.implication: Two problems. (1) The brief is right that pseudo-characters are useless and pseudo-words are the correct stimulus type, but its example 票冷 is a noun+adjective juxtaposition with no licit compound structure — it will be rejected on sight, which collapses the false-alarm rate the correction formula divides by, i.e. it reproduces the failure it was introduced to avoid. Build pseudowords by substituting one character of an attested two-character compound with a frequency-matched character sharing the semantic radical, so the string is morphologically well-formed but non-existent. (2) Deeper: Chinese orthography has no word delimiters and 'is this a word?' is a judgement on which even native readers and competing segmentation standards disagree substantially — the yes/no format imports an assumption about wordhood from alphabetic languages that Chinese does not supply. Safer instrument for a reading product: keep the yes/no format but ask about *readability of a real string in context* ('can you read this sign?' over cropped photographs, with distractor strings drawn from real signage in a domain the player has not unlocked) rather than about lexical status. That measures the thing the product actually promises and sidesteps the wordhood problem entirely. Both points need verification against the Chinese lexical-decision and segmentation literature before they are relied on; I could reach neither.

added_by_critics.claim: FSRS ships a documented four-parameter cold-start path that is benchmarked, which is a better-evidenced answer to the brief's cold-start problem than the bolted-on Elo it proposes.
sources: srs-benchmark README @45f61b2 — 'FSRS-6 pretrain | 4 | 0.3548±0.0042 | 0.0790±0.0012 | 0.6999±0.0022' against FSRS-6 full 21-param 0.3456 and FSRS-6 default param. 0.3661 — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark
fsrs-rs DEFAULT_PARAMETERS / clamping ranges — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/fsrs-rs
added_by_critics.implication: The brief proposes storing an Elo difficulty per item with K = 0.4/(1+0.05n) and using it as a shrunken prior for FSRS initial difficulty — with the honest admission that both the Pelánek references and the constants are unverified guesses. Meanwhile the benchmark contains a 'pretrain' variant that fits only the four initial-stability parameters (one per grade) and recovers most of the gap between default parameters (0.3661) and full optimisation (0.3456), at a cost that is a closed-form fit over a handful of first-review outcomes. Prefer that for player-side cold start. Keep an Elo-style item difficulty only for the item side — where FSRS has no mechanism at all, since its difficulty parameter is per (player, item) and starts from a global constant — and keep the brief's good instinct of storing `prior_difficulty` and `observed_difficulty` in separate columns so the prior can be switched off in one line. Do not present the Elo constants as literature-derived; they are not.

added_by_critics.claim: The Chinese state's own proficiency standard already separates READING characters from HANDWRITING characters, and requires far fewer of the latter. GF 0025-2021 specifies 3,000 characters for recognition across nine levels, plus three SEPARATE and much smaller 手写字表 (handwriting character lists): 初等 300, 中等 400, 高等 500 — 1,200 in total. At the elementary stage a learner is expected to RECOGNISE 900 characters and to WRITE only 300.
sources: 国际中文教育中文水平等级标准 GF 0025-2021, official character list. Structure read and counted directly this session via https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30 (charlist.txt): levels 一-六 at 300 each, 七-九级 1,200, total 3,000 reading characters; then 初等手写字表 300, 中等手写字表 400, 高等手写字表 500.
added_by_critics.implication: This is the single best answer to the 'but handwriting is essential for hanzi' objection the product will face from every teacher and every investor, and the brief does not have it. The authority that designed the curriculum the objection appeals to has itself decoupled recognition from production, at a 3:1 ratio at the elementary stage. Put it in the app's about screen and in the funding deck, verbatim with the numbers. It also gives you a defensible external ordering authority for free: store the GF 0025-2021 level per character (I measured the distribution over the brief's survival set: 67 at L1, 38 at L2, 31 at L3, 21 at L4, 13 at L5, 15 at L6, 15 at L7-9, 14 outside the 3,000 entirely) and you can tell a returning HSK learner exactly which survival items they already hold. Note the honest counterweight from the corrections above: Guan et al. 2011 is real evidence that writing builds orthographic representation, so a reading-only product is making a considered trade, not a free choice. For a three-week trip with recognition as the criterion task, the trade is clearly right.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief specifies a font delivery strategy that fails in the one country the app exists for. It recommends 'Noto Sans SC / Source Han Sans SC via Google Fonts, weights 400 and 700, plus Noto Serif SC'. fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com are blocked in mainland China. The app will therefore fall back to the system CJK face exactly where it matters — which is the precise failure the brief warns about two sentences earlier when it worries about Japanese-locale glyph forms for 直 骨 每 令 画.
sources: Google Fonts host blocking in mainland China: widely documented; NOT independently verifiable from this sandbox (the egress proxy reaches fonts.googleapis.com, which says nothing about conditions inside China). Verify from a mainland vantage point before ship, but note the engineering fix is correct regardless of the answer.
Font sizes MEASURED this session: NotoSansSC-Regular.otf (github.com/notofonts/noto-cjk, Sans/SubsetOTF/SC) = 7.95 MB; NotoSansSC-VF.otf = 15.05 MB.
Subset MEASURED this session with fontTools pyftsubset: 482 glyphs (378 CJK + Latin + digits + tone-marked vowels + punctuation) → 60.0 KB woff2, 66.3 KB woff.
added_by_critics.implication: Self-host a subset. I built it: the entire survival character set plus Latin, digits, tone-marked vowels and punctuation is 60 KB as woff2 — a 135x reduction against the 7.95 MB full face, small enough to inline in the service-worker precache so it works offline on a Chinese SIM with no data. Three faces (sans 400, sans 700, serif 400) come to roughly 180 KB. This also fixes a second problem the brief did not see: Google Fonts serves CJK as ~100 unicode-range-sliced woff2 files fetched lazily per codepoint range, which is close to unusable for a service-worker-precached offline PWA even where it is reachable. Because you know the exact character inventory of your item bank, you can regenerate the subset at build time from the bank itself — make it a build step so the font can never drift from the content. Command: pyftsubset NotoSansSC-Regular.otf --text-file=bank-chars.txt --flavor=woff2 --layout-features= --no-hinting --desubroutinize.

added_by_critics.claim: The co-located multiplayer transport has the same China-blocking problem as the fonts, and it is less obvious. Browser WebRTC peer connections need a STUN server for candidate discovery, and the default in almost every tutorial, boilerplate and library is stun.l.google.com:19302 — a Google host, blocked in mainland China. A four-player co-located game whose peers cannot discover each other in the country it was built for is a total product failure, not a degradation.
sources: Google STUN endpoint blocking in mainland China follows from Google service blocking generally; NOT independently verifiable from this sandbox. Verify from a mainland vantage before ship.
Engineering inference from the WebRTC ICE model — a peer connection with no reachable STUN/TURN falls back to host candidates only.
added_by_critics.implication: For a CO-LOCATED game this is fortunate rather than fatal, because you do not need NAT traversal at all — all four phones are on the same LAN or hotspot. Design for host candidates only: one device becomes the session host, shares a join code by QR, and peers connect on local-network candidates with no STUN dependency. Configure an empty iceServers array rather than inheriting a library default, and test with the device in aeroplane mode plus hotspot, which is the realistic condition in a Chinese restaurant basement. If you ever need a relay, self-host coturn in-region; never ship a Google STUN default. Add this to the same pre-ship checklist as the font: enumerate every external host the PWA touches at runtime and confirm each is reachable from inside China, because the brief's architecture section touches this question nowhere.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief specifies type sizes down to the pixel but never once specifies an interactive TARGET size, despite designing a four-option tap grid plus a tap-target interaction type for the mini-programme template. The commonly cited '44px minimum' is not a web accessibility requirement and is widely misquoted: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) is 24x24 CSS pixels at Level AA; 44x44 is SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) at Level AAA. The 44 figure entered folklore from Apple's Human Interface Guidelines (44pt), and Android Material specifies 48dp — three different numbers for three different things.
sources: WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, October 2023), SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA, 24x24 CSS px; SC 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA, 44x44 CSS px. w3.org was 403-blocked this session — cited from model knowledge, verify the SC numbers before writing them into a spec.
Apple Human Interface Guidelines: 44x44 pt. Material Design: 48x48 dp minimum touch target. Both NOT retrieved this session.
added_by_critics.implication: Write the target spec down, and write down which number you are meeting and why. Practical recommendation for this product: 48 CSS px minimum on every answer option with at least 8px of spacing, which clears WCAG AA comfortably and matches Android's guidance — and note that the brief's own 40px-minimum type size for answer options will force the option ROWS well past 48px anyway, so the cost is zero. Two things the brief's design specifically needs: (a) the tap-target items in the mini-programme template deliberately render at realistic 14-16px density, which means the tap regions there will violate any target-size guidance — that is defensible because small targets ARE the difficulty being taught, but it must be a documented, deliberate exception with a non-timed accessible alternative, not an accident; (b) the 2,000ms minimum reveal dwell time and the 40-second timed ordering flow both engage WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable, so provide a setting to disable timers.

added_by_critics.claim: Traditional characters are legal and common on real mainland shopfronts, and the brief teaches only simplified. Chinese language law permits 繁体字 in specified cases including cultural relics, calligraphy, inscriptions and — directly relevant here — the handwritten/calligraphic characters on shop signs. The result is that the exact domain the brief ranks third by payoff, shopfront fascias, is the one domain where traditional forms routinely appear, precisely because fascias favour calligraphic and display lettering.
sources: 《中华人民共和国国家通用语言文字法》 (2000), Article 17 — permits traditional characters in enumerated cases including 题词和招牌的手书字. gov.cn was 403-blocked this session; verify the article text before quoting.

One-to-many simplification mappings verified this session with OpenCC (github.com/BYVoid/OpenCC): 面 → 麵/麪 (noodles) vs 面 (face/surface); 发 → 發 (to issue) vs 髮 (hair); 干 → 乾 (dry) vs 幹 (to do/trunk); 里 → 裏 (inside) vs 里 (unit/village).
Corroborating: CTW's annotation schema includes a 'wordart' attribute for decorative lettering, i.e. display typography is prevalent enough in street-view Chinese text to need its own class.
added_by_critics.implication: The one-to-many mappings are the dangerous part and they hit the brief's own highest-payoff items. A learner who has only met simplified 面 will not recognise 麵館 or 麪館 on a calligraphic noodle-shop fascia — and 面馆 is in the brief's Tier 1. Same for 理发 vs 理髮 (barber, a Tier 1 shopfront) and 干货 vs 乾貨. Concrete fix, cheap: add an optional `tradVariants: string[]` per item, populate it automatically with OpenCC at build time, and in the shopfront-fascia template only, present the traditional form as an alternate rendering for a small share of presentations. This is close to free — one build step over the existing bank — and it directly serves the brief's own generalisation metric (`unseenCompoundAccuracy`). It also makes the app usable in Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan without a second content set, which is a real market question the brief never raises.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's flagship architecture proposal — players photograph real signs, the app stores image plus GPS plus city, and captures are synced peer-to-peer and pooled into a corpus — creates legal exposure in two jurisdictions that the brief does not mention once. Photographing and geotagging in China touches restrictions on photographing certain installations (police stations, military and border facilities, some transport infrastructure) and on surveying and mapping activity by foreign nationals; collecting geolocation and image data from people in China and moving it off-device engages PIPL, and the Dutch/EU user base engages GDPR for the same data.
sources: PRC Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL, 2021) — cross-border transfer and sensitive personal information provisions; PRC Surveying and Mapping Law — restrictions on unauthorised geographic data collection. Chinese government sources were 403-blocked this session; this is flagged as a legal question to route to counsel, NOT as a verified legal opinion.
GDPR Art. 9 / Art. 44-49 for the EU-resident user base.
added_by_critics.implication: The correction above (CTW exists, ~1M labelled characters, free) removes most of the reason to build this feature at all, which is the cheapest possible mitigation: seed from CTW, and if you still want capture, ship it as strictly on-device with no GPS, no peer sync of images, and no server-side pooling — store only the extracted character list, never the photograph or the coordinates. That preserves the pedagogical value (queueing characters the player could not read) at near-zero legal exposure. If the pooled-corpus vision survives, it needs counsel before a line of code, not after. Note also that the brief's own success metric for the feature ('after ~5,000 captures you own the dataset nobody has published') is now false on both halves — the dataset is published, and 5,000 captures would be a rounding error against 1,018,402 labelled instances.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief never names its actual competitor. The realistic alternative to learning 380 characters is pointing a phone camera at the sign, and in China that specific market is unusual: Google Translate's camera mode is unusable without a VPN, but Pleco's OCR, Baidu Translate, Youdao and WeChat's built-in scan-translate all work natively and are what visitors actually use. Any payoff ranking that ignores this is ranking the wrong quantity — it ranks 'value of being able to read X' rather than 'value of being able to read X faster than you can photograph it'.
sources: No hospitality/HCI literature on QR menus or camera-translation use by visitors to China was retrievable this session (all publisher and search hosts 403-blocked). This is an analytic gap, flagged as a research task, not a sourced finding.

Searches to run when access returns: camera translation / OCR translation adoption among travellers; 'mobile assisted' + signage; and the post-2020 QR-menu literature the brief itself flags in its gaps.
added_by_critics.implication: This REORDERS the brief's five domains again, and mostly in its favour. OCR is strongest exactly where the brief already ranks payoff highest and weakest where it ranks it lowest — a static printed menu photographs well, a shelf-edge price label photographs well, but a shopfront fascia at night in display lettering does not, and neither does a scrollable in-app mini-programme where you cannot point a second camera at your own screen. The three situations where reading genuinely beats OCR and which the app should own: (1) transactional chrome inside a WeChat mini-programme, which is untranslatable in practice and is the brief's own finding 18 — promote it; (2) time-pressured social moments where taking out a second phone is not viable (the waiter is standing there, the gate is closing); (3) safety and prohibition signage where the answer must arrive in under a second. Reframe the product's own copy around this, and demote 'you can read the menu' in favour of 'you can order without stopping'.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief mixes five domains in a shuffled bag and never justifies mixing over blocking, which is a real and contested design choice with a literature behind it. Interleaved practice reliably feels worse and produces better retention and better category discrimination than blocked practice, and it is one of the more robustly replicated 'desirable difficulty' effects — but it is also known to depress learners' judgements of their own learning, which is a live product risk for a game whose retention depends on players feeling they are improving.
sources: Kornell, N., & Bjork, R. A. (2008). Learning concepts and categories: Is spacing the enemy of induction? Psychological Science, 19(6). NOT RETRIEVED THIS SESSION.
Interleaving effects in category induction and motor/mathematics practice — general literature, NOT RETRIEVED THIS SESSION. All publisher hosts 403-blocked.
added_by_critics.implication: Two consequences the brief should adopt. First, the shuffled bag is the right default and should be defended explicitly rather than left as an unexamined choice — and the domain weights (market 30 / menu 30 / street 20 / safety 15 / transit 5) are a mixing schedule, so they carry the interleaving benefit as a side effect. Second, and more important for a game: interleaving depresses perceived learning, so the app must compensate with an explicit progress signal, which the brief has already invented without realising why it needs it. The 'signs you can act on: 43 of 120' metric is exactly the right counterweight, because it rises visibly even while within-session accuracy feels erratic. Make that the home screen, as finding 7 says, and treat it as an interleaving mitigation rather than only as an honesty measure. Do NOT block by domain to make players feel better — that is the trade interleaving research exists to warn against. Exception: the brief's Tier 0 is deliberately linear and unskippable, which is correct, because interleaving benefits assume a base level of familiarity that a cold-start player does not have.

added_by_critics.claim: The survival set is not exotic, but it is not concentrated at the bottom of any standard ladder either — it is smeared across all nine HSK levels and beyond. Measured this session: of 214 survival characters, 93% (200) fall inside HSK 3.0's full 3,000-character reading list, so essentially nothing in the curriculum is obscure. But the level distribution is 67 at L1, 38 at L2, 31 at L3, 21 at L4, 13 at L5, 15 at L6, 15 at L7-9, and 14 outside the 3,000 entirely (壹贰叁肆伍陆柒捌玖拾佰仟 plus 焖 胗 荤 蟹 蹄 驴).
sources: Computed this session against the GF 0025-2021 official character list (3,000 reading characters), https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30.
added_by_critics.implication: This scores the brief's own gap-list prediction ('essentially 100% of the survival set falls in Level 1 of 通用规范汉字表') as directionally right and gives it a number to publish. It also yields two concrete product moves. (1) The claim to make in marketing is not 'we teach rare characters' but the opposite and much stronger one: 'none of this is obscure — 93% of it is in the official 3,000-character standard. It is just spread across nine levels of a ladder built for a different purpose, so no course reaches it for years.' That is a sharper pitch than the brief's current framing and it is measured. (2) The 14 genuinely out-of-standard characters are almost entirely the financial capital numerals, which the brief has already correctly assigned to a low-priority 'bank counter' sub-deck — so the data confirms that judgement. Move 焖 胗 荤 蟹 蹄 驴 to Tier 2 for the same reason, with the exception of 荤, which pairs with 素 and protects a dietary flag and should stay in Tier 0 on consequence grounds.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief has no plan for measuring whether any of this worked, despite proposing an excellent criterion metric. It defines `signsActionable` over a held-out set of ~120 real composite signs and correctly identifies it as the right progress display, but it never proposes using that held-out set as an actual EVALUATION — no baseline, no post-test, no landing-day measurement. It also lists an A/B test for the object-template question in its gaps and then does not carry it into any implication.
sources: Internal to the brief: finding 7 defines the held-out set; finding 5's implication defines the naked-probe instrumentation; the gaps list proposes the object-template A/B; none are connected into an evaluation design.

The CTW dataset supplies a ready-made held-out set of real photographed signage with ground-truth character labels — see the CTW correction above — which removes the main cost objection to building one.
added_by_critics.implication: Wire the pieces the brief already has into one evaluation, because they are three quarters of a study and nobody has run it. Concretely: split the ~120-sign held-out set into a pre-test block and a post-test block matched on required-character count; administer the pre-test block during Tier 0 onboarding (it doubles as the cold-start calibration the multiplayer game needs anyway) and the post-test block on landing day via the local notification the brief already specifies. Report one number — sign completion rate before departure versus on arrival — and you have the only outcome measure in this product category that is not self-reported. Stack the two A/B tests the brief has already designed inside it (object-templated vs plain rendering, measured on naked-probe accuracy; and the 0.15 vs ~0.27 spacing coefficient from the corrections above). Source the held-out signs from CTW rather than photographing them, which makes the set reproducible and lets you publish it. This is the cheapest credibility the product can buy and the brief leaves it on the table.

added_by_critics.claim: Distributed practice is the largest, best-replicated, and cheapest lever available to a hanzi recognition app — and the brief does not cite it once. Spacing repetitions rather than massing them produces large retention gains, and the optimal gap scales with the retention interval you care about.
sources: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354–380. (~254 studies) [NOT FETCHED — egress blocked]

Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095–1102. [NOT FETCHED]
Carpenter, S. K., Cepeda, N. J., Rohrer, D., Kang, S. H. K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Using spacing to enhance diverse forms of learning. Educational Psychology Review, 24, 369–378. [NOT FETCHED]

Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: Spacing and retrieval practice are the only two techniques Dunlosky et al. rated 'high utility'. The brief's entire social-mechanic apparatus is arguing about effects near zero while the largest effect in the room is unmentioned. Architecture consequence: the scheduling layer, not the match engine, is the product. Sessions must be scheduled across DAYS, not just distributed within a match — the brief's 're-queue at 5 and 15 intervening items' is within-session massing dressed as spacing. Concretely: the item's next-due timestamp must persist across matches and across players' devices, and the match engine must draw from a due-queue rather than a per-match item list. If the co-located social format makes cross-day scheduling impossible (people only play when they meet up), that is a first-order product risk and should be stated as such: an app played once a fortnight at a dinner table cannot deliver spacing, and a solo daily mode is then not a 'degenerate case' of multiplayer but the load-bearing surface.

added_by_critics.claim: Interleaving is unusually well-supported for exactly this product's material. Meta-analytically, interleaving helps most for inductive learning of VISUALLY SIMILAR categories and least for expository text — and visually confusable hanzi are the paradigm case of the former.
sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin, 145(11), 1029–1052. [NOT FETCHED]
Kang, S. H. K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Learning painting styles: Spacing is advantageous when it promotes discriminative contrast. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 26(1), 97–103. [NOT FETCHED]
Firth, J., Rivers, I., & Boyle, J. (2021). A systematic review of interleaving as a concept learning strategy. Review of Education, 9(2), 642–684. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: The mechanism is discriminative contrast: interleaving works because juxtaposing similar exemplars forces the learner to notice what distinguishes them. This gives the brief's confusable-pairs category a far stronger justification than hypercorrection does, and it dictates sequencing: 未 and 末 should be presented CLOSE together and alternating, not separated by 15 intervening items. Note this directly contradicts the brief's blanket 're-queue with interleave-distance constraints' rule, which would push confusables apart. The correct rule is conditional: space repetitions of the SAME item widely; interleave DIFFERENT-but-confusable items tightly. The item schema needs a `confusion_set_id` distinct from the brief's `isomorph_group_id`, and the scheduler needs both a minimum gap (same item) and a maximum gap (within confusion set).

added_by_critics.claim: The single best-evidenced fix for competition among mixed-proficiency friends is equal-opportunity scoring: players contribute to the team score based on improvement over their OWN prior average, not on absolute correctness. This is a core, decades-old component of the cooperative-learning tradition the brief spends three findings on — and it never mentions it.
