sources: Slavin, R. E. (1980). Cooperative learning. Review of Educational Research, 50(2), 315–342. [NOT FETCHED]
Slavin, R. E. (1995). Cooperative Learning: Theory, Research, and Practice (2nd ed.). Allyn & Bacon. [NOT FETCHED]
Slavin, R. E. (2011). Instruction based on cooperative learning. In Mayer & Alexander (Eds.), Handbook of Research on Learning and Instruction. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: A co-located game among friends or family will have wildly heterogeneous Chinese proficiency — that is the condition under which competitive structures do their documented damage, because outcome and ability become perfectly confounded. Slavin's Student Teams-Achievement Divisions solves this directly: every player has a personal base score, and points contributed to the team are a function of performance RELATIVE TO THAT BASE, so the weakest player can contribute the maximum. This subsumes and improves on the brief's proposed 'team score × proportion of members contributing' formula, which still rewards raw correctness and therefore still makes the beginner a liability. It also delivers the mastery-goal / self-referenced-progress framing the brief wants from Ames (1992) as a scoring rule rather than as a UI afterthought. Implement as: contribution = f(correct_this_round − personal_rolling_baseline), clipped, with the baseline recomputed after each match.

added_by_critics.claim: Adaptive item difficulty targeting roughly a 75% success rate is the standard, empirically-grounded way to run a mixed-ability practice GAME, and there is a directly analogous production system with published evidence at national scale.
sources: Klinkenberg, S., Straatemeier, M., & van der Maas, H. L. J. (2011). Computer adaptive practice of maths ability using a new item response model for on the fly ability and difficulty estimation. Computers & Education, 57(2), 1813–1824. (Math Garden / Rekentuin) [NOT FETCHED]
van der Maas, H. L. J., & Nyamsuren, E. (2017). Cognitive analysis of educational games: The number game. Topics in Cognitive Science, 9(2), 395–412. [NOT FETCHED]

Wauters, K., Desmet, P., & Van den Noortgate, W. (2010). Adaptive item-based learning environments based on the item response theory. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 26(6), 549–562. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: Math Garden runs an Elo rating on players AND items simultaneously, updated after every response with a scoring rule that incorporates response time, and deliberately serves items at a target success probability (Klinkenberg et al. used a user-selectable difficulty corresponding to roughly 60/75/90% success). This is the mechanism the brief gropes toward with its invented '≥5 prior exposures' gate, and it is strictly better: it makes the opponent-dealing mechanic safe by construction, because the dealing algorithm can be constrained to items within a rating band of the target player rather than to a hand-set exposure count. It also gives you the difficulty estimates needed to make Slavin-style improvement scoring fair, and an Elo update is a few lines of code with no training data requirement — it works from the first match. This is the highest value-per-line-of-code item in the whole review.

added_by_critics.claim: Team scoring without individual identifiability produces social loafing — a well-established meta-analytic effect of moderate size. The brief asserts 'individual accountability' as a principle but proposes to show contributions only PRIVATELY and only AFTER the match, which is close to the condition under which loafing occurs.
sources: Karau, S. J., & Williams, K. D. (1993). Social loafing: A meta-analytic review and theoretical integration. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 65(4), 681–706. (~78 studies) [NOT FETCHED]
Latané, B., Williams, K., & Harkins, S. (1979). Many hands make light the work: The causes and consequences of social loafing. JPSP, 37(6), 822–832. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: Karau & Williams's Collective Effort Model identifies the moderators that eliminate loafing: individual contributions must be identifiable and evaluable, the task must be seen as meaningful, and the group must be small and valued. The brief's design satisfies 'small and valued' but deliberately hides identifiability to protect against ability attributions — and those two goals are in direct tension, which the brief never acknowledges. The resolution is to make contribution identifiable IN REAL TIME to the contributor and to the team in a form that carries no ability implication: show that each player HAS contributed (a filled dot per player per round) without showing how much or how accurately. Presence-of-contribution is an effort cue, which is what Ames (1992) wants made salient; magnitude-of-contribution is the ability cue to suppress. That resolves the tension rather than trading one harm for the other.

added_by_critics.claim: Do not build a neural knowledge-tracing model. Deep knowledge tracing's reported advantage over simple logistic and Bayesian models largely evaporates once the simpler models are given equivalent features, and it reverses on small datasets — which is what a v1 with a few hundred players has.
sources: Khajah, M., Lindsey, R. V., & Mozer, M. C. (2016). How deep is knowledge tracing? Proceedings of the 9th International Conference on Educational Data Mining (EDM). [NOT FETCHED]
Gervet, T., Koedinger, K., Schneider, J., & Mitchell, T. (2020). When is deep learning the best approach to knowledge tracing? Journal of Educational Data Mining, 12(3), 31–54. [NOT FETCHED]
Wilson, K. H., Karklin, Y., Han, B., & Ekanadham, C. (2016). Back to the basics: Bayesian extensions of IRT outperform neural networks for proficiency estimation. EDM 2016. [NOT FETCHED]
Settles, B., & Meeder, B. (2016). A trainable spaced repetition model for language learning. Proceedings of ACL 2016. (Duolingo half-life regression) [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: Khajah et al. showed that adding forgetting, item difficulty, and student ability to Bayesian Knowledge Tracing closes most of the gap DKT claimed; Gervet et al. found logistic-regression approaches competitive or superior, with the neural advantage appearing only on large datasets with long interaction sequences. Settles & Meeder's half-life regression — a logistic model of recall probability as a function of lag and feature-weighted memory strength, trained on Duolingo's own data and reported to beat Leitner and Pimsleur baselines in production A/B tests — is the right reference implementation for this product and is publicly described in the ACL Anthology. Combined with the Elo item/player ratings above, that is the entire modelling stack: no training corpus required, interpretable enough to debug, and it degrades gracefully at n=20 users.

added_by_critics.claim: General running-text character coverage statistics are the WRONG basis for sequencing this item bank, and the brief quotes no coverage figure at all. Signage, menus and labels have a restricted, high-skew lexicon that a general-frequency list orders badly.
sources: Jun Da (2004). Chinese text computing — Modern Chinese character frequency list, derived from a ~258-million-character corpus of modern Chinese. Middle Tennessee State University. [NOT FETCHED]
中华人民共和国教育部 (2013). 通用规范汉字表 (Table of General Standard Chinese Characters) — 8,105 characters; Level 1 = 3,500. [NOT FETCHED]
中外语言交流合作中心 (2021). 国际中文教育中文水平等级标准 (Chinese Proficiency Grading Standards for International Chinese Language Education / 'HSK 3.0') — 3,000 characters, ~11,092 words across 9 levels. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: The commonly cited figures from Jun Da's corpus — roughly 89% running-text coverage at 1,000 characters, ~94% at 1,500, ~98% at 2,500, ~99.5% at 3,500 — are real but describe general modern prose. They should never be quoted in this design doc without naming that corpus, and they should not drive sequencing. A menu is dominated by cooking-method and ingredient characters (炒 chǎo stir-fry, 蒸 zhēng steam, 煮 zhǔ boil, 炖 dùn stew, 烤 kǎo roast, 辣 là spicy, 汤 tāng soup, 面 miàn noodles, 饭 fàn rice); a supermarket label by 净含量 jìng hánliàng net weight, 保质期 bǎozhìqī best-before, 配料 pèiliào ingredients, 生产日期 shēngchǎn rìqī production date; a shopfront by 营业 yíngyè open-for-business, 折 zhé discount, 元 yuán. Several of these are mid-to-low frequency in general text and top-decile in domain. The correct move is to build or license a small domain corpus — photograph a few hundred real menus, labels and shopfronts — and sequence on domain frequency, reporting coverage against THAT corpus with its size stated. Any coverage percentage that ships without a named corpus should be struck from the doc.

added_by_critics.claim: Simplification merges distinct traditional characters into single simplified forms, and several of those merges land directly on menu and signage vocabulary. This is a content-correctness risk the brief does not mention, and it also determines whether the app can ever serve Taiwan/Hong Kong.
sources: Direct knowledge of standard simplified/traditional correspondences in modern Mandarin. [No dictionary fetched — egress blocked; every pair below should be spot-checked against a reference such as 现代汉语词典 before authoring]
added_by_critics.implication: The consequential merges for this product: 面 in simplified covers both 面 miàn 'face/surface' and 麵 miàn 'flour/noodles' (traditional keeps them distinct) — so 牛肉面 niúròumiàn 'beef noodles' is 牛肉麵 in Taipei. 干 in simplified covers 干 gān, 乾 gān 'dry', and 幹 gàn 'to do' — so 干炒牛河 gān chǎo niú hé is 乾炒牛河, and a naive gloss of 干 as 'to do' on a menu is simply wrong. Also 里/裡 (lǐ, inside), 后/後 (hòu, after — vs 后 hòu 'queen'), 发/發 (fā) vs 髮 (fà, hair), 谷/穀, 松/鬆, 云/雲. Product consequences: (1) the item schema needs separate `simplified`, `traditional`, and `sense_id` fields, because one simplified form can map to two traditional forms with different meanings, and a one-to-one mapping table WILL generate wrong content; (2) the meaning gloss must be attached to the sense in context, not to the character in isolation — 干 on a menu means 'dry', full stop; (3) if traditional is ever supported, it is not a font swap or a table lookup, it is a re-authoring of the affected items. Decide now whether v1 is simplified-only and write that into the schema, rather than discovering the merge problem during localisation.

added_by_critics.claim: The 'read the subway' pillar is the weakest of the brief's four target situations, because mainland metro signage is systematically bilingual and romanised, while menus, supermarket labels and shopfronts are frequently Chinese-only.
sources: Direct knowledge of Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen metro signage conventions, which pair Chinese station names with Hanyu Pinyin and/or English, and use standardised bilingual wayfinding. [Not verified against a signage corpus or the relevant GB standard — egress blocked; verify against GB/T 30240 'Guidelines for the use of English in public service areas' before relying on it]
added_by_critics.implication: A learner who cannot read 换乘 huànchéng 'transfer' will read 'Transfer' printed underneath it. That does not make subway items worthless — line names, exit lettering, 首/末班车 shǒu/mòbānchē first/last train, and service notices are often Chinese-dense — but it means subway signage should be the SMALLEST of the four content pillars, not an equal quarter. The genuinely Chinese-only reading demand, and therefore the strongest product wedge, is: supermarket labels (ingredients, allergens, best-before), menus at non-tourist restaurants, and shopfront/service signage (opening hours, 营业中 yíngyè zhōng, discount notices). Rebalance the item budget accordingly, and validate the premise cheaply by photographing the actual environments before authoring 400 items against an assumption.

added_by_critics.claim: On handwriting: the brief defers it and is right to, but not for the reason it implies. There is real evidence that handwriting practice strengthens orthographic representations in learners of Chinese — 'handwriting is unnecessary' is as overstated as 'handwriting is essential'.
sources: Guan, C. Q., Liu, Y., Chan, D. H. L., Ye, F., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Writing strengthens orthography and alphabetic-coding strengthens phonology in learning to read Chinese. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 509–522. [NOT FETCHED]

Xu, Y., Chang, L.-Y., Zhang, J., & Perfetti, C. A. (2013). Reading, writing, and animation in character learning in Chinese as a foreign language. Foreign Language Annals, 46(3), 423–444. [NOT FETCHED]

Cao, F., Vu, M., Chan, D. H. L., et al. (2013). Writing affects the brain network of reading in Chinese: A functional magnetic resonance imaging study. Human Brain Mapping, 34(7), 1670–1684. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: Guan et al. compared handwriting practice against pinyin/alphabetic coding in learning to read Chinese and found writing practice specifically benefited orthographic knowledge — the very skill this app targets — while alphabetic coding benefited phonology. The animation studies (Xu et al.) find that watching stroke animations captures some but not all of the benefit. So the honest framing for the design doc is: deferring handwriting is a legitimate SCOPE decision that trades a measurable orthographic benefit for build cost and for the fact that handwriting cannot be done well on a phone at a dinner table. It is not an evidence-backed conclusion that handwriting is unnecessary. Cheap partial capture: show a stroke-order animation inside the explanation card on first exposure and on error, which costs one asset per character and no interaction design.

added_by_critics.claim: If tone is ever added: tone colour-coding is unsupported folklore, while high-variability phonetic training has direct experimental support for Mandarin tone.
sources: Wang, Y., Spence, M. M., Jongman, A., & Sereno, J. A. (1999). Training American listeners to perceive Mandarin tones. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America, 106(6), 3649–3658. [NOT FETCHED]
Wang, Y., Jongman, A., & Sereno, J. A. (2003). Acoustic and perceptual evaluation of Mandarin tone productions before and after perceptual training. JASA, 113(2), 1033–1043. [NOT FETCHED]
Sadakata, M., & McQueen, J. M. (2014). Individual aptitude in Mandarin lexical tone perception predicts effectiveness of high-variability training. Frontiers in Psychology, 5, 1318. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: Tone colour-coding (the Pleco/Hanping convention of colouring characters by tone) is ubiquitous in learner tools and I could locate no controlled evidence that it improves tone acquisition or transfers to uncoloured text; the obvious risk — that learners become dependent on a cue absent from all real-world signage — is untested. Treat it as unsupported and, if used at all, as a temporary scaffold that must be fadeable. The supported route is high-variability phonetic training: Wang et al. trained American listeners with multiple talkers and reported large identification gains with generalisation to new talkers and new words, plus retention months later, and a follow-up showed transfer to production. Since this product's target skill is reading signage, none of this is v1 work — but it should be recorded so that a later 'add tones' decision does not default to colouring.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief wants a 'discriminating cue (radical, component, position)' field on every item. That is sound for MEANING but will produce wrong content if applied to PRONUNCIATION, because the phonetic component of a Chinese compound character is an unreliable pronunciation cue.
sources: Shu, H., Chen, X., Anderson, R. C., Wu, N., & Xuan, Y. (2003). Properties of school Chinese: Implications for learning to read. Child Development, 74(1), 27–47. [NOT FETCHED]
Shen, H. H., & Ke, C. (2007). Radical awareness and word acquisition among nonnative learners of Chinese. The Modern Language Journal, 91(1), 97–111. [NOT FETCHED]
Taft, M., & Chung, K. (1999). Using radicals in teaching Chinese characters to second language learners. Psychologia, 42(4), 243–251. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: In analyses of the characters children actually encounter, the semantic radical is a useful meaning cue for a clear majority of compound characters, but the phonetic component gives the exact syllable-plus-tone for only a minority — commonly reported in the region of a quarter to two-fifths depending on whether tone is required. Shen & Ke additionally found that CFL learners' radical awareness develops slowly and that semantic-radical knowledge outpaces phonetic-radical knowledge. Content-pipeline consequence: make the discriminating-cue field TYPED — `semantic_radical` | `contrast_character` | `position_in_compound` | `phonetic_hint` — and make `phonetic_hint` optional and individually verified, never auto-generated from a component table. An auto-generated phonetic hint will be wrong often enough to teach errors, and a wrong hint delivered as 'elaborated feedback' in the resolution moment is worse than no elaboration at all.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's anxiety reasoning is one step away from Krashen's Affective Filter, which is unfalsifiable and should be kept out of the design document. The defensible mechanism for 'pressure degrades performance' is attentional control / working-memory competition, which also supplies a better account of the Beilock finding.
sources: Gregg, K. R. (1984). Krashen's monitor and Occam's razor. Applied Linguistics, 5(2), 79–100. [NOT FETCHED]
McLaughlin, B. (1987). Theories of Second-Language Learning. Edward Arnold. [NOT FETCHED]
Eysenck, M. W., Derakshan, N., Santos, R., & Calvo, M. G. (2007). Anxiety and cognitive performance: Attentional control theory. Emotion, 7(2), 336–353. [NOT FETCHED]
Sweller, J., van Merriënboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 261–292. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: The Affective Filter Hypothesis makes no falsifiable prediction — it explains success and failure equally well after the fact — and has been rejected as a scientific theory in the SLA methodology literature for forty years, while remaining popular in practitioner writing. If it appears in the design doc, a reviewer with SLA training will discount the surrounding argument. Attentional Control Theory gives the same practical guidance with a testable mechanism: anxiety impairs the inhibition and shifting functions of executive control, degrading processing EFFICIENCY (effort and time) more than effectiveness (accuracy). That predicts something the product can actually measure: under the adversarial mechanic, expect response LATENCY to inflate before accuracy drops. Latency is therefore the early-warning metric, and it is already in the brief's logging schema — this finding tells you what to do with it.

added_by_critics.claim: The 44×44 px touch target is a platform standard, not an empirical finding — and the empirical mobile-HCI work points to a somewhat different number in physical units. The brief specifies ≤14px and ≥17px type without any accessibility reference.
sources: Parhi, P., Karlson, A. K., & Bederson, B. B. (2006). Target size study for one-handed thumb use on small touchscreen devices. MobileHCI '06, ACM. [NOT FETCHED]
Colle, H. A., & Hiszem, K. J. (2004). Standing at a kiosk: Effects of key size and spacing on touch screen numeric keypad performance and user preference. Ergonomics, 47(13), 1406–1423. [NOT FETCHED]
W3C (2018/2023). WCAG 2.1 SC 2.5.5 Target Size (AAA, 44×44 CSS px); WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA, 24×24 CSS px). [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: 44×44 originates in Apple's Human Interface Guidelines and is echoed in WCAG 2.1 as a AAA criterion; Google Material specifies 48dp; WCAG 2.2's AA minimum is 24×24 CSS px with spacing exceptions. The empirical work is in physical units and gives roughly 9.2mm for discrete one-handed thumb tapping and ~9.6mm for serial tapping (Parhi et al.), which at typical modern phone densities is comfortably above 44 CSS px. Practical consequence for this product: answer-option targets are pressed under time pressure, one-handed, possibly on a table in a bar — pick ~9–10mm physical, verify with a device-pixel-ratio-aware measurement rather than a CSS constant, and cite WCAG 2.2 AA as the floor and Parhi as the target. Separately, the brief's ≤14px / ≥17px type sizes have no source and will fail WCAG 1.4.4 resize and 1.4.3 contrast checks if 'muted colour at 14px' is taken literally — specify type in rem with a contrast ratio, not in fixed px.

added_by_critics.claim: There is a small but real literature on CO-LOCATED digital play specifically, which the brief lists as an unfilled gap. It supports the format on enjoyment and social-presence grounds — which is the honest basis for this product's format choice.
sources: Gajadhar, B. J., de Kort, Y. A. W., & IJsselsteijn, W. A. (2008). Shared fun is doubled fun: Player enjoyment as a function of social setting. Fun and Games 2008, LNCS. [NOT FETCHED]
Emmerich, K., & Masuch, M. (2017). The impact of game patterns on player experience and social interaction in co-located multiplayer games. CHI PLAY '17, ACM. [NOT FETCHED]
Vorderer, P., Hartmann, T., & Klimmt, C. (2003). Explaining the enjoyment of playing video games: The role of competition. ICEC '03, ACM. [NOT FETCHED]
added_by_critics.implication: Gajadhar et al. compared solo, mediated-social and co-located play and found co-located play produced the highest enjoyment and perceived social presence — the effect of physical co-presence exceeded that of merely knowing a human opponent existed. Combined with Wouters et al.'s group-play moderator, this is a defensible evidential basis for the co-located format on the ENGAGEMENT axis, which is exactly where the brief already concludes competition earns its place. It is not evidence for a learning benefit, and the brief should claim only the former. Emmerich & Masuch is the more directly useful reference for the design question the brief actually faces — which co-located game patterns (shared goal, direct competition, asymmetric roles) produce which social outcomes — and is in the ACM DL, one of the sources the brief was told to use and never reached.

added_by_critics.claim: 通用规范汉字表 (Table of General Standard Chinese Characters, GF 0023-2013) is a strictly better character spine than HSK for this product, and there is an MIT-licensed machine-readable copy that also solves the heteronym and traditional-variant problems the brief created for itself.
sources: https://github.com/jaywcjlove/table-of-general-standard-chinese-characters — cloned and analysed this session. MIT. data/characters.json = 8,105 characters in the three official tiers (3,500 / 3,000 / 1,605); data/pinyin.duo.json = 597 多音字 with all readings; data/simplified.convert.json = 1,489 simp→trad with 1:many arrays; data/traditional.convert.json = 1,520 trad→simp; data/pinyin.json per-character readings
Cross-check computed this session: HSK 3.0's 3,000 characters are 98.9% inside TGH tier 1 (2,967), 33 in tier 2, 0 outside TGH entirely
added_by_critics.implication: TGH strictly CONTAINS HSK 3.0 and adds the ~500 tier-1 characters HSK omits — which is exactly where the brief's own missing signage characters live (笋 藕 韭 are TGH tier 1 but absent from HSK 3.0). Use TGH tier as the difficulty spine and HSK band only as a secondary signal, which also reduces your dependence on the HSK trademark the brief correctly warns about. Take the 597-entry 多音字 table directly — it is the fastest fix for the pinyin-correctness problem. Take the 1:many trad tables as a HAZARD LIST, not a converter: any string containing 干, 发, 只, 台, 历, 钟, 复, 尽, 系 must be hand-authored if you ever render traditional. LEGAL CAVEAT, same shape as the HSK one the brief analysed well: GF 0023-2013 is a PRC national standard, so a third party's MIT grant covers their transcription labour only, not any rights the issuing body may assert. Attribute the repo, and treat the underlying list as facts.

added_by_critics.claim: The photographed-signage corpus — the brief's single highest-value recommendation and claimed moat — has an unexamined copyright, trademark and privacy problem, and the brief's proposed marketing claim ('we photographed 200 real menus in Chengdu') makes it worse by advertising the provenance.
sources: Legal analysis from first principles; no case law reachable this session (all scholarly and legal domains 403 at the egress proxy). Graded moderate and flagged for counsel, not asserted as settled.
Brief's own text: 'Consider shipping a "we photographed 200 real menus in Chengdu" provenance claim' and 'every item carries {string, gloss, …}' with photographs implied as item media
added_by_critics.implication: Separate the TEXT from the IMAGE — they have completely different risk profiles. Individual dish names and station names are short factual phrases with thin-to-no copyright, and a frequency count over them is your own work; that half of the moat is clean. The photographs are not: menu layout and typography, dish photography, package artwork and shopfront logos are all protected expression, and shipping them in a commercial app is redistribution. Trademark compounds it — a photographed shopfront carries a live mark. Privacy compounds it again: a Dutch controller photographing inside private premises engages GDPR the instant a person is in frame, and PRC PIPL applies at collection. CONCRETE PIPELINE REQUIREMENT: ship transcribed text set in your own licensed font, never the source photograph. Use photographs as internal reference material only, kept out of the repo and out of the bundle. If a photograph must appear in-app for authenticity, shoot it yourself, frame out people, logos and third-party food photography, and record per-item provenance (location, date, permission asked). Drop the 'we photographed 200 real menus' marketing line — it converts a private research practice into a public admission, for no product benefit that a plain 'built from real-world signage' claim does not also deliver.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's typography spec (48–64 px hanzi) is not just unverified — it is dimensionally ambiguous in a way that makes it unimplementable, and it conflicts with the brief's own layout requirements.
sources: Internal-consistency analysis of the brief against its own layout requirements; no CJK legibility literature reachable this session (all scholarly domains 403)

Brief's own conflicting requirements: 'primary hanzi at 48–64 px minimum', 'hanzi that the player must discriminate between at no less than 56 px', plus a grid of candidate hanzi strings, plus a gloss, plus bid controls, on one phone screen
added_by_critics.implication: The spec never says CSS px or device px, and the two differ by a factor of 2–3 across the phones at any real table. At 56 CSS px on a 360 CSS-px-wide phone you fit six characters per line with no margin — but the brief also demands a Codenames-style grid of candidate strings AND a visible gloss AND bid controls on the same screen. Those requirements cannot all hold. The right spec unit is not font size at all, it is STROKE SEPARATION IN DEVICE PIXELS: a 15-stroke character such as 蔬 needs roughly one device pixel of clear space between adjacent strokes to stay resolvable, which lands near 24–28 CSS px on a 3x display and near 40 CSS px on a 2x display. Branch the type scale on window.devicePixelRatio rather than shipping one number. Keep the brief's sound sub-claims — weight 400/500 never 300, AAA 7:1 contrast on hanzi, generous line-height — and resolve the size by testing the actual subset font on the oldest supported phone, as the brief itself says. Also drop the '48–64 px' figure from any design system doc until that test is done; a number in a spec gets implemented whether or not it carries a caveat.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's blanket exclusion of handwriting rests on a contested empirical premise it does not need, and defending it weakens an otherwise correct decision.
sources: No literature reachable this session (all scholarly domains 403). The writing-supports-reading line associated with Tan, Spinks, Eden, Perfetti & Siok (PNAS, 2005) and subsequent work on motor traces in orthographic learning is cited from knowledge and was NOT accessed; later work reporting small or absent effects for adult L2 learners is likewise cited from knowledge only.
Brief's own claim: 'Handwriting practice is slow (tens of seconds per item versus 1–3 seconds for a recognition item)' — a turn-budget argument, which is independently sound
added_by_critics.implication: Keep the decision, drop half the justification. The turn-budget argument alone is decisive and needs no literature: a 30-second turn idles three players for 90 seconds and the table's attention collapses. That is sufficient. The additional claim that handwriting has no transfer to reading is NOT established — there is a real research line arguing the opposite for character recognition specifically — and asserting it in a design document invites a reviewer to reopen a settled decision on the weakest available ground. If you want the benefit without the cost: offer an optional off-the-clock finger-trace on items a player has failed repeatedly, outside the turn timer, never as a scored interaction. That is the same shape as the brief's own (correct) handling of optional mnemonics.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's confusable-distractor mandate is asserted without evidence and is in direct tension with its own critique of Duolingo; as specified it is likely to induce interference rather than discrimination.
sources: Internal-contradiction analysis of the brief; no paired-associate or contextual-interference literature reachable this session (all scholarly domains 403)

Brief's own text: 'pick 2–3 distractors that share a component with the target (same radical, or same phonetic, or same overall stroke silhouette)' vs its Duolingo criticism that 'three distractors that are not visually confusable' let a learner shape-match
added_by_critics.implication: Duolingo's failure mode is distractors that are too EASY. The brief's fix is maximum confusability, which is the opposite extreme, not the correct point — and a learner who has never seen 请 will not learn it by being shown 请 清 情 晴 simultaneously; they will learn a fuzzy blend of all four. Make confusability a FUNCTION of the player's exposure state for that item: first correct encounter uses semantically and visually distant distractors; component-sharing distractors unlock only after the item has been answered correctly at least once. This also fits the brief's deterministic-reducer constraint — exposure count is already per-player state, and the distractor tier is a pure function of (item, exposure_count, seed), so every phone still derives an identical set. Log the distractor set alongside the outcome so this can be settled on your own data rather than asserted, which is currently the only way it will ever be settled.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's signature UX mechanic — 'make the gloss cost points, in public' — has zero support and is contradicted by the brief's own co-operative-mode finding.
sources: Internal-contradiction analysis; no retrieval-practice or desirable-difficulties literature reachable this session (all scholarly domains 403)

Brief's own text: 'Revealing a gloss should deduct from the current bid, and the other players at the table should see that it happened. The social cost of asking for help is the mechanism' vs, two findings later, 'purely competitive language games punish the weakest player publicly, which is the fastest way to end a game night'
added_by_critics.implication: Both cannot be right. Making help publicly expensive is precisely the mechanism the brief elsewhere identifies as the fastest way to end a game night — and the predictable failure is that a beginner stops requesting glosses and starts guessing, which converts a retrieval attempt into a coin flip and teaches nothing while the score still moves. Separate the two variables the brief has fused: make the gloss cost POINTS (private, real, preserves the retrieval incentive) but not VISIBILITY (public, social, punishes the weakest player). Ship the public-cost variant behind a flag, default it OFF for any table containing a first-time player, and treat it as the first thing to A/B once you have tables. This is the highest-risk unvalidated bet in the brief and it is currently presented as its central design insight.

added_by_critics.claim: The severe method caveat is unchanged after this review: no scholarly source was reachable to me either, so the entire pedagogy and landscape half remains unverified — but the reachable surface is larger than the brief realised, and that is where the next sweep should start.
sources: Egress probe run this session: 403 CONNECT from the agent proxy for scholar.google.com, api.semanticscholar.org, arxiv.org, aclanthology.org, journals.plos.org, doi.org, api.openalex.org, files.eric.ed.gov, osf.io, ncbi.nlm.nih.gov, en.wikipedia.org, www.unicode.org, www.mdbg.net, tatoeba.org, commonvoice.mozilla.org, huggingface.co, cdn.jsdelivr.net. WebSearch: 'used its web search budget (200 of 200)'.
Reachable and exploited this session: github.com, api.github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, registry.npmjs.org, pypi.org / files.pythonhosted.org
added_by_critics.implication: npm and PyPI are reachable and the brief never used them — that is how I measured every font and stroke-data figure it had to estimate, and how I installed fonttools/brotli to test its subsetting recommendation empirically. Any claim of the form 'this dataset is N megabytes' or 'this package ships X' is answerable TODAY without a search budget: npm pack it and measure. Reserve the next sweep's search budget strictly for claims that need a paper, in this priority order — (1) whether any efficacy study of Duolingo Chinese exists, since 'the market leader has no evidence for its Chinese course' is a positioning claim you would repeat publicly and must not get wrong; (2) a recent meta-analysis on keyword-mnemonic durability, which decides whether mnemonics are core or optional; (3) the phono-semantic PREDICTIVENESS figure (not the type-count), which decides whether phonetic-series ordering earns one to two weeks of content authoring; (4) CJK mobile legibility, which sets the type scale. Everything else in Part 1 is descriptive product observation that a search will not improve. And do not re-run Part 2's licence readings — re-run Part 2's NUMBERS, which is where the errors actually are.

added_by_critics.claim: SPACING IS THE LARGEST OMISSION IN THE BRIEF. It is the best-evidenced manipulation in L2 vocabulary learning specifically, and the brief mentions it only as one word in a list of 'the canonical five' — deriving no architecture from it at all.
sources: Kim, S. K., & Webb, S. (2022). The Effects of Spaced Practice on Second Language Learning: A Meta-Analysis. Language Learning, 72(2), 269–319. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/lang.12479 — 98 effect sizes, 48 experiments, N = 3,411; compares spaced vs massed, longer vs shorter spacing, and equal vs expanding spacing, on both immediate and delayed post-tests, with nine moderators.
Does spaced practice have the same effects on different L2 vocabulary learning activities? Fill-in-the-blanks versus flashcards. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/376584142
added_by_critics.implication: Two consequences the brief misses. (1) Scheduling is the highest-leverage architectural decision in any vocabulary product and there is no finding covering it — the whole brief is about a single session's encoding. Add a between-session scheduler and make the spaced-vs-massed contrast, plus the equal-vs-expanding question, a first-class design decision with this meta-analysis as its evidence base. (2) A co-located party game is structurally MASSED: a table plays one sitting, and the brief's own high-confidence-miss rule (finding 22) requeues the missed item WITHIN THE SAME SESSION, which is the weakest schedule this literature identifies. That rule is defended by hypercorrection ('a test must intervene after feedback'), which is fine, but it should not be mistaken for good scheduling. The product needs a reason for players to return, or its best-evidenced lever is unavailable to it — and that is a business-model finding, not just a memory one.

added_by_critics.claim: HANDWRITING/TRACING IS THE BEST-EVIDENCED CHINESE-SPECIFIC ENCODING MANIPULATION IN THE FIELD, AND IT IS THE ONE THING THE BRIEF EXPLICITLY BANS.
sources: Guan, C. Q., Liu, Y., Chan, D. H. L., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Writing strengthens orthography and alphabetic-coding strengthens phonology in learning to read Chinese. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 509–522 — 48 adult CFL learners, five consecutive days, handwriting-to-read vs pinyin-typing-to-read. https://sites.pitt.edu/~perfetti/PDF/Writing%20strengthens%20Guan%20JEP.pdf

Cao, F., et al. (2013). Journal of Neurolinguistics, 26(4), 440–461 — writing vs visual chunking vs reading-only training in adult CFL learners, with follow-up at three months. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0911604413000043
Comparison studies of typing and handwriting in Chinese language learning: A synthetic review. System (2021). https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0883035521000100
Writing quality predicts Chinese learning. Reading and Writing (2015). https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11145-015-9549-0
added_by_critics.implication: A single finger-trace of one component on the reveal — not full stroke-order drilling, not scored, not gating — is a defensible cheap experiment with better Chinese-specific evidence behind it than the typeface-variability mechanic the brief promotes to a MUST. It also fits the co-located phone/tablet form factor exactly. Caveat honestly: Guan et al. ran five days with 48 learners and measured form recognition and meaning; whether a two-second trace in a party game reproduces any of that is untested. But 'untested' is a reason to instrument it, not a reason to write 'never' into the spec.

added_by_critics.claim: SEMANTIC VERSUS PHONETIC COMPONENTS IS A MISSING DIMENSION OF THE DECOMPOSITION SCHEMA. Phonetic radicals predict a character's pronunciation only about 40% of the time; semantic radicals carry more reliable meaning cues.
sources: Perfetti, C. A., Liu, Y., & Tan, L. H. The Lexical Constituency Model. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/8098601_The_Lexical_Constituency_Model_Some_Implications_of_Research_on_Chinese_for_General_Theories_of_Reading — for compound characters, meaning cues from semantic radicals are more reliable than pronunciation cues from phonetic radicals, the latter at approximately 40% accuracy.
The interaction of orthography, phonology and semantics in L2 learners' Chinese character production. Frontiers in Psychology (2023), 14:1076810. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10017467/
Teaching Semantic Radicals Facilitates Inferring New Character Meaning in Sentence Reading for Nonnative Chinese Speakers. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5660119/
added_by_critics.implication: The brief's `transparency` enum (transparent | semi | opaque) operates at the WORD level, on multi-character compounds. It has no equivalent at the CHARACTER level, where the majority of Chinese characters are semantic-plus-phonetic compounds and where the inference rule the learner is being taught is right about meaning and wrong about sound roughly 60% of the time. Add a per-component `role` field: semantic | phonetic | neither. The breakdown screen should gloss semantic components ('this part means water') and must NOT invite meaning inference from a phonetic component — that installs exactly the misfiring rule the brief warns about for opaque compounds, at far greater frequency. This is the same argument the brief makes correctly about 东西, applied one level down where it bites harder.

added_by_critics.claim: CURIOSITY CAN IMPAIR MEMORY FOR INCIDENTAL INSTRUCTIONAL CONTENT — the direct counter-evidence to the brief's reveal-screen architecture, published and unaddressed.
sources: States of epistemic curiosity interfere with memory for incidental scholastic facts. npj Science of Learning (2024). https://www.nature.com/articles/s41539-024-00234-w — memory was POORER for scholastic facts presented after trivia questions that had elicited high versus low curiosity.
Temporal proximity to the elicitation of curiosity is key for enhancing memory for incidental information. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7812865/
Curiosity Killed the Cat but Not Memory. Brain Sciences (2022), 12(7), 846. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9313209/

Fandakova, Y., & Gruber, M. J. (2021). States of curiosity and interest enhance memory differently in adolescents and in children. Developmental Science. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/desc.13005
added_by_critics.implication: The brief proposes putting the component breakdown into the high-curiosity reveal window BECAUSE curiosity boosts incidental encoding. The nearest published analogue — incidental SCHOLASTIC FACTS following a curiosity-eliciting question, rather than Gruber's unrelated faces — found the opposite. Do not build the reveal-screen placement on this rationale. There are two better ones available and already in the brief: spatial/temporal contiguity with the answer (finding 20's split-attention argument) and feedback timing on a pretest (finding 23). Both are stronger and neither requires an fMRI paper. If the team wants to keep the curiosity rationale, it is a hypothesis to A/B, not a warrant.

added_by_critics.claim: VISUAL WORKING MEMORY IS NOT ESTABLISHED AS A SLOT SYSTEM, so no integer UI constant can be derived from it. The slots-versus-continuous-resource question is open.
sources: Ma, W. J., Husain, M., & Bays, P. M. (2014). Changing concepts of working memory. Nature Neuroscience — the slots/resources debate is explicitly unresolved.
Resources masquerading as slots: Flexible allocation of visual working memory. Cognitive Psychology (2016). https://www2.psy.unsw.edu.au/Users/CDonkin/publications/cp16b.pdf
Failure of self-consistency in the discrete resource model of visual working memory. Cognitive Psychology (2018). https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0010028518300239
Suchow, Fougnie, Brady & Alvarez (2014). Terms of the debate on the format and structure of visual memory. https://bradylab.ucsd.edu/pdfs/SuchowFougnieBradyAlvarez2014.pdf
Modelling Working Memory Capacity: Is the Magical Number Four, Seven, or Does it Depend on What You Are Counting? Journal of Cognition (2024). https://journalofcognition.org/articles/10.5334/joc.387
added_by_critics.implication: Generalises beyond finding 5. Any design rule in this product of the shape 'show at most N items' is inheriting a contested parameter and should be written as a load rule instead: how many elements must be INTEGRATED to grasp the item, and how many are reference material the eye can re-sample. The brief already has the right tool for this in its own findings on element interactivity and split attention — it should use that tool consistently rather than reaching for a capacity constant when it wants a number.

added_by_critics.claim: THE BRIEF IS CLEAN ON THE FIELD'S FIVE CLASSIC FRAUDS — and that is worth recording explicitly, because their absence is a decision, not an oversight.
sources: Verified by inspection of all 27 findings: no learning-styles claim (the field's most thoroughly refuted idea) appears anywhere; no Ebbinghaus forgetting curve is quoted (the usual quotation misrepresents a single-subject nonsense-syllable self-experiment as a universal law); no '10,000 hours' claim appears; no bizarreness effect appears (it is unreliable outside mixed-list designs and reverses in pure lists); no method of loci claim appears (its evidence base is serial recall of ordered lists, which does not transfer to the recognition and meaning-retrieval this product needs).

Dunlosky, J., et al. (2013). Improving Students' Learning With Effective Learning Techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58 — already cited in the brief; the source that rates these techniques.
added_by_critics.implication: Two things follow. First, do not let a later revision reintroduce them: put an explicit exclusion list in the design document naming learning styles, the Ebbinghaus curve, 10,000 hours, the bizarreness effect, and method of loci as banned rationales, so nobody adds a 'visual learner' onboarding question or a memory-palace mode in six months. Second, the failure mode the brief was screened for DOES appear, just in a more sophisticated dress: the fMRI-as-design-warrant in finding 24 and the WM-capacity-as-layout-constant in finding 5 are the same error wearing better citations. Those two are where the review effort should go, not on the classic frauds.

added_by_critics.claim: THE BRIEF'S OWN ACCESS CAVEAT IS TOO PESSIMISTIC AND THEREFORE TOO PERMISSIVE. Its central gap says every academic domain was blocked and every number is unverified; in fact search-level verification is available and catches real errors.
sources: Verified in this review by search-level checking: Kurita (2026) r=.31 and its moderators — confirmed as stated. Bisra et al. (2018) g=.55, 69 effect sizes, 64 reports, 20 moderators — confirmed exactly. Yanagisawa & Webb (2021) 398 effect sizes, N=4,628, 15.0%/5.1%, evaluation > need > search — confirmed exactly. Morris, Bransford & Franks (1977) crossover, replicated at immediate and delayed test in Exp 2 — confirmed. Lee & Kalyuga (2011) vertical-format advantage attributed to eliminating split attention — confirmed. Higdon et al., 'Distinctiveness, not dual coding' — confirmed (QJEP 78(1), 180–191; picture superiority eliminated when physical distinctiveness was equated).

Errors caught the same way: Symons & Johnson d (0.65 unverifiable, ~0.50 reported); Rowland's format moderators (free recall g≈0.79 vs MC g≈0.36) understated; Pelzl typeface effects (one-to-two words, single session) overstated; Cao et al. 2013 misattributed; Wang/Thomas/Ouellette authors and two-day interval omitted; Murre 2021's failed-replication result unstated; Kang & Pashler DOI mismatched.
added_by_critics.implication: Rewrite the access caveat. Publisher full text is genuinely blocked, but abstracts, effect sizes, sample sizes and moderator structures are recoverable through search indexes for essentially every source in this brief — I verified fourteen claims and found errors in six of them without reading a single Methods section. 'I could not check it' therefore does not excuse a number appearing in a spec. Concretely: before any figure in this brief becomes load-bearing, run the same search-level check, and mark each claim with a `verified_at` level (search-abstract / full-text) rather than a blanket 'abstract-only' that flattens a verified meta-analytic g together with an unverifiable d.

added_by_critics.claim: Multiple-choice testing with plausible lures reliably produces later intrusions of those lures — learners subsequently produce the wrong alternatives they read. This is a documented cost of exactly the format 看不懂 is built on, and it is mitigated primarily by immediate corrective feedback.
sources: Roediger, H. L., & Marsh, E. J. (2005). The positive and negative consequences of multiple-choice testing. JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 31(5), 1155–1159. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION — all scholarly hosts 403 at the egress gateway; cited from reviewer's own knowledge.

Butler, A. C., & Roediger, H. L. (2008). Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing. Memory & Cognition, 36(3), 604–616. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Marsh, E. J., Roediger, H. L., Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2007). The memorial consequences of multiple-choice testing. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
added_by_critics.implication: This is the single largest omission in the brief. The app's core mechanic — four options, deliberately confusable — is the exact configuration that produces lure intrusions, and the brief's recommendation to pair 出口 with 入口 maximises the risk. Design consequences, all mandatory: (1) feedback is not optional and must be immediate at reveal; a round must never end without correction. (2) Feedback must be corrective, not merely verdictive — it must display the correct answer, and where the player chose a lure it must name that lure and mark it wrong explicitly, because feedback that only says 'incorrect' leaves the lure unopposed in memory. (3) An item answered wrong should have its *specific chosen lure* recorded in the schedule, so the next exposure of that item can present the same lure and force the discrimination that failed, rather than a random distractor set.

added_by_critics.claim: Making an unsuccessful guess before receiving the answer improves subsequent learning of that item, relative to studying it directly for the same total time — the pretesting or prequestion effect. Errors committed before feedback are not merely harmless, they are productive.
sources: Kornell, N., Hays, M. J., & Bjork, R. A. (2009). Unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance subsequent learning. JEP: LMC, 35(4), 989–998. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Richland, L. E., Kornell, N., & Kao, L. S. (2009). The pretesting effect: Do unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance learning? JEP: Applied, 15(3), 243–257. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Carpenter, S. K., & Toftness, A. R. (2017). The effect of prequestions on learning from video presentations. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
added_by_critics.implication: This replaces the Reggente 'explicit binding' analogy as the justification for the bet, and it is a much better fit: the bet is literally a commitment made before the answer is available, which is the pretesting manipulation. Two design consequences the Reggente framing would not have given you. (1) A wrong bet is pedagogically valuable, so the game must not punish wrong bets so heavily that players hedge or disengage — the scoring should keep guessing attractive. (2) The benefit comes from the guess-then-feedback sequence, so the gap between commitment and reveal should be short and guaranteed; never allow a round to leave a bet unresolved.

added_by_critics.claim: For material that must be retained until a fixed future date, the optimal spacing gap between study episodes scales with the retention interval — roughly on the order of ten to twenty percent of the time until the test — and both much shorter and much longer gaps lose substantial retention.
sources: Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T., & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 132(3), 354–380. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.

Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095–1102. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
added_by_critics.implication: The brief declares spacing out of scope and then makes scheduler recommendations anyway ('do not lengthen the interval', 'retire to a long interval'), which is not a tenable position. This finding answers the brief's own gap about a player learning weeks before a trip: the scheduler should take the trip date as an explicit input and space exposures as a proportion of the time remaining, rather than running a generic ease-factor algorithm. Concretely, add a target_date field to the player profile; if the trip is eight weeks out, gaps on the order of a week are indicated, not the one-to-three-day gaps a default SRS curve will produce. This is also the only intervention in the whole review that is evidenced at the retention interval the product actually cares about.

added_by_critics.claim: The scholarly refutation of pictographic character-story systems is not a blog post — it is a well-known body of sinological work establishing that the great majority of Chinese characters are phono-semantic compounds, not pictographs, and that the 'ideographic' account of the script is a persistent myth.
sources: DeFrancis, J. (1984). The Chinese Language: Fact and Fantasy. University of Hawaii Press — Ch. 8, 'The Ideographic Myth'. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Boltz, W. G. (1994). The Origin and Early Development of the Chinese Writing System. American Oriental Society. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Standard estimates that phono-semantic compounds constitute roughly 80–90% of the character inventory. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION — cited from reviewer's own knowledge.
added_by_critics.implication: The brief could only source its Chineasy criticism to Language Log and flagged as a gap that it found no peer-reviewed critique. The gap is an artefact of searching for 'Chineasy' rather than for the underlying claim. Cite DeFrancis for the design rule instead: because most characters are phono-semantic rather than pictographic, a system that supplies a picture-story for every character must be fabricating for the majority of them. This converts the brief's 'etymological vs mnemonic-only' data flag from a nice-to-have into a necessity, and gives it a defensible threshold: a component gloss may be marked etymological only where the component's role is semantic or phonetic on standard reference grounds, and everything else is marked invented.

added_by_critics.claim: Semantic radicals are only partially reliable as meaning cues, and their informativeness depends on position regularity and on the specific radical — so a component-decomposition feature that presents every radical as a dependable meaning clue will teach some confident falsehoods.
sources: Taft, M., & Zhu, X. (1997). Submorphemic processing in reading Chinese. JEP: Learning, Memory, and Cognition. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Feldman, L. B., & Siok, W. W. T. (1999). Semantic radicals contribute to the visual identification of Chinese characters. Journal of Memory and Language. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Shu, H., & Anderson, R. C. (1997). Role of radical awareness in the character and word acquisition of Chinese children. Reading Research Quarterly. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
added_by_critics.implication: Qualifies the brief's strongest positive recommendation. The component tree should carry a per-component reliability marker, not just a gloss — some semantic radicals are highly predictive of meaning, many are weakly or historically predictive, and phonetic components are unreliable for a learner who does not already know the component's reading (as the brief itself notes). Render high-reliability components prominently and low-reliability ones as background structure rather than as a meaning clue. Without this, the transfer engine the brief is counting on will generate confident wrong inferences on unseen characters, which is the Chineasy failure mode arriving through the front door.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's two flagship content recommendations pull against each other: crowding a learner with orthographically and semantically similar competitors is a documented source of associative interference, and the same similarity that makes a contrast instructive makes the items harder to keep apart in memory.
sources: Anderson, J. R. (1974). Retrieval of propositional information from long-term memory — the fan effect. Cognitive Psychology. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Anderson, M. C., Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (1994). Remembering can cause forgetting: Retrieval dynamics in long-term memory. JEP: LMC. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Nation, I. S. P., and the applied-vocabulary literature on the costs of teaching semantic sets and antonym pairs together. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION — cited from reviewer's own knowledge.
added_by_critics.implication: The brief recommends both simultaneous confusable pairing (出口 beside 入口) and component-family surfacing (after 口 in 出口, surface 入口, 门口, 窗口). Run together, these guarantee that a beginner meets a dense cluster of near-identical forms with related meanings in a short window — the configuration most likely to produce durable confusion. Resolve it by separating the two functions in time: use simultaneous pairing at the *resolution/teaching* moment, where the contrast is explained and feedback is present, and do not use component-family membership as a reason to schedule those items *close together in the deal*. Add an explicit anti-adjacency rule on component-family siblings, which is the opposite of what the brief specifies.

added_by_critics.claim: The instinct that a harder-to-read typeface improves memory is folklore. The widely publicised disfluent-font result failed in large, well-powered replications.
sources: Diemand-Yauman, C., Oppenheimer, D. M., & Vaughan, E. B. (2011). Fortune favors the bold (and the italicized). Cognition — the original claim. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Meyer, A., Frederick, S., et al. (2015). Disfluent fonts don't help people solve math problems. JEP: General — large-sample null. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Eitel, A., & Kühl, T., and subsequent replication work reporting null or negligible disfluency effects on learning. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
added_by_critics.implication: Pre-empt this before a stakeholder proposes it. A brief that recommends typeface variability invites the adjacent and much more famous 'make it harder to read' idea, which is not supported. State explicitly in the design doc: vary typefaces for perceptual generalisation to real-world signage; do not degrade legibility on the theory that difficulty aids memory. Weathered, low-contrast or grimy sign treatments should be included only where they reflect real signage the player will actually encounter, not as a deliberate difficulty manipulation.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief's resolution card is heading for cognitive overload. Splitting a learner's attention across multiple simultaneous sources that must be integrated, and duplicating the same information in redundant channels, both reliably impair learning — which is a direct constraint on how much can be stacked at the reveal moment.
sources: Sweller, J., Ayres, P., & Kalyuga, S. (2011). Cognitive Load Theory. Springer — split-attention and redundancy effects. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Mayer, R. E. (2009/2021). Multimedia Learning. Cambridge University Press — coherence, redundancy and signalling principles. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Kalyuga, S., Chandler, P., & Sweller, J., on the expertise reversal effect. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
added_by_critics.implication: Counted up, the brief wants the resolution card to carry: a component tree, a simultaneous confusable pair, a mnemonic line, a paired image, pinyin, a per-item speed indicator, and a timed unison say-it-aloud prompt. That is seven competing elements in a party-game reveal lasting a few seconds. Cut it. A defensible reveal is: the character on its substrate, the meaning, the one discriminating feature against the specific lure the player chose, and the say-aloud beat. Push the component tree and the confusable pair into a separate, self-paced 'why' view the player can open after the round. Note also the expertise-reversal implication: scaffolding that helps a first-time viewer actively costs a player who already knows the item, so the resolution card should thin out as an item's accuracy record improves.

added_by_critics.claim: On the three specific pieces of folklore this review was told to hunt — learning styles, the ten-thousand-hour rule, and the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve as usually quoted — the brief is clean: none of them appears. That is genuinely unusual for a memory-science brief and deserves recording, but the Ebbinghaus curve is likely to enter later via the scheduler, and should be pre-emptively barred.
sources: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2008). Learning styles: Concepts and evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3), 105–119. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.

Macnamara, B. N., Hambrick, D. Z., & Oswald, F. L. (2014). Deliberate practice and performance: A meta-analysis. Psychological Science — deliberate practice explains a modest fraction of variance. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
Murre, J. M. J., & Dros, J. (2015). Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve. PLOS ONE, 10(7), e0120644. UNVERIFIED THIS SESSION.
added_by_critics.implication: Credit where due: kill nothing here. But add a standing prohibition to the design doc for the spacing/scheduler sweep that follows, because that is where the forgetting curve always enters. The original curve is a single subject — Ebbinghaus on himself — memorising nonsense syllables, with savings-in-relearning as the dependent measure rather than recall, and the modern replication recovered a curve while documenting substantial variability. It is not a law and it does not supply the '70% forgotten in 24 hours' figure that scheduler design documents habitually quote. Any forgetting function in the scheduler should be fitted to the app's own per-item outcome data, which the brief's item-state schema already makes possible.

added_by_critics.claim: The literature gap the brief identifies — that no study tests a mnemonic technique against four-option recognition of Chinese characters with confusable distractors — is real, but the brief draws the wrong conclusion from it. The absence is an argument for building measurement into v1, not an argument for reasoning harder from mismatched studies.
sources: Derived from the brief's own gap analysis plus the standing state of the character-learning literature. No external source fetched — all scholarly hosts returned 403 at the egress gateway this session.
added_by_critics.implication: Every one of the brief's twenty-six findings is an extrapolation across at least one of: outcome measure, material type, retention interval, or population. Given that, the highest-value engineering decision is not any single feature — it is instrumentation that lets the app settle these questions on its own data within weeks. Minimum viable measurement: log per-exposure item id, substrate/typeface id, scaffolding rung, chosen option (not just correct/incorrect), response latency, and time since last exposure. That schema turns five of the review's open questions — does say-it-aloud help, does the finger trace help, does substrate variety help, does colour-coding hurt, what is the real forgetting function for these items — into A/B tests the product can run, rather than literature arguments it cannot win.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief never cites the retrieval-practice (testing) effect, despite retrieval being the app's entire core loop. This is the largest omission in the document, and it is the best-supported effect in the whole area.
sources: Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432–1463. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

Adesope, O. O., Trevisan, D. A., & Sundararajan, N. (2017). Rethinking the use of tests: A meta-analysis of practice testing. Review of Educational Research, 87(3), 659–701. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
added_by_critics.implication: Every scheduling and presentation decision in the brief is downstream of a decision the brief never argues for: that the app tests rather than shows. Cite the meta-analytic testing effect explicitly, because it is the strongest justification the product has and it is currently missing. Concretely it also settles a design question the brief leaves open: when an item is due, default to a retrieval attempt (with the sign shown and the meaning withheld) rather than a review/restudy card, and never let the UI offer a 'just show me the answers' review mode as the default path through a due queue.

added_by_critics.claim: The brief asserts there is no relevant L2-vocabulary spacing meta-analysis; there is, and it is more directly on-point for the product than Cepeda's trivia-fact ridgeline.
sources: Kim, S. K., & Webb, S. (2022). The effects of spaced practice on second language learning: A meta-analysis. Language Learning, 72(1), 269–319. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
Nakata, T. (2015). Effects of expanding and equal spacing on second language vocabulary learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 37(4), 677–711. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
added_by_critics.implication: Replace Cepeda as the primary scheduling citation with L2-specific spacing evidence, which is the correct material and population. Two design consequences the brief misses: (a) expanding and equal spacing schedules perform similarly in L2 vocabulary, so the engineering complexity of an expanding-interval algorithm is not obviously worth paying for — an equal-interval schedule is a defensible v1; (b) the L2 spacing literature is where the moderators the product actually cares about (learner proficiency, item difficulty, number of encounters) have been estimated, unlike the two-session trivia paradigm.

added_by_critics.claim: The optimal spacing gap is a function of the item's current memory strength, not of the calendar horizon alone — which is the correct replacement for the brief's fixed 15%-of-horizon formula and the basis for every adaptive scheduler that has been validated at scale.
sources: Pavlik, P. I., & Anderson, J. R. (2005). Practice and forgetting effects on vocabulary memory: An activation-based model of the spacing effect. Cognitive Science, 29(4), 559–586. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
Pavlik, P. I., & Anderson, J. R. (2008). Using a model to compute the optimal schedule of practice. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied, 14(2), 101–117. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
Settles, B., & Meeder, B. (2016). A trainable spaced repetition model for language learning. Proceedings of ACL 2016, 1848–1858. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
added_by_critics.implication: Architecture, and it directly patches the bug in the brief's scheduler: gap length must be conditioned on estimated item strength (encounters so far, recency, past success rate, per-item difficulty) as well as on the trip date. Practically — model each item with a strength estimate updated on every trial, schedule when predicted recall crosses a threshold, and let the trip date set the THRESHOLD (higher threshold as the trip approaches) rather than set the gap. This also gives the product a principled place to put the confusion-matrix signal from Nakata & Suzuki: sibling-confusion events should lower the item's strength estimate even when the answer was correct.

added_by_critics.claim: Handwriting or finger-tracing practice improves visual RECOGNITION of Chinese characters for L2 learners, specifically by strengthening orthographic representations — the exact deficit a confusable-pair app is trying to fix. The brief scopes the app to recognition and never engages this.
sources: Guan, C. Q., Liu, Y., Chan, D. H. L., Ye, F., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Writing strengthens orthography and alphabetic-coding strengthens phonology in learning to read Chinese. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 509–522. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

Cao, F., Vu, M., Chan, D. H. L., et al. (2013). Writing affects the brain network of reading in Chinese: A functional magnetic resonance imaging study. Human Brain Mapping, 34(7), 1670–1684. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
added_by_critics.implication: UI, and it is a cheap addition to an existing screen. A brief finger-trace of the distinguishing component at resolution time is a production-side intervention with direct evidence for improving the recognition outcome the app measures — and it is a better-grounded way to 'direct attention to the critical difference' than the colour ban the brief proposes. Scope it tightly: trace only the differing component (the top of 出 versus 入; the 公 in 公斤), only on the resolution screen for form-confusable pairs, and never as a required input on the timed card. This should be A/B'd against the passive side-by-side panel on delayed discrimination accuracy.

added_by_critics.claim: Learners' judgments about which study conditions work are systematically inverted for exactly the manipulations this app depends on, and the inversion is not limited to interleaving — it covers spacing, retrieval practice, and difficulty generally.
sources: Bjork, R. A., Dunlosky, J., & Kornell, N. (2013). Self-regulated learning: Beliefs, techniques, and illusions. Annual Review of Psychology, 64, 417–444. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
Kornell, N., & Bjork, R. A. (2008). Psychological Science, 19(6), 585–592. [cited in the brief; generalisation not drawn]
added_by_critics.implication: Product-metrics governance, and it is broader than the brief's single note about the confusable panel. Write it into the experimentation policy: no learning-relevant feature in this app may be killed or shipped on the basis of self-reported difficulty, perceived helpfulness, in-session accuracy, or session-satisfaction scores — all four move in the wrong direction for effective practice. The only admissible primary metric is delayed performance at ≥1 week, ideally on transfer items (a sign in a rendering the player has not seen). This constraint should be stated once at the top of the brief rather than buried in one finding, because it invalidates the default analytics stack a consumer app will otherwise use.

added_by_critics.claim: Perceptual disfluency as a learning aid — harder-to-read fonts, degraded stimuli — is folklore. The best-known instance failed to replicate in large, well-powered studies.
sources: Geller, J., Still, M. L., Dark, V. J., & Carpenter, S. K. (2018). Would disfluency by any other name still be beneficial? Memory & Cognition. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]

Taylor, A., Sanson, M., Burnell, R., Wade, K. A., & Garry, M. (2020). Disfluent difficulties are not desirable difficulties: The (lack of) effect of Sans Forgetica on memory. Memory, 28(7), 850–857. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
added_by_critics.implication: Pre-emptive negative recommendation, of the same kind the brief correctly makes for sleep-audio. A team that has absorbed 'desirable difficulties' will at some point propose degrading the sign rendering to make recognition harder — blurring, low contrast, a deliberately awkward typeface. There is no support for it and the best-publicised version failed replication. Distinguish clearly in the brief between difficulty that comes from RETRIEVAL demands (supported: spacing, testing, withholding the answer) and difficulty that comes from PERCEPTUAL degradation (unsupported). Note this does not conflict with the multiple-renderings recommendation: varying realistic renderings is variability, not degradation.

added_by_critics.claim: 'Storage strength versus retrieval strength' provides the same two-state item model the brief wants, without any neuroscience — and it makes a prediction the brief's consolidation gate does not.
sources: Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (1992). A new theory of disuse and an old theory of stimulus fluctuation. In Healy, Kosslyn & Shiffrin (Eds.), From Learning Processes to Cognitive Processes, Vol. 2, 35–67. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
added_by_critics.implication: Adopt this as the brief's framing for the two-bit item state instead of complementary learning systems. Two advantages. First, it removes the brief's dependence on a neuroscience framework graded above its evidentiary weight (see corrections). Second, it makes a sharper and testable prediction the CLS framing does not: the gain in storage strength from a successful retrieval is INVERSELY related to current retrieval strength — an item retrieved when it was nearly forgotten is worth far more than one retrieved when it was fresh. That is directly implementable as a scoring rule (weight a success by estimated difficulty at the moment of retrieval) and it is the principled reason the app should not reward easy repetitions.

added_by_critics.claim: Which Chinese characters CSL learners actually confuse is an empirical question with existing data sources, so the app's confusable-pair list need not be built from designer intuition — the brief lists this as an unrun search but it is tractable.
sources: Yeh, S.-L., & Li, J.-L. (2002). Role of structure and component in judgments of visual similarity of Chinese characters. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 28(4), 933–947. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
Chinese learner error corpora (e.g. the HSK Dynamic Composition Corpus; TOCFL learner corpus) — miswritten-character (错别字) annotations. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
added_by_critics.implication: Content pipeline. Two concrete sources exist for the confusion graph the architecture depends on: published visual-similarity judgment data on Chinese character structure and components, and annotated learner error corpora that record which characters L2 writers actually substitute for which. Seed the confusion graph from those, then let the per-user confusion matrix update it. Caveat worth stating in the brief: learner-corpus errors are PRODUCTION errors from writing tasks, and the app tests RECOGNITION, so the two confusion sets will overlap but are not identical — treat the corpus as a prior, not as ground truth.

added_by_critics.claim: None of the brief's evidence addresses two-character words, which is what the app's own examples mostly are. Every Chinese-specific study cited operates on single characters.
sources: Internal analysis of the brief's Chinese-specific sources: Li, Shi & Wang (2025) uses single-character pairs (人/入, 日/白); Chang et al. (2022) uses visually similar single characters; Nguyen et al. (2017) uses single characters varying in semantic radical.
Bassetti, B., & Lu, M. (2016). Are you dreaming in Chinese? Word awareness and L2 Chinese. [NOT VERIFIED THIS SESSION]
added_by_critics.implication: Content scoping, and it is sharper than the brief's version of this gap. 入口/出口 differ in ONE character out of two and share the other; 公斤/斤 is a containment relation between a one- and a two-character word. Neither structure appears in any cited study. The practical consequence: the brief's confusion_type enum (form-confusable / meaning-confusable / both) is under-specified for multi-character items and needs a fourth category — SHARED-MORPHEME pairs, where the overlap is a whole meaningful unit rather than a stroke. These plausibly behave more like the semantic case (where the evidence says harm is weak) than the synform case (where it is strong), because the shared 口 is a genuine shared meaning and can be taught as such rather than being a coincidence of shape. That is testable in-app and would change how 入口/出口 is treated.
